<C><B>PREFACE</B></C>
<SHL>
<P><SC>The</SC> plan of the preceding volumes of this edition has been fol-
lowed in the preparation of the present volumes. It is modified
only by the necessity of making the impossible attempt to condense
within a certain number of pages a whole literature.
<P>Of the imperfect success which has crowned the labour no one can
be so fully aware as the Editor. Nevertheless, the work is given to
the public in the trust that it will furnish some facilities to the study
of this great poem, and aid in preparing the way for better editions
than this.
<P>The First Volume contains <I>The Text,</I> with a collation of the texts of
the Quartos and Folios, and of some thirty modern editions, together
with Notes and Comments from the Editors whose texts are collated,
and, added to these, such verbal and grammatical criticisms from
other quarters as seemed to be valuable; in some instances, notes are
given that have little or no value, except as hints of the progress or
of the madness of Shakespearian criticism.
<P>As a general rule, in the Commentary preference is given to verbal
over &aelig;sthetic criticism. Whenever editors whose texts are collated
have indulged in &aelig;sthetic suggestions, these, in the main, have been
retained. But in other cases &aelig;sthetic criticisms have been reserved
for Volume II, except where the notes were of too brief and frag-
mentary a character to be separated from the context.
<P>This difference in the treatment of verbal and &aelig;sthetic criticism
is observed solely with reference to the arrangement of the mass
of material, not because &aelig;sthetic criticism is inferior in value to
verbal. Indeed, does not the value of the latter depend in many
cases more or less directly upon the former?
<PB N=vi>
<HE>vi <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>There is a disposition abroad to disparage &aelig;sthetic criticisms of
<SC>Shakespeare</SC>. An excellent edition of the Poet, now issuing from the
press, discards it wholly; the editor, whose opinions are entitled to
great respect, regarding it as an impertinence, and stigmatising it gene-
rally as &lquo;sign-post criticism.&rquo; Unquestionably, there has been much
commenting upon <SC>Shakespeare</SC>, which, ignoring the humblest intel-
ligence in the reader, is flat, stale, and unprofitable, a nuisance and a
weariness of the flesh. But shall we ignore the possible existence
of a keener insight than our own? Is the gift of reading between the
lines, so essential to the appreciation of dramatic literature, universal?
Have the generality of us eyes to see what is there written? Who
can fail to be enlightened and delighted with such fine criticism (as
is given in Volume II, p. 167) of the very first scene of this tragedy,
and which the Editor regrets did not come to his notice in time to be
inserted in the Commentary, where it vitally belongs? Are we not to
listen eagerly and reverently when <SC>Coleridge</SC> or <SC>Goethe</SC> talks about
<SC>Shakespeare</SC>? Can we fail to prize the flashes of light (all too few)
thrown here and there upon <SC>Shakespeare</SC> by <SC>Charles Lamb</SC>, that
genius, wasted in the India House, whom, had England known
the gift of God, she would have pensioned bountifully and set to re-
cording the thoughts these plays evoked in him, that we might be
brought into nearer communion with the great Poet than, with all
our laborious verbal criticism, we have yet been able to reach?
<P>To be sure, such commentators as these, and <SC>Schlegel</SC>, and <SC>Haz-
litt</SC>, and Mrs <SC>Jameson</SC>, and <SC>Christopher North</SC>, and <SC>Garrick</SC> (such
acting as his was &aelig;sthetic criticism of a high order) are rare, and ex-
ception may be made in favour of all master-minds like these. But
the present Editor, in full memory of the many weeks and months
spent in reading criticisms on <I>Hamlet,</I> fully agrees with a keen and
eloquent critic in <I>Blackwood's Magazine</I> (more likely than not,
<SC>Thomas Campbell</SC>) when he says: &lquo;We ask not for a picture of the
&lquo;whole landscape of the soul, nor for a guide who shall point out all its
&lquo;wonders. But we are glad to listen to every one who has travelled
&lquo;through the kingdoms of Shakespeare. Something interesting there
&lquo;must be even in the humblest journal; and we turn with equal pleasure
&lquo;from the converse of those who have climbed over the magnificence
<PB N=vii>
<HE><I>PREFACE</I> vii</HE>
<P>&lquo;of the highest mountains there, to the lowlier tales of less ambitious
&lquo;pilgrims, who have sat on the green and sunny knoll, beneath the
&lquo;whispering tree, and by the music of the gentle rivulet.&rquo;
<P>Moreover, the present Editor freely acknowledges the great inter-
est he has taken in witnessing the power of <SC>Shakespeare's</SC> genius as
shown in its stimulating effect upon minds of a high order. In the
endeavour to solve the mystery of Hamlet, the human mind, not only
in its clear radiance but in the sad twilight of its eclipse, has been
subjected to the most searching analysis. This ideal character,
Hamlet, has been assumed to be very nature, and if we fail to reach
a solution of the problem it presents, the error lies in us and in our
analysis; not in <SC>Shakespeare</SC>. Such have been the revelations of
the wisdom and genius of the First of Poets found in the works
which attempt to ravel all this matter out, and from which extracts
have been made in the second of these volumes, that the present
Editor was not long in making up his mind to bear patiently, for
the sake of these, the sea of troubles (sign-post criticisms) that he
has been compelled to encounter in the prosecution of his work.
To appreciate what is beautiful is one thing; to be informed of
what it is that delights us is a different and an added pleasure.
To vary the language of another: &lquo;The worth of [Shakespeare]
&lquo;must rise as his grandeurs are comprehended, and our joy in
&lquo;his harmony and beauty will be heightened the more fully he is
&lquo;understood.
<BQ>
&lquo;&ldquo;I grieve not that ripe knowledge takes away<LB>
&lquo;The charm that [Shakespeare] to my boyhood bore,<LB>
&lquo;For with the insight cometh day by day<LB>
&lquo;A greater bliss than wonder was before.&rdquo;&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>The Editor has availed himself of the liberty to form his own text
afforded him by the fact that the texts of all the ancient authoritative
editions are virtually printed on the same page. He has followed no
other. If his text appears to follow the <I>Cambridge Edition,</I> it is
merely because that edition has been used to print from.
<P>It has been his settled principle, as it was that of Dr <SC>Johnson</SC>:
&lquo;that the reading of the ancient books is probably true, and there-
<PB N=viii>
<HE>viii <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;fore not to be disturbed for the sake of elegance, perspicuity, or
&lquo;mere improvement of the sense. For though much credit is not
&lquo;due to the fidelity, nor any to the judgement of the first publishers,
&lquo;yet they who had the copy before their eyes were more likely to
&lquo;read it right than we who read it only by imagination. . . . . My
&lquo;first labour is always to turn the old text on every side, and try if
&lquo;there be any interstice through which light can find its way. . . . .
&lquo;I have adopted the Roman sentiment, that it is more honourable
&lquo;to save a citizen than to kill an enemy, and have been more
&lquo;careful to protect than to attack.&rquo;
<P>A list of editions collated in the <I>Textual Notes,</I> and an explana-
tion of the abbreviations and symbols there employed will be found
at the close of the Appendix.
<P>In the Second Volume is given, first: a Reprint of the <I>Quarto of</I>
1603. This earliest Quarto differs from the rest so materially that
a full or intelligible record of its various readings in the form of
foot-notes is simply impossible. In a note on &lquo;<I>The Date and the
Text</I>&rquo; will be found an account of the different theories respecting
its origin.
<P>Then follows <I>The Hystorie of Hamblet,</I> the story on which, per-
haps, was founded either this tragedy or the lost original drama
which <SC>Shakespeare</SC> afterward changed to its present shape.
<P>After this comes a translation of a curious old German tragedy
called <I>Fratricide Punished, or Prince Hamlet of Denmark.</I> An
account of it will be found in a short prefatory note.
<P>Then come the <I>English Critics,</I> and a discussion of the one great
insoluble mystery of Hamlet's sanity. Without for one moment
wishing to assume the responsibility of umpire, the present Editor
thinks it no more than right to call attention to one fact which it
seems to him should be kept in view on entering upon this dis-
cussion&mdash;viz. where the testimony of experts is invoked, and their
testimony is unanimous, the speculations and opinions of others,
laymen and inexpert, cannot be expected to carry much weight. In
courts of justice, every day, the testimony of experts is accepted
in cases involving liberty or confinement, life or death, and we
<PB N=ix>
<HE><I>PREFACE</I> ix</HE>
<P>cannot, it is submitted, be so inconsistent as wholly to rule out
that testimony here. If, therefore, we listen to experts at all, we
can hardly refuse our assent to their unanimous verdict. Despite
all this, the present Editor's opinion, which, after what he has
just said, he cannot, as a layman, expect to have any value, and
which, in view of the magnitude of the discussion, he would be
the last, as an Editor, to set forth at length, is that Hamlet is
neither mad, nor pretends to be so. And in view of the fact that
he has faithfully read and reported all the arguments on that side,
the Editor begs the advocates of the theory of feigned insanity to
allow him, out of reciprocal courtesy, to ask how they account for
Hamlet's being able, in the flash of time between the vanishing of
the Ghost and the coming of Horatio and Marcellus, to form, horror-
struck as he was, a plan for the whole conduct of his future life?
<P>Then follow Notes on <I>The Names and Characters,</I> on the <I>Duration
of the Action,</I> on <I>Garrick's Version,</I> and on <I>Actors' Interpretations;</I>
it is greatly to be regretted that in this last department our accounts
of <I>how</I> great actors spoke are so meagre. As <SC>Cibber</SC> says of <SC>Bet-
terton</SC>: &lquo;Pity it is that the momentary Beauties flowing from an
&lquo;harmonious Elocution cannot, like those of Poetry, be their own
&lquo;Record: That the animated Graces of the Player can live no
&lquo;longer than the instant Breath and Motion that presents them,
&lquo;or at best, can but faintly glimmer through the Memory or im-
&lquo;perfect Attestation of a few surviving Spectators. Could how Bet-
&lquo;terton spoke be as easily known as what he spoke, then might you
&lquo;see the Muse of Shakespeare in her Triumph, with all her Beau-
&lquo;ties, rising into real Life, and charming the Beholder. But, since
&lquo;this is so far out of the reach of description, how shall I show
&lquo;you Betterton?&rquo;
<P>Next comes the <I>German Criticism.</I>
<P>With the rashness of ignorance, the present Editor, in laying out
his plan for this edition, proposed to himself to preface it with an
essay upon the remarkable literature which this great drama has
created in Germany. His idea was to give the views of all the wri-
tings on <I>Hamlet</I> which have appeared down to the present time in
that country,&mdash;of a l, that is, which he could procure. But, in the
<PB N=x>
<HE>x <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>work of preparation for such an essay, after going carefully through
what, at a rough and moderate computation, amounts to some two
thousand pages and upwards, he finds himself,&mdash;no surprising dis-
covery,&mdash;quite unequal to the task. The sense of his incompetency
is, however, greatly relieved by the one very clear conviction with
which he emerged from the metaphysical atmosphere: the proposed
essay, could it be written, would utterly defeat a purpose to be kept
religiously in view in the preparation of this edition of <I>Hamlet,</I>&mdash;
namely, compression. It would far exceed in bulk all the rest of
the volumes. The Editor therefore must restrict himself to a simple
statement of the principles by which he has been guided in the
selection of extracts from the German critics.
<P>First: All unfavourable criticism of fellow-critics is excluded as
much as possible. Although our German friends are somewhat jeal-
ous of their well-deserved reputation as a nation of thinkers, they
sometimes seem, individually, very much disposed to grudge one an-
other a share in that distinction. The propriety of the exclusion
observed is obvious. To confound <SC>Goethe, Schlegel</SC>, or <SC>Tieck</SC> is
one thing, to elucidate <SC>Shakespeare</SC> is another. It is curious to
observe how much of Shakespearian criticism,&mdash;and this applies to
English as well as German,&mdash;is devoted to hostile criticism of fellow-
critics, living and dead. It is submitted that this it is, and not
&lquo;sign-post criticism&rquo; alone, which has tended to bring disrepute on
this branch of literature. &lquo;I know not,&rquo; says Dr <SC>Johnson</SC>, &lquo;why
&lquo;our editors should with such implacable anger persecute their pre-
&lquo;decessors. <G>*oi( nexpoi\ mh\ da/xnousin</G>, the dead, it is true, can make
&lquo;no resistance, they may be attacked with great security; but, since
&lquo;they can neither feel nor mend, the safety of mauling them seems
&lquo;greater than the pleasure; nor, perhaps, could it much misbecome
&lquo;us to remember, amidst our triumphs over the <I>nonsensical</I> and
&lquo;<I>senseless,</I> that we likewise are men; that <I>debemur morti,</I> and, as
&lquo;Swift observed to Burnet, shall soon be among the dead ourselves.&rquo;
<P>Second: The selection is confined as closely as possible to one
point: the character of Hamlet. It has been hardly possible to ob-
serve this rule with absolute strictness. <SC>Tieck's</SC> theory in regard to
Ophelia's relationship to Hamlet bears so intimately upon the cha-
<PB N=xi>
<HE><I>PREFACE</I> xi</HE>
<P>racter of both, and has made so deep an impression upon the popular
mind, as to demand its insertion here.
<P>Lastly: Whatever has been found that is strikingly original, although
not of necessity true, has been included among these extracts; such as
the wonderful connection which <SC>Karpf</SC> imagines he has discovered
between the &lquo;courtier's kibe&rquo; and Thor's frozen toe, and <SC>Flathe's</SC>
opinions concerning the family of Polonius. Of course the reader
will not suppose where no bracketed exclamation-marks appear, that
all these criticisms or commentaries are adopted by the present Edi-
tor; and this remark the Editor wishes most emphatically to apply
to all the comments and notes, English and German, throughout
these volumes. He has an especial aversion to that cheap and easy
way of expressing dissent, or, as it most commonly reads, contempt.
He can recall but one instance of its use, and even there it would
have been avoided could the structure of the sentence, condensed
to save space, have left the paternity of the note unambiguous.
Those who read or study these volumes may be safely trusted to dis-
cover for themselves the wisdom or the folly of the critics, and the
Editor gladly forgoes the pleasure of displaying how much wiser he
is than those whom he cites.
<P>The endeavour, in all honesty, has been to select from every author
the passages wherein he appears to most advantage, and wherein also
he contributes his best thought to the elucidation of the great tragedy.
At the same time, it must be confessed, there has been a little amuse-
ment had, now and then, in citing passages where our admirable
friends stumble and fall in the interpretation of words, as when
<SC>Gerth</SC> states that <I>slings</I> (in the &lquo;slings and arrows of outrageous
&lquo;fortune&rquo;) are the cables with which buoys are attached to sunken
anchors or are placed to indicate hidden reefs or shoals.
<P>Notwithstanding these trivial deductions, no one who has made
any acquaintance with the labours of Shakespeare students in Ger-
many can fail to be impressed by the excellence they show even in
the department of verbal criticism. It is too late a week with
<SC>Schmidt's</SC> <I>Lexicon</I> and a dozen <I>Shakespeare Yearbooks</I> on our
shelves to cast any slurs on German Shakespeare criticism. Were
such the intention, German criticism could well endure them with
<PB N=xii>
<HE>xii <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>equanimity. For the indefatigable labour, the keen analysis, the
sympathetic and loving appreciation which characterise the treat-
ment of <SC>Shakespeare</SC> by German men of letters, command the
warmest admiration. Their devotion to this tragedy in particular
is impressive. Everywhere throughout the length and breadth of
their land commentators on it arise; not only at the prominent
centres of culture, but in towns and villages, whose names English-
speaking people have perhaps never heard of, do these writers spring
up. Even while the Editor is closing his labours, two more volumes
on <I>Hamlet</I> have been added to the list. Although it would be a
comfort to think that he had collected all, yet,&mdash;<I>Rusticus exspectat,
&amp;c.</I> Verily, given a printing-press on German soil (and the print-
ing-press is indigenous there), and, lo! an essay on <I>Hamlet.</I> Let
Germans themselves ridicule this devotion if they will. No man
born to the inheritance of the language of <SC>Shakespeare</SC> can regard
it otherwise than with respectful admiration and pride, or fail to
welcome the aid which it contributes to an enlightened apprecia-
tion of the great Poet. We all hold ourselves partakers of his
glory, and such fine adoration of our household divinity we accept
as a flattering tribute to ourselves.
<P>And what a tribute is it to <SC>Shakespeare's</SC> genius! Here, at last,
we may venture to set a limit to his imagination. Not even he could
have imagined such a fame. No one of mortal mould (save Him
&lquo;whose blessed feet were nailed for our advantage to the bitter
&lquo;cross&rquo;) ever trod this earth, commanding such absorbing interest
as this Hamlet, this mere creation of a poet's brain. No syllable
that he whispers, no word let fall by any one near him, but is
caught and pondered as no words ever have been, except of Holy
Writ. Upon no throne built by mortal hands has ever &lquo;beat so
fierce a light&rquo; as upon that airy fabric reared at Elsinore.
<P>In <SC>Shakespeare's</SC> allusions to Wittenberg the Germans have
found a direct intimation that <I>Hamlet</I> was written with especial
reference to their own nation; and <SC>Freiligrath</SC> struck a keynote,
which found an echo in all hearts, when he exclaimed: &lquo;Germany
&lquo;is Hamlet.&rquo; <SC>Lessing</SC>, that most healthy and earnest of German
scholars, &lquo;the Englishman born in Germany&rquo;, was the first, now
<PB N=xiii>
<HE><I>PREFACE</I> xiii</HE>
<P>more than a hundred years ago, to announce to his countrymen
the advent of <SC>Shakespeare</SC>. His masterly criticisms of the Ham-
burg Theatre, written in the interest of the great English Poet.
levelled Voltaire and the French school of taste, and opened the
path ten years later for the extraordinary success that attended
<SC>Brockmann's</SC> Hamlet. The enthusiasm which <SC>Brockmann</SC> inspired
in this character was unprecedented in Germany, and can be
paralleled only by Mr <SC>Irving's</SC> recent success in London. Fine
steel engravings appeared, representing different scenes of the trag-
edy; silver medals were struck in honour of the popular actor,
and, what was before unheard of on the Berlin stage, he was called
before the curtain after the play.
<P>The enthusiasm for <I>Hamlet,</I> thus kindled, has not died out to this
day. <SC>Goethe's</SC> interpretation, everywhere as widely known as the
play itself, quickened the popular admiration by apparently reliev-
ing the tragedy of its painful mystery; and although there are not
wanting keen critics who dissent from <SC>Goethe's</SC> interpretation of
Hamlet's character, yet as a piece of criticism it filled Lord <SC>Ma
caulay</SC> &lquo;with wonder and despair,&rquo; and still underlies most of the
theories, English and German, that have since appeared.
<P>The last theory of Hamlet's character, which has arrested special
attention in Germany by the bold and animated way in which it
has been set forth by its chiefest expounder, <SC>Werder</SC>, was first
proposed in strong terms by <SC>Klein</SC>. It sweeps aside every vestige
of <SC>Goethe's</SC> explanation, with all theories akin to it. It affirms
Hamlet to be a man of action, never at a loss, never wavering,
taking in at once the position of affairs, adjusting himself thereto
with admirable sagacity, and instantly acting with consummate tact
as occasions require. A theory so directly opposed to all accepted
ideas of Hamlet claims a full exposition. It has been found im-
possible, in justice, to compress it into a narrower space than it
occupies in the Appendix.
<P>The Editor is well aware that he incurs some hazard in thus
selecting extracts from the German essayists. If he has unwittingly
committed any injustice, and omitted to notice theories for which
their authors claim originality, he can only plead innocence of in-
<PB N=xiv>
<HE>xiv <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>tention, and the difficulty he has found in fathoming the precise
meaning of metaphysical treatises, dive as deeply as he might into
&lquo;the depths of his consciousness.&rquo;
<P>German actors and stage-managers have long felt a want unknown
in English-speaking lands. There are probably not three theatres
in Germany that use the same translation or adaptation of Shake-
speare. To meet this want of uniformity, a selection of the dramas
was issued by <SC>Eduard</SC> and <SC>Otto Devrient</SC>, a name that will ensure
everywhere a respectful attention to all suggestions thus endorsed,&mdash;
suggestions, be it understood, never the crude conceits of the mo-
ment, but practically tested during many years of highly-famed
practice on the stage. In their rendition of <I>Hamlet</I> by the Messrs
<SC>Devrient</SC>, it is a noteworthy fact that for scenic representation the
First Quarto has been proved by them to be more effective than
the Second Quarto or Folio, which is the basis of the ordinary act-
ing copies. Over thirty years ago <SC>Hunter</SC> in England and <SC>Rapp</SC>
in Germany maintained the higher dramatic power of the First
Quarto over the Second Quarto in the order of the scenes and in
its general effectiveness. But it was reserved for the Messrs <SC>Dev-
rient</SC> to put these theories to the test with the best possible result,
as they say, and as their fame warrants the belief.
<P>The claim for Hamlet's youth, urged by the Messrs <SC>Devrient</SC>,
deserves attention. Hamlet as a youth of nineteen or twenty cer-
tainly possesses a charm which can hardly belong to the maturer age
of thirty; besides, this idea of him reconciles many discrepancies
which have set commentators at variance. It accords with his wish
to return to Wittenberg; with the election of his uncle over him
as king by the nobles; and it also lessens the age of the Queen
and our disgust at the mutiny in a matron's bones. A discussion
of this question will be found in the notes on V, i, 153. This
puzzle about Hamlet's age arises, to a large extent, it is submitted,
from our losing sight of <SC>Shakespeare's</SC> method of dealing with
the dramatic element of time,&mdash;a method whereby in the most
artful manner he conveys two opposite ideas of its flight: swiftness
and slowness; by one series of allusions we receive the impression
that the action of the drama is driving ahead in storm, while by
<PB N=xv>
<HE><I>PREFACE</I> xv</HE>
<P>another series we are insensibly beguiled into the belief that it
extends over days and months. Attention was called to this won-
drous art of <SC>Shakespeare's</SC> by both <SC>Halpin</SC> and <SC>Christopher
North</SC>, at about the same time; the former admirably analyzed,
with reference to it, the <I>Merchant of Venice,</I> and the latter re-
vealed its working in the case of <I>Macbeth</I> and <I>Othello.</I> If we
turn to this present play of <I>Hamlet,</I> we see how throughout, wher-
ever <I>time</I> comes in as an element, we are subject to <SC>Shakespeare's</SC>
glamour and gramarye. Horatio is introduced to us as one famil-
iar with all the every-day occurrences in Denmark, the gossip of
the court, the cause of the post haste and rummage in the land;
in the next scene, on the very same day, Hamlet greets him with
such surprise that we get the impression that he is fresh from
Wittenberg; if we stop to think, we remember that he came to
see the old king's funeral, and that took place nearly two months
before, and in that time he might well have learned all the polit-
ical news; but then he must have been about the court, and it is
a little strange that hamlet had not met him. As spectators of
the play, we do not stop to think this out, but accept without
question each impression that the poet intends to make on us.
Again, Polonius, who assuredly knew the latest item of court
gossip, seems as much surprised at Ophelia's account of Hamlet's
strange behaviour as Ophelia herself; it was evidently a new thing
to him, and yet when he goes directly to the King, the latter has
been so long cognisant of Hamlet's &lquo;transformation&rquo; that he had
sent for Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to help him find out its
cause; and Polonius, too, speaks of Hamlet's &lquo;lunacy&rquo; as a fact
well known and of long standing; and the very next day after
this Hamlet has a second interview with Ophelia, when she asks
him how he does &lquo;this <I>many</I> a day,&rquo; and tells him that she has
remembrances of his which she has longed <I>long</I> to re-deliver.
Again, Hamlet tells Rosencrantz and Guildenstern that he has
&lquo;of late foregone all custom of exercises.&rquo; In the last scene
Hamlet tells Horatio that he has been in &lquo;continual practice of
&lquo;late.&rquo; These are not inconsistencies. They are not oversights
on the part of <SC>Shakespeare</SC>. They belong to the two series of
<PB N=xvi>
<HE>xvi <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>times, the one suggestive and illusory, and the other visible and
explicitly indicated. <SC>Halpin</SC> calls them the <I>protractive</I> series and
the <I>accelerating</I> series. <SC>Christopher North</SC> calls them <SC>Shake-
speare's</SC> &lquo;two clocks.&rquo; As another instance of the way in which
the <I>long time</I> is adroitly insinuated in this Play, note the passage,
where Claudius describes to the Queen the events that have fol-
lowed the death of Polonius: &lquo;the people are muddied, thick,
&lquo;and unwholesome in their thoughts and whispers,&rquo; which of
course was the work not of an hour nor of a day, but perhaps of
weeks; it must have taken some time for this knowledge to have
reached the king's ears; then Laertes has &lquo;returned in secret
&lquo;from France, feeds on his wonder, keeps himself in clouds.&rquo;
This, too, consumes time, and the very time which we feel, with-
out stopping to compute it, is necessary for Laertes to gather the
populace to his side and mature his plans for rebellion. From
what we here learn, Laertes may have returned from France
weeks before, and yet when he bursts into the King's presence
and demands his father, the <I>short time</I> which is essential for
keeping up the tension of the passion comes into play, and we
get the impression that Laertes has just landed and has rushed in
hot haste to the King's palace. And so vivid is this impression
that Laertes is always held up by critics and commentators as an
example to Hamlet in the speed with which he sweeps to avenge
his father's death; whereas, as we see from this speech of Clau-
dius, Laertes may have been almost as dilatory as Hamlet, and
may have allowed &lquo;buzzers&rquo; day after day &lquo;to infect his ears,&rquo; or
kept himself &lquo;in clouds&rquo; for weeks. The <I>short time</I> is again
thrust upon us by showing us Laertes ignorant of Ophelia's in-
sanity. Apparently, Laertes has not even taken the time to go
to his own home after landing from France. And these instances
may be multiplied, doubtless, by any attentive reader of the trag-
edy. Indeed, is not the whole theory of Hamlet's procrastination
to a large extent due to this &lquo;legerdemain&rquo; of <SC>Shakespeare's</SC> in
the matter of time? There are not wanting critics who, counting
off the days on only one of &lquo;<SC>Shakespeare's</SC> clocks,&rquo; conclude
<PB N=xvii>
<HE><I>PREFACE</I> xvii</HE>
<P>the whole action within a week or ten days,&mdash;scant room for pro-
crastination, where the killing of a king is the aim. As <SC>Chris-
topher North</SC> says: &lquo;Shakespeare, in his calmer constructions,
&lquo;shows in a score of ways, weeks, months; that is therefore the
&lquo;true time, or call it the historical time. Hurried himself, and
&lquo;hurrying you, on the torrent of passion, he forgets time; and a
&lquo;false show of time, to the utmost contracted, arises. . . . . If
&lquo;any wiseacre should ask, &ldquo;How do we manage to stand the
&lquo;&ldquo;<I>known</I> together-proceeding of two times?&rdquo; the wiseacre is an-
&lquo;swered, &ldquo;We don't stand it,&mdash;for we know nothing about it.
&lquo;&ldquo;We are held in a confusion and a delusion about the time.&rdquo;
&lquo;We have effect of both,&mdash;distinct knowledge of neither. We
&lquo;have suggestions to our Understanding of extended time,&mdash;we
&lquo;have movements of our Will by precipitated time. . . . . If you
&lquo;ask me,&mdash;which judiciously you may,&mdash;what or how much did
&lquo;the Swan of Avon intend and know of all this astonishing leger-
&lquo;demain, when he sang thus astonishingly? Was he, the juggler,
&lquo;juggled by a&euml;rial spirits,&mdash;as Puck and Ariel? I put my finger to
&lquo;my lip, and nod to him to do the same. . . . . A good-natured
Juggler has cheated your eyes. You ask him to show you how
&lquo;he did it. He does the trick slowly,&mdash;and you see. &ldquo;Now,
&lquo;&ldquo;good Conjurer, <I>do it slowly and cheat us.</I>&rdquo; &ldquo;I can't. I
&lquo;&ldquo;cheat you by doing it quickly. To be cheated, you must <I>not</I>
&lquo;&ldquo;see what I do; but you must <I>think</I> that you see.&rdquo; When we
&lquo;inspect the Play in our closets, the Juggler does his trick slow-
&lquo;ly. We sit at the Play, and he does it quick.&rquo; Just as <SC>Shake
speare</SC> has dealt with the time of the whole tragedy he has dealt
with the age of Hamlet; in the earlier scenes he is in the very
hey-day of primy nature, but the effect of the fearful experience
which he undergoes is to quicken and stimulate mightily his
powers of thought,&mdash;to ripen his intellect prematurely. Therefore
at the close, as though to smoothe away any discrepancy between
his mind and his years, or between the execution of his task and
his years, a chance allusion by the Grave-digger is thrown out,
which, if we are quick enough to catch, we can apply to Ham-
let's age, and we have before us Hamlet in his full maturity.
<PB N=xviii>
<HE>xviii <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>In the selection of <I>French Criticisms</I> which follow the <I>German,</I> it
may be thought strange that no reference is to be found to <SC>Ducis's</SC>
version of <I>Hamlet,</I>&mdash;that unlucky butt for English and German
ridicule. No extracts would do it justice, and to insert the whole
was impossible. But would it not be well, between our fits of
laughter over it, to recall the year in which it first appeared?
In 1769 the first German translation of <I>Hamlet</I> was only three
years old, and <SC>Lessing</SC> almost single-handed was in the thick of
his battle-royal with the French school of art, then supreme in
Germany, and of which <SC>Ducis's</SC> <I>Hamlet</I> is no unfair representa-
tive in the main features; seven years later, <SC>Brockmann</SC>, the idol
of the German stage, played Hamlet at first in <SC>Heufeld's</SC> ver-
sion, in which Laertes is omitted and Hamlet is the prosperous
successor of Claudius (afterwards, it is true, <SC>Brockmann</SC> acted
<SC>Schroeder's</SC> version, which is nearer the original, although Ham-
let survives the King's attempt to poison him, and the fencing-
scene is omitted). And at that time, on the English stage, <SC>Gar-
rick</SC> and his &lquo;showmen&rquo; were &lquo;drawing about&rquo; Lear with <SC>Nahum
Tate's</SC> &lquo;hook in the nostrils of the Leviathan.&rquo; It is to be ap-
prehended that no German nor English tongue dare wag in rude
noise at <SC>Ducis</SC>, who, after all, did not assume to translate <SC>Shake-
speare</SC>, but merely adapt him. From the French point of view
(and is it not unreasonable to demand that a Frenchman should
have any other?) it is not difficult to regard <SC>Ducis's</SC> version as
a powerful drama; and we know that in the hands of <SC>Talma</SC> its
effect was signal.
<P>There now remains the agreeable duty to record the names of
those from whom I have received aid.
<P>At the very outset, however, it is with sorrow that I am reminded
that Professor <SC>Allen</SC>, upon whom in years past I leaned so heavily,
and to whom it was a pleasure to be indebted, has joined the
group of

&lquo;Precious friends, hid in death's dateless night.&rquo;<LB>

<PB N=xx>
<HE>xx <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;him,&rquo; says Dr <SC>Johnson</SC>, &lquo;that is yet unacquainted with the
&lquo;powers of Shakespeare, and who desires to feel the greatest
&lquo;pleasure that the drama can give, read every play, from the first
&lquo;scene to the last, with utter negligence of all his commentators.
&lquo;When his fancy is once on the wing, let it not stoop at cor-

&lquo;actness and read the commentators.&rquo; H. H. F.

<P><B>Scene I</B>] <SC>Gildon</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> &amp;c., 1709, p. 404): This scene, I have been assured,
Sh. wrote in a Charnal House, in the midst of the Night. <SC>Seymour</SC> (p. 138): This
whole scene appears unnecessary to the design and conduct of the play, and might
with advantage be omitted. The hand of Sh. is visible in it occasionally, but it is
part of that undigested plan which is manifest throughout the play. [Seymour finds
the same fault in <I>Macbeth</I> and <I>Lear.</I> <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>: In this play the Acts and Scenes are marked in the Ff only
as far as II, ii, and not at all in the Qq.
<P>1. <B>Who's there</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 148): That Shakespeare meant to put an effect
in the actor's power in these very first words is evident from the impatience expressed
by the startled Francisco in the line that follows. A brave man is never so per-
emptory as when he fears that he is afraid. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> finds a &lquo;psychological
motive&rquo; in thus representing Bernardo as so forgetful of all military use and wont as
to challenge Francisco who is on guard. Evidently Bernardo is afraid to meet the
Ghost all alone, and it is because he feels so unmanned that his last words to Fran-
cisco are to bid Horatio and Marcellus make haste. [For other instances of irregu-
larities in metre, which may be explained by the custom of placing ejaculations,
appellations, &amp;c. out of the regular verse, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 512. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>2. <B>me</B>] <SC>Jennens</SC>: This is the emphatic word. [<SC>Hanmer</SC> printed it in italics. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
Francisco, as the sentinel on guard, has the right of insisting on the watch-word,
which is given in Bernardo's answer.
<P>3. <B>king</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> supposed this sentence to have been the watch-word, but <SC>Pye</SC>
(p. 308) believes that it corresponds to the former usage in France, where, to the
common challenge <I>Qui vive?</I> the answer was <I>Vive le Roi,</I> like the modern answer,
&lquo;A friend.&rquo; And <SC>Delius</SC> points out that shortly afterwards to the same challenge
Hor. and Mar. give a different response.
<P>6. <B>upon your hour</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: An unusual phrase, meaning &lquo;just as your
hour is about to strike.&rquo; Compare <I>Rich. III:</I> III, ii, 5; IV, ii, 115; <I>Meas. for
Meas.</I> IV, 1, 17. As Fran. speaks the clock is heard striking midnight. [See
<SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 191; <I>Macb.</I> III, i, 16; V, iii, 7.]
<P>7. <B>now</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC>: Is not the sense the same whether we read <I>new</I> or &lquo;now&rquo;?
<P>8. <B>much</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 51: <I>Much, more,</I> is frequently used as an ordinary adjective
like the Scotch <I>mickle,</I> and the Early English <I>muchel.</I>
<P>9. <B>heart</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 212): As no particular reason appears for the melancholy
of this insignificant personage, it is probable that the poet meant by this little artifice to
prepare the minds of the spectators for a tragical story. Such a remark at the open-
ing of a play disposed their minds, unconsciously perhaps to themselves, to the
solemnity of thought and feeling which suited the awful scenes soon to be unfolded.
<SC>Strachey</SC> (p. 24): The key-note of the tragedy is struck in the simple preludings of
this common sentry's midnight guard, to sound afterwards in ever-spreading vibra-
tions through the complicated though harmonious strains of Hamlet's own watch
through a darker and colder night than the senses can feel.
<P>10. <B>Not a mouse stirring</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 148): The attention to minute
sounds,&mdash;naturally associated with the recollection of minute objects, and the more
familiar and trifling, the more impressive from the unusualness of their producing
any impression at all,&mdash;gives a philosophic pertinency to this image; but it has like-
wise its dramatic use and purpose. For its commonness in ordinary conversation
tends to produce the sense of reality, and at once hides the poet, and yet approxi-

<P>19. <B>A piece</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: He says this as he gives his hand [to this effect War-
burton inserted a stage-direction]. <SC>Heath</SC> and <SC>Steevens</SC>: It is merely a humorous,
cant expression. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: The philosophic Horatio conceives the personality
of man, in its outward manifestation merely, as only a piece of himself. <SC>Moltke</SC>:
It is not without significance that Sh. makes Horatio return a different answer to
this question than did Bernardo. The latter by his reply of &lquo;He&rquo; implies that he is
present body and soul (for he and Marcellus have no longer any doubt; they have
already seen the apparition with their own eyes); whereas Horatio by his answer
implies that owing to his incredulity he is not wholly present, that he is not there
with his body and soul, but that he had undertaken to share the watch with the cor-
poreal part only of his entire individuality. <SC>Moberly</SC>: As we say, &lquo;something
like him.&rquo;
<P>20. <SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 149): The actor should be careful to distinguish the expecta-
tion and gladness of Bernardo's &lquo;Welcome, Horatio!&rquo; from the mere courtesy of his
&lquo;Welcome, good Marcellus!&rdquo;
<P>21. Whether this should be spoken by Mar. or Hor. has occasioned discussion,
<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 122) asks, &lquo;Can it be imagined that the same person, who, but a line or two
after, calls the apparition &ldquo;this dreaded sight,&rdquo; should, in this line, call it &ldquo;this
thing&rdquo;? The levity of the expression, and the question itself, are suited to the un-
believing but eager Hor.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> gives it to Hor., because Hor. had come pur-
posely to inquire about the Ghost. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: Mar. is a firm believer in the
Ghost, and the allusion to it as a &lquo;thing&rquo; betokening contempt and doubt can come
only from the skeptic, Hor. <SC>Hudson</SC>: There is a temperate skepticism well befitting
a scholar in this speech of Horatio's. On the other hand, <SC>Elze</SC> advocates Mar.
&lquo;Horatio, being the invited guest, remains in the background, attentive and expect-
ant, while Marcellus is more forward in his zeal to convince Horatio of the truth of
his story.&rquo; <SC>White</SC>: Horatio does not yet believe that the Ghost appeared at all.

<P>is as if &lquo;let us tell you&rquo; had been used instead of &lquo;let us assail your ears.&rquo; It is an

<P>33. <B>sit we</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 361, considers this so-called imperative in the first person
plural as the subjunctive, <I>i. e.</I> &lquo;suppose we sit down?&rquo; &lquo;what if we sit down?&rquo; Com-
pare &lquo;Break we our watch up,&rquo; line 168 of this scene.
<P>35. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: In the deep feeling which Ber. has of the solemn nature of what
he is about to relate, he makes an effort to master his own imaginative terrors by an
elevation of style,&mdash;itself a continuation of the effort,&mdash;by turning off from the ap-
parition, as from something which would force him too deeply into himself, to the
outward objects, the realities of nature, which had accompanied it. This passage
seems to contradict the critical law that what is told makes a faint impression com-
pared with what is beholden; for it does indeed convey to the mind more than the
eye can see; whilst the interruption of the narrative at the very moment when we
are most intensely listening for the sequel, and have our thoughts diverted from the
dreaded sight in expectation of the desired, yet almost dreaded, tale,&mdash;this gives all
the suddenness and surprise of the original appearance.
<P>36. <B>star</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: Nothing more natural than for a sentinel to watch the course
of a particular star while on his lonely midnight watch; and what a radiance of
poetry is shed on the passage by the casual allusion!
<P><SC>Hudson</SC>: Of course the north star is meant, which appears to stand still while the
other stars in its neighborhood seem to revolve around it.
<P>37. <B>illume</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Not used elsewhere by Sh.
<P>39. <B>beating</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Tolling&rquo; of Q<SUB>1</SUB> perhaps imparts additional solemnity
to this impressive preparation for the appearance of the spectre.

<P>41-44. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Note the judgement displayed in having the two persons
present, who, as having seen the Ghost before, are naturally eager in confirming
their former opinions,&mdash;whilst the skeptic is silent, and, after having been twice ad-
dressed by his friends, answers with two hasty syllables,&mdash;&lquo;Most like,&rquo;&mdash;and a con-
fession of horror. O heaven! words are wasted on those who feel, and to those who
do not feel, the exquisite judgment of Sh. in this scene, what can be said? Hume
himself could not but have had faith in this Ghost dramatically, let his anti-ghostism
have been as strong as Samson against other ghosts less powerfully raised.
<P>42. <B>scholar</B>] <SC>Douce</SC>: Exorcisms were performed in Latin, and therefore only
by scholars. <SC>Reed</SC>: Thus Toby in Beau. and Fl.'s <I>Night Walker</I> II, i,&mdash;&lquo;Let's call
the butler up, for he speaks Latin, And that would daunt the devil.&rquo; In like manner
the honest butler in Addison's <I>Drummer</I> recommends the steward to speak Latin to
the ghost in that play. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: Evil spirits were not exorcised by the sign
of the cross alone, but cried out to the exorciser the Latin hexameter <I>Signa te signa,
temere me tangis et angis,</I> a verse which being a palindrome reveals its diabolic
origin. <SC>Moltke</SC>: See <I>Much Ado</I> II, i, 264: &lquo;I would to God some scholar would
conjure her.&rquo;
<P>44. <B>harrows</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Compare Milton: &lquo;Amazed I stood, harrow'd with grief
and fear.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Comus,</I> 565. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: It is natural that the surprise and terror of
the speaker should bear some proportion to the degree of his former confidence and
incredulity. <SC>Clarke</SC>: Horatio's previous levity makes his subsequent awe, and
trembling, and paleness seem like the effects of our own awe-stricken imaginations.
<SC>Wedgwood</SC>: <I>Harrow!</I> a cry of distress; Old French, <I>hare! harau! Crier haro
sur,</I> to make hue and cry after. Bohem. <I>hr! hrr!</I> interjection of excitement (fre-
mentis), <I>hurrah!</I> Old High German, <I>haren,</I> to cry out. A harrowing sight is one
which leads to the exclamation <I>harrow!</I>
<P>45. <B>It would</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: There was, and is, a notion that a ghost cannot speak
till it has been spoken to. [See <I>Macb.</I> I, v, 19; <I>Ham.</I> III, iii, 75; V, i, 77, or <SC>Ab
bott</SC>, &sect; 329. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>46. <B>usurp'st</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: Zeugma: the Ghost invades the night and assumes the
form of the king.

<P>63. <B>sledded Polacks</B>] German commentators have found more difficulty in this
phrase than the English. <SC>Tieck</SC> supposes (and so translates) that the king &lquo;dashed
his sliding Pole axe on the ice.&rquo; &lquo;<I>Sledded,</I>&rquo; he adds, &lquo;according to a license frequent
in Sh., stands for &lquo;sledding,&rquo; which Tieck mistook for &lquo;sliding.&rquo; The folly of this
interpretation and its errors were exposed by <SC>Delius</SC>. But the spelling of the Qq
<I>sleaded,</I> and the lack of a capital P in <I>pollax,</I> together with its Roman letters (proper
names in the old copies being usually printed in Italics), still presented inexplicable
difficulties. <SC>Friesen</SC> inclined to Tieck, believing it more &lquo;conceivable that the king
dashed down on the ice his <I>sleaded</I> battle-axe (whatever that might be) than that he
struck an enemy or smote him to the ground, for in this case the king's visor would
have been down, and Horatio could not have seen the frown on his face.&rquo; Wherefore,
he concludes, there is greater likelihood of finding verbal obscurities in Sh.'s text than
downright nonsense. <SC>Elze</SC> and <SC>Delius</SC> follow the English commentators, and scout
the idea of &lquo;poleaxe.&rquo; The former follows Pope, on the ground that Polack is gen-
erally found in the singular, and refers to the Polish king, just as &lquo;the Dane&rquo; is used
in line 15 of this scene. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> also follows Pope, because the plural
<I>Polacks</I> would signify the whole Polish army, and it would be monstrous to suppose
that the whole army could travel in sleighs; the &lquo;sledded Polack&rquo; is therefore merely
the Polish king, who, and who alone, had come to the conference on a sled. If the
word &lquo;Poleaxe&rquo; be adopted, insuperable difficulties attend the interpretation of
&lquo;sledded.&rquo; If it mean <I>sledged,</I> it refers to a battle-axe, to which a war-club (Old
North German <I>sleggja</I>) has been added, and the words &lquo;on the ice&rquo; are used instead
of the more natural phrase <I>on the ground</I> to indicate that the parle took place on
some frozen neutral river. <SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Notes and Queries,</I> November 19, 1864):
&lquo;I always regarded &lquo;sleaded,&rquo; or, as the modern editors read, &lquo;sledded,&rquo; as
nonsense. What a ridiculous position it must have been to see a king, in full
armour, smiting down a sledded man, <I>i. e.</I> a man sitting in a sledge! It would
rather not have been a king-like action. And it was, of course, not a remarkable,
not a memorable, fact, that in the cold Scandinavian country in winter-time, people
were found sitting in a sledge; nobody would have wondered at it,&mdash;perhaps more
at the contrary. When the king frowned in an angry parle he must have been pro-
voked to it by an irritating behaviour of the adversary, and Horatio, remembering
the fact, will also bear in mind the cause of it, and so, I suppose, he used an epithet
which points out the provoking manner of the Polack; and, following as much as
possible the form &ldquo;sleaded,&rdquo; I should like to propose the word <I>sturdy,</I> or, as it would
have been written in Shakespeare's time, <I>sturdie.</I>&rquo; <SC>Moltke</SC> believes that he has
discovered the correct reading on &aelig;sthetic as well as philological grounds; Sh.
wishes to portray to us the character of the deceased king, which must be full of

<P>grandeur and dignity. Such rage as Tieck's interpretation implies would be most
unseemly; besides, by dashing down his poleaxe, he would disarm himself, which
would be silly. The idea, therefore, conveyed by the word &lquo;smite&rquo; must be per-
sonal to the king; it must be some gesture, not a blow delivered on an enemy. What,
therefore, more natural than that he should strike his Poleaxe violently on the ice,
just as any honest citizen is wont by way of emphasis to strike his fist on the table?
&ldquo;Sledded&rdquo; is a sophistication of the printers, and the correct text is <I>his leaded pole-
axe,</I> i. e. his poleaxe loaded with lead; or <I>his edged poleaxe,</I> i. e. sharpened; or, for
aught to the contrary, <I>his sledged poleaxe.</I> This emendation of Moltke's <SC>Clarendon</SC>
pronounces an anticlimax; Sh. having mentioned &lquo;Norway&rquo; in the first clause would
certainly have told us with whom the &lquo;angry parle&rquo; was held. Curiously enough,
this emendation of Moltke's has been anticipated not by a German, but by an
Englishman. In the <I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 3d April, 1875, <SC>C. Eliot Browne</SC> gives some
notes on <I>Hamlet</I> by the Earl of Rochester, 1761, and on the present passage is the
following: &lquo;<I>Sleaded</I> agrees with an axe, but not with a man; and signifies loaded
with lead. . . . The king was then in an angry parle (which can't signify fighting),
and because he could not have his will most furiously struck his loaded or heavy
battle-axe into the ice.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Polack&rquo; is the name of an inhabitant of Poland.
<I>Polaque</I> is French. As in Davison's translation of Passeratius's <I>Epitaph on Henry
III of France,</I> published by Camden: &lquo;This little stone a great king's heart doth
hold, Who ruled the fickle French and Polacks bold.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: The corrupted
form in the Qq shows that Sh. wrote &lquo;Polacks.&rquo; Since, as <SC>Dyce</SC> adds, the singular
is afterwards spelled in this play &lquo;Polacke,&rquo; &lquo;Pollacke,&rquo; &lquo;Poleak,&rquo; &lquo;Pollock,&rquo; and
&lquo;Polake.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC> preferred the singular, because we cannot well suppose that in
a parley the king belaboured many, as it is not likely that provocation was given by
more than one, or that on such an occasion he would have condescended to strike a
meaner person than a prince. <SC>Boswell</SC>: May not <I>Poleax</I> be put for the person
who carried the pole-axe, a mark of rank,&mdash;as we should talk at the present day &lquo;of
<I>the gold stick in waiting.</I>&rquo; &lquo;He sent a great and glorious duke, one of them that
<I>held the golden pole-axe,</I> with his retinue,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;Milton's <I>Brief Hist. of Moscovia.</I>
<P>65. <B>jump</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: In the folio we sometimes find a familiar word substituted

jumpe at three.&rquo;&mdash;Chapman's <I>May-Day.</I> <SC>Halliwell</SC>: <I>Jump</I> is rather more ex-

the retrospective narrative! And observe, upon the Ghost's reappearance, how much

general thought and past experience,&mdash;and the sympathy of Mar. and Ber. with his

<P>72. <B>toils</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Causes to toil. Many verbs which we only use as in-

taken from the French &lquo;prest,&rquo; <I>ready,</I> and is so written in Henry VII's Book of
Household Expenses. The word is here used in its ordinary signification, as shown
by the Concordance. <SC>Lord Campbell</SC> (p. 103): Such confidence has there been in
Shakespeare's accuracy, that this passage has been quoted both by text-writers and
by judges on the bench as an authority upon the legality of the <I>press-gang,</I> and upon
the debated question whether <I>shipwrights,</I> as well as <I>common seamen,</I> are liable to

tolerate the idea of impressment, which he says is an injustice of wholly modern

<P>107. <B>romage</B>] <SC>Wedgwood</SC> (<I>s. v.</I> Rummage): Two words seem confounded.
1. <I>Rummage,</I> the proper stowing of merchandise in a ship; from Du. <I>rui<*>,</I> Fr.
<I>rum,</I> the hold of a ship. Hence <I>to rummage,</I> to search among the things stowed
in a given receptacle. 2. But in addition to the foregoing the word is sometimes
used in the sense of racket, disturbance [as here in <I>Hamlet</I>]. In this sense it may
be a parallel form with <I>rumpus.</I> <SC>Caldecott</SC> connects it with &lquo;<I>Romelynge,</I> privy
mysterynge. Ruminacio, mussitacio.&rquo;&mdash;Prompt. Parv.
<P>108-125. <SC>Knight</SC> explains the omission of these lines in the Ff on the ground
that Shakespeare probably suppressed this magnificent description of the omens
which preceded the fall of &lquo;the mightiest Julius&rquo; after he had written <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I>
<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 214): I wonder that the commentators should have overlooked so
obvious an origin of this passage as Lucan's description (<I>Pharsalia,</I> lib. i) of the
prodigies which preceded the death of C&aelig;sar. We have the tenantless graves, the
sheeted dead seen on the streets, the stars with trains of fire, and the moon's eclipse.
It is of little moment to ask if Lucan had been translated when Sh. wrote <I>Hamlet</I>
The earliest published translation, I believe, is that by Sir Arthur Gorges, 1614.
<P>108. <B>be</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 299: As a rule it will be found that <I>be</I> is used with some
notion of doubt, question, thought, &amp;c.; 1, in questions, as in III, ii, 100; V, i,
94; and 2, after verbs of thinking, as in the present case. Very significant is this
difference in &lquo;I <I>think</I> my wife <I>be</I> honest, and <I>think</I> she <I>is</I> not,&rquo; <I>Oth.</I> III, iii, 384.
<P>109. <B>sort</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The cause and effect are proportionate and suitahle.
<P>112. <B>mote</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> (<I>King John,</I> IV, i, 92): The modern spelling of <I>moth.</I>
Thus, &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; they are in the aire, like <I>atomi in sole,</I> mothes in the sonne.&rquo;&mdash;Preface
to Lodge's <I>Incarnate Devils,</I> 1596. Also, &lquo;<I>Festucco,</I> a little sticke, a fease-strawe,
a tooth-picke, a moth, a little beame.&rquo;&mdash;Florio, 1598.

and for ever &lquo;State&rquo; with a towering capital. . . . It is for the Republic and City
what Realm or Kingdom is to us,&mdash;at once place and indwelling Power. &lquo;State,&rquo;&mdash;
properly Republic,&mdash;here specifically and pointedly means Reigning City. The
Ghosts walked in the City,&mdash;not in the Republic. . . . Every hackneyer of this

<P>116. <SC>Jennens</SC>: Perhaps a line has been omitted here, by mistake, somewhat like
the following: &lquo;Tremendous prodigies in heav'n appear'd.&rquo; <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 2, 15)
suggests, &lquo;In the heavens above strange portents did appear.&rquo;
<P>117, 118. <SC>Malone</SC>: When Sh. had told us that the &lquo;graves stood tenantless,&rquo; &amp;c.,
which are wonders confined to the earth, he naturally proceeded to say (in the line
now lost) that yet other prodigies appeared in the sky; and the phenomena he ex-
emplified by adding, &lquo;As [<I>i. e.</I> for instance] stars with trains,&rquo; &amp;c. I suspect that
the words &lquo;As stars&rquo; are a corruption, and that the lost words, as suggested by the
passage in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> II, ii, which describes the prodigies preceding his death, con-
tained a description of &lquo;<I>fiery warriors fighting in the clouds,</I>&rquo; or of &lquo;<I>brands burning
bright beneath the stars.</I>&rquo; What makes me believe that the corruption lies in &lquo;As
stars&rquo; is the disagreeable recurrence of &lquo;stars&rquo; in the next line. Perhaps Sh. wrote:
<I>Astres</I> with trains of fire&mdash;and dews of blood Disastrous dimm'd the sun! &lquo;<I>Astre</I>&rquo;
is an old word for <I>star;</I> see <I>Diana,</I> a collection of poems, printed circa 1580. [See
also Florio, &lquo;<I>Stella:</I> a starre, an aster, a planet.&rquo; <SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Knight</SC> rather favors
Malone's emendation, and thinks that it gets rid of the difficulty. <SC>Caldecott</SC> finds
no difficulty in conceiving the meaning of the passage as it stands, reading or under-
standing it thus: &lquo;The graves opened, the dead were seen abroad [spectacles such]
as,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.,</I> Feb. 1845): This line has merely got out of its
place; there is nothing wanting. Transpose it to follow line 121, and read, &lquo;As
stars with . . . . . . blood, <I>Are</I> harbingers preceding,&rquo; &amp;c. A. E. B [<SC>rae</SC>] (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I>
24 Jan. 1852): It is only by the occurrence of such difficulties as the present,
which, after remaining so long obscure, are at last only resolvable by presup-
posing in Sh. a depth of knowledge far exceeding that of his triflers, that his
wonderful and almost mysterious attainments are beginning to be appreciated. In
the present case he must not only have known that the fundamental meaning of
<I>aster</I> is a spot of light, but he must also have taken into consideration the power of
<I>dis</I> in producing an apsolute reversal in the meaning of the word to which it may
be prefixed. Thus, <I>service</I> is a benefit, <I>disservice</I> is an injury, while <I>unservice</I> (did

<P>118. <B>moist star</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: That is, the moon. See <I>Wint. Tale,</I> I, ii, 1. Voss

<P>121. <B>precurse</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Only found here in Sh., though he uses &lquo;precurrer&rquo;

<P>121. <B>fierce</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> explains this as <I>terrible;</I> <SC>Steevens</SC>, as <I>conspicuous,

<I>bloody</I> and <I>terrible,</I> as elsewhere it means <I>extreme, excessive,</I> citing <I>King John,</I> V,
vii, 13, and Jonson's <I>Sejanus,</I> V, x (p. 140, ed. Gifford), &lquo;O most tame slavery, and
fierce flattery.&rquo;
<P>122. <B>harbingers</B>] See <I>Macb.</I> I, iv, 45.
<P>122. <B>still</B>] Constantly, always. See II, ii, 42; <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> II, ii, 172, 174.
V, iii, 106; <I>Macb.</I> V. vii, 16; and <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 69.
<P>123. <B>omen</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: &lquo;Prologue&rquo; and &lquo;omen&rquo; are synonymous, whereas Sh.
means that these phenomena are forerunners of the events presaged by them, and
such sense the addition of a single letter gives. <SC>Upton</SC> says that the &lquo;omen&rquo; is the
event itself, which happened in consequence of the omens, and cites Virgil, <I>&AElig;n.</I> i,
349. <SC>Heath</SC> expressed the same idea in the phraseology of a grammarian: &lquo;Omen,&rquo;
by metonymy of the antecedent for the consequent, is here put for the event pre-
dicted by the omen. <SC>Farmer</SC> appositely cited a distich from Heywood's <I>Life of
Merlin:</I> &lquo;Merlin, well vers'd in many a hidden spell, His countries omen did long
since foretell.&rquo;
<P>124. <B>demonstrated</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: This word is accented on the first syllable also
in <I>Hen. V:</I> IV, ii, 54.

<P>125. <B>climatures</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Possibly used for those who live under the same
climate. Otherwise it would be better to read &lquo;climature&rquo; with Dyce. The French
<I>climature</I> appears to be a modern word in that language, for it is not found in Cot-
grave, and Littr&eacute; gives no early example of its use.
<P>127. <SC>White</SC>: The stage direction of the Qq may be a misprint for &lquo;<I>He</I> spreads,&rquo;
&amp;c., indicating Horatio's action in his attempt to stay the Ghost. &lquo;His&rquo; might, of
course, refer to the Ghost through &lquo;it;&rquo; but there seems to be no occasion for the
Ghost to make such a gesture.
<P>127. <B>cross</B>] <SC>Blakeway</SC>: Whoever crossed the spot on which a spectre was
seen became subject to its malignant influence. Among the reasons for supposing
the Earl of Derhy (who died 1594) to have been bewitched is the following: &lquo;On
Friday there appeared a tall man who twice <I>crossed him</I> swiftly; and when the Earl
came to the place where he saw this man, he first fell sick.&rquo;&mdash;Lodge's <I>Illustrations
of British History,</I> vol. iii, p. 48.
<P>129, 132, 135. See I, i, 1, and <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 512.

can be not infrequently laid, especially when a living person accomplishes that for
him which he, when alive, should have himself accomplished.&rquo;
<P>134. <B>happily</B>] <SC>Nares</SC> and <SC>Clarendon</SC> consider this as equivalent to <I>haply;</I>
<SC>Tschischwitz</SC> and <SC>Hudson</SC>, as equivalent to <I>luckily.</I> The latter says: &lquo;Which
<I>happy</I> or <I>fortunate foreknowledge</I> may avoid:&rquo; a participle and adverb used in the
sense of a substantive and adjective. The structure of this solemn appeal is almost
identical with that of a very different strain in <I>As You Like It,</I> II, iv, 33-42.

<P>139. <B>Cock crows</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Few Notes,</I> &amp;c., p. 134): The cock used to crow
when Garrick acted Hamlet, and, perhaps, also when that part was played by some
of his successors; but now-a-days managers have done wisely in striking the <I>cock</I>
from the list of the Dramatis Person&aelig;. <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Cursory Notes,</I> &amp;c., p. 43): It
is said in the life of one of the actors, I think of George Cooke, that on one occa-
sion not fewer than <I>six cocks</I> were collected in order to summon the spirit to his
diurnal residence, lest one cock, like one single <I>clock,</I> might not keep time exactly,
when the matter was of importance.
<P>139, 141. <SC>Steevens</SC> is unwilling to believe that the speeches &lquo;Stop it, Marcellus,&rquo;
and &lquo;Do, if it will not stand,&rquo; are correctly given to Horatio, who, as a scholar, must
have known the folly of attempting to commit any act of violence on a shadow; he
therefore proposes to give them to Bernardo, whose first impulse, as an unlettered
officer, would be to strike at what offends him. &lquo;The next two speeches, &ldquo;'Tis
here!&rdquo; &ldquo;'Tis here!&rdquo; should be allotted to Mar. and Ber., and the third, &ldquo;'Tis
gone!&rdquo; to Hor. As the text now stands, Mar. proposes to strike the Ghost with his
partisan, and yet, afterwards, is made to descant on the indecorum and impotence
of such an attempt.
<P>140. <B>partisan</B>] See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> I, i, 66.
<P>141, 142. <B>Do . . . gone!</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 261): To avoid the broken line:
'Tis gone!&rquo; which <I>here</I> seems to me irregular, arrange &lquo;Do&rquo; as belonging to line
140, reading &lquo;If <I>'t will</I> not . . . gone!&rquo; as one line.

<P>150. <B>cock</B>] <SC>Farmer</SC>: Bourne of Newcastle, in his <I>Antiquities of the Common
People,</I> informs us: &lquo;It is a received tradition among the vulgar, that at the time of
cock-crowing the midnight spirits forsake these lower regions and go to their proper
places. Hence it is that in country places, where the way of life requires more
early labour, they always go chearfully to work at that time.&rquo; And he quotes some
lines from the first hymn of Prudentius, <I>Ad Gallicinium:</I> &lquo;Ferunt, vagantes d&aelig;monas,
L&aelig;tos tenebris noctium, Gallo canente exterritos Sparsim timere, et cedere. Hoc

ventum Dei.&rquo; <SC>Douce</SC> quotes from another hymn, said to have been composed by
Saint Ambrose, and formerly used in the Salisbury service: &lquo;It contains the follow-
ing lines, which so much resemble the speech of Hor. that one might almost suppose
Sh. to have seen them: &ldquo;Preco diei jam sonat, Noctis profund&aelig; pervigil; Nocturna
lux viantibus, A nocte noctem segregans. Hoc excitatus Lucifer Solvit polum
caligine; Hoc omnis errorum chorus Viam nocendi deserit. Gallo canente spes
redit,&rdquo;&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Philostratus, giving an account of the apparition of Achilles's

the cock crowed.&mdash; <I>Vit. Apol.</I> iv, 16. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: No Addison could be more care-
ful to be poetical in diction than Sh. in providing grounds and sources of its pro-
priety. But how to elevate a thing almost mean by its familiarity, young poets may
learn in this treatment of the cock-crow.
<P>153. <B>sea</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: According to the pneumatology of that time, every element

earth, or earthly spirits ranging the air, return to their station, to their proper limits,
in which they are confined. We might read:&mdash;&lquo;at his warning Th' extravagant and
erring spirit hies To his confine, whether in sea, or air, Or earth, or fire. And of,&rquo;
&amp;c. But change is unnecessary.

<P>158. <B>season</B>] <SC>Moltke</SC>: This passage, in connection with Francisco's remark,
&lquo;'Tis bitter cold,&rquo; I, i, 8, and then with, &lquo;But two months dead,&rquo; I, ii, 138, and lastly
with, &lquo;Sleeping within my orchard,&rquo; I, v, 59, intimates to us in the clearest manner
the time of year in which Sh. wishes us to conceive the opening of this tragedy&mdash;
namely, in winter, but a little before Advent; for, two months previously, about
September, the older Hamlet could have taken his after-dinner nap in the open air.
<SC>Caldecott</SC> (in a note on &lquo;the morn,&rquo; line 166) says, that the almost momentary
appearance of the Ghost, and the short conversations preceding and subsequent to it,
could not have filled up the long interval of a winter's night in Denmark, from
twelve till morning. <SC>Knight</SC> asks, How do we know it was a <I>winter's</I> night?
Francisco, indeed, says &lquo;'tis bitter cold;&rquo; but even in the nights of <I>early summer</I> in
the north of Europe, during the short interval between twilight and sunrise, &lquo;the air
bites shrewdly.&rquo; That this was the season intended by Sh. is indicated by Ophelia's
flowers. Her pansies, her columbines, and her daisies belong not to winter, and her
&lquo;coronet of weeds&rquo; were the field flowers of the latter spring hung upon the willow
in full foliage, &lquo;That shows its hoar leaves in the glassy stream.&rquo; Knight might have
added that the reference to &lquo;the <I>dew</I> of you high eastern hill&rquo; is also inappropriate
to midwinter.

<P>163. <B>takes</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC>: To bewitch, to affect with malignant influence, to strike with

<P>164. <B>gracious</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Partaking of the nature of the epithet with which it
is associated, with &lquo;blessedness;&rquo; participating in a heavenly quality, of grace in its
scriptural sense; not in the sense in which it is used in <I>King John,</I> III, iv, 81.
Frequently, in Sh., it does not mean, as has been interpreted, graceful, elegant, win-
ning, pleasing simply, but touched with something holy, instinct with goodness.
<P>165. <B>in part believe</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: This assent of Horatio's to so imaginative a creed
is peculiarly appropriate, coming, as it does, immediately upon a supernatural appear-
ance, when his mind is softened to impressions, and is prepared to admit the possi-
bility of spiritual wonders. <SC>Moberly</SC>: A happy expression of the half-sceptical,
half-complying spirit of Shakespeare's time, when witchcraft was believed, antipodes
doubted.
<P>166, 167. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 216): It must have been in emulation of these lines that
Milton wrote, &lquo;Now morn her rosy steps in th' eastern clime Advancing, sowed the
earth with orient pearls.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Par. Lost,</I> v, 1. We have the same characteristics of
morning in both. &lquo;Russet,&rquo; <I>rosy;</I> &lquo;eastern hill,&rquo; <I>eastern clime;</I> &lquo;the dew,&rquo; <I>orient
pearls.</I> <SC>Strachey</SC> (p. 27): We are brought out of the cold night into the warm
sunshine, and we realize, in this lyrical movement, that harmony of our feelings
which it was one of the objects of the Chorus to produce in the Greek Tragedy.
<P>167. <B>eastern</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> pronounced in favor of <I>eastward.</I> <SC>Steevens</SC> denied

in the morn, &lquo;&mdash; cheareful Chaunticlere with his note shrill Had warned once, that
Ph&oelig;bus&rquo; fiery Car In haste was climling up the <I>Eastern Hill,</I> Full envious that

<P>170. <B>Hamlet</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 151): Note the unobtrusive and yet fully adequate
mode of introducing the main character, &lquo;young Hamlet,&rquo; upon whom is transferred
all the interest excited for the acts and concerns of the king his father.
<P>171. <B>dumb</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> quotes from <SC>Simrock</SC> (p. 488) that only those per-
sons have any influence over spirits, who are themselves guileless, such as Priests,
young scholars, &amp;c. This essential qualification Horatio attributes to Hamlet.
<P>173. <B>loves</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC> (Note on <I>Rich. II:</I> IV, i, 315): The plural is fre
quently used by Sh. and writers of the 16th and 17th centuries when designating
an attribute common to many, in cases where it would now be considered a solecism.
Thus &lquo;sights,&rquo; <I>Lear,</I> IV, vi, 35; <I>Rich. III:</I> IV, i, 25; <I>Timon,</I> I, i, 255; <I>Pericles,</I> I,
i, 74; so &lquo;loves,&rquo; &lquo;consents,&rquo; <I>Two Gent.</I> I, iii, 48, 49; &lquo;wills&rquo; in <I>Hen. VIII:</I> III, i,
68; see also <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 14, 250, 253; II, ii, 14; IV, vii, 30; <I>Macb.</I> III, i, 121.
<P>173. <B>duty</B>] <SC>Hudson</SC>: These last three speeches are admirably conceived. The
speakers are in a highly kindled state; when the Ghost vanishes, their terror pres-
ently subsides into an inspiration of the finest quality, and their intense excitement,
as it passes off, blazes up in a subdued and pious rapture of poetry.
<P><B>Scene II.</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC>: The audience are now relieved by a change of scene
to the royal court, in order that Ham. may not have to take up the leavings of ex-
haustion. In the king's speech, observe the set and pedantically antithetic form of
the sentences when touching that which galled the heels of conscience,&mdash;the strain
of undignified rhetoric,&mdash;and yet in what follows concerning the public weal, a
certain appropriate majesty. Indeed was he not a royal brother?

he says, &lquo;the sense required, the distinction made between &ldquo;drop&rdquo; and &ldquo;droop&rdquo; in

reduplication of the wrong letter in both type-setting and chirography.&rquo; <SC>Francke</SC>

<P>29. <B>bed-rid</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Earle gives the following doubtful, but ingenious,
etymology of this word: &lquo;The Saxons called a sorcerer &ldquo;dry:&rdquo; . . . out of this word
a verb was made, &ldquo;be-drian,&rdquo; to bewitch or fascinate. . . . The participle of this verb,
&ldquo;be-drida,&rdquo; a disordered man, has, by a false light of cross analogy, generated
the modern &ldquo;bed-ridden,&rdquo; a half-sister of &ldquo;hag-ridden.&rdquo;&rquo; (<I>Philology of the English
Tongue,</I> p. 22.) The etymology commonly given explains it of one who is carried
or rides on a bed. &lquo;Bed-rid&rquo; occurs in <I>Wint. Tale,</I> IV, iv, 412. <SC>Moberly</SC>: If
Earle's derivation be rejected, and the connection with ride still assumed, we must
suppose that from the idea of a &lquo;ridden&rquo; or trained horse comes the more general
one of &lquo;accustomed to,&rquo; and thence &lquo;perpetually on,&rquo; the bed. Compare the way
in which <G>h)_qos</G> is used in Homer and Herodotus simply to mean &lquo;a place&rquo; (<G>ta<*> *skuqe/wn
h<*>qea</G>).
<P>31. <B>gait</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: Here used metaphorically, for proceeding in a business.

<P>33. <B>subject</B>] See I, i, 72. That this is used absolutely, see <I>Lear,</I> IV, vi, 107,
&lquo;see how the subject quakes.&rquo;

&lquo;we'll shift <I>for</I> ground&rquo;

<P>38. <B>dilated</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The tenor of these artieles set out at large. <SC>Claren-
don</SC>: According to Minsheu, &lquo;delate&rquo; is only another form of &lquo;dilate,&rquo; meaning &lquo;to
speak at large.&rquo; Compare &lquo;defused&rquo; and &lquo;diffused.&rquo; Bacon uses &lquo;delate&rquo; in the
sense of &lquo;carry,&rquo; &lquo;convey.&rquo;
<P>38. <B>allow.</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> says Sh. should have written <I>allows,</I> and that many
writers fall into this error, when a plural noun immediately precedes the verb.
<SC>Steevens</SC> asserts that all such defects in Sh. were merely the errors of illiterate
transcribers or printers. <SC>Caldecott</SC> boldly maintains that Sh. was fully justified,
in cases like the present, by the usage of the best scholars and writers of the time,
and gives instances from Queen Elizabeth's <I>Seneca,</I> and King James's <I>Reylis and
Cautelis of Scottis Poesie,</I> from Puttenham's <I>Arte of English Poesie,</I>
and Daniel's
<I>Apologie for Ryme;</I> and, further, that this usage was proper because the ear abhors
the caeophony of an accumulation of <I>ss,</I> more especially in poetry, whose prov-
ince is to please the ear, not offend it. <SC>Knight</SC> says that the use of the plural
verb with the nominative singular, a plural genitive intervening, can searcely be
detected as an error. &lquo;The truth is, that it is only within the last half century that
the construction of our language has attained that uniform precision which is now
required. . . . It is remarkable that the very commentators, who were always ready
to fix the charge of ignorance of the rudiments of grammar upon Sh., have admitted
the following passage in a note to 2 <I>Hen. IV</I> by that elegant modern scholar, T.
Warton: &ldquo;Beaumont and Fletcher's play contains many <I>satirical strokes</I> against
Heywood's comedy, <I>the force</I> of which <I>are</I> entirely lost to those who have not seen
that comedy.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Elze</SC> ingeniously suggests that &lquo;allow&rquo; may be in the subjunctive,
and <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> roundly asserts that it is, &lquo;because it is preceded by the idea
of comparison implied by &ldquo;than,&rdquo; which in Old English and Anglo-Saxon usually
governed the subjunctive.&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC> gives this as an instance of confusion of agree-
ment by proximity (&sect; 412). For many instances (which <SC>Dyce</SC> with truth says might
be multiplied without end) of apparent lack of agreement between the nominative
and the verb, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 332 <I>et seq.; Macb.</I> II, i, 61, and <I>Ham.</I> III, ii, 194; III,
iii, 14.

<P>53. <B>coronation</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: As an instance of the minute attention with which
the finished play was elaborated from the early sketch, it may be noteworthy that, in
Q<SUB>1</SUB>, the motive of Laertes's visit is said to be his desire to attend the late king's
funeral. But it evidently oeeurred to Sh. that the acknowledgement of such an
object was as little consistent with the character of Laertes as it would be palatable
to the living monarch, and, accordingly, in the augmented piece the reason given
by Laertes for his coming is more courtier-like.
<P>56. <B>pardon</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Leave to depart. So in III, ii, 303. It is equivalent
to &lquo;leave&rquo; in <I>Cymb.</I> I, iv, 46, and 3 <I>Hen. VI:</I> IV, i, 87.
<P>57. <B>Polonius</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 32): A critic who should suggest that &lquo;Polo
nius&rquo; was a corruption of <I>Apollonius</I> would perhaps &lquo;make much laugh,&rquo; as Man
Friday says; yet I know not that it is more strange than &lquo;Laertes&rquo; and fifty other
similar names in our old plays.
<P>63. <B>graces</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: May the exercise of thy fairest virtues fill up thy time,

<P>64. <B>cousin</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: This word was used to denote &lquo;uncle&rquo; and &lquo;aunt,&rquo;
&lquo;nephew&rquo; and &lquo;niece,&rquo; as well as in the modern sense. Compare <I>Twelfth Night,</I> I,
iii, 5, where it means &lquo;niece,&rquo; and III, iv, 68, where it means &lquo;uncle.&rquo;
<P>64. <B>and</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> suggested &lquo;<I>Kind</I> my son,&rquo; or, as we now say, &lquo;Good

which it otherwise lacks.
