<P>65. [<B>Aside</B>] The propriety of this &lquo;aside,&rquo; which was first marked by Warburton,
and has been adopted by every succeeding editor, is denied by <SC>Moltke</SC> for the fol-
lowing reasons: There is no other instance in Shakespeare's plays where the hero is
first introduced with such a very brief soliloquy; secondly, no one plays upon words
when speaking to one's self; thirdly, Sh. invariably strikes the keynote of his dramas
at the very outset. In this instance, after having in the first scene made us take sides
with Hamlet against the King, and after having still further fostered this feeling of
sympathy for the one and dislike for the other by the King's hypocritical speech
from the throne, it is of the utmost importance that this opposition between the two
should be emphasized, and that Hamlet himself should be shown, not only as per-
fectly aware of it himself, but as equally determined that the King himself should
be aware of it. All these objects fail if the speech be spoken aside.
<P>65. <B>kin ... kind</B>] <SC>Hanmer</SC>: Probably a proverbial expression for a relationship
so confused and blended that it was hard to define it. <SC>Johnson</SC> supposes &lquo;kind&rquo; to
be here the German word for <I>child.</I> That is, &lquo;I am more than <I>cousin</I> and less than
<I>son.</I>&rquo; This conjecture <SC>Steevens</SC> properly disposes of by requiring some proof that
&lquo;kind&rquo; was ever used by any English writer for <I>child.</I> He adds: A jingle of the
same sort is found in <I>Mother Bombie,</I> 1594, &lquo;&mdash;the nearer we are in blood, the fur-
ther we must be from love, the greater the <I>kindred</I> is, the less the <I>kindness</I> must be.&rquo;
Again, in <I>Gorboduc,</I> 1561, &lquo;In kinde a father, but not kindelynesse.&rquo; As &lquo;kind,&rquo;
however, signifies <I>nature,</I> Hamlet may mean that his relationship bad become an
<I>unnatural</I> one, as it was partly founded on incest. &lquo;Kind&rquo; is used for <I>nature</I> in
<I>Jul. C&aelig;s., Ant. &amp; Cleo., Rich. II,</I> and <I>Tit. And.</I> So, too, we have &lquo;kindness,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I>
unnatural, in <I>Ham.</I> II, ii, 609. <SC>Malone</SC> gives substantially the best paraphrase: &lquo;I
am a little more than thy kinsman (for I am thy step-son), and am somewhat less
than kind to thee (for I hate thee, as being the person who has incestuously married
my mother). <SC>Steevens</SC> says that it was the King who was &lquo;less than kind;&rquo; so also
does <SC>Caldecott</SC>, who somewhat darkly interprets (yet <SC>Moberly</SC> quotes it approv-
ingly): More than a common relation, having a confusedly accumulated title of rela-
tionship, you have less than benevolent, or less than even natural, feeling; by a play
upon &lquo;kind&rquo; in its double use and double sense&mdash;its use as an adjective, signifying
<I>benevolent;</I> and its sense as a substantive, signifying <I>nature.</I> We have &lquo;unkind&rquo; in
this sense in <I>Ven. &amp; Ad.</I> 204. &lquo;Surely,&rquo; says <SC>Knight</SC>, &lquo;Hamlet applies these words
to himself. The King has called him, &ldquo;My cousin Hamlet.&rdquo; He says, in a sup
pressed tone, &ldquo;A little more than kin,&rdquo;&mdash;a little more than cousin. The King adds,
&ldquo;and my son.&rdquo; Hamlet says, &ldquo;less than kind;&rdquo;&mdash;I am little of the same <I>nature</I>
with you.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC> follows Steevens and Caldecott in applying these words to the
King. &lquo;By &ldquo;less than kind&rdquo; Hamlet means <I>degenerate and base.</I> &ldquo;Going <I>out of
kinde,</I> (says Baret,) which goeth <I>out of kinde, which doth, or worketh dishonour to his

<P>other work is the word &lquo;kind&rquo; used so frequently and so unambiguously as in <I>The
Tragedie of Gorboduc.</I> <SC>White</SC> and <SC>Hudson</SC> follow Steevens, Caldecott, and Singer
in referring these words to the King. The former paraphrases: In marrying my
mother, you have made yourself something more than my kinsman, and, at the same
time, have shown yourself unworthy of our race, our kind. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: This
playing on words may be attributed to many causes or motives; as, either to an exu-
berant activity of mind, as in the higher comedy of Sh. generally; or to an imitation
of it as a mere fashion, as if it were said,&mdash;&lquo;Is not this better than groaning?&rquo;&mdash;or
to a contemptuous exultation in minds vulgarized and overset by their success, as in
the poetic instance of Milton's Devils in the battle; or it is the language of resent-
ment, as is familiar to every one who has witnessed the quarrels of the lower orders,
where is invariably a profusion of punning invective, whence, perhaps, nicknames
have in a considerable degree sprung up: or it is the language of suppressed passion,
and especially of a hardly-smothered personal dislike. The first and last of these
combine in Hamlet's case; and I have little doubt that <SC>Farmer</SC> is right in suppos-
ing the equivocation carried on in the expression, &lquo;too much i' the sun,&rquo; or son.
<P>67. <B>i' the sun</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: A probable allusion to the proverb: &lquo;Out of heaven's
blessing into the warm sun.&rquo; <SC>Farmer</SC> suggested that a quibble was here intended
between &lquo;sun&rquo; and <I>son.</I> <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Adopting this suggestion of Farmer's, the pas-
sage must mean, &lquo;I have too much about me of the character of expectancy, at the
same time that I am torn prematurely from my sorrows, and thrown into the broad glare
of the sun and day; have too much of the son and successor and public staging without
possession of my rights, and without a due interval to assuage my grief.&rquo; But a closer
observer, (continues Caldecott), here says: &lquo;One part of Farmer's suggestion is right,
Hamlet means that he had not <I>possession of his rights;</I> but there was no quibble;
the allusion is to the proverb referred to by Johnson, which means, &lquo;to be out of
house and home,&rquo; or, at least, to be in a worse temporal condition than a man was,
or should be. Thus in <I>Lear,</I> II, ii, 168, and &lquo;&mdash; they were brought from the good
to the bad, and from Goddes blessyng (as the proverbe is) in to a warme sonne.&rquo;&mdash;
Preface to Grindal's <I>Profitable Doctrine,</I> 1555. And again, &lquo;By such art he thought
to have removed him, as we say, out of God's blessing into the warm sun.&rquo;&mdash;
Raleigh's <I>Hist. of the World,</I> 1677. His being deprived of his right, <I>i. e.</I> his suc-
cession to the kingdom, Hamlet might therefore call &lquo;being too much i' the sun.&rquo;
<SC>Knight</SC>: There is no quibble. His meaning is explained by the old proverb.
<SC>Staunton</SC>: Hamlet may mean, &lquo;I am too much in the way; a mote in the royal
eye;&rquo; but his reply is purposely enigmatical. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I> s. v. <I>heaven's benediction,</I>
&amp;c.): The proverbial expression alluded to by Johnson is found in various authors,
from Heywood down to Swift; the former has, &lquo;In your running from him to me, yee
runne Out of God's blessing into the warme sunne.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Dialogue on Proverbs,</I> Workes,
sig. G 2 ver. 1598; and the latter: &lquo;<I>Lord Sparkish.</I> They say, marriages are made
in heaven; but I doubt, when she was married, she had no friend there. <I>Neverout.</I>
Well, she's got out of God's blessing into the warm sun.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Polite Conversation,</I>
Dialogue 1, Works, vol. ix, p. 423. Ray gives as its equivalent, <I>Ab equis ad asinos.</I>

<P><I>&mdash;Proverbs,</I> p. 192, ed. 1768. <SC>Hudson</SC> inclines to Farmer's suggestion, and ados:
&lquo;Perhaps there is the further meaning implied, that he finds too much sunshine
of jollity in the Court, considering what has lately happened.&rquo; In <I>Much Ado,</I>
II, i, 331, Beatrice says of herself, &lquo;I am sun-burned,&rquo; and this phrase <SC>Hunter</SC>
(i. 250) ingeniously explains, and gives it a signification akin to the present passage.
&lquo; &ldquo;To be in the sun,&rdquo; &ldquo;to be in the warm sun,&rdquo; &ldquo;to be sun-burned,&rdquo; were phrases,&rquo;
says Hunter, &lquo;not uncommon in the time of Sh., and for a century later, to express
the state of being without family connections, destitute of the comforts of domestic
life. There must have been some reason for this association of discomfort with what
is generally considered comfort, at least among northern nations, and this reason is
found in the old English version of the One Hundred and Twenty-first Psalm, in
which occurs the passage, &ldquo;So that the sun shall not burn thee by day, nor the moon
by night;&rdquo; and as this psalm, in the earlier Rituals of the Church, was used in the
Churching of Women, it followed that the matron who was surrounded by her hus-
band and children was one who had received the benediction that the <I>sun should
not burn</I> her, while the unmarried woman, who had received no such benediction, came
to be spoken of by those who allowed themselves to use such jocular expressions as
one &ldquo;still left exposed to the burning of the sun,&rdquo; or, as Beatrice says, &ldquo;sun-burned.&rdquo;
When the translation of the Scriptures was revised, in the reign of James I, the
word &ldquo;smite&rdquo; was substituted in this verse for &ldquo;burn,&rdquo; probably on account of these
ludicrous associations; and for the same reason, on the last revision of the Liturgy,
this psalm was left out of the service altogether. In the first and original use of this
phrase, then, it denoted the state of being unmarried; thus Beatrice uses it. It then
expanded so as to include the state of those who were without family connections of
any kind; thus Hamlet uses it. It expanded still wider and included the state of
those who have no home, and thus it is used in <I>Lear,</I> II, ii, 168. And it seems to have
expanded wider still, and to have been sometimes used for any species of destitution, or
distress, or evil. Hamlet therefore means, &ldquo;I have lost father and mother; you heap
upon me the terms &lquo;cousin&rquo; and &lquo;son,&rquo; but I find myself forlorn, with none of the
comforts remaining which arise out of the charities of kindred.&rdquo;&rquo; Ingenious as
this explanation of Hunter's is, it applies with more force to the phrase used by
Beatrice than to that used by Hamlet; we have no examples given us that &lquo;to be in
the sun&rquo; was ever thus understood, and for it we must take Hunter's unsupported
assertion. <SC>Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 25 May, 1867) thus paraphrases: Ham. turns
off the King's query with an apparently courtly compliment,&mdash;Nay, my lord, I am
too much in the sunshine of your favour, where I show but as a shadow (too much
am I in that sunshine which I detest); deposed by you as heir and successor to the
throne on which by God's providence I was placed, I am now gone to the world;
instead of being in clouds and rain, amid sorrow and tears for my dead father and
king, I find myself in the midst of marriage festivities and carousings. <SC>Moberly</SC>
thinks the proverb may have meant that a person loses all special advantages, and
is reduced to light and sunshine, which are the common inheritance of all.
<P>68. <B>nighted</B>] For the general rule that participles formed from an adjective mean
&lquo;made of (the adjective),&rquo; and derived from a noun, mean &lquo;endowed with, or like
(the noun),&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 294.

often treat Claudius as an <I>usurper,</I> who had deprived young Hamlet of his <I>right</I>
by <I>heirship</I> to his father's crown? Hamlet calls him drunkard, murderer, and
villain; one who had carried the election by low and mean practices; had &lquo;Popp'd
in between the election and my hopes&mdash;;&rquo; had &lquo;From a shelf the precious diadem
stole, And put it in his pocket;&rquo; but never hints at his being an <I>usurper.</I> His dis-
content arose from his uncle's being preferred before him, not from any legal right
which he pretended to set up to the crown. Some regard was probably had to the
recommendation of the preceding prince in electing the successor. And therefore
young Hamlet had &lquo;the voice of the king himself for his succession in Denmark;&rquo;
and he at his own death prophesies that &lquo;the election would light on Fortinbras,
who had his dying voice,&rquo; conceiving that by the death of his uncle he himself had
been king for an instant, and had therefore a right to recommend. When, in the
fourth Act, the rabble wished to choose Laertes king, I understand that autiquity
was forgot, and custom violated, by electing a new king in the lifetime of the old
one, and perhaps also by the calling in a stranger to the royal blood. <SC>Elize</SC>: It is
not exactly consistent with this elective character that the queen should be called
&lquo;the imperial jointress of this warlike state.&rquo; <SC>Marshall</SC> (p. 16): Perhaps the com
parative youth of Ham., and the fact that the kingdom was threatened by the Nor-
wegians, were the reasons which induced the royal councillors to place the sceptre
in the hands of Claudius.
<P>110. <B>nobility</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Magnitude. <SC>Johnson</SC>: Rather <I>generosity.</I> <SC>Heath.</SC>
Eminence and distinction.
<P>110-112. <B>with . . . impart</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: The king had declared Hamlet his im-

says &lquo;impart&rquo; is <I>impart myself, communicate</I> whatever I can bestow; and <SC>Heath</SC>
and <SC>Capell</SC> both approve of this interpretation. <SC>Mason</SC> (p. 374): &lquo;To impart
<I>toward</I>&rquo; a person is not English. Moreover &lquo;impart&rquo; is never neuter. Read, there-
fore, &lquo;and <I>still</I> no less nobility of love&rquo; instead of &lquo;<I>with</I> no less,&rquo; &amp;c.; or else read,
&lquo;Do I <I>my part</I> toward you&rquo; instead of &lquo;do I impart.&rquo; <SC>Delius</SC> suggests that Sh.
probably regarded &lquo;no less<*> nobility of love&rquo; as the object of &lquo;impart,&rquo; and forgot,

thus: &lquo;And with nobility no less of love,&rquo; &amp;c. The nobility that he grants him is
that of heir-presumptive. <SC>Dyce</SC> pronounces this reading of Badham's &lquo;very improper.&rquo;

<P>127. <B>rouse</B>] <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: The radical sense of the word is shown in Platt
Deutsch <I>ruse, rusie,</I> noise, racket, disturbance; German <I>rauschen,</I> to rustle, roar, to
do things with noise and bustle. <I>Rausch</I> is a flare-up, a sudden blaze; the same
word is metaphorically applied to excitation from drink. Platt Deutsch <I>runsk,</I> Old
Norse <I>r&uacute;ss,</I> Dutch <I>roes,</I> tipsiness. When transferred to the cognate sense of a full
glass or bumper, English <I>rouse</I> was not unnaturally supposed to be contracted from
<I>carouse</I> (German <I>garaus</I>), with which it has a merely accidental resemblance&mdash;
<I>Rouse,</I> noise, intemperate mirth. [See I, iv, 8.]
<P>127. <B>bruit</B>] See <I>Macb.</I> V, vii, 22. <SC>Staunton</SC>: This plainly imports not simply
a deep draught, but the accompaniment of some outcry, similar, perhaps, to our
&lquo;hip, hip, hurrah!&rquo;
<P>129. <B>too too</B>] <SC>Nares</SC> pointed out the intensive effect of this reduplication, giving
instances from Holinshed and Spenser, and adding that it is common. <SC>Halliwell</SC>
(<I>Sh. Soc. Papers,</I> 1844, i, 39) showed that &lquo;too-too&rquo; is a provincial word recognized
by Ray, and explained by him as meaning &lquo;very well or good,&rquo; and that Watson a
few years afterwards says it is &lquo;often used to denote <I>exceeding.</I>&rquo; In proof &lquo;<I>that</I> <SC>too-
too</SC>, <I>as used by our early writers, is one word, denoting</I> &ldquo;<I>exceedingly,</I>&rdquo; <I>and that it
ought to be so printed,</I>&rquo; Halliwell gives from the poets twelve instances, from Skelton
down to Hudibras, and refers to over thirty other passages where the phrase is
found, extending from <I>Promos and Cassandra</I> to Young's <I>Night Thoughts.</I> [After
all, Halliwell did not so print it in his edition.] <SC>Hunter</SC> doubts if this reduplica-
tion be emphatic. It appears to him to have been in sense neither more nor less
than <I>too,</I> and he cites many instances from prose writers. Palsgrave, he adds, has
beside <I>to-much, to-little,</I> &amp;c., <I>to to much, to to great, to to little, to to small,</I> answering
to <I>par trop trop peu, par trop trop grant, par trop trop petit.</I> The prouunciation
was too-too, as appears by this line of Constable's: &lquo;But I did too-too inestimable
wey her.&rquo; That the phrase was used with intensifying iteration, <SC>White</SC> thinks is
clear from instances like the present, and from the similar iteration of other adverbs
and adjectives in the literature of Shakespeare's day. For instance: &lquo;Thy wit dost
use <I>still still</I> more harmes to finde,&rquo;&mdash;Sidney's <I>Arcadia,</I> ii, p. 225, ed. 1603; &lquo;While
he did live <I>far, far</I> was all disorder,&mdash;<I>Ib.</I> v, p. 430; &lquo;&mdash;your lesson is <I>Far far</I> too
long to learne it without bocke,&rquo;&mdash;<I>Astrophel and Stella,</I> St. 56, <I>Ib.</I> p. 537; &lquo;Stop you

<P>my mouth with <I>still still</I> kissing me,&rquo;&mdash;<I>Ib.</I> St. 81, <I>Ib.</I> p. 547; &lquo;Even to thy pure

<P>129-159. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: This <I>t&aelig;dium vit&aelig;</I> is a common oppression on minds cast
in the Hamlet mould, and is caused by disproportionate mental exertion, which
necessitates exhaustion of bodily feeling. Where there is a just coincidence of
external and internal action, pleasure is always the result; but where the former is
deficient, and the mind's appetency of the ideal is unchecked, realities will seem
cold and unmoving. In such cases passion combines itself with the indefinite alone.
In this mood of his mind the relation of the appearance of his father's spirit in
arms is made all at once to Hamlet: it is&mdash;Horatio's speech, in particular&mdash;a perfect
model of the true style of dramatic narrative; the purest poetry, and yet in the
most natural language, equally remote from the inkhorn and the plough.
<P>129. <B>solid flesh</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: The base affinities of our nature are ever present
to Hamlet's mind. Here he thinks of the body as hiding from us the freshness,
life, and nobleness of God's creation. If it were to pass away, silently and sponta-
neously, like the mist on a mountain-side, or if, curtain-like, we might tear it down
by an act of violence, it may be that we should see quite another prospect; at any
rate, the vile things now before us would be gone for ever.
<P>130. <B>resolve</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This means the same as <I>dissolve.</I> <SC>Nares</SC> cites: &lquo;I
could be content to resolve myself into tears, to rid thee of trouble.&rquo;&mdash;Lyly's
<I>Euphues,</I> p. 38. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;To thaw or resolve that which is frozen, regelo.&rquo;
Baret's <I>Alvearie.</I>

artillery, but to a divine decree. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 218): This is an unhappy word to use
here. I fear the truth is that the noise of the cannon in the King's speech was still
ringing in the Poet's ears. <SC>Grant White</SC> (<I>The Galaxy,</I> Oct. 1869): Here and in
<I>Cym.</I> III, iv, 77-80, there is a particular assertion of the existence of a specific pro-
ibition of suicide by Divine law. Sh. may have known the Bihle, as he knew all
other things in his day knowable, so much better than I do that I may not without
presumption question what he says with regard to it. But I have not been able to
discover any such specific prohibition. <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Knowledge and
Use of the Bible,</I> p. 149): Unless it be the Sixth Commandment, the &lquo;canon&rquo; must
be one of natural religion.

pare line 82, where &lquo;shows of grief&rquo; is defined by Hunter to be &lquo;mourning apparel,&rquo;
nay, by Hamlet himself, to be &lquo;the trappings and the suits of woe.&rquo; What, then,
are the <I>shows</I> with which Gertrude followed her husband's body to the grave but
&lquo;customary suits of solemn black?&rquo; What were her Niobe's tears but &lquo;th' fruitful
river in the eye?&rquo; What were these but the &lquo;forms and <I>shows</I> of grief?&rquo; Let the
text he thus paraphrased, &lquo;Before my mother's &ldquo;mourning weeds&rdquo; (2 <I>Hen. VI</I>)
were worn out, the doffed them for the wedding-gear. Oh! wicked speed,&rquo; &amp;c.

<P>150. <B>discourse of reason</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC> (<I>Dict.</I>): <I>Discourse.</I> The act of the under-
standing, by which it passes from premises to consequences. <SC>Gifford</SC> (note on
Massinger's <I>Unnatural Combat,</I> Works, vol. i, p. 148, ed. 1813): It is very diffi-
cult to determine the precise meaning which our ancestors gave to <I>discourse,</I> or to
distinguish the line which separated it from <I>reason.</I> Perhaps it indicated a <I>more</I>
rapid deduction of consequences from premises than was supposed to be effected by
reason;&mdash;but I speak with hesitation. . . . Whatever be the sense, it frequently
appears in our old writers, by whom it is usually coupled with <I>reason</I> or <I>judgement,</I>
which last would seem to be the more proper word. . . . &lquo;Discourse <I>of</I> reason&rquo; is so
poor and perplexed a phrase, that [in <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 150] I should dismiss it at once
for what I believe to be the genuine reading: &lquo;discourse <I>and</I> reason.&rquo; <SC>Boswell</SC>:
The text may be supported by numerous examples. The very same phrase is used
in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> II, ii, 116. In the preface to Davys's <I>Reports:</I> &lquo;And this idea I
have conceived of him, not out of mine own imagination, or weak discourse of
reason;&rquo; and Saville's Tacitus's <I>Agricola,</I> 1591, p. 242: &lquo;Agricola, though brought
up in the field, upon a naturall wit, and discourse of reason,&rquo; cap. ix. Hamlet him-
self explains the phrase in IV, iv, 36. <SC>Caldecott</SC> adds, <I>Oth.</I> IV, ii, 153, &lquo;dis-
course of thought.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. 2): &lquo;Discourse of reason&rquo; means <I>ratiocination.</I>
Brutes have not this reasoning faculty, though they have what is <I>instinct</I> and memory.
Hamlet opposes the <I>discursive</I> power of the intellect of men to the instinct of
brutes. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) cites: &lquo;There was no discourse of reason strong enough to
diuert him from thinking that he was betrayed.&rquo;&mdash;<I>A Tragi-comicall History of ovr
Times,</I> &amp;c., p. 34, 1627.
<P>151. <B>with</B>] See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 194.
<P>154. <B>unrighteous</B>] <SC>Badham</SC> (p. 282): The Queen's tears were not unrighteous,
but every way due; and though it may be urged that they were hypocritical, we learn
nothing of the kind from Sh.; nor is it conceivable that where there was so much
that deserved to be called by the worst names, Hamlet should be made to select
such a trifle as the mere feigning of sorrow as something <I>most unrighteous.</I> I have
little doubt that Sh. wrote, &lquo;<I>moist and righteous</I> tears.&rquo;
<P>155. <B>flushing</B>] <SC>Hudson</SC>: This refers to the redness of the eyes, caused by what

<P>177. <B>pray thee</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: This reading of F<SUB>1</SUB> suits the required deliberateness
of the expression better. There is an earnest entreaty meant.
<P>180. <B>baked-meats</B>] <SC>Collins</SC>: It was anciently the general custom to give a cold
entertainment to mourners at a funeral. In distant counties this practice is continued
among the yeomanry. See <I>The Tragique Historie of the Faire Valeria of London,</I>
1598: &lquo;His corpes was with funerall pompe conveyed to the church, and there sol-
lemnly enterred, nothing omitted which necessitie or custom could claime; a sermon,
a <I>banquet,</I> and like observations.&rquo; Again, in the old romance of <I>Syr Legore,</I> no
date: &lquo;A great <I>feaste</I> would he holde Upon his quenes mornynge day, That was
buryed in an abbay.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: See, also, Hayward's <I>Life and Raigne of King
Henrie the Fourth,</I> 1599, p. 135: &lquo;Then hee [King Richard II] was obscurely in-
terred,&mdash;without the charge of a <I>dinner</I> for celebrating the funeral.&rquo; <SC>Douce</SC>: This
practice was certamly borrowed from the <I>c&oelig;na feralis</I> of the Romans, alluded to in
Juvenal's 5th <I>Satire</I> and in the Laws of the Twelve Tables. It consisted of the
offering of a small plate of milk. honey, wine, flowers, &amp;c. to the ghost of the
deceased. In the North this teast is called an <I>arval</I> or <I>arvil-supper:</I> and the loaves
that are sometimes distributed among the poor, <I>arval-bread.</I> <SC>John Addis, Jun.</SC>
(<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 9 Feb. '67) cites an apposite passage from Massinger: &lquo;The same rose
mary that serves for the funeral will serve for the wedding.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Old Law,</I> IV, i.
<SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: This is one word. See Chaucer (<I>Cant. Tales,</I> v. 344): &lquo;With-
outen bake mete never was his house.&rquo; The combination of a funeral and a mar-
riage feast contained nothing repugnant to the ancient Northern mind. At the end
of cap. 14 of <I>Frithiof's Saga,</I> it is related that Frithiof prepared a sumptuous feast,
to which came all his followers, and thereupon was held the funeral feast of Hring
the King, and likewise the marriage feast of Frithiof and Ingiborg. Here in
Hamlet what was so abhorrent was that the <I>widow</I> should have married so quickly.
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: We have &lquo;bakemeats&rquo; in Gen. xl, 17.

&lquo;dearest foe,&rquo; his uncle, lest he should send him to heaven.

<P>two opposite meanings from the single Anglo-Saxon word <I>derian,</I> to hurt, thence
deriving our word <I>dear</I> = not cheap (when the season <I>dereth</I> the crops, causing a
<I>dearth</I>); hence what is not cheap is precious, valued; whence comes the secondary
meaning of <I>dear</I> = beloved. In this passage &lquo;dearest&rquo; has reverted to its original
meaning of <I>hurtful, mischievous.</I> This plausible derivation, or rather explanation,
of the two distinct and contrary meanings of the word has been followed by Rich-
ardson in his <I>Dictionary,</I> and by the edd. above named, except Craik, who detected
Tooke's error in tracing the word, in both its meanings, to one root, by showing
that the word dear = high-priced, precious, beloved, is the Anglo-Saxon <I>de&oacute;re, d&uacute;re,
d&ycirc;re,</I> from the verb <I>de&oacute;ran</I> or <I>d&yacute;ran,</I> to hold dear, to love. Craik thus explains
the different senses which the word assumes: the notion properly involved in it of
<I>love</I> having first become generalized into that of a strong affection of any kind,
thence passes on into that of such an emotion the very reverse of love, or as
<SC>Clarendon</SC> concisely states it: &lquo;dear&rquo; is used of whatever touches us nearly either
in love or hate, joy or sorrow. <SC>M&auml;tzner</SC> (i, 196) gives a list of two hundred
and thirty-five words which had originally different forms (and of course different
meanings), but which now are found in only one form; among them (i, 206) is
<I>dear,</I> with the different original forms pointed out by Craik. See &lquo;dear soul,&rquo; III
ii, 58.

rades were <I>melted</I> to &lquo;jelly,&rquo; for jelly is no longer jelly when melted, but that they

ment&rquo; as procured by distillation from &lquo;cursed hebenon.&rquo; Therefore we feel morally
certain that Shakespeare's word here was &lquo;bechill'd.&rquo; <SC>Bailey</SC> (i, 47) dissents from

<P>216. <B>it head</B>] <SC>Craik</SC> (Note <I>on Jul. C&aelig;s</I> I, ii, 124): The word <I>its</I> does not
occur in the authorized translation of the Bible; it is, however, found in Sh. There
is one instance [the only one, according to <SC>Rolfe</SC>, where it is not spelled <I>it's,</I> with
an apostrophe] in <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> I, ii, 4. But the most remarkable of the plays
in this particular is probably <I>Wint. Tale;</I> where in I, ii, 151-158, we have as many
as three instances in a single speech of Leontes; again in I, ii, 266, and III, iii.
46. On the other hand, we have the following instances in F<SUB>1</SUB> of the use of <I>it</I> in
possessive sense, where we now use <I>its: Wint. Tale,</I> II, iii, 178; III, ii, 101;
<I>King John,</I> II, i, 160, 161, 162; <I>Lear,</I> I, iv, 235 (<I>bis</I>); the passage &lquo;that nature which
contemnes it origin,&rquo; in <I>Lear,</I> IV, ii, 32, is not in Ff; but Q<SUB>1</SUB> has <I>ith</I> and Q<SUB>2</SUB> <I>it.</I> There
is also one passage in our English Bible, <I>Levit.</I> xxv, 5, in which the reading of the
original edition is &lquo;of it own accord.&rquo; The modern reprints give &lquo;its.&rquo; [<SC>Rolfe</SC>
adds: In the Geneva Bible, 1579, we have &lquo;it owne accorde,&rquo; in <I>Acts,</I> xii, 10.]
Trench (<I>English Past and Present</I>) doubts whether Milton has once admitted <I>its</I>
into <I>Paradise Lost,</I> &lquo;although, when that was composed, others frequently allowed
it.&rquo; But he does use it occasionally, <I>e. g.</I> &lquo;The mind is its own place.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Par.
Lost,</I> i, 254; and &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; falsehood . . . returns Of force to its own likeness.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Ib.</I> iv,
813. [<SC>Rolfe</SC>: See also <I>Hymn on the Nativity,</I> 106.] Generally, however, he
avoids the word, and easily does so by personifying most of his substantives; it is
only when this cannot be done that he reluctantly accepts the services of the little
<I>parvenu</I> monosyllable. Bacon has frequently <I>his</I> in the neuter. Trench notices
the fact of the occurrence of <I>its</I> in Rowley's <I>Poems</I> as decisive against their genuine-
ness. The modern practice is the last of three distinct stages through which the
language passed, as to this use of <I>its,</I> in the course of less than a century. First,
we have <I>his</I> serving for both masculine and neuter; secondly, we have <I>his</I> restricted
to the masculine, and the neuter left with hardly any recognized form; thirdly, we
have the defect of the second stage remedied by the frank adoption of the hereto-
fore rejected <I>its.</I> And the most curious thing of all in the history of the word <I>its</I>
is the extent to which, before its recognition as a word admissible in serious com
position, even the occasion for its employment was avoided or eluded. This is very
remarkable in Sh. The very conception which we express by <I>its</I> probably does not
occur once in his works for ten times that it is to be found in any modern writer.
So that we may say the invention or adoption of this form has changed not only our
English style, but even our manner of thinking. The Saxon personal pronoun was,
in the nominative singular, <I>He,</I> masculine; <I>He&oacute;,</I> feminine; <I>Hit,</I> neuter. <I>He</I> we still
retain; for <I>He&oacute;</I> we have substituted <I>She,</I> apparently a modification of <I>Se&oacute;,</I> the
feminine of the demonstrative; <I>Hit</I> we have converted into <I>It</I> (though the aspirate
is still often heard in the Scottish dialect). The genitive was <I>Hire</I> for the feminine
(whence our modern <I>Her</I>), and <I>His</I> both for the masculine and the neuter. It is to
be understood, of course, that <I>its.</I> however convenient, is quite an irregular forma-

<P>tion; the <I>t</I> of <I>it</I> (originally <I>hit</I>) is merely the sign of the neuter gender, which does
not enter into the inflection, leaving the natural genitive of that gender (<I>hi, hi-s</I>)
substantially identical with that of the masculine (<I>he, he-s, hi-s</I>).
<P>To the foregoing <SC>Rolfe</SC> adds the following instances of <I>it's</I> in F<SUB>1</SUB>: <I>Temp.</I> I, ii,
95; <I>Ib.</I> I, ii, 393; 2 <I>Hen. VI:</I> III, ii, 393; <I>Hen. VIII:</I> I, i, 18. <I>It,</I> or <I>yt,</I> pos-
sessive is found in F<SUB>1</SUB> in fourteen passages. The following are not mentioned by
Craik: <I>Temp.</I> II, i, 163; 2 <I>Hen. IV:</I> I, ii, 131; <I>Hen. V:</I> V, ii, 40; <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I>
I, iii, 52; <I>Timon,</I> V, i, 151; <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 216; <I>Ib.</I> V, i, 209; <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> II, vii,
49; <I>Ib.</I> II, vii, 53; <I>Cym.</I> III, iv, 160. Rolfe concludes: No argument in regard
to the date of the plays can be based upon the occurrence of these various forms of
the possessive <I>its.</I> We find all three in some of the earliest plays, two different
forms in the very same play, and <I>it's</I> in <I>Hen. VIII,</I> which, according to White, is
the latest of the plays. The simple fact is, that Sh. wrote in the early part of that
transitional period when <I>its</I> was <I>beginning</I> to displace <I>his</I> and <I>her</I> as the possessive
of <I>it,</I> and that just at that time the forms <I>it</I> and <I>it's</I> were more common than <I>its,</I>
though this last was occasionally used even before the end of the 16th century. See
Wright's <I>Bible Word-Book,</I> and Marsh, <I>Lectures on Eng. Lang.,</I> First Series, p.
397. [See also <SC>M&auml;tzner</SC>, i, 296, and <SC>Mommsen</SC>, <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.,</I> p. 22. Indeed,
this whole note ought to have been given in the Variorum ed. of <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I>
I, iii, 52, but my only apology for this and similar omissions in that volume is
the terror with which the endless pages in prospect inspired me in those early
days; and I have not outgrown it yet. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>217. <B>like as it would</B>] As if. See II, i, 91, 95; III, iv, 135; <I>Macb.</I> I, iv, 11;
or <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 107, or <SC>M&auml;tzner</SC>, ii, 128, and iii, 494.
<P>218. <B>even</B>] Just, exactly. See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 38, or <SC>Schmidt</SC>, (s. v.) 4.
<P>219. <B>shrunk</B>] <SC>Warton</SC>. It is a most inimitable circumstance in Sh. to make the
Ghost, which has been so long obstinately silent, and of course must be dismissed
by the morning, begin or rather prepare to speak, and to be interrupted at the very
critical time of the crowing of a cock. Another poet, according to custom, would
have suffered his Ghost tamely to vanish without contriving this start, which is like
a start of guilt,&mdash;to say nothing of the aggravation of the future suspense, occasioned
by this preparation to speak and to impart some mysterious secret. Less would have
been expected had nothing been promised.
<P>221. <B>As</B>] See <SC>M&auml;tzner</SC>, iii, 493, <G>bb</G>; and for the old preterite &lquo;writ&rquo; in the next
line, see <I>Ib.</I> i, 368.

<P>226. <B>Arm'd</B>] <SC>Knight</SC>. This passage is sometimes read and acted as if it applied
to the manner in which Hor. and Mar. were to hold their watch; and we have
somewhere seen a criticism which notes line 228 as a memorable example of an
abrupt transition. Without doubt it is asked with reference to the Ghost. Hamlet an-
ticipates the re-appearance of the figure when he asks, line 225, and proceeds to those
minute questions which carry forward the deep impressions of truth and reality with
which everything connected with the supernatural appearance of the Ghost is invested
<P>229. <B>beaver</B>] Florio (<I>A Worlde of Wordes,</I> 1598) gives: <I>Baui&eacute;ra,</I> the chin peece
of a caske or head-peece. Bullokar (<I>English Expositor,</I> 1616) defines: <I>Beauer</I>
In armour it signifieth that part of the helmet which may bee lifted vp, to take breath
the more freely. <SC>Douce</SC> (i, 439) shows that it is frequently used to denote the
whole helmet, as in 3 <I>Hen. VI:</I> I, i, 12, and gives representations of the helmet
and its parts; as also <SC>Knight</SC> at 2 <I>Hen. IV:</I> IV, i, 120. <SC>Worcester</SC> cites Stephen-
son as deriving it from Fr. <I>buvoir,</I> because it enabled the wearer to drink. The
definitions of <SC>Richardson</SC> and <SC>Wedgwood</SC> are not borne out by references to Sh.
<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 219): Some say it ought to be &lquo;he wore his beaver <I>down,</I>&rquo; but Sh. has
the authority of one who ought to know something concerning what belongs to
knights and chivalry: &lquo;they their bevers up did rear.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Faerie Queene,</I> IV, vi, 25.
<P>232. <B>Pale or red</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: The meaning is marred without the comma of F<SUB>1</SUB>

cise Horatio (e'en the justest man Ham. had ever found) to draw a nice distinction

being held. Furthermore, in addition to these three reasons, the <I>point</I> of the line

<P><SC>Scene iii.</SC>] <SC>Coleridge</SC>: This scene must be regarded as one of Shakespeare's
lyric movements in the play, and the skill with which it is interwoven with the
dramatic parts is peculiarly an excellence of our poet. You experience the sensa-
tion of a pause without the sense of a stop.
<P>1. <B>embark'd</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: As applied to things, <I>imbark't</I> or <I>inbark't</I> seems prefer-
able to &lquo;embark'd.&rquo;
<P>2. <B>as</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 109: We almost always apply <I>as,</I> like <I>because,</I> to the past and
the present; Sh. often uses it of the future, in the sense of &lquo;according <I>as.</I>&rquo; In the
present passage a modern reader would at first naturally suppose &lquo;as&rquo; to mean <I>since,</I>
or <I>because,</I> but the context shows it means &lquo;according <I>as.</I>&rquo;
<P>2. <B>benefit</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 94): It is to be observed that the words <I>benefit</I>
and <I>beneficial,</I> in our old writers, almost uniformly involve the idea of a <I>benefactor,</I>
which has since been dropped, except in cases where the context implies that idea,
<I>e. g. conferring</I> or <I>receiving a benefit.</I>
<P>3. <B>convoy</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, conveyance. See <I>All's Well,</I> IV, iv, 10.
<P>5. <B>trifling</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: That is, gay and thoughtless intimation.
<P>6. <B>fashion</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That which is changeable and temporary. See Lyly's
<I>Euphues,</I> ed. Arber, p. 81: &lquo;Tush Philautus was liked for fashion sake, but neuer
loued for fancie sake.&rquo;
<P>6. <B>toy</B>] That is, <I>caprice,</I> as in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> IV, i, 119: &lquo;inconstant toy.&rquo; Sh.
uses this word, as Staunton says (<I>King John,</I> I, i, 232), with great latitude. See
its use in I, iv, 75. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: A pastime and fancy, not a deep affection. See
<I>Oth.</I> I, iii, 269.
<P>6. <B>blood</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): Disposition, inclination, temperament, impulse. [See
line 116 of this scene, and III, ii, 64.]

<P>7. <B>primy</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: Early, belonging to the spring; perhaps, peculiar to this passage.
<P>8. <B>Forward</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Early, ripe before due season; and thence having in
it the principles of premature decay.
<P>8. To aid the scansion of this line different expedients have been devised (see
Text. Notes). <SC>Mommsen</SC> (<I>Perkins-Shakespeare,</I> Berlin, 1854, pp. 360, 496) throws
the accent on the second syllable of &lquo;lasting,&rquo; as we sometimes find it in words
which are now paroxytone; <I>e. g.</I> sembl&aacute;nce, march&aacute;nt, &amp;c. To pronounce it as a
trochee, l&aacute;sting, is against the Shakespearian usage of admitting a trochee only after
a pause. But, <SC>Elze</SC> asks, Why cannot both the last two feet be trochees: &lquo;sw&eacute;et
not &verbar; l&aacute;sting&rquo;? <SC>Abbott</SC> and <SC>Clarendon</SC> prolong &lquo;sweet&rquo; into a dissyllable (&sect; 484,
and see <I>Macb.</I> I, ii, 5). <SC>Moberly</SC> finds the solution in &lquo;permanent.&rquo; &lquo;The mean-
ing of this word induces a slight pause, and so gives it the time of an additional
syllahle.&rquo; [In other words, the voice of an intelligent reader cures instinctively
such defects in metre; if they be defects.]
<P>9. <B>suppliance</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: It is plain that <I>perfume</I> is necessary to exemph<*>y the
idea of <I>sweet, not lasting.</I> With the word <I>suppliance</I> I am not satisfied, and yet
dare hardly offer what I imagine to be right. I suspect that <I>soffiance,</I> or some such
word, formed from the Italian, was then used for the act of fumigating with sweet
scents. <SC>Mason</SC>: An amusement to fill up a vacant moment. <SC>Steevens</SC>: What was
supplied us for a minute. It is found in Chapman's ninth <I>Iliad.</I>
<P>10. <B>so?</B>] <SC>Corson</SC> [who prefers the punctuation of the QqFf]: This speech is
certainly meant to express Ophelia's submissiveness to her brother's opinion, not to
question the correctness of it.
<P>11-14. <B>For . . . withal</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> transposes these lines to follow line 32,
because, as he alleges, they afford not the slightest explanation to &lquo;Think it no
more,&rquo; and because they have been evidently inserted in the wrong place through
some blunder, and are intelligible only when restored to their proper order, as he
deems it.

<P>all the three instances in which Sh. uses the word (the third is 2 <I>Hen. IV:</I> III, ii, 276).
It comes from the Saxon <I>theow</I> or <I>theoh,</I> whence also <I>thigh,</I> and must not be con-
founded with the obsolete <I>thews</I> = manners, or qualities of mind, which is from the
Saxon <I>theaw.</I> This latter <I>thews</I> is common in Spenser, Chaucer, and earlier writers;
the former is found very rarely before Shakespeare's day. It occurs (as cited by
<SC>Nares</SC>) in Turbervile's <I>Ovid's Epistles,</I> 1567: &lquo;the thews of Helens passing form.&rquo;
In the earlier version of <I>Layamon's Brut,</I> at the end of the twelfth century (verse
6361): &lquo;Monnene strengest of maine and of <I>theawe</I> of alle thissere theode&rquo; (of
men strongest of main, or strength, and of sinew, of all this land). But Sir F.
Madden remarks (III, 471): &lquo;This is the only instance in the poem of the word
being applied to bodily qualities, nor has any other passage of an earlier date than
the sixteenth century been found in which it is so used.&rquo; <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: The <I>s</I> is
probably not a sign of the plural, but a derivative affix for <I>th,</I> whence we may infer
an abstract <I>the&ocirc;vth,</I> denoting <I>growth,</I> in later English <I>thewth.</I>
<P>12. <B>this</B>] <SC>Corson</SC> (p. 12): &lquo;His&rquo; of F<SUB>1</SUB> stands for &lquo;nature&rquo;: as nature's temple
grows, the service within widens. There is a metaphor implied.
<P>12. <B>temple</B>] See <I>Macb.</I> II, iii, 64; <I>R. of L.</I> 719, and 1172, in proof of <SC>Calde-
cott's</SC> remark that this is never but on grave occasions applied to the body.
<P>13. <B>inward service</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: As the body increases in hulk, the duties
calling forth the offices and energies of the mind increase equally. <SC>Moberly</SC>:
<G>*)aucauome/nw| tw_| sw/mati sunau/contai kai\ ai( fpe/nes</G>.&mdash;Herodotus, iii, 134.
<P>14. <B>Grows</B>] <SC>Hudson</SC>: The passage would seem to imply that Hamlet is not so
old as he is elsewhere represented to be.
<P>15. <B>cautel</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): Craft, deceit. &lquo;Cautelle: <I>A wile, cautell, sleight;
a craftie reach, or fetch, guilefvl deuise or endeuor; also, craft, subtiltie, trumperie,
deceit, cousenage.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Cotgrave. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Only used elsewhere by Sh. in <I>L. C.</I>
303. <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh.'s Testamentary Language,</I> p. 43): Sh. may have written these
lines remembering the following passage from Swinburn's <I>Treatise on Wills,</I> 1590:
&lquo;There is no cautele under heaven, whereby the libertie of making or revoking his
testament can be utterly taken away,&rquo;&mdash;p. 61. Again Laertes says, line 20, &lquo;He may
not carve for himself,&rquo; and according to Swinburn, &lquo;it is not lawful for legataries
to <I>carve for themselves,</I> taking their legacies at their own pleasure,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;p. 50.
<P>16. <B>virtue</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: It here seems to comprise both <I>excellence</I> and <I>power,</I> and
may he explained the <I>pure effects.</I> <SC>Mason</SC>: His virtuous intentions. <SC>Staunton</SC>:
It here seems to import <I>essential goodness:</I> as we speak of the <I>virtues</I> of herbs, &amp;c.
<P>16. <B>will</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The Ff contain a clear misprint by the eye catching and
giving the same word twice.

<P>20. <B>Carve</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC> (Note on &lquo;Carver,&rquo; <I>Rich. II:</I> II, iii, 144). Sh. uses the
verb to &lquo;carve&rquo; very expressively to signify &lquo;hew recklessly&rquo; and to &lquo;select selfishly.&rquo;
<P>21. <B>safety</B>] <SC>Theorald</SC> (<I>Sh. Rest.</I> p. 22) conjectured that &lquo;sanctity&rquo; of Ff should
be <I>sanity,</I> because the welfare, preservation of the state was in some degree con-
cerned by Hamlet's choice of a wife. Theobald calls attention to the same mis-
print of one word for the other in II, ii, 208, and <I>Macb.</I> IV, iii, 144. <SC>Walker</SC>
(<I>Crit.</I> iii, 88, also <I>Vers.</I> 159) makes the same conjecture: &lquo;<I>Sanity</I> must surely be
the right reading; <I>sanctity,</I> at any rate, is absurd. <I>Frequentius, ut s&aelig;<*>e fit, pro
rariori;</I> the pulpit having familiarized <I>sanctity</I> to men's minds.&rquo; Both <SC>Dyce</SC> and
<SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 484, agree with Walker. The latter says that the present line could not
be scanned without prolonging both &lquo;health&rquo; and &lquo;whole.&rquo; &lquo;Such a double pro-
longation is extremely improbable, considering the moderate emphasis required.
More probably, Theobald's suggestion is right.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: The editor of F<SUB>1</SUB>, finding
the metre defective, in consequence of the article being omitted before &lquo;health,&rquo;
instead of supplying it, for &lquo;safety&rquo; substituted a word of three syllables. <SC>Collier</SC>:
&lquo;Safety&rquo; was often of old, as here, pronounced as a trisyllable.
<P>21. <B>this</B>] <SC>Corson</SC> (p. 12): <I>The</I> of Ff is better than &lquo;this;&rquo; &lquo;state&rquo; being used
abstractly.
<P>26, 27. <B>As . . . deed</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC> [see Text. Notes]: As he, in that peculiar rank
and class that he fills in the state, and the power and means thereto annexed, may
enable himself to give his professions effect. <SC>Collier</SC>: <I>Sect and force</I> may be
strained into a meaning, but &lquo;act and place&rquo; require no such effort. The latter is the
reading of the (MS) also. <SC>White</SC>: What tolerable sense has either Q<SUB>2</SUB> or F<SUB>1</SUB> in con-
nection with the context? F<SUB>1</SUB> manifestly corrects two errors, but makes one&mdash;&lquo;force&rquo;
for <I>place.</I> &lquo;Sect&rquo; is class, rank, or, in the slang of so <*>iety, <I>set.</I> So in <I>Lear,</I> V, iii, 18.

<P>43. <B>best</B>] The not uncommon omission of the article before superlatives is
perhaps to be explained, according to <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 82, by the douhle meaning of
the superlative, which means not only &lquo;<I>the</I> best of the class,&rquo; but also &lquo;very
good.&rquo;
<P>43. <B>safety</B>] <SC>Francke</SC>: See <I>Macb.</I> III, v, 32. Also <I>Velleius Paterculus,</I> ii, 218:
<*>equentissimum initium esse calamitatis securitatem. <SC>Elze</SC>: See <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> II,
ii, 14: &lquo;the wound of peace is surety, Surety secure.&rquo;
<P>44. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: In the absence of any tempter, youth rebels against itself, <I>i. e.</I>
the passions of youth revolt from the power of self-restraint; there is a traitor in
the camp.
<P>44. <B>though . . . near</B>] For instances of the omission of the predicate verb, see
<SC>M&auml;tzner</SC>, ii, 43, though I can find no parallel instances in the conjunctive clauses
there noted. <SC>Clarendon</SC> appositely cites <I>Cymb.</I> IV, iv, 23.
<P>45. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: You will observe in Ophelia's short and general answer to the
long speech of Laertes the natural carelessness of innocence, which cannot think
such a code of cautions and prudences necessary to its own preservation.
<P>47. <B>ungracious</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Graceless. So 1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> II, iv, 490.
<P>47. <B>pastors</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> does &lquo;not scruple to change&rquo; this to the sing.
&lquo;pastor,&rquo; parsing the first &lquo;Do&rquo; as the auxiliary verb to the second, as well as to
&lquo;show,&rquo; while &lquo;Himself&rquo; remains in grammatical agreement with what has pre-
ceded.
<P>47-50. <B>pastors . . . Himself</B>] See III, ii, 181, for a construction the reverse of
this: a plural relative and a singular antecedent. <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 415: &lquo;Himself . . .
treads&rquo; is for &lquo;Whiles you tread.&rquo; The construction is changed by change of
thought.
<P>49. <B>puff'd and reckless</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Bloated and swollen, the effect of excess;
and heedless and indifferent to consequences. &lquo;Ignavus, inefficax, <I>rechetesse.</I>&rquo;&mdash;
<I>Ortus Vocab.</I> 1514.
<P>50. <B>primrose</B>] See <I>Macb.</I> II, iii, 17.

prudence to his son Robert, afterwards Earl of Salisbury, which may be read in the
<I>Desiderata Curiosa;</I> and in <I>The Harleian Miscellany</I> is a letter from Sir Henry Sydney
to Philip his son, containing divers lessons of prudence delivered in a didactic form.

racter of Polonins I can entertain no doubt, nor that some attentive observer of the
men of those times will one day trace the Poet home. Could it be the Lord Cham-

and names particularly the Lord Admiral, the Lord Treasurer, and Count Gondomer,
as persons with whom the stage had made free. <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Euphuism,</I>

joined to thee in heart.&rquo; Lines 66, 67, Euphues:&mdash;&lquo;Be not quarrellous for every
light occasion: they never fight without provoking, and once provoked they never
cease.&rquo; Line 68, Euphues: &lquo;It shall be there better to hear what they say, than to
speak what thou thinkest.&rquo; [See also II, ii, 86; and <SC>French</SC>, in Appendix, p. 239.]

<P>74. <B>Are...that</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Chief&rquo; may be used adverbially, a practice common
in Sh.: &lquo;chiefly generous.&rquo; I would more willingly read, &lquo;Select and generous. are
most <I>choice</I> in that.&rquo; <SC>Ritson</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> &amp;c. p. 193): The nobility of France are
select and generous above all other nations, and chiefly in the point of apparel; the
richness and elegance of their dress. <SC>Malone</SC>: May we suppose that &lquo;chief&rquo; of
the Ff is a word borrowed from heraldry? They in France approve themselves to
be of a most select and generous <I>escutcheon</I> by their dress. <I>Chef,</I> in heraldry, is the
upper third part of the shield. See Minsheu. This is very harsh; yet I hardly
think that the words &lquo;of a&rquo; could have been introduced without some authority
from the MS. &lquo;Generous&rquo;=<I>generosus.</I> &lquo;Chief,&rquo; however, may have been used as a
substantive, for <I>note</I> or <I>estimation.</I> <SC>Knight</SC>: It is scarcely necessary to go to her-
aldry for an explanation of the word: we have it in composition, as in <I>mischief,</I> and
the now obsolete <I>bonchief.</I> &lquo;Chief,&rquo; literally the head, here signifies <I>eminence, supe-
riority.</I> Those of the best rank and station are of a most select and generous
superiority in the indication of their dignity by their apparel. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 1):
The meaning perhaps is: &lquo;Are of a most select and generous rank and station,
<I>chiefly</I> in that.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC>, in his <I>Remarks,</I> &amp;c. p. 206, while approving of Collier's
rendering of &lquo;chief in that&rquo; (&lquo;the words can be used here in no other sense&rquo; than
<I>chiefly in that</I>), objects to the violent ellipsis which is implied by inserting &lquo;rank
and station&rquo; after &lquo;select and generous,&rquo; and adds: &lquo;During the many hours which
I have spent (perhaps wasted) in collating early dramas, I have known four or five
editions of a play, though differing from each other materially elsewhere, yet coin-
cide in some one most erroneous reading (which was corrected by a fortunately
extant MS): the text of that particular place having been once vitiated, the corrup-
tion had been retained in all the subsequent impressions. Such is evidently the
case here (where there is unluckily no MS <I>Hamlet</I> to refer to); and the probability
seems to be, that the strangely impertinent words, &ldquo;of a,&rdquo; found their way into the
line, while the eye of the transcriber or compositor, glancing away from it for a
moment, was arrested by &ldquo;of the&rdquo; immediately above.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): &lquo;Choice&rquo;
was formerly not unfrequently spelt <I>choise,</I> and the long <*> led to the misprinting of
&lquo;choice,&rquo; first, <I>chiefe,</I> and afterwards <I>cheff.</I> The (MS) substitutes &lquo;choice,&rquo; and the
whole difficulty is removed, for Polonius says that the French are &lquo;of a most select

<P>and generous choice&rquo; in all matters relating to dress. <SC>White</SC> [see this line and the

of &lquo;chief&rquo; in the first,&mdash;a kind of misprint which often occurs in the old texts of
these plays. The two errors last named were perpetuated (as errors sometimes unac-
countably are), although &lquo;chief&rquo; in the first line was changed to &lquo;best.&rquo; This reading
of White's the <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC> (<I>Preface,</I> viii) approve of as &lquo;probably&rquo; what
Sh. had &lquo;originally written;&rquo; the corruption in Q<SUB>1</SUB> and Q<SUB>2</SUB> which, they say, is clearly
due to an error in the transcript from which both were copied, may have arisen
from Shakespeare's having &lquo;given between the lines, or in the margin, &ldquo;of,&rdquo;
&ldquo;chief,&rdquo; meaning these as alternative readings for &ldquo;in&rdquo; and &ldquo;best&rdquo; in line 73.
The transcriher by mistake inserted them in line 74.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC>: The slight
change of <I>sheaf</I> for &lquo;chiefe&rquo; or &lquo;cheff,&rquo; a change for which we alone are answer-
able, seems to impart a better and more poetic meaning to the passage than any vari-
ation yet suggested; and it is supported, if not established, by the following extracts
from Ben Jonson: &lquo;&mdash;Ay, and with assurance, That it is found in noblemen and
gentlemen Of the best <I>sheaf.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Magnetic Lady,</I> III, iv. &lquo;I am so haunted at
the court and at my lodging with your refined choice spirits, that it makes me clean
of another garb, another <I>sheaf.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>Every Man Out of His Humour,</I> II, i. <SC>Ingleby</SC>
(<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 13 Sept. 1856) strongly upholds Staunton's <I>sheaf</I> in the sense of <I>a
clique, class,</I> or <I>set</I> in fashionable society. &lquo;And for this meaning we must have re-
course to Euphuism. If <I>sheaf</I> be Shakespeare's word, it is not the only instance of
Euphuism in Polonius's speech. In line 65, <I>courage</I> of the Qq is Euphuistic for <I>a
gallant.</I> It is so used by Scott in <I>The Monastery,</I> and is put into the mouth of that
prince of Euphuists, Sir Piercie Shafton. Archers spoke of &ldquo;arrows of the first
sheaf,&rdquo; and the Euphuists appropriated the metaphor, and called their friends &ldquo;gen-
tlemen of the first sheaf.&rdquo; Every archer of this day has his <I>best set</I> (a set = 12
arrows); and every archer of Shakespeare's day had his <I>first sheaf</I> (a sheaf = 24
arrows). Thus: &ldquo;In my time, it was the usual practice for soldiers to choose their
<I>first sheaf</I> of arrows, and cut those shorter which they found too long,&rdquo; &amp;c.&mdash;<I>Dis-
course on Weapons.</I>&rquo; Ingleby then cites the passages from Ben Jonson afterwards
cited by Staunton, and concludes his note with the expression of his belief that the
metaphor in the present case, as well as in <I>Every Man Out of His Humour,</I> was
taken, not wholly from archery, but from husbandry. H. C. K. (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 11 Oct.
1856) upholds the Ff, and explains <I>cheff</I> as a measure by which, according to Skin-
ner, cloth and fine linen were sold. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> thinks that the uniformity of the
QqFf in the reading &lquo;of a&rquo; is an insuperable objection to any change or omission
in that direction. The only suspicious words in the line are &lquo;in that&rquo; at the end of
it, because, as he says, we should rather expect them to be written &lquo;therein.&rquo; &lquo;In
that&rquo; he believes to be the beginning of another line, of which the conclusion is
lost, but which expressed in substance &lquo;In that they clothe themselves simply.&rquo;
Accordingly, in his text the line is: In that <I>their show denies extravagance.</I> <SC>Mo-</SC>

<P>109. <B>Running</B>] This emendation, which is <SC>Collier's</SC> conj., afterwards corrob-

&lquo;almost obvious,&rquo; and <SC>Clarendon</SC> adopts it as more in accordance with the figure
in the preceding line. <SC>Pope's</SC> emendation <SC>Johnson</SC> supported, believing that <I>wrong-
ing</I> had reference not to the phrase, but to Ophelia, the &lquo;it&rquo; being the redundant &lquo;it&rquo;
common enough in poetry, as in Pope's, &lquo;To sinner it or saint it.&rquo; <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh.
Rest.</I> p 25) conjectured <I>ranging, i. e.</I> you, behaving yourself with so much careless-
ness and liberty, will bring me into contempt, &amp;c. <SC>Heath</SC> referred <I>wronging</I> to the
&lquo;poor phrase,&rquo; for &lquo;whoever cracks the wind of anything may surely be said with
propriety to wrong or abuse it.&rquo; <SC>Warburton</SC> preferred <I>wringing, i. e.</I> not farther
to crack the wind of the phrase by <I>twisting</I> or <I>contorting</I> it. <SC>Caldecott</SC> para-
phrases the <*> by: &lquo;ranging so far, becoming so wildly excursive, and running into
so many senses of the word <I>tender.</I>&rquo; <SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Cam. Essays,</I> 1856, p. 283): Per-
haps some readers will think with me that <I>wrong</I> is a corruption of <I>worrying.</I> The
same description of persons will probably read in line 118 &lquo;extinct in <I>birth</I>&rquo; instead
of &lquo;extinct in both.&rquo; <SC>Keightley</SC>: &lquo;To wrong it thus&rquo; is most probably correct.
We might read,&mdash;supposing the allusion to be to a horse,&mdash;<I>To run,</I> as in, You run
this humour out of breath, <I>Com. of Err.</I> I, i. <SC>Corson</SC>: The Ff are probably right;
Polonius has reference to his varying application of the word &lquo;tender.&rquo;
<P>115. <B>woodcocks</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: Proverbial for a simpleton; probably from the ease

phrase here means &lquo;arts to entrap simplicity.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Compare Gosson,
<I>Apologie for the Schoole of Abuse.</I> p. 72 (ed. Arber): &lquo;When Comedie comes vpon
the Stage, Cupide sets vpp a Springe for Woodcockes, which are entangled ere they
descrie the line, and caught hefore they mistruste the snare.&rquo; <SC>Harting</SC> (p. 229):
The woodcock for some unaccountable reason was supposed to have no brains, and
the name of this bird became a synonym for a fool.

<P>117. <SC>Malone</SC> and <SC>White</SC> believe that some epithet to &lquo;blazes&rquo; has been omitted.
<SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 153): A spondee has, I doubt not, dropped out of the text. Either
insert <I>Go to</I> after &lquo;vows,&rquo; or read, &lquo;these blazes, daughter, <I>mark you.</I>&rquo; Sh. never
introduces a catalectic line without intending an equivalent to the foot omitted in
the pauses, or the dwelling emphasis, or the diffused retardation. I do not, however,
deny that a good actor might by employing the last-mentioned means, namely, the
retardation or solemn knowing drawl, supply the missing spondee with good effect.
But I do not believe that in this or any other of the foregoing speeches of Polonius,
Sh. meant to bring out the senility or weakness of that personage's mind. In the
great ever-recurring dangers and duties of life, where to distinguish the fit objects
for the application of the maxims collected by the experience of a long life requires
no fineness of tact; as in the admonitions to his son and daughter, Pol. is uniformly
made respectable. But if an actor were even capable of catching these shades in
the character, the pit and the gallery would be malcontent at their exhibition. It is
to Hamlet that Pol. is, and is meant to be, contemptible, because in inwardness and
uncontrollable activity of movement, Hamlet's mind is the logical contrary to that
of Pol., and besides Ham. dislikes the man as false to his true allegiance in the
matter of the succession to the crown. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> p. 206) gives ten or twelve
instances from Sh. and other dramatists, among them the present passage, in proof
of his assertion that &lquo;daughter&rquo; is sometimes a trisyllable. &lquo;It is observable,&rquo; he
adds, &lquo;that in almost all these instances there is a pause&mdash;in at least half of them a
full stop&mdash;after <I>daughter.</I> What was the original form of the word? Compare
<G>quga/thp</G>. In Chaucer, as far as I am acquainted with him. it is uniformly a dissylla-
ble.&rquo; In a foot-note <SC>Lettsom</SC> asks: &lquo;Quere, when did the guttural become mute in
this word? When pronounced, it would have facilitated a trisyllabic pronunciation.&rquo;
<SC>Moberly</SC> adopts one of Coleridge's suggestions, and thinks that the strong irony on
the word &lquo;vows,&rquo; which is spoken with a laugh of contempt, makes it occupy the
time of three syllables.

<P>darus; &lquo;implorators of unholy suits&rquo; is an exact description of a bawd. All such
of them as are crafty in their trade put on the appearance of sanctity, and are &lquo;not
of that dye that their investments shew.&rquo; <SC>Collier's</SC> (MS) also substitutes &lquo;bawds.&rquo;
<SC>Singer</SC> pronounces <I>bonds</I> nonsense. <SC>White</SC> says that the &lquo;context does not leave a
question as to the propriety of Theobald's emendation,&mdash;&ldquo;bawds&rdquo; having probably
been spelled <I>bauds.</I>&rquo; On the other hand, the advocates of the Ff are as follows:
<SC>Warburton</SC>, after sneering at Theobald, paraphrases: Do not believe Hamlet's
amorous vows made <I>to you;</I> which pretend religion in them (<I>the better to beguile</I>),
like those sanctified and pious vows (<I>or bonds</I>) made <I>to heaven.</I> <SC>Heath</SC> pronounces
the sense of <I>bonds</I> unexceptionable, and interprets thus: Vows, uttered in the sem-
blance of sanctified and pious engagements, such as have marriage for their object.
<SC>Malone</SC> follows Heath, and affirms that by <I>bonds</I> were meant <I>the bonds of love.</I>
<SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 155): &lquo;His vows are implorators breathing like bonds (<I>i. e.</I> similar
bonds, or sanctified vows) to those which are breathed by implorators of unholy suits.
<SC>Caldecott</SC>: Like the protestations of solemn contracts entered into with all the
formalities and ceremonies of religion. [<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i) pronounces this note of Cal
decott's &lquo;quite as silly as Malone's.&rquo;] <SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;At one time we were strenu-
ously in favour of Theobald's alteration; we are now persnaded the Ff are right.&rquo;
<SC>Clarke</SC>: We cannot help believing <I>bonds</I> to be right, because Sh. uses the word
elsewhere to signify &lquo;pledged vows,&rquo; &lquo;plighted assurances of faith and troth;&rquo; see
<I>Mer. of Ven.</I> Ii, vi, 6; <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> V, ii, 156. <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 287):
The whole passage is merely a poetic periphrasis of seduction under promise of
marriage; and had the word been <I>Sounding,</I> not &lquo;Breathing,&rquo; there would probably
have been no mistake. <SC>Corson</SC>: <I>Bonds</I> makes good sense. The general term,

<P><SC>Scene iv.</SC>] <SC>Coleridge</SC>: The unimportant conversation with which this scene
opens is a proof of Shakespeare's minute knowledge of human nature. It is a well-
established fact, that, on the brink of any serious enterprise, or event of moment,
men almost invariably endeavor to elude the pressure of their own thoughts by
turning aside to trivial objects and familiar circumstances; thus the dialogne on the
platform begins with remarks on the coldness of the air, and inquiries obliquely
connected, indeed, with the expected hour of the visitation, but thrown out in a seem-
ing vacuity of topics, as to the striking of the clock, and so forth. The same desire to
escape from the impending thought is carried on in Hamlet's account of, and moral
ising on, the Danish custom of wassailing; he runs off from the particular to the
universal, and in his repugnance to personal and individual concerns, escapes, as it
were, from himself in generalisations, and smothers the impatience and uneasy feel-
ings of the moment in abstract reasoning. Besides this, another purpose is answered;
&mdash;for by thus entangling the attention of the audience in the nice distinctions and
parenthetical sentences of this speech of Hamlet's, Sh. takes them completely by
surprise on the appearance of the Ghost, which comes upon them in all the sudden-
ness of its visionary character. Indeed, no modern writer would have dared, like
Sh., to have preceded this last visitation by two distinct appearances,&mdash;or could have
contrived that the third should rise upon the former two in impressiveness and
solemnity of interest. But in addition to all the other excellences of Hamlet's
speech concerning the wassail-music,&mdash;so finely revealing the predominant idealism,
the ratiocinative meditativeness of his character,&mdash;it has the advantage of giving
nature and probability to the impassioned continuity of the speech instantly directed
to the Ghost. The <I>momentum</I> had been given to his mental activity; the full cur-
rent of the thoughts and words had set in, and the very forgetfulness, in the fervor

<P>of his argumentation, of the purpose for which he was there, aided in preventing
the appearance from benumbing the mind. Consequently, it acted as a new impulse,
&mdash;a sudden stroke which increased the velocity of the body already in motion,
whilst it altered the direction. The co-presence of Hor., Mar., and Ber. is most
judiciously contrived; for it renders the courage of Ham., and his impetuous elo-
quence, perfectly intelligible. The knowledge,&mdash;the unthought-of consciousness,&mdash;
the sensation,&mdash;of human auditors,&mdash;of flesh and blood sympathists,&mdash;acts as a sup-
port and a stimulation a <I>tergo,</I> while the front of the mind, the whole consciousness
of the speaker, is filled, yea, absorbed, by the apparition. Add, too, that the appari-
tion itself has by its previous appearances been brought nearer to a thing of this
world. This accrescence of objectivity in a Ghost, that yet retains all its ghostly
attributes and fearful subjectivity, is truly wonderful.
<P>1. <B>it is</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> &amp;c. p. 209): The reading of F<SUB>1</SUB> would greatly

not entirely unworthy of consideration, because Shakespeare's purpose might well

when the air bites shrewdly, although it is not very cold. Horatio's reply is not
that it is cold, but that the air has this quality. However, that the Qq are right is
shown in the first scene.

<P>8. <B>rouse</B>] <SC>Gifford</SC> (<I>The Duke of Milan.</I>&mdash;Massinger, vol. i, p. 237, ed. 1805):
A &lquo;rouse&rquo; was a large glass (&lquo;not past a pint,&rquo; as Iago says) in which a health was
given, the drinking of which by the rest of the company formed a <I>carouse.</I> Bar-
naby Rich is exceedingly angry with the inventor of the custom, which, however,
with a laudable zeal for the honour of his country, he attributes to an Englishman,
who, it seems, &lquo;had his brains beat out with a pottlepot&rquo; for his ingenuity. There
could be no <I>rouse</I> or <I>carouse</I> unless the glasses were emptied. In process of time
both these words were used in a laxer sense. They are used in their primal and
appropriate signification in &lquo;I've ta'en, since supper, A <I>rouse</I> or <I>two</I> too much,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;
<I>Knight of Malta.</I> This proves Johnson and Steevens are wrong: a <I>rouse</I> has here
a fixed and determinate sense. As we should now say, &lquo;a bumper or two too much.&rquo;
[See I, ii, 127.]
<P>9. <B>wassail</B>] Festivity, a drinking-bout. See <I>Macb.</I> I, vii, 64.
<P>9. <B>up-spring</B>] Four explanations have been proposed. First: <SC>Pope</SC> (followed
by <SC>Hanmer</SC>) referred it to the King, and changed it into <I>upstart;</I> <SC>Johnson</SC> re-
tained &lquo;up-spring,&rquo; but adopted in a paraphrase Pope's emendation, &lquo;a blustering
upstart.&rquo; <SC>Nares</SC> adds the definition: &lquo;one insolent from sudden elevation.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC>
also prefers this interpretation. Second: <SC>Steevens</SC> started the correct explanation
when he showed by the following passage from Chapman's <I>Alphonsus,</I> that the
&lquo;up-spring&rquo; was a <I>German dance:</I> &lquo;We Germans have no changes in our dances.
An <I>Almain</I> and an <I>upspring,</I> that is all.&rquo; <SC>Elze</SC> confirmed it when, in his edition of
Chapman's <I>Alphonsus</I> [p. 144], he showed that this &lquo;up-spring&rquo; was &lquo;the &ldquo;H&uuml;pfauf.&rdquo;
the last and consequently the wildest dance at the old German merry-makings. See
Ayrer's <I>Dramen,</I> ed. by Keller, iv, 2840 and 2846: &ldquo;Ey, jtzt geht erst der hupffauff
an. Ey, Herr, jtzt kummt erst der hupffauff.&rdquo; No epithet could therefore be more
appropriate to this drunken dance than Shakespeare's &ldquo;swaggering.&rdquo; I need hardly
add that &ldquo;up-spring&rdquo; is an almost literal translation of the German name. <SC>Staun-
ton</SC>, while assuming that &lquo;up-spring&rquo; refers to a dance, understands &lquo;reels&rquo; as a plural
noun, qualified by &lquo;up-spring.&rquo; [I have always supposed it to be a verb, in the
same construction as &lquo;keeps.&rquo; <SC>Ed.</SC>] Third: Steevens, in his note on &lquo;rouse,&rquo; having
quoted from Decker's <I>Gul's Hornbook:</I> &lquo;Teach me, thou soveraigne skinker, how
to take the German's upsy freeze, the Danish rousa,&rquo; &amp;c., <SC>Caldecott</SC> inferred that
the &lquo;up-spring&rquo; dance might be like the &lquo;upsy freeze,&rquo; both connected with the music
and riot of a German dehauch. <SC>Badh<*>m</SC> (<I>Cambridge Essays,</I> 1856, p. 283) went

<P>12. <B>custom</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The royal custom in Denmark near the date of this
play may be seen in Howell's <I>Letters:</I> &lquo;The King [Christian IV., who reigned
from 1588 to 1649] feasted my Lord once, and it lasted from eleven of the clock
till towards evening; during which time the King began thirty-five healths. . . .
The King was taken away at last in his chair.&rquo; [Caldecott cites several other
authorities to the same effect.] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 221): The English, in the Tudor
reigns, appear to have been a remarkably sober people, and the introduction of the
vice of drunkenness is attributed by contemporary writers to the connection with the
Netherlands.
<P>14, 15. <B>native . . . manner born</B>] <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. Illust. by Old Authors,</I> i, 47):
In the manumission by Henry VIII of two villeins the following words are used:
&lquo;We think it pious and meritorious with God to manumit Henry Knight, a taylor,
and John Herle, a husbandman, our natives, as being born within the manor of Stoke
Clymmysland.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Barr. Stats.</I> 276. Hamlet, therefore, may speak of Denmark, or
Elsinore as the manor, himself as <I>nativus,</I> to the manor born, and the &lquo;heavy-headed
revel&rquo; as a custom incident to the manor. &lquo;Manor&rquo; is here used, probably, in a
double sense, as in <I>Love's Lab.</I> I, i, 208, where it is contrasted with <I>manner.</I> It is of
little importance whether the word be speit <I>manner</I> or <I>manor,</I> the mention of one
would suggest the other, which is <I>idem sonans,</I> but different in meaning.

<P>16. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> p. 210): I once heard an eminent poet maintain that this
<*>me, though it has passed into a sort of proverbial expression, is essentially non-
sense: &lquo;how.&rquo; said he, &lquo;can a custom be <I>honoured in the breach?</I>&rquo; Compare the
following line of a play attributed to Jonson, Fletcher, and Middleton: &lquo;He keeps
his promise best that breaks with hell.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Widow,</I> III, ii. <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent.
Maga.</I> Feb. 1845): The meaning is: &lquo;It is a custom that will more honour those
that break it than those who observe it;&rquo; &lquo;honoured&rquo; is put for <I>honourable,</I> and
transferred to the subject. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 221): We may regard Sh. as again making
an effort, like that in <I>Oth.</I> II, iii, 79 (and efforts by a genius such as his are not lost),
to free his countrymen from so baneful a vice.
<P>17. <B>east and west</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, &lquo;makes us traduced east and west of
other nations.&rquo; [Not as <SC>Warburton</SC> says, &lquo;this revel from morn till night.&rquo;]
<P>17-38. As these lines are not in Q<SUB>1</SUB>, <SC>Malone</SC> supposes that they were omitted out
of deference to Anne of Denmark, the queen of James <SC>I. Knight</SC>, on the other
hand, ingeniously conjectures that they were added in Q<SUB>2</SUB> in order to qualify the
harsh description of royal riot in lines 8-12. A trait of Shakespeare's character may
be herein indicated: he would not suppress the lines offensive to royalty, because
the description given in them was true; he only made it less severe by adding a
tolerant exposition of the mode in which one ill quality destroys the lustre of many
good ones. After the queen's death the passage was omitted in the Ff. <SC>Elze</SC> be
lieves that they were erased by Sh., but restored by the printer of Q<SUB>2</SUB> in order to
justify his title-page, wherein it was stated that the play was &lquo;enlarged to as much
again as it was,&rquo; and is inclined to believe them spurious.
<P>18. <B>of</B>] For other instances of &lquo;of&rquo; used for <I>by,</I> see III, i, 154; IV, ii, 12; <I>Macb.</I>
III, vi, 27, or <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 170.
<P>19. <B>clepe</B>] From the Anglo-Saxon, <I>cleopian,</I> to call. See <I>Macb.</I> III, i, 93.
<P>19. <B>drunkards</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: And well our Englishmen might; for in 1604 the
following mention is made of a Dane in London, in <I>Looke to it: For Ile Stabbe ye</I>
[by Samuel Rowlands, p. 21, ed. <I>Hunterian Club</I>]: &lquo;You that will drinke <I>Reynald<*></I>
vnto death: The <I>Dane,</I> that would carowse out of his Boote.&rquo;
<P>19. <B>swinish</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 221): This seems to allude to some parody on the
style of the kings of Denmark, which bore allusion to this habit. <SC>Clarendon</SC>;

of the kings of Denmark?

<P>25. <B>As</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 127): <I>As</I> is here used, I think, not in the sense of <I>for

not a selection from them by way of example. This is a frequent&mdash;perhaps, indeed,
the one exclusive&mdash;signification of <I>as</I> when employed in this construction; as in 3

struction of <I>as</I> in a number of passages, where it has been, or is likely to be, mis-
taken for the modern usage.

<C>[36. &lquo;<B>The dram of eale,</B>&rquo; &amp;c.]</C>
<P>should rather suspect Sh. might have written &lquo;The dram of base Doth all the noble
substance <I>oft eat</I> out,&rquo; &amp;c. But granting a little farther departure from the printed
text, I should think it still more probable that the true reading is: &lquo;Doth all the
noble substance <I>soil with doubt.</I>&rquo; That is: A dram of base alloy stains all the noble
substance of his virtues with the suspicion that they are mere tinsel appearances only,
and not of the true sterling standard. <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> &amp;c. i, 126), after citing Heath
with approval, adds, &lquo;But it should seem, from the comment that the same author makes
upon his second amendment, that the line stands in need of a substantive, following
&lquo;of&rquo; to perfect the sense of it. And this, in truth, is the light in which the editor
has view'd the corruption all along; that some word was slipt out of the copy, and
&lquo;<I>out</I>&rquo; changed to &lquo;a doubt&rquo; by the printer's ingeniousness: the vacancy cannot be
fill'd better than by the word in possession; and the line may be cur'd of it's bald-
ness by no very great licence, the change of &lquo;all&rquo; into <I>eat;</I> after which, the comment
that has been given above [Heath's] is both a just and a perfect one.&rquo; [Which means
that Capell would read the line &lquo;Doth <I>eat</I> the noble substance of <I>worth out.</I>&rquo; In
Capell's list of &lquo;Various Readings of Hamlet&rquo; he cites the reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB> thus: of eale
4&degree;.a. (f. ill). This, I presume, indicates, what the Cam. Edd. ascribe to him, the con-
jecture of <I>ill</I> for &lquo;eale.&rquo; Hereby Capell anticipated <SC>Jennens</SC>, who merely states that
he ventures to read: &lquo;The dram of <I>ill</I> Doth all the noble substance of <I>good out,</I> To
his own scandal.&rquo;] In the Var. of 1773, <SC>Steevens</SC> says: &lquo;Mr <SC>Holt</SC> reads, The dram
of base Doth all the noble substance <I>oft adopt,</I> &amp;c. I would read Doth all the noble
substance (<I>i. e.</I> the sum of good qualities) <I>oft do out.</I>&rquo; &lquo;To <I>do a thing out</I> is <I>to efface,</I>
or <I>obliterate anything in drawing.</I>&rquo; Perhaps we should say, &lquo;To <I>its</I> own scandal.&rquo;
[<I>Vide infra,</I> Steevens, 1793.] <SC>Davies</SC> (<I>Dramatic Misc.</I> 1784, iii, 10): The very tri-
fling alteration of adding a letter to one word, and the changing two letters for one
in another, will restore to us the original reading, &lquo;The dram of base Doth all the
noble substance <I>oft work</I> out,&rquo; &amp;c. When I read this proposed emendation to the
reverend and learned Mr Robertson, he not only concurred with me, but assured
me he had himself made the same amendment. The apostle James hath a senti-
ment very similar to the present passage; &lquo;For, whosoever shall keep the whole
law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.&rquo; [In the Var. 1785, S[tephen]
W[eston] proposes the same emendation. <SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Mason</SC> (1785): I offer as an amend-
ment (which is at least as near the old text as any yet proposed, and which is sup-
ported by line 35), &lquo;Doth all the noble substance <I>of 't corrupt.</I>&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC> (1790):
&lquo;The dram of base Doth all the noble suhstance of <I>worth dout,</I> To,&rquo; &amp;c. To <I>dout</I>
signified in Shakespeare's time, and yet signifies in Devonshire and other western
counties, to <I>do out,</I> to efface, to extinguish. Thus they say, &lquo;<I>dout</I> the candle, <I>dout</I> the
fire,&rquo; &amp;c., just as <I>don</I> signifies <I>do on</I> [or <I>doff,</I> do off&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>]. &lquo;Dout&rquo; having
been written by the transcriber <I>doubt,</I> and the word &lquo;worth&rquo; having been inadver-
tently omitted, probably the line, in the copy for the press, stood: Doth all the noble
substance of <I>doubt.</I> The editor or printer of the Qq, finding the line too short, in-
serted the indefinite article, without attending to the context. Theobald's insertion
of <I>worth</I> is fully justified by his citation from <I>Cymbeline.</I> [Malone, in Var. 1785,
proposed &lquo;<I>By</I> his own seandal;&rquo; but did not repeat it in his own edition. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
