&lquo;The dram <I>of doubt</I> Doth all the noble substance <I>oft anneal</I> To,&rquo; &amp;c. That is, the
dram of doubtful or base metal doth often, in the operation of annealing, cause the
whole substance to become durably as base as itself. Whether this emendation
will be made out by a comparison with the processes used in the arts, I know uot,
as everything connected with chemical science, or any branch of philosophy, ap-
peareth to me too insignificant to bestow upon it one moment's attention. <SC>Zachary
Jackson</SC> says that he has endeavored to give the passage some sense, but cannot
speak with that perfect confidence which he does in reference to &lquo;most of my restora-

ventured to read <I>bale</I> (<I>i. e</I> evil) as nearer to the reading of the first edition. <SC>Stearns</SC>
(<I>Sh. Treas.</I> p. 373) adopted this reading of Singer's, and explains it as a reference
to the commerce in drugs, in which a great deal of adulteration is practiced; for
the word <I>bale</I> we have now only the word <I>alloy.</I> <SC>Collier</SC>: It is easy to see how

In MS <I>andout,</I> run into one word, would be readily mistaken for <I>a doubt,</I> especially

to its own vileness&rquo;? We by no means pretend that <I>pound</I> was the actual word
misrendered &lquo;doubt;&rquo; it is inserted merely because it occurs in opposition to
&lquo;<I>dram</I>&rquo; in a line of Quarles's <I>Emblems,</I> b. ii, E 7,&mdash;&lquo;Where ev'ry <I>dram</I> of gold
contains a <I>pound</I> of dross,&rquo;&mdash;and because it is extremely probable <I>some such</I> antithesis
was intended here. So in Spenser's <I>Faerie Queene,</I> b. i, c. iii, s. 30:&mdash;&lquo;A <I>dram</I> of
sweete is worth a <I>pound</I> of sowre.&rquo; <SC>Swynfen Jervis</SC> (<I>Proposed Emendations,</I> &amp;c.
1860, p. 23): Read, The dram of <I>evil</I> Doth all the noble substance <I>oft outdo,</I> To,
&amp;c. Compare <I>Cor.</I> II, i, 150; &lquo;So heavenly love shall outdo hellish hate.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Par.
Lost.</I>; &lquo;Wherein the graver had a strife With nature, to outdo the life.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Jonson.</I>
In <SC>Chambers's</SC> <I>Household Sh.</I> is the following note: &lquo;We have adopted &ldquo;<I>oft subdue</I>&rdquo;
[for &ldquo;of a doubt&rdquo;], suggested by Mr Swynfen Jervis, and thus supported:&mdash;<I>Son.</I> iii,
6; and <I>All's Well,</I> V, iii, 217.&rquo; <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 2): For &lquo;eale&rquo; read <I>evil;</I> for &lquo;of a
doubt&rquo; read <I>oft weight down.</I> &lquo;<I>Weigh,</I> in some of the old copies of Hamlet, is
spelt <I>way.</I>&rquo; Compare <I>Rich. III:</I> V, iii, 153; <I>Timon</I> V, i, 154. <SC>Corson</SC> (<I>Jottings,</I> &amp;c.
p. 13, 1874): All the difficulty of the passage is removed, I think, by understanding
&lquo;noble,&rquo; not as an adjective, as all the commentators have understood it, qualifying
&lquo;substance,&rquo; but as a noun opposed to &lquo;eale,&rquo; and the object of &lquo;substance,&rquo; a verb
of which &lquo;doth&rquo; is its auxiliary. Thus: &lquo;the dram of eale doth all the noble, sub-
stance of&rquo; (<I>i. e.</I> &lquo;with,&rquo; a sense common in the English of the time) &lquo;a doubt (which
works) &lquo;to his own scandal.&rquo; &lquo;Substance&rquo; is used in the sense of &lquo;imbue with a cer-
tain essence;&rquo; &lquo;his&rquo; is a neuter genitive, standing for &lquo;noble,&rquo; and = &lquo;its.&rquo; The
dram of ill <I>transubstantiates</I> the noble, <I>essences</I> it to its own scandal. (In regard to
the uses of &lquo;of&rquo; and &lquo;to,&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect;&sect; 171, 186.) The use of &lquo;substance,&rquo; in
the sense of &lquo;essence,&rquo; was, of course, sufficiently common, and had been for more
than two centuries, to justify the interpretation given. In <I>Macb.</I> I, v, 48, we have
&lquo;sightless substances&rquo;=&lquo;invisible essences,&rquo; &lquo;sightless&rquo; being used objectively. &lquo;Be-
ing of one suhstance with the Father.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Book of Common Prayer.</I> Chaucer, in <I>The
Prologe of the Nonne Prestes Tale</I> (l. 14809 of Tyrwhitt's edition, l. 16289 of
Wright's), uses the word to express the <I>essential</I> character or nature of a man. The
Host objects to the Monk's Tale, as being too dull for the occasion; and, that the
fault may not be thought to lie in himself, says, &lquo;And wel I wot the substance is in
me, If eny thing schal wel reported be.&rquo; That is, I am so <I>substanced,</I> so constituted,
so tempered, such is my <I>cast</I> of spirit, that I can appreciate and enjoy, as well as the
next man, a good story well told. Whether &lquo;substance&rquo; can be found, in this sense,
as a verb, matters not. The free functional application of words which character-
ized the Elizabethan English, allowed, as every Eaglish scholar knows, of the use
of any noun, adjective, or neuter verb, as an active verb. This interpretation I
communicated in the main to <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> [4 Oct. 1862]; but I did not then recog-
nize an important element in it, that the pronoun &lquo;his&rquo; is a neuter genitive, standing
for &lquo;noble&rquo; used as a noun. <SC>Arrowsmith</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Editors,</I> &amp;c. 1865, p. 6)
thus quotes the passage: &lquo;The dram of base Doth all the noble substance <I>often</I>

The sentence, we may see, is not complete, and it should also be recollected that

&lquo;eale,&rquo; and that it was identical with the &lquo;esil&rquo; in V, i, 264, meaning vinegar? In that
case Sh. may perhaps have written &lquo;Doth all the noble substance <I>over-clout.</I>&rquo; In the
next scene, the posseting of the blood by poison is described like &lquo;eager droppings
into milk.&rquo; Thus Sh. here means that the small quantity of vinegar or other acid
matter <I>over-clouts,</I> or <I>curdles over,</I> the whole of the substance to which it is added,
so as to impart its own scandalous character to that suhstance. He has just used
the word &lquo;o'erleavens.&rquo; Clout, to clot or curdle, is a well-known provincial expres-
sion. The unfamiliar word, <I>clout,</I> was mistaken hy the eye for <I>dout,</I> and <I>over,</I> by
the ear for &lquo;of a.&rquo; <SC>The Writer of the Article on Shakespearian Glos-
saries in the Edinburgh Review</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 23 Oct. 1869): <I>Evil</I> is used by
Elizabethan writers, and by Sh. himself, as a monosyllable, and it might, then, by a
mistake of the ear, easily have been written as pronounced: <I>eale.</I> Again, the verb
<I>dout</I> is used not only in its literal sense of <I>do out,</I> but in the secondary meaning of
obscure, eclipse, prevent the manifestation of, as by Laertes in IV, vii, 192. This
secondary sense very much does away with the force of Lettsom's objection to <I>dout.</I>
Read, then, &lquo;The dram of <I>e'il</I> Doth all the noble substance <I>often dout</I> To&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>W.

wine so used shall ever afterward lothe wine.&rquo; May not wine thus treated have
been technically termed <I>eel</I> (eale)? Read, then: The dram of <I>eel</I> Doth,&rquo; &amp;c., <I>i. e.</I>
the dram of eel-dressing (vitiated wine) doth often doubt (bring into suspicion and
disrepute) the noble substance (of pure wine) to the scandal of the said substance.

eale&rquo; may be assigned, viz.: &lquo;An extremely small weight, or quantity, even the six-
teenth part of an ounce, of the eel-fish,&rquo; taking dram in its quantitative sense. <SC>J.

<SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Euphuism,</I> p. 93, 1871): &lquo;Dram of eale&rquo; may be a misprint
or abbreviation, of <I>dram of hellebore,</I> or &lquo;<I>ele-</I>bore,&rquo; which old authors speak of as being

<I>meale</I> (the old spelling of meal), the change of the preceding word, &lquo;dram,&rquo; to <I>bran</I>
is obvious, and we have a sentence singularly in accordance with the argument of
Hamlet's speech, which he illustrates by the homely simile of <I>bran</I> doubting or dis-

change of &lquo;of a&rquo; to <I>of it</I> hardly needs apology. In <I>So,</I> the <I>S</I> being next the <I>T</I> in the
printer's &lquo;case,&rquo; the error would be easily accounted for. <I>His</I> and <I>this</I> are so fre-
quently confounded in the old eopies, that no one would hesitate to correct where the
sense of a passage required the change. The corruption of <I>one</I> into &lquo;own&rquo; prohably
arose from the similarity in sound of the two words. The simile of <I>bran and meal</I>
seems to have been a favorite one with Elizabethan writers. Sh. uses it twice else-
where, in <I>Cym.</I> IV, ii, 27; <I>Cor.</I> III, i, 322. <SC>Hudson</SC> (1870): &lquo;The dram of <I>vile</I> Doth

which was often used by old writers in the sense of <I>cast down</I> or depress. Perhaps
<I>attaint</I> would give a slightly more congruous sense. <SC>Miles</SC> (<I>Review of Hamlet,</I> p.
16, 1870): &lquo;The dram of <I>ill</I> Doth all the noble substance <I>throw</I> in doubt&rquo; seems to

<P>39. In <SC>Davies's</SC> <I>Dram. Misc.</I> (iii, 29) an account is given from Cibber of Better-
ton's acting in this scene; Betterton was taught by Sir William Davenant, who had
seen Taylor, one of the original performers of Hamlet [see V, ii, 274]: &lquo;He opened
the scene with a pause of mute amazement; then, rising slowly to a solemn, trem-
bling voice, he made the Ghost equally terrible to the spectator and himself; and,
in the descriptive part of the natural emotions which the ghastly vision gave him,
the boldness of his expostulation was still governed by decency; manly, but not
braving; his voice never rising to that seeming outrage or wild defiance of what he
naturally revered.&rquo; Booth said: &lquo;When I acted the Ghost with Betterton, instead
of my awing him, he terrified me. But divinity hung round that man.&rquo; On the
other hand, Macklin, after the first line, spoke the rest of the address calmly but re-
spectfully, and with a firm tone of voice, as from one who had subdued his timidity
and apprehension. Booth, says Davies, has never been surpassed in his acting of
the Ghost; his slow, solemn, and undertone of voice, his noiseless tread, as if he had
been composed of air, created a powerful impression. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 222): &lquo;The idea
of surprise predominates over the idea of apprehension. He did not mean that he

<P>45. <B>Royal Dane</B>] <SC>Pye</SC> (p. 312): The change of punctuation proposed in the
following anonymous observation, published in the <I>St. James's Chronicle,</I> 15 Oct.
1761, is so convincing that I shall without hesitation adopt it: &lquo;[To put a colon
after &ldquo;Dane&rdquo;] seems to be a strange climax (if not an anti-climax). But a slight
alteration in the pointing will remove all objections, preserve the beanty of the
climax, and perhaps give an additional force to the whole passage. Thus, &ldquo;I'll call
thee Hamlet, King, Father,&mdash;Royal Dane, O answer me.&rdquo; The climax naturally
and beautifully ends with the endearing appellation of &ldquo;Father.&rdquo; He then addresses
the Ghost by the general appellation, &ldquo;Royal Dane, O answer me.&rdquo;&rquo; This seems
the criticism of no mean critic. [Mr Edwin Booth has informed me that his father
always spoke the line thus, and that he himself has always so spoken it. I believe
Mr Irving has also adopted it. To me it is unquestionably the true reading, and I
have not hesitated to punctuate the text accordingly. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>47. <B>canoniz'd</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Bones over which the rites of sepulture have been
performed, or whicb were buried according to the canon. <SC>Blakeway</SC>: The accent
is on the second syllable. [See <SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Vers.</I> 197; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 491.]
<P>47-50. <SC>Johnson</SC> has a long note on these lines, called forth by <SC>Warburton's</SC>
superfluous change of &lquo;hearsed in <I>earth,</I>&rquo; and sums up the whole sentence in:
&lquo;Why dost thou appear, whom we know to be dead?&rquo; <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 531): By the ex-
pression <I>hearsed in death</I> is meant, shut up and secured with all those precautions
which are usually practised in preparing dead bodies for sepulture, such as the wind-
ing-sheet, shroud, coffin, &amp;c. So that <I>death</I> is here used, by a metonymy of the
antecedent for the consequent, for the rites of death, such as are generally esteemed
due, and practised with regard to dead bodies.

<P>49. <B>in-urn'd</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC>: In my <I>Few Notes,</I> &amp;c., p. 137, I remarked: &lquo;Perhaps the
reading of the Qq is preferable, because <I>in-urn'd</I> implies that the body had been re-
duced to ashes,&rquo;&mdash;a remark which I now wish to recall. Compare <I>Cor.</I> V, vi, 145.
146. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Urn&rquo; is used for &lquo;grave&rquo; in <I>Hen. V:</I> I, ii, 228.
<P>52. <B>complete</B>] Accented on the first syllable. See <SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Vers.</I> 292; <I>Crit.</I>
ii, 21: <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 492. <SC>Douce</SC>: It is accented on the second syllable in <I>King John,</I>
II, i, 433, 434.
<P>52. <B>steel</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Probably Sh. introduced the Ghost in armour for the sake
of greater solemnity; though it was really the custom of the Danish kings to be
buried in that manner. Vide Olaus Wormius, cap. vii: &lquo;. . . postquam . . . rex collem
sibi . . . extruxisset, cui post obitum regio diademate exornatum, armis indutum, in-
ferendum esset cadaver.&rquo;
<P>53. <B>Revisits</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 128): <I>Qu&aelig;re,</I> in cases where <I>st</I> would produce
extreme harshness, and where at the same time the old copies have <I>s,</I> whether we
ought not to write the latter? [The text which I have adopted is my answer. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>53. <B>glimpses</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 223): The scene is thus made more picturesque by
introducing the moon sending forth her beams on the platform, either through in-
terstices of dark clouds, or, what is more probable, through the openings among the
battlements.
<P>54. <B>we</B>] <SC>Theobald, Caldecott</SC>, and <SC>Clarendon</SC> say that in strict grammar <I>us</I>
should be here used; but <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 58) evidently, as <SC>Lettsom</SC> notes, con-
nects &lquo;we fools&rquo; with &lquo;That,&rquo; and so does <SC>Moberly</SC> in his excellent paraphrase:
&lquo;What may it mean that we with our blind nature (are made) so horribly to shake
our composure of spirit with thoughts beyond the reach of our souls?&rquo; adding: &lquo;This
random connexion of the clause suits well with the headlong impetuosity of the
speech.&rquo; On the same grammatical grounds <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> reads, &lquo;So horridly <I>do</I>
shake.&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 216, thus explains &lquo;and we&rquo;: After a conjunction and before an
infinitive we often find <I>I, thou,</I> &amp;c., where in Latin we should have &lquo;me,&rquo; &lquo;te,&rquo; &amp;c.
The conjunction seems to be regarded as introducing a new sentence, instead of
connecting one clause with another. Hence the pronoun is put in the nominative,
and a verb is, perhaps, to be supplied from the context. So, too, we have &lquo;we&rquo; for
<I>us</I> in III, ii, 231, since it stands quasi-independently at some distance from the gov-
erning word, &lquo;touches.&rquo;
<P>54. <B>fools</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Intimating that we are only kept (as formerly fools in
a great family) to make sport for nature, who lies hid only to mock and laugh at us
for our vain searches into her mysteries. <SC>Mason</SC> (p. 378): A paraphrase of the

<P>73. <B>deprive</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: In this place it signifies simply <I>to take away.</I> So also
<SC>Dyce</SC> interprets it in &lquo;deprives our own sight.&rquo;&mdash;Beau. &amp; Fl. <I>The Maid in the Mill,</I>
IV, iii, 8. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 261): That is, depose reason from her throne in
your mind. &lquo;Deprive&rquo; is here synonymous with <I>depose.</I> <SC>Lettsom</SC> (<I>Foot-note</I> to
the foregoing): I have observed two examples of this use of the word in <I>R. of L.</I>
1186 and 1752. Again, &lquo;And join together to deprive my breath.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Woman Kill'd
with Kindness,</I> Dodsley vii, p. 261; &lquo;What son, what comfort that she (<I>Fortune</I>)
can deprive?&rquo;&mdash;Marston, <I>Antonio &amp; Mellida,</I> Part i, III, i. <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 200: &lquo;De-
prive,&rquo; meaning to &lquo;take away a thing from a person,&rquo; like &lquo;rid,&rquo; can dispense with
&lquo;of&rquo; before the impersonal object. This explains the present passage: &lquo;which might
<I>take away</I> your controlling principle of reason.&rquo; Compare also the tendency (&sect; 290)
to convert neuter verbs into active verbs. See also I, iii, 51.
<P>73. <B>sovereignty of reason</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The same as sovereign or supreme
reason. Thus, &lquo;At once to betray the sovereignty of reason in my soul.&rquo;&mdash;King Charles,

p. 352, ed. 1816): &lquo;Sovereignty&rquo; here is merely a title of respect, and the whole
phrase means neither more nor l<*>s than to deprive your lordship, or your honour,
or your highness, of reason. [<I>Aliquando dormit<*>t,</I> &amp;c. As <SC>Hunter</SC> says, Hamlet
was no sovereign. <SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Dispossess the sovereignty of your reason

<P><B>Stage Direction</B>] Owing to the length of time that elapses before the companions
of Ham. rejoin him, <SC>Delius</SC> thinks it unlikely that the dialogue with the Ghost took
place on the same Platform where Ham. broke loose from his friends. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>
changes the scene to &lquo;A Wilderness,&rquo; because &lquo;Ham. must have followed the Ghost
a long distance, since he refuses to go farther. His question also, &ldquo;Whither wilt
thou lead me?&rdquo; shows that, despitc his courage, horror is beginning to creep over
him; and at the close of the scene the Ghost speaks from under the ground.&rquo; The
earliest change in this stage direction that I can find is in <SC>Schroeder's</SC> adaptation
of the play for the Hamburg theatre, in 1781. Here the scene is laid in &lquo;<I>A Grave-
yard with the Church in the background.</I>&rquo;

<P>6. <B>bound</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: Hamlet uses the word in the sense of <I>ready addressed</I> [past
part. of Old Norse <I>buinn,</I>&mdash;see Wedgwood], the Ghost uses it as the past participle
of the verb <I>to bind.</I>
<P>11. <B>to fast in</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Rest.</I> p. 45) conjectured that we should read
<I>roast,</I> but afterwards in his correspondence with his &lquo;most affectionate friend,&rquo;
Warburton (see Nichols, <I>Lit. Hist.</I> vol. ii. p. 559), he said, &lquo;<I>sed facti p&oelig;nitet,</I>&rquo; and
suggested instead, <I>confined fast:</I> presumably he withdrew them both, since he does
not allude to them in his ed., where he says: The expression is purely metaphorical,
for <I>fasting</I> could be no great punishment for a <I>Spirit.</I> According to the Roman
Catholic religion, <I>fasting</I> purifies the soul here, as the <I>fire</I> does in the <I>Purgatory</I> here
alluded to; the soul must be purged either by fasting here or by burning hereafter.
<SC>Heath</SC> and <SC>Johnson</SC> both conjectured <I>to lasting,</I> which the former considered jus
tified by the next line, the meaning being: fires which were to last till the purgation
was completed; and which the latter interpreted as <I>unremitted</I> and <I>unconsumed.</I>
<SC>Collier's</SC> (MS) has the same. <SC>Smith</SC> [cited by Steevens]: Chaucer has a similar
passage with regard to the punishments of hell, <I>Persones Tale,</I> p. 291, ed. Tyrwhitt,
4to: &lquo;And moreover the misese of helle shall be in defaute of mete and drink.&rquo;

<P>to <I>fast</I> might be considered as one of the punishments inflicted on the wicked. <SC>Dyce</SC>
(ed. i.): If the old text be wrong, and certainly the passages in Chaucer, &amp;c., as

most probable alteration yet proposed. [This remark about Steevens's conj. is
omitted in <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii), and citations from Chaucer, &amp;c. alone are given.] <SC>White</SC>:
These fires were those of Purgatory, in which the Ghost was confined for the day
only, and so were not lasting in any sense. &lquo;Fast&rquo; may be used here in its radical
sense of religious observance, and without any allusion to abstinence from food, or
there may be a reference to the old notion contained in the extract from Chaucer.
<SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: <I>Lasting</I> cannot be right, because the Ghost was in Purgatory, nor
is <I>to fast in</I> any better, since the old king wanders about outside his &lquo;prison-house,&rquo;
and could, if he chose, satisfy his hunger. Clearly, the true opposite to &lquo;walk&rquo;
is what I have adopted in my text, &lquo;confined fast.&rquo; [See Theobald <I>supra.</I> <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>14. <B>burnt and purged</B>] <SC>Farmer</SC>: Thus Gawain Douglas, in his translation of
<I>&AElig;n.</I> vi, 740, says that &lquo;it is a nedeful thing to suffer panis and torment, . . . some
in the wyndis, sum under the watter, and in the fire uthir sum. Till the mony vices
Contrakkit in the corpis be done away And purgit.&rquo;
<P>17, 18. <B>Make . . . start . . . to</B>] For the omission and insertion of &lquo;to&rquo; in the
same sentence, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 350, and I, v, 178.
<P>19. <B>an end</B>] For instances of nouns, adjectives, and participles with the prefix <I>a,</I>
see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 24, where it is shown that <I>a</I> represents some preposition, as &lquo;in,&rquo; &lquo;on,&rquo;
&lquo;of,&rquo; &amp;c., contracted by rapidity of pronunciation, and takes an <I>n</I> before a vowel for
euphony. See also &sect; 182, and of this play, I, iii, 119; II, ii, 466; III, i, 165; III,
iv, 122; and <I>Macb.</I> V, v, 49. <SC>Eastwood</SC> and <SC>Wright</SC> (<I>Bible Word-Book,</I> p. 2):
This prefix <I>a-</I> or <I>an-</I> is generally said to be a corruption of the Anglo-Saxon particle
<I>on-,</I> but more probably the two are essentially identical, and only different dialectical
forms of the same. In many instances the two forms remain side by side, as in <I>aboard</I>
and <I>on-board, aground</I> and <I>on ground.</I>

<P>of &lquo;an inaccurate use of words in Sh., some of them owing to his imperfect scholar-

<P>21. <B>blazon</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;Such promulgation of the mysteries of eternity must
not be made to beings of a day.&rquo; <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: 1. To blow abroad, to spread
news, to publish. 2. To portray armorial bearings in their proper colours. <SC>Moberly</SC>:
&lquo;A blaze&rquo; is a white mark upon a horse; whence <I>to blaze trees</I> is to notch them with
an axe, so as to mark the way back. To &lquo;blazon,&rquo; therefore, means properly to
mark out; hence &lquo;to reveal.&rquo;
<P>24. <B>O God!</B>] <SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 159) considers this as an unnecessary interpolation of
some actors; so also the Ghost's repetition of &lquo;Murder&rquo; in line 27.
<P>27. For this line <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> substitutes the two corresponding lines of Q<SUB>1</SUB>.
<P>30. <B>meditation</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This word is consecrated by the <I>mysticks</I> to sig-
nify that flight of mind which aspires to the enjoyment of the supreme Good. So
that the two most rapid things in nature are here employed: the ardency of divine
and human passion in an <I>enthusiast</I> and a <I>lover.</I> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This is so ingenious
that I hope it is just. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: That is, &lquo;as the course and process of thought
generally.&rquo; We have &lquo;I'll make him fly swifter than meditation,&rquo; in the Prologue to
<I>Wily Beguiled.</I> It was not improbably, therefore, a common saying.
<P>31. <B>sweep</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Rest.</I> p. 50) conjectured <I>swoop,</I> not only from the
fitness of the word, but from its use in <I>Macb.</I> IV, iii, 219. He did not repeat the
conj. in his edition.
<P>32. <B>shouldst</B>] For instances of &lquo;should&rquo; where we now use <I>would,</I> see <SC>Abbott</SC>,

<P>32, 34. <B>shouldst...Wouldst</B>] <SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Misc. Obs.</I> 1752, p. 17): As the passage
stands, we must read it with a note of interrogation, and even then it is scarce passa-
ble. Transpose the &lquo;shouldst&rquo; and the &lquo;Wouldst:&rquo; &lquo;And duller <I>wouldst</I> thou be,&rquo; &amp;c.
This is pertinent and natural, and we find the Ghost speaks a little more to the purpose.
<P>33. <B>roots</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 127): The moderns have sunk a great beauty by not
following the Ff; for in &lquo;roots&rquo; is an idea of action that diminishes the compari-
son's beauty, which consists in <I>in</I>action. <SC>Steevens</SC> (quoted by <SC>Dyce</SC> in his ed. i)
paraphrases Capell, and adds: This dull root pluck'd from Lethe flood.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The
Humorous Lieutenant,</I> IV, iii, Beau. &amp; Fl. vol. vi, ed. Dyce. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: We have
the phrase [&lquo;rot&rquo;] again in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> I, iv, 47: &lquo;To rot itself with motion.&rquo;
<SC>Knight</SC>: Whiter, in his <I>Etymological Dict.,</I> speaking of this passage, in connection
with the theory of <I>ease</I> belonging to the idea of being <I>earthed</I>&mdash;fixed, resting&mdash;
says, &lquo;It is curious that Sh. uses <I>ease</I> as connected with a term which most strongly
expresses the idea of being <I>fixed</I> in a certain spot, or <I>earth.</I>&rquo; <SC>White</SC>: The Qq are
confirmed by the passage from <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> If in the one case the flag <I>rots</I> itself
with <I>motion,</I> it seems clear that in the other it must <I>root</I> itself with <I>ease.</I> The oppo-
sition of &lquo;roots&rquo; to &lquo;stir&rquo; in the next line also supports this reading. <SC>Staunton</SC><*>
It is difficult to determine which expression deserves the preference.

<P>56. <B>sate</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: The reading of Qq makes excellent sense, even with-
out changing &lquo;in&rquo; to <I>from.</I> &lquo;Even in a celestial bed lust will separate, detach
itself, &amp;c.&rquo; Not only &lquo;link'd,&rquo; but also &lquo;prey,&rquo; shows <I>sort</I> to be the emphatic word.
It is small wonder if German commentators prefer &lquo;sate&rquo; to <I>sort,</I> but Englishmen,
before whose vision the enormous breadth of their own almost square beds must have
instantly arisen, ought to have conceived the right idea of <I>separation in bed.</I>
Moreover, &lquo;sate itself&rquo; cannot be connected with &lquo;prey on garbage&rquo; on physiological
grounds.
<P>59. <B>orchard</B>] See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> II, i, 5.
<P>60. <B>custom</B>] Instances are given in the Var. '21 to show that an &lquo;after-dinner
sleep&rquo; (<I>Meas. for Meas.</I> III, i, 33) was in general customary.
<P>60. <B>in</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: A somewhat similar use of the preposition <I>of,</I> in the Qq,
occurs in <I>Love's Lab.</I> I, i, 43. For the use of <I>of,</I> see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 176.
<P>61. <B>secure</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 292): Accent on the first syllable, as in <I>Oth.</I> IV, i,
72, and as &lquo;complete&rquo; in <I>Ham.</I> I, iv, 52. <SC>Staunton</SC> (Note on <I>Lear,</I> IV, i, 20):
Careless, unguarded. Thus, in Sir T. More's <I>Life of Edward V:</I> &lquo;When this lord
was most afraid, he was most secure; and when he was secure, danger was over his
head.&rquo; Again, Judges, viii, 11: &lquo;And Gideon . . . smote the host: for the host was
secure.&rquo;
<P>62. <B>hebenon</B>] <SC>Grey</SC> (ii, 287): This stands, by metathesis, for <I>henebon,</I> that is,
<I>henbane,</I> of which the most common kind (<I>Hyoscyamus niger</I>) is certainly narcotic,

<P><I>Philosopher's Fourth Satire of Mars,</I> by Anton, 1616: &lquo;The poison'd henbane, whose

hecause Sh. was perfectly well acquainted with the supposed properties of the hen-

Shakespeare's day believed that poison might be introduced into the system through
the ears; the eminent surgeon, Ambroise Par&eacute;, Shakespeare's contemporary, was
suspected of having, when he dressed the ear of Francis II, infused poison into it.
Dr Sherwen informs us that in Gower's <I>Confessio Amantis</I> the couch of the god of
sleep was made &lquo;Of <I>Hebenus,</I> that sleepie tree.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC>: The French word

to read the line: &lquo;With juice of curs&egrave;d hebon in a phial.&rquo; Or perhaps should we
not conjecture that <I>hemlock</I> was intended here? <SC>Beisley</SC> (<I>Sh.'s Garden,</I> p. 4):
&lquo;Hebenon&rquo; might have been originally written <I>enoron,</I> one of the names at that time
of <I>Solanum maniacum,</I> called also <I>deadly</I> nightshade, a more powerful poison than
henbane. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: The <I>hebona</I> of the Qq can be only a mistaken substitu-
tion of the Spanish and Italian, <I>ebano;</I> French, <I>&eacute;b&egrave;ne;</I> Latin, <I>ebenus</I> and <I>hebenus.</I>
Probably the <I>-on</I> of &lquo;hebenon&rquo; was caused by the following &lquo;in,&rquo; so that we may
suppose that originally the word here was <I>heben,</I> the only correct etymological form,
although it was sometimes incorrectly written <I>hebon.</I> <SC>Moberly</SC>: Not surely <I>ebony</I>
(<I>Diospyros</I>), the fruit of which is often edible; but henbane, or <I>Hyoscyamus,</I> which
is a strong narcotic poison. It does not indeed produce any leprous symptoms; but
the belief of its doing so would, on the theory of signatures, be founded on the
clammy appearance of the plant.

<P>69. <B>eager</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cotgrave gives: &lquo;Aigre: Eagre, sharpe, tart, biting,

<P>80. Oh] <SC>Corson</SC>: A distinction should be made between the emotional interjec-
tion, &lquo;Oh,&rquo; and the &lquo;O,&rquo; vocative. It can be seen, I think, that the distinction was
intended in the Ff, although it is not invariable. But in a modernized text consist-
ency requires that the distinction should be made, as it is one that is observed in
modern orthography. It is a distinction, too, not merely factitious, as might be sup-
posed, but based on good ground. &lquo;There is a difference between &ldquo;O sir!&rdquo; &ldquo;O
King!&rdquo; and &ldquo;Oh! sir,&rdquo; &ldquo;Oh! Lord,&rdquo; both in sense and pronunciation. As to the
sense, the <I>O</I> prefixed merely imparts to the title a vocative effect; while the <I>Oh</I>
conveys some particular sentiment. And as to the sound, the <I>O</I> is enclitic; that is
to say, it has no accent of its own, but is pronounced with the word to which it is

<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 225): This expression is the first in which we have anything like the
unsettling of the intellect, and what follows, to the end of the scene, can scarcely be
reconciled to an opinion of the perfect sanity of Hamlet, except on the supposition
that even now he began to put on the appearance of madness, which is not likely.
At the same time, it is to be observed that the light and sportive sallies which follow
are not absolutely out of nature, even if we suppose him sane, very powerful events
not producing their natural effect <I>at once.</I> Some hours commonly intervene before
the mind is awakened, as it were, to a sense of the change which has taken place,
and during the interval men do act, not unfrequently, strangely and fantastically.
When they begin to consider, then they begin to act in a manner correspondent to
their situation and character. <SC>Brae</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 13 Mar. 1852) denies, what Cole-
ridge asserts (see line 92), that Ham. noted down in his tables &lquo;that one may smile,
and smile, and be a villain.&rquo; &lquo;This jotting down by Ham., upon a real, substantial
table, of one of those &ldquo;generalized truths,&rdquo; which he had just excluded from the
table of his memory, would be too great a <I>literalising of the metaphor.</I>&rquo; It is not
this most trite reflection: &lquo;That one may smile,&rquo; &amp;c. that Ham. wishes to set down.
No, it is the all-absorbing <I>commandment</I> contained in the last line of the Ghost's

<P>and preparing the tables. Line 108 is an admirative comment upon line 106, and
&lquo;So, uncle, there you are,&rquo; is equivalent to the common exclamation, even at the
present day, expressive of misdeeds, or intentions, unexpectedly brought to light.
It is by no means uncommon for a sentence expressive of wonder or incredulity to
begin with <I>That,</I> as in line 108; we have, in <I>Cym.</I> I, i, 63, &lquo;That a king's children
should be so convey'd!&rquo; The best possible stage-direction is given by Sh. himself

<P>115. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: This part of the scene after Hamlet's interview with the Ghost
has been charged with an improbable eccentricity. But the truth is, after the mind
has been stretched beyond its usual pitch and tone, it must either sink into exhaus-
tion and inanity, or seek relief by change. It is thus well known that persons con-
versant with deeds of cruelty contrive to escape from conscience by connecting
something of the ludicrous with them, and by inventing grotesque terms and a certain
technical phraseology to disguise the horror of their practices. Indeed, paradoxical
as it may appear, the terrihle, by a law of the human mind, always touches on the
verge of the ludicrous. Both arise from a perception of something out of the com-
mon order of things&mdash;something, in fact, out of its place; and if from this we can
abstract danger, the uncommonness will alone remain, and the sense of the ridicu-
lous be excited. The close alliance of these opposites,&mdash;they are not contraries,&mdash;
appears from the circumstance, that laughter is equally the expression of extreme
anguish, and horror, as of joy; as there are tears of sorrow and tears of joy, so there
is a laugh of terror and a laugh of merriment. These complex causes will naturally
have produced in Ham. the disposition to escape from his own feelings of the over-
whelming and supernatural by a wild transition to the ludicrous,&mdash;a sort of cunning
bravado, bordering on the flights of delirium. For you may, perhaps, observe
Hamlet's wildness is but half false; he plays that subtle trick of pretending to act
only when he is very near really being what he acts.

<P>123. <B>Denmark</B>] <SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 162): Hamlet begins these words in the ardour

off hastily: &lquo;There's ne'er a villain in all Denmark&rquo; that can match (perhaps he
would have said) my uncle in villainy; and then recollecting the danger of such a
declaration, he pauses for a moment and then abruptly concludes: &lquo;but he's an
arrant knave.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: Hamlet turns his words off into a strange and baffling
jest, as a kind of refuge from the horror which would else overmaster him, with a
feeling, at the same time, that this will be the best way to defeat enquiry.

<P>137. <B>offence</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: Hamlet purposely misunderstands his friends' words, in
order to evade their enquiries. At first he pretends that his words have given offence,
whereas his friends have merely found them vague; and when they reply that there
is no offence, he takes &lquo;offence&rquo; in a wider sense as a &lquo;crime,&rquo; and refers it to the
crime of his uncle that had just been divulged to him.

Saint Patrick, but there is, my Lord, And much offence too, touching this Vision
here.&rquo;

always had upon the hilt. <SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 229): In consequence of this practice, the
name of <I>Jesus</I> was sometimes inscribed on the handle or some other part. <SC>Nares</SC>:
The singular mixture of religious and military fanaticism which arose from the
Crusades gave rise to the extraordinary custom of taking a solemn oath upon a
sword. In a plain, unenriched sword, the separation between the blade and the
hilt was usually a straight transverse bar, which, suggesting the idea of a cross,
added to the devotion which every true knight felt for his favorite weapon, and evi-
dently led to this practice; of which the instances are too numerous to be collected.
The sword or the blade were often mentioned in this ceremony without reference to
the cross. It is ludicrously referred to in 1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> II, iv, 371. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>):
The custom of swearing by a sword prevailed even among the barbarous worshippers
of Odin: &lquo;The Seythians commonly substituted a sword as the most proper symbol
to represent the supreme god. It was by planting a spear in the middle of a field
that they usually marked out the place set apart for prayers and sacrifices; and when
they had relaxed from their primitive strictness, so far as to build temples and set up
idols in them, they yet preserved some traces of the ancient custom by putting a
sword in the hands of Odin's statues. The respect they had for their arms made
them also swear by instruments so valuable and so useful, as being the most sacred
things they knew. Accordingly, in an ancient Icelandic poem, a Scandinavian, to
assure himself of a person's good faith, requires him to swear, &ldquo;by the shoulder of
a horse, and the edge of a <I>sword.</I>&rdquo; This oath was usual more especially on the eve
of some great engagement; the soldiers engaged themselves by an oath of this kind
not to flee, though their enemies should be never so superior in number.&rquo;&mdash;Mallet's
<I>Northern Antiquities,</I> &amp;c., transl. by Percy, vol. i, p. 216, ed. 1770. [For many
instances of oaths taken upon swords, see <SC>Farmer, Steevens</SC> and <SC>Caldecott. Ed.</SC>]
<SC>Knight</SC>: We have little doubt that Sh. was aware of the peculiar custom of the
Gothic nations, and did not make Hamlet propose the oath merely as a practice of
chivalry.
<P>147. <B>already</B>] <SC>Hudson</SC>: The oath they have already sworn is &lquo;<I>in faith.</I>&rquo; But
this has not enough of ritual solemnity in it to satisfy Hamlet.
<P>148. <B>Indeed</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: The meaning of Hamlet unquestionably is, Not
in words only, but <I>in act, in form;</I> upon the cross of my sword, pledge your-
selves.
<P>149. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: These subterraneous speeches of the Ghost are hardly defen-
sible; but I would call your attention to the characteristic difference between the
Ghost, as a superstition connected with the most mysterious truths of revealed re-
ligion,&mdash;and Shakespeare's consequent reverence in his treatment of it,&mdash;and the
foul earthy witcheries and wild language in <I>Macbeth.</I>

<P>150. <B>true-penny</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This word, as well as some of Hamlet's former
exclamations, we find in <I>The Malcontent,</I> 1604. <SC>Collier</SC>: This word is also found
in Nash's <I>Almond for a Parrot.</I> It is (as I learn from some Sheffield authorities)
a mining term, and signifies a particular indication in the soil of the direction in
which ore is to be found. Hence Hamlet may with propriety address the Ghost
under ground by that name. <SC>Forby</SC> (<I>Vocab. of East Anglia</I>): Hearty old fellow;
staunch and trusty; true to his purpose or pledge. <SC>Halliwell</SC> suspects that it
was sometimes applied to a sexton, therefore very appropriate here. <SC>Upton</SC> (p.
9, note): &lquo;The Vice,&rquo; in our old <I>Moralities,</I> was used to make fun with the Devil,
and he had several trite expressions, as, &lquo;I'll be with you in a trice,&rquo; &lquo;Ah, ha, boy,
are you there?&rquo; &amp;c. And it was great entertainment to the audience, to see their
old enemy belaboured in effigy. Now, Ham. is resolved to break the subject of
the discourse to none but Hor.; to others he intends to appear as a sort of madman,
he therefore now addresses the Ghost as <I>The Vice</I> does the Devil, at the same time he
wishes the sentinels to imagine that this was a shape the Devil had put on; and in
II, ii, 575, he is somewhat of this opinion himself. This manner of speech was what
the audience were well acquainted with; and it takes off in some measure from
the horror of the scene.
<P>153. <B>seen</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 263): The inversion [by putting only a comma
after &lquo;seen&rquo;] is anti-Shakespearian. <SC>Corson</SC>: Horatio asks Hamlet to propose the
oath, which he does, namely: &lquo;Never to speak of this that you have seen,&rquo; and then,
having done so, he tells them to swear by his sword, which is additional.

<P>sion of this scene is a remnant, word for word, of the earlier tragedy by Shake-
speare's predecessor; and this little snatch of Latinity upholds this view. The
dramatic predecessors of Shakespeare were very fond of interlarding their pieces
with such little snatches of Latin, and Shakespeare yielded to the practice only in
his very earliest plays, not in his later ones. Therefore, from the use of these little
phrases alone we might infer that Shakespeare retained all of these concluding lines
from the earlier drama, perhaps from no other reason than that the scene had become
a popular favorite.
<P>158. <B>upon my sword,</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 263) was the first to advocate this
punctuation of F<SUB>1</SUB>; and <SC>Corson</SC> says: &lquo;The true meaning is indicated by the
comma after &ldquo;sword.&rdquo; The &ldquo;swear by my sword&rdquo; is but a repetition of the same
idea.&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC> adds: &lquo;The Ghost's &ldquo;Swear by his sword&rdquo;&mdash;if this reading be
correct&mdash;is, as it were, an echo of Hamlet's words.&rquo; In the textual notes the punc-
tuation of those editors alone is given who have followed the arrangement of the Ff.
<P>163. <B>pioner</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: A pioneer; an attendant on an army, whose office is to

warlike tools, as spades, &amp;c. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): They are generally soldiers who, on
account of misconduct, had been degraded to the office. [For the spelling, see
<SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Vers.</I> 217; <I>Crit.</I> iii, 263; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 492. Also I, ii, 172; III, iv, 206. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>64. <B>of reach</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Far-sighted. See I, iv, 56. Compare &lquo;we of taste and
feeling.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> IV, ii, 30. <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 168: &lquo;Of&rquo; here means <I>by means of.</I>
<P>65. <B>windlasses</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: Metaphorically, art and contrivance, subtleties; <I>e. g.</I>
&lquo;Which, by slie drifts, and windlaces aloof, They brought about.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Mirror for
Magistrates,</I> p. 336. <I>Windlaies</I> is used by Fairfax, for sudden turns; whether he
meant this word or another, is not quite clear: perhaps, rather, <I>windings:</I>&mdash; &lquo;The
beauties faire of shepherd's daughters bold, With wanton windlaies runne, turne,
play, and passe.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Tasso,</I> xiv, 34. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 226): <I>Windlaces</I> is used in a sense
now forgotten. We find it in Golding's Ovid, the seventh book, the book in which
Sh. was so well read: &lquo;&mdash;like a wily fox he runs not forth directly out, Nor makes a
windlasse over all the champion fields about,&rquo; &amp;c. It is also used by Bishop Hacket.
<SC>Edinburgh Review</SC> (<I>Shakespearian Glossaries,</I> July, 1869): In Shakespeare's
day, <I>windlace,</I> literally, a winding, was used to express taking a circuitous course,
fetching a compass, making an indirect advance, or, more colloquially, beating about
the bush instead of going directly to a place or object; and in this sense it exactly
harmonizes with the other phrase used by Polonius to express the same thing,&mdash;
&lquo;assays of bias,&rquo;&mdash;attempts in wbich, instead of going straight to the object, we seek
to reach it by a curved or winding course, the bias gradually bringing the ball round
to the Jack. Thus, in Golding's Ovid: &lquo;The winged God . . . Continued not directly
forth, but gan me down to stoupe, And fetched a windlasse round about.&rquo; <SC>Claren-
don</SC>: Also Lily's <I>Euphues and his England</I> (ed. Arber), p. 270: &lquo;I now fetching
a windlesse, that I myght better haue a shoote, was preuented with ready game.&rquo;
<P>65. <B>assays of bias</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: A metaphor from the game of bowls, in
which the player does not aim at the Jack (or &lquo;mistress,&rquo; as it was called in Shake-
speare's time) directly, but in a curve, so that the bias brings the ball round. &lquo;Assays
of bias&rquo; are therefore indirect attempts.
<P>66. <B>indirections</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Indirect methods. We find out indirectly, says
Polonius, what we wish to know directly. See <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> IV, iii, 75.
<P>69. <B>God be wi' you</B>] See <I>Macb.</I> III, i, 43, or <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 228).
<P>69. <B>fare you well</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: Although the double leave-taking is quite

<P>in keeping with the loquacity of Polonius, we are justified, nevertheless, in expecting
a reply from the departing servant. I have therefore given the words &lquo;God be wi'
you&rquo; (which, by the contraction of <I>with</I> into &lquo;wi',&rquo; express a certain condescension)
to Polonius, and &lquo;fare you well&rquo; to Reynaldo.
<P>70. <B>Good my lord</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC>: Reynaldo has previously said &lquo;Very good, my lord,&rquo;
and he afterwards says, &lquo;Well, my lord,&rquo; but the present speech is not therefore to
be pointed &lquo;Good, my lord.&rquo; Compare II, ii, 521.
<P>71. <B>in yourself</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Perhaps this means, in your own person, not by
spies. <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 129): &lquo;In yourself&rquo; is put for&mdash;observe <I>of</I> yourself, or with your
own eyes; for he had been lesson'd before to pick up his &lquo;inclination&rquo; from others.
C. (in <I>Var.</I> 1821): The temptations you feel, suspect in him. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: It seems
no more than &lquo;<I>of</I> or <I>by</I> yourself,&rquo; and as if the word &lquo;in&rquo; had been altogether
omitted. He was at first to discover Laertes's inclination by enquiry from others;
but now to find them out by personal observation. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: I find it hard
to persuade myself that &lquo;in&rquo; is anything more than a misprint, which arose from the
last syllable of the preceding word. A change of &lquo;in&rquo; into <I>then</I> could be easily
made except for the uniformity of the old copies. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Possibly it means,
Conform your own conduct to his inclinations.
<P>73. <B>music</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: Let him go on, to what tune he pleases; let him conduct
himself in any style and at any rate he chooses. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Eye him sharply, but
do it <I>slyly,</I> and let him fiddle his secrets all out. <SC>Vischer</SC> (<I>Sh. Jahrbuch,</I> ii. p.
149): Here we have the key to the whole scene. His son may gamble, drink,
swear, quarrel, drab, enter houses of sale, videlicet, brothels, only&mdash;let him ply his
music: true cavalier-breeding!
<P>74. <B>matter</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: There is a wonderfully fine contrast between the prolix
slyness of Polonius's attempt to find out what had better be unknown, and the scene
of distracting and passionate misery which shows how Hamlet's soul has been shat-
tered by an unsought-for revelation.

<P>The supposition that Hamlet went to Ophelia directly after the interview with the
Ghost is incorrect, and for the following reasons: first, the interview between Po
lonius and Reynaldo implies that some little time has elapsed since the departure of
Laertes for Paris; secondly, during this time Ophelia has returned Hamlet's letters,
and denied him access; her father asks her, &lquo;Have you given him any hard words
of late?&rquo; The letter which Polonius reads to the King must, therefore, have belonged
to a period before the opening of the drama. Ophelia had strictly obeyed her father's
commands, and returned all Hamlet's letters. Thirdly, Polonius goes at once to the
King, and yet, when he speaks to him of Hamlet, the King already knew of Ham-
let's (feigned) insanity, and therefore must himself have seen the Prince before
Ophelia saw him. Fourthly, between the close of the first act and the present
scene, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern must have been summoned on account of
Hamlet's changed demeanor, and of the King's suspicions which that demeanor
had aroused.
<P>77. <B>closet</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: A private apartment. Hence the King's private secre-
tary was called &lquo;clerk of the closet.&rquo; See III, ii, 315; and <I>King John,</I> IV, ii, 267.
<P>78. <B>unbraced</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Unfastened. Compare <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> I, iii, 48; and
II, i, 262.
<P>79. <B>foul'd</B>] <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>: Theobald reads <I>loose</I> on the authority, as he
says, &lquo;of the elder Qq.&rquo; It is not the reading of any of the first six, but of those
of 1676, 1683, 1695, and 1703. Had Capell been aware of this, he would scarcely
have designated Theobald's mistake as a &lquo;downright falsehood.&rquo; Theobald at the
time of writing his <I>Sh. Restored</I> knew of no Quarto earlier than that of 1637 (<I>Sh.
Rest.</I> p. 70), and it is just possible that some copy of this edition (Q<SUB>6</SUB>) from which
that of 1676 was printed may have had the reading &lquo;loose.&rquo; [The Cam. Edd. refer
to a note on III, iv, 59, where they give two different readings in two different copies
of Q<SUB>6</SUB>: &lquo;a heaven-kissing&rquo; in Ingleby's copy, and &lquo;a heaue, a kissing,&rquo; in Capell's
copy. This variation in copies of the same date has long been known to exist in
the older Qq, but, I confess, I was not prepared to find much variation in later Qq of
the same date. In no less than twenty-four instances, however, I have found that
my copy of Q'76 differs from that of the Cam. Edd., as recorded in their notes. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>80. <B>Ungarter'd</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: It was the regular amorous etiquette, in the reign of
Elizabeth, for a man professing himself deeply in love to assume a certain negligence
in dress. His garters, in particular, were not to be tied up. See <I>As You Like It,</I>
III, ii, 398.
<P>80. <B>down-gyved</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> interprets his reading, <I>down-gyred,</I> as &lquo;rolled
down to the ancle,&rquo; and derives <I>gyred</I> from <G>gupw_</G>, to bend, to round. <SC>Heath</SC> gives
the true definition of &lquo;down-gyved&rquo;: fallen down to the ancle, after the fashion of
gyves, or fetters.
<P>82. <B>purport</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (iii, 264): Pronounce &lquo;purp&oacute;rt,&rquo; not &lquo;pit&emacr;ous.&rquo;
<P>82, 83. <B>so . . . As</B>] See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 275; and II, ii, 177; or <I>Macb.</I> I, ii, 43.
<P>84. <SC>Keightley</SC> completed the rhythm of this line by the insertion of <I>in</I> after
&lquo;comes.&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 478, makes the second syllable of &lquo;horrors&rquo; a foot by itself on
the principle that &lquo;<I>er</I> [or <I>or</I>] final seems to have been sometimes pronounced with a
kind of &ldquo;burr,&rdquo; which produced the effect of an additional syllable.&rquo; A process
which neither my tongue nor my imagination can compass. Why not let Ophelia's
strong emotion shudderingly fill up the gap?
<P>90. <B>perusal</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Examination. See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> V, iii, 74; <I>Rich.
II:</I> III, iii, 53; <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> IV, v, 232. [Also, <I>Ham.</I> IV, vii, 137.]
<P>91, 95. <B>As</B>] See I, ii, 217.
<P>91. <B>stay'd</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 507: As <I>ed</I> is pronounced after <I>i</I> and <I>u,</I> so it might be
after <I>y</I> in &lquo;stayed,&rquo; but the effect would be painful. The pause after &lquo;it&rquo; must supply
the extra syllable.

<P>100. <SC>Miles</SC> (<I>Review of Hamlet,</I> p. 28): We are not permitted to see Hamlet in

should bring him to such a pass!&mdash;his knees knocking each other!&mdash;knees that had
firmly followed a beckoning ghost! There is more than the love of forty thousand
brothers in that hard grasp of the wrist,&mdash;in that long gaze at arm's length,&mdash;in the
force that <I>might,</I> but <I>will</I> not, draw her nearer! And never a word from this king
of words! His <I>first</I> great silence,&mdash;the <I>second</I> is death!

<P>118, 119. <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, this must be made known to the King, for (being
kept secret) the hiding of Hamlet's love might occasion more mischief to us from him
and the Queen, than the uttering or revealing of it will occasion hate and resent-
ment from Hamlet. The poet's obscure expression seems to have been caused by
his affectation of concluding the scene with a couplet. <SC>Heath</SC>: The concealment
of it may be attended with consequences productive of greater calamity than the
displeasure can possibly be with which the disclosing it may be received. <SC>Calde-
cott</SC>: At the close of an act, or when the scene is shifted, and there is a pause in
the action of the drama, it was the usage of our dramatists, down to the middle of
the last century, not simply to divert attention from the main object, as here, by the
introduction of a couplet or rhymes, but to make the subject of such couplet foreign
altogether to the interests of the drama, an unconnected flourish, and that, not un-
frequently, a labored and florid simile. Such a custom in Sh., so far from being
what Warburton calls it, was the very opposite of &lquo;affectation;&rquo; not to have done it
occasionally would have been an affectation of singularity. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: In the
couplets which conclude scenes the sense is frequently sacrificed to the rhyme. The
sense here seems to be&mdash;Hamlet's mad conduct might cause more grief if it were
hidden than the revelation of his love for Ophelia would cause hatred, <I>i. e.</I> on the
part of the King and Queen. Yet the Queen afterwards expresses her approval of
the match, III, i, 38. Compare also, V, i, 231-234. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> cannot per-
suade himself that the author of the <I>Sonnets</I> and of <I>Venus &amp; Adonis</I> could have
composed Iines so faulty in Iogic and style as these, and he therefore thinks that even
sticklers for the authorized text will pardon him for changing line 119 into &lquo;More
grief to him, than hate to us their love.&rquo; He also marks &lquo;Ophelia exit&rquo; after line 117.

<P>2. <B>Moreover that</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: Over and above that we longed to see you. On
the other hand, &lquo;more above,&rquo; in line 125, means &lquo;moreover.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Besides

<P>5. <B>transformation</B>] On the pronunciation of the final <I>ion</I> as a dissyllable, see
<SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Vers.</I> 230; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 479, and V, ii, 217.
<P>6. <B>Sith</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: The oldest meaning of this difficult word may be seen from
the <I>Fairy Queen</I> (iii, 10, 33), &lquo;he humbly thanked him a thousand sith,&rquo; literally,
&lquo;a thousand steps&rquo; (M&auml;tzner, i, p. 390 [? 410]). Hence, apparently, &lquo;sithen the
fathers died,&rquo; in Wickliffe's Bible, means &lquo;from the time when;&rquo; the preposition
being omitted, as in many English phrases even now. Then come the absolutes
&lquo;sith, sithence, since,&rquo; as in line 12 below. Lastly, the adverb becomes a causative
conjunction; on the principle that &lquo;propter hoc&rquo; may be practically, though loosely,
expressed by &lquo;post hoc.&rquo; That is, &lquo;Sin thou are righteous judge&rquo; means &lquo;following
on the fact that thou art a righteous judge.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Marsh (<I>Lectures on the
English Language,</I> pp. 584-586) says, that in the latter half of the sixteenth century
&lquo;good authors established a distinction between the forms, and used <I>sith</I> only as a
logical word, an illative, while <I>sithence</I> and <I>since,</I> whether as prepositions or as
adverbs, remained mere narrative words confined to the signification of <I>time after.</I>&rquo;
Sh., it is clear, did not observe this distinction, whether we take the quartos or the
folios to represent his exact text. [See IV, iv, 45.]
<P>8, 9. <B>put...from</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Compare <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> III, v, 107.
<P>10. <B>dream of</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: <I>Deem of,</I> that is, the just estimate of himself I
cannot judge of, or comprehend. <SC>White</SC>: Sh. not improbably wrote as it stands
in the Ff. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The <I>of</I> is superfluous, as in <I>Rich. III:</I> I, iii, 6.
<P>11. <B>of so young</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 167: &lquo;Of,&rquo; applied to time, in cases like the present,
means <I>from.</I> So still &lquo;<I>of</I> late.&rquo; Compare &lquo;Of long time he had bewitched them.&rquo;
&mdash;<I>Acts,</I> viii, 11. [See also <SC>M&auml;tzner</SC>, ii, 221.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>45. <B>and</B>] <SC>Knight</SC>: The reading of the Ff means that Polonius holds that his

the error, <I>one,</I> of the Ff, have proved unsuccessful. <SC>Hudson</SC>: I hold my duty both

<P>80. <B>It likes</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 297): An abundance of impersonal verbs is a mark of
an early stage in a language, denoting that a speaker has not yet arrived so far in
development as to trace his own actions and feelings to his own agency. There are
many more impersonal verbs in Early English than in Elizabethan, and many more
in Elizabethan than in modern English. See &lquo;Well be (it) with you,&rquo; II, ii, 362,
III. iv, 173; V, ii, 63. <SC>M&auml;tzner</SC> (iii, 174) gives the same phrase: &lquo;It likes us
well,&rquo; from <I>King John,</I> II, i, 533, with the following explanation: &lquo;The dative in
Germanic verbs passes completely into the accusative where the consciousness of
the language abandons the substitute for the dative by the periphrasis with <I>to.</I> &rquo;
[&lquo;Zounds! I was never so bethumped with words since first I called my brother's
father, dad.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>81. <B>consider'd</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: When we have more time for considering. For
instances of an indefinite and apparently not passive use of passive participles, see
<SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 374.

<P>84. <B>feast</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The king's intemperance is never suffered to be forgotten.
<P>86. <SC>Johnson</SC>: Polonius is a man bred in courts, exercised in business, stored with
observation, confident in his knowledge, proud of his eloquence, and declining into
dotage. His mode of oratory is truly represented as designed to ridicule the prac-
tice of those times, of prefaces that made no introduction, and of method that em-
barrassed rather than explained. This part of his character is accidental, the rest is
natural. Such a man is positive and confident, because he knows that his mind was
once strong, and knows not that it is become weak. Such a man excels in general
principles, but fails in the particular application. He is knowing in retrospect, and
ignorant in foresight. While he depends upon his memory, and can draw from his
repositories of knowledge, he utters weighty sentences, and gives useful counsel;
but as the mind in its enfeebled state cannot be kept long busy and intent, the old
man is subject to sudden dereliction of his faculties; he loses the order of his ideas,
and entangles himself in his own thoughts, till he recovers the leading principle, and
falls again into his former train. This idea of dotage encroaching upon wisdom will
solve all the phenomena of the character of Polonius. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Nothing can
be more easily conceivable or intelligible than the &lquo;idea of dotage encroaching upon
wisdom&rquo;; but does this apply to Polonius? To be extinguished, talent or faculty
must first have existence. Now we have nothing that directly goes to establish the
fact of his having at any time a clear and commanding intellect. Almost everything
has, on the contrary, an opposite bearing; for the very quality relied upon by Dr
Johnson appears to us to be that which most strongly indicates imbecility of mind,
viz. having the memory stored with sage rules and maxims, fit for <I>every</I> turn and
occasion, without the faculty of making effective use of them upon <I>any.</I> In Polo-
nius's general conduct, unmixed folly or dotage is visible at every turn. <SC>Moberly</SC>:
In estimating this character we should do well to remember that the use of language
like that of Polonius would not in Shakespeare's euphuistic days argue the complete
folly that it would at the present time. [See also I, iii, 59. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>86. <B>expostulate</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: To show by discussion, to put the pros and cons,
to answer demands upon the question, &lquo;Pausanias had now opportunity to visit her
and to expostulate the favorable deceit, whereby she had caused his jealousie.&rquo;&mdash;
Stanley's <I>Aurore,</I> 1650, p. 44. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 228): &lquo;Expostulate&rquo; is of rare occur-
rence. It occurs in <I>A Brief Relation of the Shipwreck of Henry May,</I> 1593, in-
corporated in Captain Smith's book on <I>Virginia:</I> &lquo;How these isles came by the
name of the Bermudas, . . . I will not <I>expostulate,</I> nor trouble your patience with
these uncertain antiquities,&rquo; p. 172. It means, to inquire, and when it is an inquiry
from a superior in a state of displeasure, we get at once to what is the present sig-
nification of the world. Thus, in the manuscript book of <I>Anecdotes</I> collected by Sir

<P>109. <SC>Alfred Roffe</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 5 Oct. 1861) gives a list of no less than nine
metrical and musical adaptations of this letter of Hamlet's. One of them, in date
about 1800, &lquo;Composed for and dedicated to Miss Abrams by Michael Kelly,&rquo; is as
follows: &lquo;Doubt (O most beautified), that the stars are fire, Doubt (my soul's idol), that
the sun doth move, Doubt that eternal Truth may prove a liar, But, sweet Ophelia,
never doubt I love. My mind no skill in these fond numbers owns, Yet these de-
clare I love thee best, most best, And though no Muses reckon up my groans, These
lines may shelter in thy snowy breast.&rquo;
<P>109. <B>beautified</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> objected to this word, because of its two meanings,
viz. artificial and natural beauty; the first would be manifestly inappropriate here,
and the second Sh. has used in <I>Two Gent.</I> IV, i, 55, and would not, therefore, here
call it a &lquo;vile phrase.&rquo; He therefore substituted <I>beatified,</I> which is less of an anti-
climax than &lquo;beautified,&rquo; after &lquo;Celestial and soul's idol,&rquo; and which, moreover,
would be the more likely to excite the Roman Catholic Polonius to anger, since it is
almost peculiarly applied to the Virgin Mary. <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 130) prefers <I>beatified,</I> be-
cause of &lquo;its concordance with &ldquo;celestial&rdquo; and &ldquo;idol,&rdquo; and because the passage de-
mands it, which is certainly verse.&rquo; Accordingly, he reads lines 109 to 112, inclu-
sive, as verse, dividing at &lquo;idol&rquo; (which, <I>metri grati&acirc;,</I> he reads &lquo;fair idol&rquo;), &lquo;Ophelia,&rquo;
&lquo;beautified&rquo; (which he reads &lquo;<I>that</I> beatify'd&rquo;), &lquo;these.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Beautified&rquo;
seems to be a vile phrase for the ambiguity of its meaning. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Nash dedi-
cates his <I>Christ's Tears over Jerusalem,</I> 1594, &lquo;To the most beautified lady, the lady
Elizabeth Carey.&rquo; <SC>Nares</SC>: A common word in those times, particularly in the
addresses of letters. The examples wherein a person is said to be &lquo;beautified&rquo; with
various endowments seem hardly apposite. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: That is, accomplished.
&lquo;&mdash;metricall speach . . . by Art bewtified and adorned, and brought far from the
primitiue rudenesse.&rquo;&mdash;Puttenham's <I>Arte of English Poesie,</I> 1589 [p. 39, ed. Arber].
<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): By &lquo;beautified&rquo; (which, however &lquo;vile a phrase,&rquo; is common enough
in our early writers) I believe Hamlet meant <I>beautiful,</I> and not <I>accomplished.</I>

<P>136. <B>winking</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Connivance, as in <I>Hen. V:</I> V, ii, 332. In <I>Cym.</I>
II, iv, 89, &lquo;two winking Cupids&rquo; mean two blind Cupids, two Cupids with their eyes
shut. So <I>Acts,</I> xvii, 30.
<P>138. <B>round</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Roundly, without reserve, as in III, i, 183; III, iv, 5.
<SC>Caldecott</SC>: As here used, it cannot be more correctly interpreted than by the re-
verse of its literal meaning, <I>i. e. without</I> circuity. In this sense, and senses nearly
allied to it, this word is used with great latitude. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) gives eight different
uses of <I>round.</I> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The adjective is here used for the adverb, as in
Bacon's <I>Essay,</I> vi: &lquo;A shew of fearfulnesse, which in any businesse doth spoile the
feathers, of round flying up to the mark.&rquo; See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 60.
<P>139. <B>bespeak</B>] For the use of the prefix <I>be-,</I> see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 438.
<P>140. <B>star</B>] <SC>Boswell</SC>: &lquo;Out of thy star&rquo; is &lquo;placed above thee by fortune.&rquo; We
have &lquo;fortune's star,&rquo; I, iv, 32. <SC>Collier</SC>: &lquo;Star&rquo; is probably to be taken as <I>destiny.</I>
<SC>Singer</SC>: In <I>Twelfth Night,</I> II, v, 156, we have &lquo;in my stars I am above thee.&rquo;
<SC>White</SC>: <I>Sphere</I> is at once a plausible reading and a gloss. <SC>Staunton</SC>: Lord
Hamlet is a prince beyond the influence of the star which governs your fortunes.
<SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 6): Substitute <I>o</I> for <I>t,</I> and you have &lquo;out of thy <I>soar.</I>&rquo; It is not to be
concealed that Sh. does not elsewhere employ <I>soar</I> as a noun.
<P>141. <B>prescripts</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: He had <I>ordered, charged,</I> Ophelia to lock herself up
from Hamlet; see I, iii, 135.
<P>144. <B>fruits</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: She took the <I>fruits</I> of advice. when she obeyed advice;
the advice was then made <I>fruitful.</I>
<P>146-150. <SC>Warburton</SC>: The ridicule of this character is here admirably sustained.

<P>He would not only be thought to have discovered this intrigue by his own sagacity,
but to have remarked all the stages of Hamlet's disorder, from his sadness to his
raving, as regularly as his physician could have done; when all the while the mad-
ness was only feigned. The humor of this is exquisite from a man who tells us, with
a confidence peculiar to small politicians, that he could find: &lquo;Where truth was hid,
though it were hid indeed Within the centre.&rquo;
<P>147. <B>watch</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: A sleepless state.
<P>147, 148. <B>thence into . . . lightness</B>] Although <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vcrs.</I> 20) suggests
that here &lquo;weakness&rquo; and &lquo;lightness&rquo; be pronounced as trisyllables, yet he adds: I
rather suspect that we should write, &lquo;thence <I>to</I> a weakness, thence <I>Into</I> a lightness.&rquo;
<SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 483, while conceding the possibility that &lquo;weakness&rquo; is a trisyllable, yet
thinks that &lquo;the repeated &ldquo;thence&rdquo; may require a pause after it, which might excuse
the absence of an unaccented syllable.&rquo;
<P>148. <B>lightness</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Lightheadedness. Compare <I>Oth.</I> IV, i, 280.
<P>149. <B>madness</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: Sh. intended Hamlet should be deeply moved by
Ophelia's unexplained repulse of him, coming immediately upon the shock he re-
ceives from the Ghost's revelation, and he seizes upon the one as affording apparent
cause for his disturbance of mind arising out of the other, and as giving plausible
and ostensible ground for the madness which he assumes, and by which he wishes
to be believed to have been seized. Polonius's deduction and his report to the King
and Queen of that, and Hamlet's condition, are precisely what the prince desired
should successively accrue from his own behaviour. This all appears to us to be in
favor of our opinion with regard to Hamlet's <I>feigned</I> insanity.
<P>150. <B>all we</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 240: A feeling of the unemphatic nature of the nomi-
natives <I>we</I> and <I>they</I> prevents us from saying &lquo;all we.&rquo; [For another instance of a
transposed pronoun, see V, ii, 14. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>150. <B>for</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: The relative <I>which</I> must be supplied from the foregoing
&lquo;wherein.&rquo;
<P>151. <B>this</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: The reading of F<SUB>1</SUB>, &lquo;'tis this,&rquo; suits better what precedes, and
the reply of the Queen that follows.

<P>158. <B>centre</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: Despite the reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, I nevertheless believe
that by &lquo;centre&rquo; is meant the middle of the palm of the hand, a point important in
palmistry. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Sh., like Bacon, held to the Ptolemaic system of astron-
omy. See <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> I, iii, 85. Compare <I>Tit. And.</I> IV, iii, 12.
<P>159. <B>four</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: I formerly was inclined to adopt Tyrwhitt's proposed
emendation of <I>for</I> [anticipated by Hanmer], but have now no doubt that the text is
right. The expressions, &lquo;four hours together,&rquo; &lquo;two hours together,&rquo; &amp;c., appear to
have been common. So in <I>Lear,</I> I, ii, 170; <I>Wint. T.</I> V, ii, 148. Again in Web-
ster's <I>Duchess of Malfi</I> [ed. Dyce i, 260]: &lquo;She will muse four hours together.&rquo;
<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): It is not likely that Polonius would specify precisely how long
Hamlet walked in the lobby, and the (MS) reads <I>for.</I> <SC>White</SC>: The obvious read-
ing <I>for</I> has occurred to many critical readers; and to modern taste this would seem
an improvement. But similar phrases are of common occurrence in old books.
<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Four&rquo; here, as in <I>Cor.</I> I, vi, 84, and elsewhere, appears a mere collo-
quialism, to signify <I>some,</I> or a limited number, as <I>forty</I> is frequently used to express
a great number. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: So in Puttenham's <I>Arte of English Poesie</I> (p. 307,
ed. Arber): &lquo;laughing and gibing with their familiars foure houres by the clocke.&rquo;
<SC>Elze</SC> (<I>Shakespeare-Jahrbuch,</I> Bd. xi.) has collected many instances from Elizabethan
writers of the use of <I>four</I> and <I>forty,</I> and <I>forty thousand</I> to express an indefinite
number, and probably, with his unwearied industry, he could find <I>forty</I> more. He
also shows that this usage is not confined to England, but is common in German.
Hamlet says he loved Ophelia more than &lquo;forty thousand brothers,&rquo; V, i, 257.

<P>173. <B>fishmonger</B>] <SC>Whiter</SC> (p. 152, <I>foot-note</I>) cites a passage from Jonson's
<I>Masque at Christmas</I> (vol. vii, p. 277, ed. Gifford), where Venus, who is represented
as a deaf tire-woman, says that she was &lquo;a fishmonger's daughter.&rquo; &lquo;Probably, it
was supposed,&rquo; adds Whiter, &lquo;that the daughters of these tradesmen, who dealt in so
nourishing a species of food, were blessed with extraordinary powers of conception.&rquo;
Hence he infers some such allusion by Hamlet. <SC>Gifford</SC>, in his note on this pas-
sage in Jonson, says: &lquo;This alludes to the prolific nature of fish. The jest, which,
such as it is, is not unfrequent in our old dramatists, needs no further illustration.&rquo;
<SC>Malone</SC>: Perhaps a joke was here intended. &lquo;Fishmonger&rquo; was a cant term for a
<I>wencher.</I> In Barnabe Rich's <I>Irish Hubbub:</I> &lquo;Senex fornicator, an old fishmonger.&rquo;
<SC>Coleridge</SC>: That is, you are sent to fish out this secret. This is Hamlet's own
meaning. <SC>G. M. Zornlin</SC> (<I>Sh. Soc. Papers,</I> vol. iii, p. 157) supposes this word to
have been used in a figurative sense, perhaps somewhat as we should now apply the
word ferret, or as a dealer in baits, and that it contains an intimation that Hamlet
was aware of Polonius's being engaged in some underhand policy, &lquo;and that he
knew Ophelia was to play her part in it is evident from the caution which follows
respecting her, which the old man loses sight of in his joy at hearing his daughter
alluded to.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: Probably the meaning may be: &lquo;You deal in wares that
will not bear the sun;&rquo; that is, that Polonius has a daughter, and that all women are
as faithless and unchaste as his mother, so that the least trial overthrows them.
<SC>Tieck</SC> (<I>Kritische Schriften,</I> iii, 262): When this word is spoken the sense may be
made so obvious that one can hardly miss it: &lquo;I would you were so honest a man&mdash;
but&mdash;you are a fleshmonger.&rquo; You are a pander, not so honest a man as a fish-
monger. Hamlet casts in the teeth of Polonius that he made opportunities for him
and his daughter, and the following speech: &lquo;For if the sun,&rquo; &amp;c. is only a continu-
ation of the expression of Hamlet's contempt for both father and daughter. <SC>Friesen</SC>
(<I>Briefe &uuml;ber Hamlet,</I> 1864, p. 287) supposes that this rather refers to Polouius's
share in providing opportunities for Claudius and the Queen, during the old king's

cumque horribilia usquequaque diffundi et <I>in his operari secundum naturam suam,</I>
nec tamen inde aliqua contaminatione sordescere, cum visibilis lux visibilibus sordi-
bus sit natura coniunctior.
<P>181. <B>good kissing carrion</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This strange passage, when set right,
will be seen to contain as great and sublime a reflection as any the poet puts into his
hero's mouth throughout the whole play. We will first give the true reading, which
is this: <I>For if the Sun breed maggots in a dead dog, Being a</I> God, <I>kissing carrion</I>&mdash;.
As to the sense, we may observe that the illative particle [for] shows the speaker to
be reasoning from something he had said before; what that was we learn in these
words, <I>to be honest, as this world goes, is to be one picked out of ten thousand.</I> Having
said this, the chain of ideas led him to reflect upon the argument which libertines
bring against Providence from the circumstance of abounding <I>evil.</I> In the next
speech, therefore, he endeavors to answer that objection, and vindicate Providence,
even on a supposition of the fact, that almost all men were wicked. His argument
in the two lines in question is to this purpose: <I>But why need we wonder at this
abounding of evil? For if the sun breed maggots in a dead dog, which, though a
God, yet shedding its heat and influence upon carrion</I>&mdash;. Here he stops short, lest
talking too consequentially the hearer should suspect his madness to be feigned, and
so turns him off from the subject by enquiring of his daughter. But the inference
which he intended to make was a very noble one, and to this purpose. If this (says
he) be the case that the effect follows the thing operated upon [<I>carrion</I>], and not
the thing operating [a <I>God</I>], why need we wonder that the supreme cause of all
things diffusing its blessings on mankind, who is, as it were, a dead carrion, dead in
original sin, man, instead of a proper return of duty, should breed only corruption
and vices? This is the argument at length, and is as noble a one in behalf of
Providence as could come from the schools of divinity. But this wonderful man
had an art not only of acquainting the audience with what his actors <I>say,</I> but with
what they <I>think.</I> The sentiment, too, is altogether in character, for Hamlet is per-
petually moralizing, and his circumstances make this reflection very natural. The
same <I>thought,</I> something diversified, as on a different occasion, Sh. uses again in

<SC>Johnson</SC>: This is a noble emendation, which almost sets the critic on a level with
the author. <SC>Malone</SC>: Hamlet has just remarked that honesty is very rare in the
world. To this Polonius assents. The prince then adds, that since there is so little
virtue in the world, since corruption abounds everywhere, and maggots are <I>bred</I> by
the sun, even in a dead dog, Polonius ought to take care to prevent his daughter
from walking in the sun, lest she should prove a <I>breeder</I> of sinners; for, though <I>con
ception</I> in general be a blessing, yet as Ophelia (whom Hamlet supposes to be as
frail as the rest of the world) might chance to <I>conceive,</I> it might be a calamity. The
maggots <I>breeding</I> in a dead dog seem to have been mentioned merely to introduce
the word <I>conception,</I> on which word, as Steevens has observed, Sh. has played in
<I>King Lear;</I> and probably a similar quibble was intended here. The word, how-
ever, may have been used in its ordinary sense, for <I>pregnancy,</I> without any double
meaning. The slight connection between this and the preceding passage and Ham-
let's abrupt question, &lquo;Have you a daughter?&rquo; were manifestly intended more strongly
to impress Polonius with the belief of the prince's madness. Perhaps this passage
ought rather to be regulated thus: &lquo;being a <I>god-kissing carrion,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> a carrion that
kisses the sun. The participle <I>being</I> naturally refers to the last antecedent, <I>dog.</I>
Had Sh. intended that it should be referred to <I>sun,</I> he would probably have written,
&lquo;<I>he</I> being a god,&rquo; &amp;c. We have many similar compound epithets in these plays.
Thus, in <I>Lear,</I> II, i, 9, Curan speaks of &lquo;<I>ear-kissing</I> arguments.&rquo; Again, more ap-
positely, in the play before us, III, iv, 59, &lquo;heaven-kissing.&rquo; Again, in <I>R. of L.</I>
1370, &lquo;cloud-kissing.&rquo; However, the instance quoted from <I>Cymb.</I> by Warburton
seems in favor of the regulation that has been hitherto made; for here we find the
poet considered the sun as kissing the carrion, not the carrion as kissing the sun.
So, also, in 1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> II, iv, 113, &lquo;Didst thou never see <I>Titan</I> kiss a dish of
butter?&rquo; The following lines, also, in the historical play of <I>King Edward III,</I> 1596,
which Sh. had certainly seen, are, it must be acknowledged, adverse to the regula-
tion I have suggested: &lquo;The freshest <I>summer's day</I> doth soonest <I>taint</I> The loathed
<I>carrion,</I> that it seems to <I>kiss.</I>&rquo; <SC>Whiter</SC>, whose opinions deserve respect, fails to
make a clear explanation of the text of QqFf, which he upholds. He says (p. 149)
that Sh. considers the &lquo;blessed breeding sun&rquo; as the <I>Good</I> principle in the fecundity
of the earth, and that in the present passage the train of thought in Hamlet's mind
is somewhat thus: There is so little honesty left in the world, the world has become
so degenerate, that even what is bad becomes worse by contact with what is good.
The Sun itself, though a <I>Good,</I> and in general the source of what is excellent, be
comes the origin of <I>corruption;</I> we find this <I>Good,</I> by contact with carrion, breeding
maggots. Why, therefore, may not Ophelia herself become <I>tainted,</I> and become a
<I>breeder of sinners?</I> Let her not walk in the <I>sun,</I>&mdash;keep her removed from all possi-
bility of contamination,&mdash;even from communication with those natures which in gen-

nobody would mistake; &lquo;kissing,&rquo; in such expression, is the verbal noun used adjec-

kissing, or, to be kissed, by the sun, that thus breeds a plentiful crop of maggots
therein, the <I>agency</I> of &lquo;breed&rquo; being implied in &lquo;kissing.&rquo; In reading this speech,
the emphasis should be upon &lquo;kissing,&rquo; and not upon &lquo;carrion,&rquo; the idea of which

<P>201. <B>for yourself</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: The natural reason would have been, &lquo;For some
