<P>253. <B>shadow of a dream</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Sh. has accidentally inverted the ex-
pression of Pindar, that the state of humanity is <G>skia_s o)/nap</G>, the dream of a
shadow. [<G>*era/mepoi ti/ de/ tis; ti/ d) ou) tis; skia_s o)/nap a<*>nqpwros.</G>&mdash;<I>Pythia,</I> viii, 135
(ed. Schneidewin). But, as Collier says, Sh. applies it only to the &lquo;ambitious.&rquo; <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>257. <B>beggars bodies</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC>: I do not understand this; and Sh. seems to
have intended the meaning to be not more than snatched at.&mdash;&lquo;By my fay, I cannot
reason.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: At this rate, and if it be true that lofty aims are no more than
<I>air,</I> our beggars only have the nature of <I>substance;</I> and our monarchs and those who
are blazoned so far abroad as to be thought <I>materially</I> to fill so much space, are, in
fact, <I>shadows,</I> and in imagination only gigantic. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Hamlet loses himself in
the riddles he is making. The meaning, however, seems to be: our beggars can at
least dream of being kings and heroes; and if the substance of such ambitious men
is but a dream, and if a dream is but a shadow, then our kings and heroes are but
the shadows of our beggars. <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 76): If ambition is but a shadow, some-
thing beyond ambition must be the substance from which it is thrown. If ambition,
represented by a king, is a shadow, the antitype of ambition, represented by a beggar,
must be the opposite of the shadow, that is, the substance. <SC>Moberly</SC>: If ambition
is the shadow of pomp, and pomp the shadow of a man, then the only true substantial
men are beggars, who are stript of all pomp and of all ambition.
<P>258. <B>outstretched</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: Hamlet is thinking of the strutting stage heroes.
<P>259. <B>fay</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: A corruption probably of the French <I>foi,</I> which in its
earlier forms was <I>feid, feit, fey, f&eacute;.</I> Or it may be an abbreviation of &lquo;faith.&rquo; Com-
pare <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> I, v, 124.
<P>263. <B>attended</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: My retinue, my service, is detestable. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Prob-
ably referring to the &lquo;bad dreams&rquo; already spoken of.

<P>279, 280. <B>by...withal</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: The addition of &lquo;withal&rquo; ought to have
revealed to modern editors the error of the old text; no explanation is offered by
them of the use of two prepositions for one object. It is evident that, after using
&lquo;by&rquo; three times, the climax is reached only by using it as a substantive in the last
clause; the sense therefore is: &lquo;with what more dear &ldquo;<I>by</I>&rdquo; a better proposer could
charge you.&rquo; [Thus the pure English of William Shakespeare is amended by Benno
Tschischwitz! <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>280. <B>proposer</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: An advocate of more address in shaping his aims,
who could make a stronger appeal.
<P>282. <B>What say you?</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: Perhaps this question is addressed to Hamlet,
in order to gain time and evade, if possible, a direct answer. Furthermore, I doubt
if Sh. intended Hamlet's reply to be spoken as an Aside. Nowhere does Hamlet
take much pains to conceal the distrust with which he regards these false friends,
and he does not hesitate here to let them see that he has an eye on them.

<P>306. <B>lenten</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Sparing, like the entertainments given in Lent.
<SC>Collier</SC>: Such entertainment as players met with in Lent, when they were
often not allowed to perform. This explanation <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) pronounces erro-
neous. <SC>Halliwell</SC>: Our ancestors seem to have used this adjective constantly in
a sense of deterioration. Cotgrave defines &lquo;Amoureux de caresme: A Lenten louer;
a bashfull, modest, or maidenly woer; one thats afraid to touch his mistresse.&rquo;
<P>307. <B>coted</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Overtook. In <I>The Return from Parnassus,</I> 1606: &lquo;marry
we presently coted and outstript them.&rquo; &lquo;In the laws of coursing,&rquo; says Tollet, &lquo;a
cote is when a greyhound goes endways by the side of his fellow, and gives the
hare a turn.&rquo; <SC>Nares</SC>: To pass by, to pass the side of another. It was a common
sporting term. &lquo;Each man . . . notes Which dog first turns the hare, which first
the other coats.&rquo;&mdash;Drayton, <I>Polyolb.</I> xxiii, p. 1115. <SC>Caldecott</SC> cites from Golding's
translation of Ovid, <I>Met.</I> B, x: &lquo;With that Hippomenes coted her&rquo; (where the
original has &lquo;pr&aelig;terit&rquo;). <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): Compare what Rosencrantz afterwards
says of these players, III, i, 17: &lquo;certain players. We o'er-raught (<I>overtook, over-
passed</I>) on the way.&rquo; <SC>Anonymous</SC> (<I>New Shakespearian Interpretations.</I> Edin.
Rev. Oct. 1872): <I>Cote,</I> in the language of venery, is applied to a brace of grey-
hounds slipped together at the stag or hare, and means that one of the dogs outstrips
the other and reaches the game first. Thus we find in Turbervile: &lquo;In coursing at
a Deare, if one Greyhound go endwayes by [that is beyond] another, it is accoumpted
a Cote.&rquo; Again, &lquo;In coursing at the Hare, it is not materiall which dog kylleth her
(which hunters call bearing of an Hare), but he that giveth most Cotes, or most
turnes, winneth the wager. A Cote is when a Greyhound goeth endwayes by his
fellow and giveth the Hare a turn (which is called setting a Hare about), but if he
coast and so come by his fellow, that is no Cote. Likewise, if one Greyhound doe
go by another, and then be not able to reach the Hare himselfe and turne her, this
is but stripping, and no Cote.&rquo; <I>To cote</I> is thus not simply to overtake, but to over-
pass, to outstrip, this being the distinctive meaning of the term. Going beyond is
the essential point, the term being usually applied under circumstances where over-
taking is impossible,&mdash;to dogs who start together and run abreast until the cote takes
place. So Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, having coted the players in their way,
reach the palace first, and have been for some time in conversation with Hamlet
before the strolling company arrives.

<P>312. <B>humorous</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The fretful or capricious man shall vent the whole
of his spleen undisturbed. <SC>Staunton</SC>: Not the funny man, or jester,&mdash;he was termed
&lquo;the clown,&rquo;&mdash;but the actor who personated the fantastic characters, known in Shake-
speare's time as &lquo;humourists,&rquo; and who, for the most part, were represented as
capricions and quarrelsome. <SC>Delius</SC>: Such characters as Faulconbridge, Jaques,
and Mercutio. The &lquo;clown&rquo; is next referred to.
<P>313. <B>tickle o' the sere</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Gloss. s. v.</I> sere): Tickled, or delighted with the
dry jokes of the character spoken of. <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, those who are asthmatical,
and to whom laughter is most uneasy. This is the case (I am told) with those
whose lungs are tickled by the <I>sere</I> or <I>serum.</I> <SC>Malone</SC>: The word &lquo;sere&rquo; I am
unable to explain, and suspect it to be corrupt. Perhaps we should read: &lquo;tickled
o' the <I>scene,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> by the scene. <SC>Douce</SC>: The same expression occurs in Howard's
<I>Defensative against the poyson of supposed prophecies,</I> 1620: &lquo;Discovering the
moods and humors of the vulgar sort to be so loose and tickle of the seare,&rquo; &amp;c.,
fol. 31. Every one has felt that dry tickling in the throat and lungs which excites
coughing. Hamlet's meaning may be, &lquo;the clown shall convert even their coughing
into laughter.&rquo; <SC>White</SC>: The whole speech is ironical, and here, as in his famous
directions to the players, Hamlet is severest upon the Clown, who, he says, will have
to be content with such semblance of laughter as comes from those who are tickled
not by his jokes, but by a dry cough,&mdash;&lquo;o' the sere.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC>: Correctly, per-
haps, &lquo;tickle o' the sere.&rquo; It appears to signify those easily moved to the expression
of mirth. <SC>Halliwell</SC>: <I>Light of the seare</I> is equivalent to light-heeled, loose in
character. <I>Tickle of the sear,</I> wanton, immodest. In the present passage it means
those whose lungs are wanton, or excited to laughter by coarse ribaldry. See the
following (cited by Steevens): &lquo;She that . . . wyll abyde whysperynge in the eare,
Thynke ye her tayle is not lyght of the seare.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Commune Secretary and Jalowsye,</I>
n. d. [ed. Hindley, vol. i, p. 41]. <SC>Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 22 July, 1871): The
<I>sere,</I> or, as it is now spelt, <I>sear</I> (or <I>scear</I>) of a gun-lock is the bar or balance-lever
interposed between the trigger on the one side, and the tumbler and other mechanism
on the other, and is so called from its acting the part of a serre, or talon, in gripping
that mechanism and preventing its action. It is, in fact, a paul or stop-catch. When
the trigger is made to act on one end of it, the other end releases the tumbler, the
mainspring acts, and the hammer, flint, or match falls. Hence Lombard (1596), as
quoted in Halliwell's <I>Archaic Dict.,</I> says, &lquo;Even as a pistole that is ready charged
and bent will flie off by-and-by, if a man do but touch the <I>seare.</I>&rquo; Now if the lock
be so made of purpose, or be worn, or be faulty in construction, this sear, or grip,
may be so tickle or ticklish in its adjustment that a slight touch or even jar may dis-
place it, and then, of course, the gun goes off. Hence &lquo;light,&rquo; or &lquo;tickle of the
sear&rquo; (equivalent to, like a hair-trigger), applied metaphorically, means that which
can be started into action at a mere touch, or on the slightest provocation, or on
what ought to be no provocation at all. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The real meaning is just the re-

and <I>Poetaster</I> were performed there by the Children of Queen Elizabeth's chapel in

<C>[320. &lquo;<B>inhibition.</B>&rquo;]</C>
<P><I>Antonio's Revenge.</I> Many of Lyly's plays were represented by them about the same
time; and, in 1607, Chapman's <I>Bussy d'Ambois</I> was performed by them with great
applause. It was probably in this and some other noisy tragedies of the same kind

Winwood, 28 March, 1605, which might lead us to infer that the words found only
in the Folio were added at that time: &lquo;The plays do not forbear to present upon the
stage the whole course of this present time, not sparing the king, state, or religion,
in so great absurdity and with such liberty that any would be afraid to hear them.&rquo;&mdash;
<I>Memorials,</I> ii, 54. Or the words in the Folio might have been added in 1612, in
which year Heywood's <I>Apologie for Actors</I> was published, containing the following
passage, which leads us to infer that the little <I>eyases</I> were the persons guilty of the
<I>late innovation,</I> or practice of introducing personal abuse on the stage: &lquo;Now to
speake of some abuse lately crept into the quality, as an inueighing against the State,
the Court, the Law, the Citty, and their gouernements, with the particularizing of
priuate mens humors (yet alive) Noble-men &amp; others. I know it distastes many;
neither do I any way approue it, nor dare I by any meanes excuse it. The liberty
which some arrogate to themselues, committing their bitternesse, and liberall inuec-
tiues against all estates, to the mouthes of Children, supposing their iuniority to be a
priuiledge for any rayling, be it neuer so violent, I could aduise all such, to curbe
and limit this presumed liberty within the bands of discretion and gonernment. But
wise and iuditial Censurers, before whom such complaints shall at any time hereafter
come, wil not (I hope) impute these abuses to any transgression in vs, who haue
euer been carefull and prouident to shun the like.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC> thinks that they
were obliged to travel because of the license granted to a new description of actors,
who had met with the most extravagant applauses and success. <SC>Collier</SC> says,
that this passage probably refers to the limiting of public theatrical performances
to the two theatres, the Globe on the Bankside, and the Fortune in Golden Lane,
in 1600 and 1601. The players, by a &lquo;late innovation,&rquo; were &lquo;inhibited,&rquo; or for-
bidden, to act in or near &lquo;the city,&rquo; and therefore travelled,&rquo; or <I>strolled,</I> into the
country. See Collier's <I>Hist. of Engl. Dram. Poetry and the Stage,</I> i, 311.
<SC>Clarendon</SC> doubts the validity of Steevens's explanation of the &lquo;inhibition,&rquo; and
thinks that the &lquo;late innovation&rquo; does not clearly refer to the introduction of per-
sonal abuse on the stage, and adds the following conclusive note: For a very long
period there had been a strong opposition in the city to theatrical performances. In
March, 1573-4, the Lord Mayor and Corporation declined to license a place for
them within the city. In 1575 players were again forbidden to act there, and in
consequence, in 1576, the Blackfriars Theatre was built without the limits of the
jurisdiction of the city. In 1581 the Lord Mayor was ordered to allow performances
in the city by certain companies of actors on week days only, being holidays; but
his inhibition must have remained still in force, because in the following year, 1582,
the Lords of the Council pray the Lord Mayor to revoke his inhibition against play-
ing on holidays. In 1589 Lord Burleigh appears to have directed the Lord Mayor
to silence the players of the Lord Admiral's and the Lord Strange's companies for
introducing matters of state and religion upon the stage. To this apparently Nash
alludes in his <I>Return of the renowned Cavaliero Pasquile of England,</I> published in
1589. In this year, also, proposals were made to appoint two commissioners to act

<P>with the Master of the Revels for the purpose of examining and licensing every
play, and so restraining the abuses of the actors. About the year 1590 the Children
of St Paul's were silenced, and the interdict was apparently not removed till about
1600. In 1597 the Lord Admiral's players were restrained for a time from playing
in consequence of having brought out Nash's <I>Isle of Dogs,</I> a play in which per-
sonal satire was probably introduced, and for which the author was imprisoned. In
1601 a letter was addressed by the Lords of the Council to certain Justices of the
Peace in the county of Middlesex in which the actors at the Curtain Theatre, Shore
ditch, are charged with satirising living persons and introducing personalities into
their plays. It is difficult, therefore, to see at what precise period the explanation
offered by Steevens could be true. In 1604 the indulgence of the actors in personal
abuse could hardly be called an &lquo;innovation;&rquo; on the contrary, it was a practice
from which the stage had never been entirely free. If we were to add to the con-
jectures upon this point, we should be disposed to suggest that the &lquo;innovation&rquo; re-
ferred to was the license which had been given on 30 Jan. 1603-4 to the Children of
the Queen's Revels to play at the Blackfriars Theatre and other convenient places.
The Blackfriars Theatre belonged to the company of which Sh. was a member,
formerly the Lord Chamberlain's and at this time His Majesty's servants. The
popularity of the Children may well have driven the older actors into the country
and so have operated as an &lquo;inhibition,&rquo; though in the strict sense of the word no
formal &lquo;inhibition&rquo; was issued. If by &lquo;inhibition&rquo; Sh. merely meant, as we think
most probable, that the actors were practically thrown out of employment, it seems
also likely that by &lquo;innovation&rquo; he meant the authority given to the Children to act at
the regularly licensed theatres. It must be borne in mind, in reference to this, that
nothing is said either of &lquo;inhibition&rquo; or &lquo;innovation&rquo; in Q<SUB>1</SUB>, 1603, but that the sentence
containing both is first introduced in Q<SUB>2</SUB>, 1604. It is to the interval, therefore, that
we must look for the explanation. In offering this conjecture we have not lost sight
of the fact that, after all, remembering how chary Sh. is of contemporary allusions,
no special occurrence may be hinted at, although in what follows in the Folio edition
a satire upon the Children's performances was clearly intended. In Chalmers's
<I>Farther Account of the Early English Stage</I> (Var.'21, iii, 423-429) will be found
a list of payments, at sundry times during the reign of Elizabeth, to the Children of
Paul's, Westminster, Windsor, and the Chapel Royal, and an enumeration of the
plays performed by them and by the Children of the Revels from 1571 to 1633.
The quotation cited by Malone from Heywood shows, indeed, that the Children
indulged in personalities, but not that any &lquo;inhibition&rquo; was the consequence. Be-
sides, it refers to a subsequent date. <SC>Fleay</SC> (<I>Sh. Manual,</I> p. 41): This is not
necessarily to be applied to the first order of the Privy Council for the restraint
of the immoderate use of playhouses (made 22 June, 1600), for this order proved
ineffectual; but rather to their second order, made 31 Dec., 1601. <I>The Fortune</I>
and <I>The Globe</I> were allowed to remain open; the others were closed, owing to the
personal allusions indulged in by some of the companies. [See note III, ii, 267. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>versation; namely, that point where the dialogue is most lively, where question and
answer follow each other stroke on stroke, and the speakers are the most excited.
These &lquo;little eyases,&rquo; therefore, continually cry out as though they were at the very
height of conversation. <SC>Staunton</SC>: The phrase, derived perhaps from the defiant
crowing of a cock upon his midden, really meant, we believe, like&mdash;&lquo;Stood chal-
lenger on mount of all the age,&rquo; to crow over or challenge all comers to a conten-
tion. In line 424, Hamlet uses the phrase, &lquo;cried in the top,&rquo; where it evidently
means <I>crowed over.</I> Again, in Armin's <I>Nest of Ninnies,</I> the author, alluding to
fencers or players at single stick, talks of &lquo;making them expert till they cry it up in
the top of question.&rquo; [p. 55, <I>Sh. Soc.</I> vol. x.] <SC>White</SC>: To &lquo;cry in the top&rquo; seems
rather to mean to assume superiority;&mdash;as afterwards Hamlet, speaking of people
who set him down about the play from which he quotes, says their judgments &lquo;cried
in the top&rquo; of his. I can conjecture no specific origin of the phrase. It might well
have been formed on the mere general force of the words which compose it. <SC>Wel-
lesley</SC> (<I>Stray Notes, &amp;c.,</I> 1865, p. 33): &lquo;Question&rquo; is not <I>conversation, dialogue,</I> but
the old word, still in use in other languages, for <I>the rack.</I> The pulleys were strained,
and the witnesses hoisted to the utmost height, till the desired confession was elicited;
and so the phrase, &lquo;top of question,&rquo; came to be metaphorically applied; as, for in-
stance, to the highest stretch of the voice or the utmost force of an argument. The
<I>top of the bent</I> [III, ii, 367] was a phrase of the same kind, borrowed from those bows
which were not bent by hand, but by a <I>rack.</I> &lquo;These bows . . . were bent only by a
man's immediate strength, without the help of any bender or <I>rack</I> that are used with
others.&rquo;&mdash;Wilkins's <I>Mathematical Magick.</I> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): Recite at the very highest
pitch of the voice. Wellesley's explanation is wrong. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: I am con-
vinced that this phrase in the MS was: <I>that cry on the top, out of question,</I>&rquo; that is,
they cry at the highest pitch of the voice, where it is wholly inappropriate. [And
even so is the text amended. <SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: That is, pipe out their parts at the top
of their shrill infantine voices. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Probably, to speak in a high key,
dominating conversation. For &lquo;question&rquo; in this sense, see <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> IV, i, 70.

<P>353. <B>appurtenance</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Proper accompaniment.
<P>354. <B>comply with</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This is again apparenlly used in the sense of <I>to
compliment</I> in V, ii, 178. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: That is, compliantly assume this dress and
fashion of behaviour. <SC>Singer</SC>: Hamlet has received his old school-fellows with
somewhat of the coldness of suspicion hitherto, but he now remembers that this is
not courteous. He, therefore, rouses himself to give them a proper reception:
&lquo;Come, then, the appurtenance of welcome is <I>fashion</I> and <I>ceremony;</I> let me <SC>embrace</SC>
you in this <I>fashion,</I> lest,&rquo; &amp;c. That to <I>comply with</I> was to <I>embrace</I> will appear from
the following passages in Herrick: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash;witty Ovid, by Whom faire Corinna sits;
and doth comply With Yvorie wrists, his Laureat Head,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;[<I>Hesperides,</I> p. 279,
ed. 1846]; also, &lquo;And then a Rug of carded wooll, Which, . . . seem'd to comply,
Cloudlike the daintie Deitie.&rquo;&mdash;[<I>Ib.</I> p. 224.] <SC>White</SC>: In my judgement &lquo;comply
with&rquo; (not &lquo;comply&rquo; alone) has here, and in V, ii, 178, merely the sense of &lquo;com-
pliment.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC>: Let me <I>fraternize</I> or conjoin with you in the customary
mode; not &lquo;Let me <I>compliment.</I>&rquo; <I>To comply</I> literally means <I>to enfold.</I> <SC>Claren-
don</SC>: Use ceremony with you in this fashion. [An interpretation which applies
equally well to V, ii, 178.]
<P>354. <B>this garb</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: The reading of the Ff makes the better sense, where
&lquo;the&rquo; is used generically.
<P>355. <B>extent</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The degree of courtesy dealt out. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2):
Is there not room to doubt here whether &lquo;extent&rquo; has not been misprinted for <I>ostent,</I>
a word Sh. not unfrequently uses in the sense of external show? We have no
authority for the change, but the word &lquo;extent&rquo; is not very intelligible here, though
it may be reconciled to a meaning. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Condescension; the behaviour
of a superior to an inferior when he makes the first advances. See &lquo;extend&rquo; in <I>All'
Well,</I> III, vi, 73.

<P>360. <B>north-north-west</B>] <SC>Francke</SC>: Perhaps the meaning is: Great, powerful
tempests in the moral world, apparitions from the mysterious Hereafter, can make
me mad, can crush my reason; but such people as you are, who come around me
with sweet phrases and mock friendship, I have yet wit enough to elude.
<P>361. <B>handsaw</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Hanmer's alteration serves to show us the origin
of the proverb which was a common one in Shakespeare's day. <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 133):
The speaker's meaning is that opportunity did not serve for his purpose; when it
did, it would be seen he had his right senses. <SC>Nares</SC>: <I>Hernshaw, heronshaw,</I> or
<I>hernshew</I> is a heron or hern. &lquo;As when a cast of falcons make their flight, At an
hernshaw, that lyes aloft on wing.&rquo;&mdash;Spenser, <I>Fairie Queene,</I> VI, vii, 9. &lquo;To know
a hawk from a <I>hernshaw,</I>&rquo; was certainly the original form of the proverb. But the
corruption had taken place before the time of Sh. It is <I>handsaw</I> in Ray's <I>Proverbs,</I>
p. 196, ed. 1768. <SC>White</SC>: I suspect that in Shakespeare's time the corrupted phrase
had, to general acceptation, lost its original meaning, and that the comparison was
supposed to be between the tool called a hawk and a handsaw. There was, and I
believe there still is, a hooked cutting tool called a hawk. <SC>Halliwell</SC>: No evi-
dence in support of the supposition that &lquo;handsaw&rquo; is a corruption of <I>hernshaw</I> has
been produced; the phrase always occurs in this form. It is not necessary to believe
that the supposition is correct, the wildest incongruities being often found in pro-
verbial phrases of this description. It is suggested by C. W. H. in the <I>Athen&aelig;um</I>
(30 December, 1865), that Sh. might have become acquainted, through North's Plu-
tarch, with the significations attached by the &AElig;gyptians to the hawk and heron re-
spectively,&mdash;the former was the emblem of the North wind, and the latter of the South
wind. &lquo;Hamlet, though feigning madness, yet claims sufficient sanity to distinguish
a hawk from a hernshaw when the wind is southerly; that is, in the time of the
migration of the latter to the north, when the former is not to be seen.&rquo; J. A. G.
(<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 6 July, 1867) suggests <I>anser,</I> &lquo;the generic name for our domestic water-
fowl.&rquo; <SC>J. A. Picton</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 30 Nov. 1872) suggests that &lquo;hawk&rquo; may refer, not
only to the bill-hook, mentioned by White, but also to a plasterer's instrument so
named. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: In Suffolk and Norfolk &lquo;hernsew is pronounced &lquo;harnsa,&rquo;
from which to &lquo;handsaw&rquo; is but a single step. For the following explanation of the
earlier part of this obscure passage, we are indebted to Mr <SC>J. C. Heath</SC>, formerly
Fellow of Trinity Hall, Cambridge: &lquo;The expression obviously refers to the sport
of hawking. Most birds, especially one of heavy flight like the heron, when roused
by the falconer or his dog, would fly down or with the wind, in order to escape.
When the wind is from the north, the heron flies towards the south, and the spectator

<P>373. <B>actor</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: The fun here consists in Hamlet's mentioning an

purpose, as well as Middleton in <I>A Mad World, my Masters.</I> <SC>Blackstone</SC>: It
was an interjection used at Oxford, when any one began a story that was generally
known before. <SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 231): This expression may continue to exercise the skill
of the critics, if they are disposed to pursue the game through the following mazes:
&lquo;Anno DCCCXL Ludovicus imperator ad mortem infirmatur, cujus cibus per XL
dies solummodo die dominica dominicum corpus fecit. Cum vidisset d&aelig;monem
astare, dixit <I>buez, buez,</I> quod significat <I>foras, foras.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Alberici monachi trium fontium
<I>Chronicon,</I> Leips. 1698. Ducange, under the article <I>Buzi,</I> says, &lquo;Interpretatur
despectus vel contemptus. Papias (Ab Hebraico <I>Bus</I> vel <I>bouz,</I> sprevit).&rquo;
<P>377. <B>Then . . . ass</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: This seems to be the line of a ballad. <SC>Elze</SC>: At
all events, it contains biting ridicule of Polonius, who has just said that &lquo;The actors
are come hither&mdash;upon my honour!&rquo;

Unity of Place; &lquo;poem unlimited&rquo; refers to those that disregarded such restrictions.

given &lquo;freely to use and exercise the Arte and facultie of playing Comedies, Trage-
dies, Histories, Enterludes, Moralls, Pastoralls, Stage plaies &amp; such other like.&rquo; To
this last description, &lquo;stage plaies,&rquo; I suppose the &lquo;poem unlimited&rquo; belonged, which,
I presume, was an extemporised piece.

<P>382. <B>writ . . . liberty</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 133): This means, pieces written in rule, and
pieces out of rule. <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Writ&rquo; is used for <I>writing</I> by Shakespeare's contem-
poraries. Thus, in <I>The Apologie of Pierce Pennilesse,</I> by Nashe, 1593: &lquo;For the
lowsie circumstance of his poverty before his death, and sending that miserable <I>writte</I>
to his wife,&rquo; &amp;c. Again, in Bishop Earle's <I>Character of a mere dull Physician,</I> 1638:
&lquo;Then follows a <I>writ</I> to his drugger in a strange tongue,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;For the
observance of the rules of the drama, while they take such liberties as are allowable,
they are the only men.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>: The meaning probably is, that the players were good,
whether at written productions or at extemporal plays, where liberty was allowed to the
performers to invent the dialogue, in imitation of the Italian <I>commedie al improviso.</I>
See <I>Hist. of Engl. Dram. Poetry,</I> iii, 393. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 265): Read <I>wit.</I>
&lquo;Writ&rquo; for <I>composition</I> is not English. It is as if we should say, <I>the laws of poem</I>
for <I>the laws of poetry,</I> or talk of so and so being contrary to <I>the genius of ode,</I> mean-
ing <I>the genius of lyrical composition.</I> The passages quoted by the Var. commenta.
tors are utterly irrelevant. The same erratum occurs, <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> III, ii, 225: &lquo;For
I haue neyther <I>writ</I> nor words, nor worth.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Probably the author did
not intend that we should find a distinct meaning in Polonius's words. <SC>Corson</SC>:
The Qq and Ff connect in construction, &lquo;for the law of writ and the liberty,&rquo; with
Seneca and Plautus, and not with &lquo;these are the only men,&rquo; which evidently refers to
the actors he's talking about. &lquo;Liberty&rquo; should he construed with &lquo;law;&rquo; the law
and the liberty of writ [writing]. And &lquo;law&rquo; and &lquo;liberty&rquo; seem to refer, respec-
tively, to &lquo;heavy&rquo; and &lquo;light.&rquo; This respective construction is frequent in Sh. See
<I>Macb.</I> I, iii, 60, 61; <I>Ham.</I> III, i, 151; <I>Wint. Tale,</I> III, ii, 160-162; <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I>
III, ii, 15-18; IV, xv, 25, 26; <I>Com. of Err.</I> II, ii, 112-117; <I>Temp.</I> I, ii, 335, 336;
<I>Mid. N. D.</I> III, i, 98-101.

<P>399. <B>It came to pass</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: &lquo;As he had a daughter, of course he got
into a scrape,&rquo; is the inference suggested.
<P>400. <B>pious chanson</B>] <SC>Pope</SC> explained the reading of F<SUB>1</SUB> as the name of &lquo;old
ballads sung on bridges.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC> defines &lquo;pious chansons&rquo; as ballads containing
some scriptural history, sung about the streets, and the &lquo;first row&rquo; is the first column
of the roughly printed sheet. <SC>Nares</SC> thinks the reading of the Ff apparently non-
sense. Shakespeare intended, perhaps, to mix French and English, but both seem to
have been corrupted by the players and printers. <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. 1) really decides the
question by an appeal to Q<SUB>1</SUB>, where the corresponding phrase is &lquo;the fir$t ver$e of the
godly Ballet&rquo; [line 1016]. But <SC>Hunter</SC> (<I>New Illust.</I> ii, 232) opened the question
again by advocating the reading of the F<SUB>1</SUB>, on the score of its being the latest intention
of the poet, and the proper one. &lquo;In fact, in France, the trivial ballad, such as that re-
ferred to, is called in ordinary discourse a <I>pons chanson,</I> or a <I>chanson du Pont Neuf.</I>
&ldquo;Vaudevilles, ou Chanson du Pont Neuf, les chansons communes qui se chantent
parmi le peuple avec une grande facilit&eacute;, et sans art: <I>Trivialis cantilena.</I>&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Dic-
tionnaire de Trevoux,</I> s. v. <I>Chanson.</I>&rquo; In reply to Hunter, <SC>Knight</SC> [ap. <SC>Dyce</SC>] perti-
nently asks: &lquo;A popular ballad is called even in modern dictionaries a <I>chanson du
Pont Neuf,</I>&mdash;but where is the authority for <I>Pons Chanson?</I>&rquo; [According to <SC>Littr&eacute;</SC>,
the secondary meaning of <I>Pont-Neuf</I> is: &lquo;Chanson populaire sur un air tr&egrave;s-connu,
<I>e. g.</I> Il sait tous les ponts-neufs qui courent les rues.&rquo; (In this sense it is not
printed with capital letters.) But nowhere does he give such a phrase as <I>pons
chansons</I> nor <I>chanson,</I> used absolutely when meaning the specific <I>chansons du pont-
neuf.</I> <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>401. <B>my</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (<I>New Illust.</I> ii, 233): &lquo;My&rquo; does not necessarily refer back
to the speaker, but may he used ethically. <SC>Corson</SC>: It is so used in the Ff read-
ing; in that of the Qq it is used objectively.
<P>401. <B>abridgements</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: He calls the players afterwards [line 507] the
brief chronicles of the time; but I think he now means: those who will shorten
my talk. <SC>Steevens</SC> (Note on <I>Mid. N. D.</I> V, i, 39): By abridgement Sh. may mean
a dramatic performance, which crowds the events of years into a few hours. <SC>Dyce</SC>
(<I>Gloss.</I>): In this place it is applied to the players, as being, I presume, the persons
who represent an <I>abridgement.</I> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Hamlet uses the word in a double
sense. The players by entering abridge his talk.

<P>404. <B>valanced</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: That is, fringed with a beard. The valance is the
fringes or drapery hanging round the tester of a bed. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: That is, is be-
come manly and fierce, as in <I>As You Like It,</I> II, vii, 150, &lquo;bearded like the pard.&rquo;
<SC>Staunton</SC>: Compare the advice of Iago to Roderigo;&mdash;&lquo;Follow thou the wars; defeat
thy favour with an usurped beard,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> assume a martial aspect; and also the context
in Hamlet's speech, &lquo;comest thou to <I>beard</I> me in Denmark?&rquo; where the point is lost
without the fierceness implied by &lquo;valiant.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Valiant&rquo; is probably a mere
misprint. <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: Supposed to be from the stuff having been made at Valencia
or Valence.
<P>406. <B>By'r</B>] Pronounced <I>beer</I> (<SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Vers.</I> p. 191).
<P>406. <B>ladyship</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: In Shakespeare's time, and till after the restoration
of Charles II, female parts were played by boys. (Compare <I>Two Gent.</I> IV, iv, 165.)
Probably the first woman who ever appeared on the English stage played Desde-
mona, on Saturday, 6 December, 1660. [Who that actress was has not been ascer-
tained; a Mrs Hughs acted this part, in this company, in 1663, and to her may
belong the honour; although the received tradition is that it is due to Mrs Saunder-
son, afterwards Mrs Betterton. The gross absurdity of entrusting to boys, and even
to men, the r&ocirc;les of women is well hit off in the doggerel &lquo;Prologue, to introduce the
first woman that came to act on the stage:&rquo;
<BQ>
&lquo;Our women are defective, and so sized<LB>
You'd think they were some of the guard disguised:<LB>
For, to speak truth, men act, that are between<LB>
Forty and fifty, wenches of fifteen;<LB>
With bone so large, and nerve so incompliant,<LB>
When you call Desdemona, enter Giant.&rquo;<LB>

defines it as a personal pronoun of the first or second person, used, in familiar or
jocose style, to denote the subjective interest which the speaker or the person ad-
dressed feels in some allusion to a circumstance which objectively is regarded as
accomplished independently of that interest. See also V, i, 157.

<P>418. <B>cried in the top</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, whose judgement I had the highest
opinion of. <SC>Johnson</SC>: I think it means only, that <I>were higher than mine.</I> <SC>Heath</SC>:
Whose judgement, in such matters, was in much higher vogue than mine. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
Perhaps it means only: whose judgement was more clamorously delivered than mine.
We still say of a bawling actor, that he speaks <I>on the top of his voice.</I> <SC>Henley</SC>:
To <I>over-top</I> is a hunting term applied to a dog when he gives more tongue than the
rest of the cry. To this, I believe, Hamlet refers, and he afterwards mentions a <SC>cry</SC>
<I>of players.</I> <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Proclaimed not merely in addition to my voice and cen-
sure, but with a tone of authority that mine could not sound. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Hen-

I need only make one observation on all this; that, thus interpreted, it is the justest
picture of a good tragedy, wrote on the ancient rules. 2. A second proof that this
speech was given to be admired is from the intrinsic merit of the speech itself, which
contains the description of a circumstance very happily imagined, namely: Ilium and
Priam's falling together, with the effect it had on the destroyer. Now this circum-

have well deserved a place in Virgil's second book of the <I>&AElig;neid,</I> even though the
work had been carried on to that perfection which the Roman poet had conceived.

best character, approves it; the player is deeply affected in repeating it; and only
the foolish Polonius tired with it. The player changes color, and the tears start from
his eyes. But our author was too good a judge of nature to make bombast and un-
natural sentiment produce such an effect. But if any one will still say that Sh. in-
tended to represent a player unnaturally and fantastically affected, we must appeal
to Hamlet, that is, to Sh. himself in this matter; who, on the reflection he makes
upon the player's emotion, in order to excite his own revenge, gives not the least hint
that the player was unnaturally or injudiciously moved. On the contrary, his fine
description of the actor's emotion shows he thought just otherwise. And indeed
had Hamlet esteemed this emotion anything unnatural, it had been a very improper
circumstance to spur him to his purpose. That which supports the common opinion

<P>Hecuba are also in the Sh. speech, it is impossible to imagine that he meant these
lines for mere bombast. I do not quote the Hecuba part, as there is nothing corre-
sponding to it in Nash, and it is in every one's hands. The finest bit in Nash is the
picture of Pyrrhus:
<BQ>
&lquo;So leaning on his sword he stood stone still,<LB>
Viewing the fire wherewith rich Ilion burnt;&rquo;<LB>
</BQ>
<P>and this Sh. has capped with lines 458-466. There is a moral certainty that these
passages are competitors for popular favor. . . . . On all grounds alike, then, I hold
that this scene was written by Sh. in 1594, as a supplement to Marlowe's unfinished
play, in competition with Nash, and that it was introduced by him into the first
draught of <I>Hamlet</I> in 1601 or thereabouts.
<P>435. <B>gules</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This signifies <I>red</I> in the barbarous jargon of heraldry.
Also in <I>Timon,</I> IV, iii, 59. <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: From the red color of the mouth.
<I>Gueule,</I> the mouth, throat, gullet. <SC>Glossary</SC> <I>of Terms Used in British Heraldry:</I>
Perhaps from the Persian <I>ghul,</I> a rose; if so, it was prohably introduced by the
Crusaders.

<SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;Trick'd,&rquo; like the following participles, &lquo;bak'd&rquo; and &lquo;impasted,&rquo; belongs to
&lquo;gules,&rquo; not to &lquo;he.&rquo;

<P>456. <B>declining</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: This use of the word, which is frequent in Sh.,
I have not observed in any contemporary. See also I, v, 50. [Elsewhere Caldecott
adduces this as an argument in favor of the belief that this extract is Shakespeare's
own composition. See his note on line 437.]
<P>458. <B>painted</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Sh. was probahly here thinking of the tremendous per-
sonages often represented in old tapestry, whose uplifted swords stick in the air, and
do nothing. <SC>Delius</SC>: The simile is amplified in <I>Macb.</I> V, viii, 25-27.
<P>459. <B>neutral</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Not standing &lquo;between his will and matter.&rquo; But
indifferent to both. So &lquo;neutral&rquo; is opposed to &lquo;loyal,&rquo; in <I>Macb.</I> II, iii, 106.
<P>460. For single lines of two or three accents interspersed amid ordinary verses, see
<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect;&sect; 511, 512); so, too, II, ii, 540, 557, 563; III, iii, 78; and <I>Macb.</I> I, ii, 20.
<P>462. <B>rack</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): A mass of vapoury clouds. So Bacon's <I>Sylva Sylva-
rum,</I> &sect; 115, p. 32, ed. 1658. &lquo;The winds in the upper region, which move the
clouds ahove (which we call the rack).&rquo;
<P>464. <B>hush</B>] For other instances of the conversion of one part of speech into
another, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 22.
<P>465. <B>region</B>] <SC>C. Arendon</SC>: Originally a division of the sky marked out by the
Roman augurs. In later times the atmosphere was divided into three regions, upper,
middle, and lower. By Sh. the word is used to denote the air generally.
<P>466. <B>a-work</B>] See I, v, 19.

<P>471. <SC>Dryden</SC> (<I>Preface to Troilus and Cressida,</I> 1679): What a pudder is here
kept in raising the expression of triffling thoughts. Would not a man have thought
that the Poet had heen bound Prentice to a Wheel-wright for his first Rant? and had
followed a Ragman, for the clout and blanket, in the second? Fortune is painted
on a wheel; and therefore the writer in a rage, will have Poetical Justice done upon
every member of that Engin; after this execution be bowls the Nave downhill,
from Heaven to the Fiends: (an unreasonable long mark a man would think;) 'tis
well there are no solid Orbs to stop it in the way, or no Element of fire to consume
it; but when it came to the earth, it must be monstrous heavy, to break ground as
low as to the Center. His making milch the burning eyes of Heaven was a pretty
tollerable flight too; and I think no man ever drew milk out of eyes before him: yet
to make the wonder greater, these eyes were burning. Such a sight indeed were
enough to have rais'd passion in the Gods, but to excuse the effects of it, he tells you
perhaps they did not see it. [This passage is criticised not as Shakespeare's, but as
&lquo;written by some other poet.&rquo; <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>473. <B>fellies</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Iantes: The fellowes of a wheele; the peeces (of
wood) whereeof the ring, or the time consists.&rquo;&mdash;Cotgrave.
<P>478. <B>jig</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: A jig was not, in Shakespeare's time, only a dance, but a
ludicrous dialogue in metre, and of the lowest kind, like Hamlet's conversation
with Ophelia [III, ii, 105-115]. In <I>The Hog hath lost his Pearl,</I> 1614, one of the
players comes to solicit a gentleman to <I>write a jig</I> for him. Many of these jigs are
entered in the Stationers' Company:&mdash;&lquo;Philips his Jigg of the Slyppers,&rquo; 1595;
&lquo;Kempe's Jigg of the Kitchen-stuff Woman,&rquo; 1595. <SC>Malone</SC>: So, also, in the Pro-
logue to Fletcher's <I>Love's Pilgrimage</I> [misquoted; it should be the <I>Fair Maid of the
Inn</I>&mdash;Collier's <I>Hist. Eng. Dram. Poetry,</I> iii, 380]: &lquo;A jig shall be clapp'd at, and
every rhyme Prais'd and applauded,&rquo; &amp;c. A jig was not always in the form of a
dialogue; it signified a ludicrous metrical composition, as well as a dance. So in
Florio: &lquo;<I>Frottola,</I> a countrie gigge, or round, or countrie song, or wanton verse.&rquo;
<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Hist. Eng. Dram. Poetry,</I> iii, 380): We have no extant specimen of any
such performance. It seems to have been a ludicrous composition in rhyme, sung, or

<P>said, by the clown, and accompanied by dancing and playing upon the pipe and

<I>gigge,</I> though pronounced with <I>g</I> soft, after the Italian) was a ballad or ditty sung to
a fiddle. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Note on Prologue to Fair Maid of the Inn</I>): More persons than
one were sometimes employed in a jig; and there is reason to believe that the per-
formance was of considerable length, lasting even, on some occasions, for an hour.

is acted.&rquo; [See <SC>Chappell</SC> (<I>Popular Music of the Olden Time,</I> p. 495), where the
tune is given of <I>The King's jig,</I> which is supposed to have been one of the tunes
to which Charles II danced. <SC>Collier</SC> says that some of Tarleton's jigs, both music
and words, survive in MS.]
<P>480. <B>mobled</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is <I>veiled.</I> Sandys [<I>Travels,</I> i, 69, ed. 1637&mdash;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>], speaking of the Turkish women, says: &lquo;their heads and faces are so
mabled in fine linen that nothing is to be seen of them hut their eyes.&rquo; <SC>Upton</SC> (p.
299): This designedly affected expression seems to be formed from Virg. <I>&AElig;n.</I> ii, 40:
Magna comitante caterva, <I>i. e.</I> mob-led Queen. <SC>Farmer</SC>: &lquo;The moon does mobble
up herself.&rquo;&mdash;Shirley's <I>Gentleman of Venice.</I> <SC>Holt White</SC>: It is nothing but a
depravation of <I>muffled.</I> &lquo;Mobbled nine days in my considering cap.&rquo;&mdash;Ogilby's
<I>Fables.</I> <SC>Malone</SC>: A few lines lower we are told that she had &lquo;a clout&rquo; upon her
head. To <I>mab</I> (in the North pronounced <I>mob</I>), says Ray, in his <I>Dict. of North
Country Words,</I> is &lquo;to dress carelessly. <I>Mabs are slatterns.</I>&rquo; <SC>Coleridge</SC>: A <I>mob-
cap</I> is still a word in common use for a morning-cap, which conceals the whole head
of hair, and passes under the chin. It is nearly the same as the night-cap, that is, it
is an imitation of it, so as to answer the purpose (&lquo;I am not drest for company&rquo;), and
yet reconciling it with neatness and perfect purity. <SC>Delius</SC>: The real meaning
which Sh. attached to it here is still doubtful; that an unusual word was intended is
plain, both from Hamlet's objection to it and Polonius's approval of it. <SC>G. H. of
S.</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 23 July, 1864) suggests <I>maddled,</I> a word in use in Yorkshire, mean-
ing not absolutely mad, but bewildered almost to madness.

<P>515. <B>dozen or sixteen lines</B>] See III, ii, 178.
<P>519. <B>mock</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: Hamlet, like the true gentleman that he is, feels that he
has been betrayed into treating the old courtier with something of impatience and
discourtesy; therefore he bids the actor, whom he knows to be naturally and pro-
fessionally disposed to waggery, not forget himself to Polonius on the strength of
the example just given.
<P>522. <B>alone</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: The eagerness shown by Hamlet to be left in peace by
himself appears to be a main evidence of his merely acting a part and <I>assuming</I>
madness; he longs to get rid of the presence of persons before whom he has resolved
to wear a show of insanity. Alone, he is collected, coherent, full of introspection.
That he is neither dispassionate nor cool appears to be the result of his unhappy
source of thought, not the result of derangement; he is morally afflicted, not men-
tally affected.

<P>527. <B>wann'd</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC> upheld <I>warm'd,</I> because the effort to shed tears and the
unusual exertion in a passionate speech would warm and flush the face; no actor
can grow pale at will, and even if he could there is nothing in the fragment to make
him. <SC>Malone</SC> effectually silenced all this by referring to Polonius's speech, line
497. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: We have had an instance of a verb formed from an adjective
in &lquo;pale,&rquo; I, v, 90, where it is transitive.
<P>529. <B>function</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: That is, each power and faculty,&mdash;the whole ener-
gies of soul and body. &lquo;Nature within me seems In all her functions weary of her-
self.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Sams. Agon.</I> 596, <I>i. e.</I> using the term that imparts &lquo;performance or the doing
of a thing&rquo; for &lquo;the power or faculty by which the thing is done.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>:
The whole action of the body. See <I>Macb.</I> I, iii, 140.
<P>530. <B>conceit</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Conception, idea (of the character he was person-
ating). [See also III, iv, 114; IV, v, 43.]
<P>534. <B>cue</B>] <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: The last words of the preceding speech, prefixed to the
speech of an actor in order to let him know when he is to come on the stage. From
the letter Q, by which it was marked. &lquo;Q, a note of entrance for actors, because it
is the first letter of <I>quando,</I> when, showing when to enter and speak.&rquo;&mdash;C. Butler,
<I>Eng. Gram,</I> 1634, in <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 5 Aug. 1865. Minsheu explains it somewhat dif-
ferently: &lquo;A <I>qu,</I> a term used among stage-players, &agrave; Lat. <I>qualis, i. e.</I> at what manner
of word the actors are to begin to speak, one after another hath done his speech.
The French term is <I>replique.</I>
</CC>

<P>537. <B>free</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Free from offence, guiltless. [See &lquo;free souls,&rquo; III, ii, 231.]
<P>541. <B>peak</B>] <SC>Singer</SC>: To <I>mope,</I> to <I>act foolishly and with irresolution.</I>
<P>542. <B>John-a-dreams</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, <I>John of dreams,</I> which means only
<I>John</I> the <I>dreamer;</I> a nickname for any ignorant, silly fellow. Thus the puppet
thrown at during Lent was called <I>Jack-a-lent,</I> and the ignis-fatuus, <I>Jack-a-lanthorn.
John-a-droynes,</I> however, if not a corruption of this nickname, seems to have been
some well-known character, as I have met with more than one allusion to him.
So, in <I>Have with you to Saffron Walden,</I> by Nash, 1596: &lquo;The description of that
poor <I>John-a-droynes</I> his man, whom he had hired,&rquo; &amp;c. <I>John-a-Droynes</I> is like-
wise a foolish character in Whetstone's <I>Promos and Cassandra,</I> 1578. <SC>Collier</SC>: It
is rather a nickname for a sleepy, apathetic fellow. The only mention yet met with
of John-a-dreams is in Armin's <I>Nest of Ninnies,</I> 1608 (see <I>Sh. Soc.</I> vol. x, p. 49):
&lquo;His name is John, indeede, saies the cinnick; but neither John a nods, nor John a
dreames, yet either as you take it.&rquo; John-a-droynes was, in all probability, a different
person.
<P>542. <B>unpregnant</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Not quickened with a new desire of vengeance;
not teeming with revenge. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Having no living thoughts within relating
to my cause. In <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> I, i, 12, &lquo;pregnant in&rquo; is used for &lquo;filled with
knowledge of.&rquo;
<P>544. <B>property</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: This appears here to be used in the sense of &lquo;own
person.&rquo; Compare &lquo;proper life,&rquo; in V, ii, 66. Or possibly it may mean his &lquo;kingly
right.&rquo; The commentators, by their silence, seem to take it in the ordinary modern
sense, which can hardly be. [I suppose it refers to his crown, his wife, everything,
in short, which he might be said to be possessed of, except his life. &lquo;Property&rquo; is
used in its ordinary modern sense in <I>Merry Wives,</I> III, iv, 10. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>545. <B>defeat</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Destruction. <SC>Steevens</SC>: This word is very licen-

<P>552. <B>pigeon-liver'd</B>] <SC>White</SC>: It was supposed that pigeons and doves owed

was in a Choller wrought &ldquo;Only like me my mistress hath no gall.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;Drayton's

so <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> I, iii, 237. [See <SC>Harting's</SC> <I>Ornithology of Sh.</I> p. 185.]
<P>553. <B>oppression</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): It is <I>transgression</I> in the (MS), but &lquo;oppres-
sion&rquo; is no doubt the proper reading. Hamlet is alluding to his own lack of gall,
and to &lquo;oppression&rquo; being bitter to himself. The old annotator seems to have thought
that the hero was referring to <I>transgression</I> on the part of others, which he lacked
gall to make bitter to them. <SC>Dyce</SC>: Hamlet means he lacks gall to make him feel
the bitterness of oppression. <SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Text Vindicated,</I> p. 264) pro-
poses <I>aggression,</I> a conjecture which the Cam. Edd. mark as &lquo;withdrawn.&rquo; I gladly
accept the fact on their testimony.

<P>554, 555. <B>I . . . offal</B>] <SC>Sievers</SC> (<I>Archiv f. n. Sprachen,</I> vol. vi, 1849, p. 12) main-
tains that here Hamlet's plan is revealed, which is, not revenge, not murder, but to
bring Claudius to judgement and legal execution as a criminal, upon whose gibbeted
carcass the region kites can fatten.
<P>556. <B>kindless</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Unnatural. <SC>Singer</SC>: We have &lquo;kindly&rquo; for <I>natural,
i. e.</I> accordance with kind, elsewhere. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Observe how Hamlet checks him-
self in this strain of objurgation, and then, in mere shame of what he has done,
turns to ranting at himself for having ranted.
<P>559. <B>father</B>] <SC>Jennens</SC>: There seems to be no necessity for this word here; or

beautiful reading,&rquo; and <SC>White</SC> declares it &lquo;a fine form of speech, which needs no

of Q<SUB>2</SUB> is &lquo;inferior in both thought and rhythm.&rquo; <SC>Halliwell</SC>: The &lquo;dear departed&rquo;
is still a common phrase, and the ellipsis in the Ff was, I suspect, in consonance
with the phraseology of Shakespeare's time.
<P>561. <B>Must</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> finds a profound meaning in this use of &lquo;must,&rquo; where

<P>13. <B>Niggard</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This is given as the description of the conversation
of a man whom the speaker <I>found not forward to be sounded;</I> and who <I>kept aloof</I>
when they would <I>bring him to confession:</I> but such a description can never pass but at
cross purposes. Shakespeare certainly wrote it just the other way [see Textual Notes].
That this is the true reading, we need but to turn back to the preceding scene, for
Hamlet's conduct, to be satisfied. <SC>Mason</SC>: Warburton forgets that by <I>question,</I> Shake-
speare does not usually mean <I>interrogatory,</I> but <I>discourse;</I> yet in whichever sense the
word be taken, this account given by Ros. agrees but ill with the scene hetween him
and Ham. as actually represented. <SC>Malone</SC>: Slow to begin conversation, but free
enough in his answers to our demands. Guild. has just said that Ham. kept aloof
when they wished to bring him to confess the cause of his distraction: Ros. therefore
here must mean, that <I>up to that point,</I> till they touch'd on that, he was free enough in his
answers. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 236): According to Warburton's reading, the account is that
which the lords must have rendered of their interview with Hamlet, if they meant
to report it truly. Warburton's emendation has not had justice done to it hy other
commentators, but we find it confirmed by Q<SUB>1</SUB>. <SC>Staunton</SC>: Unless &lquo;question&rquo; is
admitted to mean argument, Warburton's emendation yields a truer description of
Hamlet's bearing towards his schoolfellows than that afforded by the old text.
<SC>Tschischwitz</SC> finds an insuperable objection to Warburton's emendation because it
would represent Hamlet as not &lquo;gentlemanlike&rquo; in asking many questions and nig-
gard in replying. &lquo;It is manifest that Rosencrantz here merely gives utterance to a
rule of good manners.&rquo; <SC>Clarke</SC>: If it be borne in mind that Sh. employs &lquo;of&rquo; very
variously, and that he occasionally uses the word &lquo;question&rquo; to signify &lquo;inquisition,&rquo;
&lquo;cross-examining,&rquo; it appears to be evident that here &lquo;niggard of question&rquo; ellipti-
cally expresses &lquo;sparing of speech when we cross-examined him;&rquo; and if it be
remembered how peculiarly Sh. sometimes employs the possessive case, we think it
will be perceived that here &lquo;of our demands&rquo; is employed to express &lquo;of demands
respecting ourselves.&rquo; Thus, then, we take the whole speech to mean&mdash;&lquo;He was
sparing of speech when we questioned him: but of demands respecting ourselves
he was very free in return:&rquo; which interpretation completely tallies with the circum-
stances as they really occurred. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Ros. and Guild. were completely
baffled, and Ham. had the talk almost to himself. Perhaps they did not intend to
give a correct account of the interview.
<P>13. <B>of our demands</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): &lquo;Of&rquo; is altered to <I>to</I> in the (MS), but
needlessly, because &lquo;of&rquo; has here the force of <I>on.</I> <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Of&rquo; may be written
either by attraction from the previous &lquo;of,&rquo; or it may he u<*>ed for &lquo;on,&rquo; as in Marlowe's
<I>Jew of Malta,</I> IV, iv: &lquo;Of that condition I will drink i<*> up.&rquo; [See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 173,
which may perhaps apply to this use of &lquo;of.&rquo; <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>14. <B>assay</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Try his disposition towards.

<C>[56. <B>To be, or not to be.</B>]</C>
<P>deavor to discover the train, and to show how one sentiment produces another.
Hamlet, knowing himself injured in the most enormous and atrocious degree, and
seeing no means of redress but such as must expose him to the extremity of hazard,
meditates on his situation in this manner: <I>Before I can form any rational scheme
of action under this pressure of distress,</I> it is necessary to decide whether, <I>after our
present state, we are</I> to be, or not to be. That is the question, which, as it shall be
answered, will determine <I>whether 'tis nobler,</I> and more suitable to the dignity of
reason, <I>to suffer the outrages of fortune</I> patiently, or to take arms against <I>them,</I> and
by opposing end them, <I>though perhaps</I> with the loss of life. If <I>to die</I> were <I>to sleep,
no more, and by a sleep to end</I> the miseries of our nature, such a sleep were <I>devoutly
to be wished;</I> but if <I>to sleep</I> in death be <I>to dream,</I> to retain our powers of sensibility,
we must <I>pause</I> to consider <I>in that sleep of death what dreams may come.</I> This con-
sideration <I>makes calamity</I> so long endured; <I>for who would bear</I> the vexations of
life, which might be ended <I>by a bare bodkin,</I> but that he is afraid of something in
unknown futurity? This fear it is that gives efficacy to conscience, which, by turn-
ing the mind upon <I>this regard,</I> chills the ardor of <I>resolution,</I> checks the vigor of
<I>enterprise,</I> and makes the <I>current</I> of desire stagnate in inactivity. We may suppose
that he would have applied these general observations to his own case, but that he
discovered Ophelia. <SC>Malone</SC>: Dr Johnson's explication of the first five lines of
this passage is surely wrong. Hamlet is not deliberating whether after our present
state we are to exist or not, but whether he should continue to live, or put an end to
his life; as is pointed out by the second and the three following lines, which are
manifestly a paraphrase on the first: &lquo;Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer, &amp;c.,
or to take arms.&rquo; The question concerning our existence in a future state is not con-
sidered till the tenth line: &lquo;To sleep! perchance to dream!&rquo; &amp;c. See <I>R. of L.</I> 1154.
<SC>Coleridge</SC>: This speech is of absolutely universal interest,&mdash;and yet to which of
all Shakespeare's characters could it appropriately have been given but to Hamlet?
For Jaques it would have been too deep, and for Iago too habitual a communion
with the heart; which in every man belongs, or ought to belong, to all mankind.
<SC>Lamb</SC> (<I>Works,</I> vol. iii, p. 88. London, 1870): How far the very custom of hear-
ing anything <I>spouted,</I> withers and blows upon a fine passage, may be seen in those
speeches from <I>Hen. V.,</I> &amp;c., which are current in the mouths of schoolboys, from
their being to be found in <I>Enfield's Speaker,</I> and such kind of books. I confess
myself utterly unable to appreciate that celebrated soliloquy in <I>Hamlet,</I> beginning,
&lquo;To be, or not to be,&rquo; or to tell whether it be good, bad, or indifferent; it has been
so handled and pawed about by declamatory boys and men, and torn so inhumanly
from its living place and principle of continuity in the play, till it has become to
me a perfect dead member. <SC>Caldecott</SC>, criticising Dr Johnson, says that the <I>train
of thought</I> is obvious enough; it is only the grammatical thread that technically
may call for some unwinding. He denies that any doubt is here raised by Hamlet
as to a future state of existence,&mdash;Hamlet is questioning solely what the condition
of such existence is to be. &lquo;A desire to be out of the world is one of the most
strongly-marked features of Hamlet's character. It is the first wish he utters when
alone: I, ii 129. But he is then restrained from anything heyond a <I>wish</I> for suicide
by religious scruples. The inclination now returns upon him more forcibly (having
more cause for such an impulse), and the prohibition of Heaven does not enter into
consideration. It is here only, what he shall change his life for. This is the lan-

<C>[56. <B>To be, or not to be.</B>]</C>
<P>guage and subject of a man's mind who is nearer death, than he who only wishes
that it were lawful to kill himself.&rquo; <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 236): This soliloquy is placed in
Q<SUB>1</SUB> at the beginning of what is now Act II. It stands there most appropriately. We
have seen, at the close of Act I, the state of Hamlet's mind immediately on having
received the dread information and the solemn command of the Ghost; we are next
presented with what was the state of his mind after a few days' reflection. He
enters <I>solus,</I> in a meditative mood, and the subjects of his meditations are among the
most awful which can engage mortal thoughts. This is to show his <I>natural</I> mind.
Then follows the dialogue with Ophelia, which is intended to show us his <I>artificial</I>
mind,&mdash;that idle, wandering folly which he assumed, the better to accomplish his
object. I can conceive nothing more dramatically proper than this. It prepares for
all the succeeding action in which the natural and the artificial Hamlet are so wildly
combined. Why there was a change in the arrangement, or by whom it was made,
I can no more explain than I can account for many other things connected with the
publication of these dramas. But that the play is greatly injured by the change I
feel a confident conviction; for not only is this soliloquy wanting in the place most
appropriate to it, but it is now found in a place not suitable to it. Such meditations
as these are not such as were likely to arise in the mind of one who had just con-
ceived a design by which he hoped to settle a doubt of a very serious kind, and
who must have been full of curiosity about the issue of his plot. If this speech
is to indicate deliberation concerning suicide, or is even allied to suicide, such de-
liberation is surely out of place when curiosity was awake, and his mind deeply in-
tent on something that he must do. To be sure, the hypothesis of Inconsistency will
explain all; but then it will explain anything. Another very material effect is pro-
duced by the change in the point at which this <I>solus</I> speech is introduced. The line,
&lquo;But look where sadly the poor wretch comes <I>reading,</I>&rquo; immediately precedes his
entry, when, supposing himself to he unobserved, he gives utterance to the musings
of his mind. See also Q<SUB>1</SUB>. It is thus manifest that the poet's intention was that
these should be meditations of Hamlet on something which he found written in a
book which he holds in his hand, a book which spoke of the evils of life, of death,
their cure, of futurity, of the question of being or not being when we have shuffled off
this mortal coil, and that what he says arises out of the argument in the book before
him, and is not to be regarded as thoughts springing up in his own mind. [See note,
line 60.] &lquo;To be, or not to be: ay, there's the point,&rquo; as it is in the Quarto, is equiva-
lent to, &lquo;You, the author, are discussing the question of what shall be hereafter; you
have a great and mighty subject in hand.&rquo; And the words as we now have them,
&lquo;To be, or not to be,&mdash;that is the question,&rquo; are much the same, if we regard, as we
may, &lquo;question&rquo; as equivalent to theme, argument, or subject. [There is also an
analysis of this soliloquy to be found in <SC>Goldsmith's</SC> <I>Works</I> (vol. iii, p. 316, Lon-
don, 1854), which attempts to prove that it is &lquo;a heap of absurdities, whether we
consider the situation, the sentiment, the argumentation, or the poetry.&rquo; This essay
and five others have been included in Goldsmith's works on the strength of their
having appeared in <I>The British Magazine</I> during the years 1761, 1762, and 1763,
but no one, I think, can read them, certainly the one in question, without agreeing
with the editor of the edition, <SC>Peter Cunningham</SC>, &lquo;that they are not by Goldsmith.&rquo;
The needless attempt, however, has been made gravely to refute this essay in <SC>Hack-

<P>59. <B>sea</B>] <SC>Pope</SC>: Perhaps <I>siege,</I> which continues the metaphor of &lquo;slings,&rquo; &lquo;arrows,&rquo;
&lquo;taking arms,&rquo; and represents the being encompassed on all sides with trouhles
<SC>Theobald</SC>: Or one might emend nearer the traces of the text: &lquo;th' <I>assay</I> of
troubles&rquo; [<SC>Singer</SC> has no doubt that this was the word], or &lquo;a <I>'say</I> of troubles,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I>
the attempts, attacks, &amp;c. But perhaps any change is unnecessary, considering
Shakespeare's freedom in combining metaphors, and that a &lquo;sea&rquo; is used to signify
a vast quantity, multitude, or confluence of anything. The prophet Jeremiah, in
chap. li, 42, calls a prodigious army, a <I>sea.</I> &AElig;schylus is frequent in the use of this
metaphor: <I>Septem contra Thebas</I> [lines 64 and 114, ed. Dindorf]. Besides, a &lquo;sea
of troubles&rquo; among the Greeks grew into proverbial usage: <G>kakw_n qa/lassa</G>. So that
the phrase means the troubles of human life, which flow in upon us, and encompass
us round, like a sea. <SC>Hanmer</SC>: <I>Assailing</I> would preserve the propriety of the
metaphor. <SC>Johnson</SC>: Sh. breaks his metaphors often, and in this desultory speech
there was less need of preserving them. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: This mode of speaking is
proverbial, and has been so in all ages and in all languages; neither can any meta-
phor be conceived more apt than that of the sea, to convey the idea of an over-
whelming mass. With the closest analogy we say, a flood of transport, a torrent of
abuse, a peck of troubles. Sh. uses it everywhere and in every form; and the in-
tegrity of his metaphor is that which he least thinks of. <SC>Garrick</SC> (<I>Oration in
Honor of Shakespeare's Jubilee</I>): Shakespeare's terms rather than his sentences are
metaphorical; he calls an endless multitude a sea, by a happy allusion to the per-
petual succession of wave on wave; and he immediately expresses opposition by
&lquo;taking up arms,&rquo; which, being fit in itself, he was not solicitous to accommodate to
his first image. This is the language in which a figurative and rapid conception
will always be expressed. A. E. B[<SC>rae</SC>] (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> vol. vi, 23 Oct. 1852): <I>To
take arms against a sea</I> neither presents an intelligible idea in itself, nor assists in
carrying on the general allusion to offensive and defensive warfare. &lquo;Slings&rquo; and
&lquo;arrows&rquo; are figurative of <I>armed</I> aggression, against which to have recourse to <I>arms</I>
in opposition is a natural sequence of idea; but if these arms are to be directed
against <I>a sea</I> of troubles, the sequence is broken, and the whole allusion becomes
obscure and uncertain. But the whole image is that of a <I>posse</I> of evils thronging to
assail us in this life,&mdash;a <I>mortal</I> coil, as it is afterwards called, in opposition to the
<I>immortal</I> coil after death of ills we know not of,&mdash;this attack we may put an end to,
or &lquo;shuffle off,&rquo; by taking arms against it, <I>scilicet,</I> &lquo;a bare bodkin!&rquo; Thus the very
necessity of the context plainly exacts some word expressive of tumultuous attack;
and such a word we obtain, bearing precisely that meaning, by the slight alteration

<C>[59. <B>&lquo;sea of troubles.&rquo;</B>]</C>
<P>of &lquo;a sea&rquo; into <I>assay.</I> It is singular that lexicographers, amongst the several defini-
tions they have ascribed to it, should have failed to include that one peculiar mean-
ing,&mdash;<I>charge</I> or <I>onset,</I>&mdash;which renders it so appropriate. See II, ii, 71. But by
Spenser the word is most frequently used, and its meaning most plainly indicated.
See <I>Faerie Queene,</I> V, ii; V, xi. As to the probability of substitution, an equally
close approximation exists between <I>assay</I> and &lquo;a sea&rquo; as between <I>asters</I> and &lquo;as stars;&rquo;
nor is it at all certain that even in sound the vowels <I>a</I> and <I>e</I> were so distinctive in
those days as in our own. The probability is still greater if it were spelt, as was
often the case, with one <I>s. Assay</I> has all the meaning of Pope's conjecture, with
the added sense, peculiar to itself, of thronging or simultaneous onset. Thus, too,
in III, iii, 69, &lquo;make assay&rquo; receives great force and beauty if interpreted, &lquo;throng
to the rescue.&rquo; [Although A. E. B. was anticipated by Theobald, yet his defence
is so vigorous that I have not scrupled to insert it; it is doubtful whether his
definition will apply to II, i, 65. <SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Bailey</SC> (i, 28) maintains that Sh. never
could have written anything so inconsequent as lines 59 and 60: &lquo;Hamlet proposes
to himself the question whether he shall or shall not continue to live; but in pro-
ceeding to amplify it he performs the operation which is called <I>changing a child at
nurse, i. e.</I> he substitutes a totally different question&mdash;namely, whether he shall con-
tinue to bear his wrongs patiently, or shall fight against them and put them down?
It is as if my neighbor Lepidus, whilst deliberating whether he should remain in his
present house or quit it, were to say: &ldquo;To remain or to quit? That is the question;
whether it is better for me to continue to endure rattling windows, &amp;c., or to call in
the carpenter, and so put an end to these annoyances.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;vol. ii, p. 305. Accordingly,
Bailey believes that logic is vindicated, and the true text restored, by reading &lquo;to
take arms against <I>the seat</I> of troubles, And by a <I>poniard,</I> or by <I>deposing,</I> end them.&rquo;
Or the line &lquo;intrinsically, or considered by itself, might be restored by reading, &ldquo;to
take arms against a <I>host</I> of troubles;&rdquo; although the principal fault of the passage
would remain unaffected.&rquo;&mdash;p. 306. <SC>Staunton</SC>: As Sh. has already furnished us
with &lquo;a sea of joys,&rquo; &lquo;a sea of glory,&rquo; &lquo;a sea of conscience,&rquo; &lquo;a sea of wax,&rquo; &lquo;a sea
of care,&rquo; any emendation is very questionable. <SC>Halliwell</SC> cites: &lquo;Whatsoever it
be (which hardly at the length can be depainted) that after a sea of troubles we

&lquo;The analogy between the <I>sea,</I> with its ebb and flow, through rivers, channels, and

arteries, must be obvious to every one upon reflection.&rquo; Sh. frequently compares
the <I>heart</I> to a &lquo;sea.&rquo; <SC>Ingleby</SC> (<I>Sh. Hermeneutics,</I> p. 88): One consideration of
the highest importance has been entirely ignored. When Ham. talked of ending
his sea of troubles, or, as he afterwards describes it, shuffling off his mortal coil,
he had a covert consciousness, a <I>conscience,</I> in fact, which stayed the hand he would
have raised against his own life; viz. that this so-called ending and shuffling off
was a mere delusion, just as much so as repelling the advancing waves of the sea
with shield and spear. Is not the metaphor then sound and whole? If there be
an incongruity in the notion of taking arms, offensively or defensively, against
the sea, is there not just as great an incongruity in using a bare bodkin against

<P>67. <B>coil</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Turmoil, bustle. <SC>Heath</SC>: The incumbrance of this

tal <I>spoil,</I>&rquo; which is the same word as the slough which the snake casts every year. In

<I>Works,</I> ed. Dyce]; and again, &lquo;a separation Betwixt this spirit and the case of flesh.&rquo;

complete parallel is &lquo;this muddy vesture of decay.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Mer. of Ven.</I> V, i, 64. <SC>Calde-

or wraps round. Snakes generally lie like the coils of ropes; and, it is conceived,
that an allusion is here had to the struggle which that animal is obliged to make in
casting his slough. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 240): He was thinking of the <I>coil</I> of a rope.
With this expression &lquo;shuffled off&rquo; better coheres. <SC>Singer</SC>: It is remarkable that
under <I>garbuglio,</I> which corresponds in Italian to our &lquo;coil,&rquo; Florio has &lquo;a pecke of

<SC>Elze</SC>: With what reason can turmoil or noise be termed mortal? And how can
we shuffle off a mortal noise? We are convinced that under &lquo;coil&rquo; is concealed an
error which we can remedy by an almost imperceptible change, if instead of &lquo;coil&rquo;
we read <I>vail.</I> Vail means a covering, an integument, and our body is the mortal
covering or integument which we must shuffle off in order to enter on the life be-
yond. In Botany <I>vail</I> is the envelope, the chalypter of mosses, which enfolds the
fructifying organs and which is burst by them, and it is not impossible that it was
used generally for the envelope of buds. We do not venture to assert that Sh. knew
this meaning of the word, but we know with what keen looks he must have exam-
ined nature. Beyond a doubt, <I>clay</I> would be better, but it would harmonise less
with the received text. Elze (<I>Shakespeare-Jahrbuch,</I> vol. ii, p. 362) advocates the
substitution of <I>soil</I> for &lquo;coil,&rquo; which word he found in the <I>Dolfull Discours,</I> quoted

<P>misery. <SC>Farmer</SC>: This has been cavilled at by Lord Orrery and others, but without
reason. The idea of a <I>traveller</I> in Shakespeare's time was of a person who gave an
account of his adventures. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Compare, &lquo;Qui nunc it per iter tenebricosum,
Illuc unde negant redire quenquam.&rquo;&mdash;Catullus. <SC>Douce</SC>: No translation of Catullus
into English is known to have been made. Both writers may have casually adopted
the same sentiment. <SC>Malone</SC> (anticipated, however, by <SC>Gentleman</SC>, in the <I>Dra-
matic Censor,</I> i, 23, 1770) asserts that Sh. meant that from the unknown regions
of the dead no traveller returns with all his <I>corporeal powers,</I> such as he who goes
on a voyage of discovery brings back. The Ghost being &lquo;invulnerable as the air,&rquo;
was consequently <I>incorporeal.</I> <SC>Schlegel</SC> (<I>Lectures,</I> &amp;c. ii, 196, footnote): Sh. wished
purposely to show that Ham. could not fix himself in any conviction of any kind
whatever. <SC>Roffe</SC> (p. 31): According to that philosophy which the Spiritualist
believes to have been Shakespeare's, Ham. was perfectly correct in using this phrase-
ology. Surely there is no skepticism in Ham., nor inadvertency in Sh.: a departed
spirit appears to the spiritual eyes of the man, and not to his natural eyes; conse-
quently does not, and cannot, overpass &lquo;the bourn&rquo; which separates the spiritual and
causal world from the natural and effect world. <SC>Coleridge</SC> silences the question
for ever: &lquo;If it be necessary to remove the apparent contradiction,&mdash;if it be not
rather a great beauty,&mdash;surely it were easy to say that no traveller returns to this
world, as to his home or abiding-place.&rquo; <SC>Hartley Coleridge</SC> (<I>Essays and Mar-
ginalia,</I> i, 170): I will not say that an apparition might not confirm the faith of an
Hereafter, where it pre-existed, but where that faith was not, or was neutralised by
an inward misery, implicated with the very sense of being, its effect would be but
momentary or occasional,&mdash;a source of perplexity, not of conviction,&mdash;throwing
doubt at once on the conclusions of the understanding and the testimony of the
senses, and fading itself into the twilight of uncertainty, making existence the mere
shadow of a shade.

<P>102. <B>There, my lord</B>] <SC>Marshall</SC> (p. 28): At this point, just as Oph. is going

notable device, pops his head out, and in so doing drops his chamberlain's staff.
Ham. hears the noise, and instantly suspects the truth, that he is being made the
object of an artfully devised scheme to entrap him into some confession of his
secret.
<P>103. <SC>Richardson</SC> (<I>Essays,</I> &amp;c., fifth ed., 1797, p. 102): Hamlet's air and manner

<P>sex from which Oph. is so free, that the mere freedom therefrom constitutes her
character. Note Shakespeare's charm of composing the female character by the
absence of characters, that is, marks and out-jottings. <SC>Lamb</SC> (iii, 95, ed. 1870): All
the Hamlets that I have ever seen, rant and rave at Oph, as if she had committed
some great crime, and the audience are highly pleased, because the words of the
part are satirical, and they are enforced by the strongest expression of satirical in-
dignation of which the face and voice are capable. But then, whether Ham. is
likely to have put on such brutal appearances to a lady whom he loved so dearly, is
never thought on. The truth is, that in all such deep affections as had subsisted
between Ham. and Oph. there is a stock of <I>supererogatory love</I> (if I may venture
to use the expression), which in any great grief of heart, especially where that
which preys upon the mind cannot be communicated, confers a kind of indulgence
upon the grieved party to express itself, even to its heart's dearest object, in the
language of a temporary alienation; but it is not alienation, it is purely a distraction,
and so it always makes itself to be felt by that object; it is not anger, but grief
assuming the appearance of anger,&mdash;love awkwardly counterfeiting hate, as sweet
countenances when they try to frown; but such sternness and fierce disgust as Ham.
is made to show is no counterfeit, but the real face of absolute aversion,&mdash;of irrecon-
cilable alienation. It may be said he puts on the madman; but then he should only
so far put on this counterfeit lunacy as his own real distraction will give him leave;
that is, incompletely, imperfectly; not in that confirmed, practised way, like a master
of his art, or, as Dame Quickly would say, &lquo;like one of those harlotry players.&rquo;
<SC>Hazlitt</SC> (p. 110): Hamlet's conduct to Oph. is quite natural in his circumstances.
It is that of assumed severity only. It is the effect of disappointed hope, of bitter
regrets, of affection suspended, not obliterated, by the distraction of the scene around
him! Amidst the natural and preternatural horrors of his situation, he might be
excused in delicacy from carrying on a regular courtship. When his &lquo;father's spirit
was in arms,&rquo; it was not the time for the son to make love in. He could neither
marry Oph., nor wound her mind by explaining the cause of his alienation, which
he durst hardly trust himself to think of. It would have taken him years to come
to a direct explanation on the point. In the harassed state of his mind he could
not have done otherwise than he did. His conduct does not contradict what he
says of his love for her when he sees her grave. <SC>Vischer</SC> (<I>Krit. G&auml;nge,</I> p. 102)
conjectures that Ham. suspects that the Queen is eavesdropping, and that what he
says here is aimed at her.
