hut that he is the leader and disposer of a whole host of offences.&rquo;
<P>126. <B>in</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: A word is dropped out; read &lquo;in <I>name.</I>&rquo; This was the
progress. The offences are first conceived and named, then projected to be put in
act, then executed. <SC>Heath</SC>: I see no business the naming hath to do in this prog-
ress. <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;To put a thing into thought,&rquo; is to &lquo;think on it.&rquo;
<P>130. <B>father</B>] <SC>Grant White</SC> (<I>The Case of Hamlet the Younger,</I> The Galaxy,
April, 1870, p. 540): There is no warrant for the opinion that Ham. had discovered
that the King and Pol. were overhearing him, which indeed is suggested only as a
support to the indefensible assumption that Ham. being good at heart, his conduct
must have been always thoroughly estimable and consistent; whereas there are no
graver offences nor grosser errors than those into which men fall for lack of resolu
tion. <SC>Marshall</SC> (<I>A Study of Hamlet,</I> p. 28): Ham., before condemning Oph. as
an accomplice in the contemptible trick of spying on him, wishes to put her to the
plain proof; he therefore turns round and holds out his hand towards her; she, for-
getting her part, and thinking, poor girl, that he is going to take her to his breast and
forgive her, flies across to him; he checks her with his outstretched hand, and, hold-
ing hers, looks straight into her eyes, as only one who loves her has a right to look
into a ma&igrave;den's eyes, and solemnly asks her the question: &lquo;Where is your father?&rquo;
She falters out her first lie. Then indignation takes the place of sorrow with
Ham.

<P>under the circumstance, &lquo;Get thee to a nunnery&rquo; was the best and only advice he
could give her. A nunnery was her best and only refuge from the impending storm.
Destruction for himself and all else around him; but for her the cloister's timely
shelter. There is no telling when the fierce wrath may seize him; when he may
shake down the pillars of that guilty palace. But not, if he can help it, on her fair
head shall the ruin fall! Since the grave is opening for <I>him,</I> let the convent open
for <I>her.</I> Not his, but never another's! O wonderful poet! Could she not guess,
had she not some shadowy perception of the jealous, selfish, masculine love, which,
despite their fell divorce, would wall her from the world, and mark her with the
seal of God, to save her from the violation of man?

<P>1. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: This dialogue of Ham. with the Players is one of the happiest
instances of Shakespeare's power of diversifying the scene while he is carrying on
the plot. <SC>Sievers</SC> (<I>Hamlet,</I> Leipzig, 1851, note 13, p. 263) maintains that this ad-

<P>9. <B>periwig-pated</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: In the time of Sh. players most generally seem
to have worn periwigs; wigs were not in common use till the reign of Charles II.
In <I>Every Woman in her Humour,</I> 1609: &lquo;&mdash; as none wear hoods but monks and
ladies; and feathers but fore-horses, &amp;c. &mdash; none periwigs but players and pictures.&rquo;
<SC>Moberly</SC>: &lquo;Periwig&rquo; is simply an anglicised pronunciation of <I>perruque.</I>
<P>10. <B>groundlings</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: In its primitive signification it means a fish, which
always keeps at the bottom of the water. In our early play-houses the pit had
neither floor nor benches. Hence the term &lquo;groundlings&rquo; for those who frequented
it. Jonson mentions them with equal contempt: &lquo;&mdash; the understanding gentlemen
of the ground here ask'd my judgement.&rquo;&mdash;[<I>Bartholomew Fair,</I> Induct. p. 366,
<I>Works,</I> ed. Gifford. There are other derisive allusions to them on the same page
and on the next. <SC>Ed.</SC>] Again: &lquo;&mdash; give me the penny, I care not for the gentle-
man, I; let me have good ground.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Case is Altered,</I> I, i [p. 327, <I>Works,</I> ed.
Gifford]. <SC>Nares</SC>: From this last extract we see that the price paid by these gentry
was then only a penny. See also, in the same play, II, iv [p. 361]. Also: &lquo;Be-
sides, sir, all our galleries and ground-stands are furnished, and the groundlings within
the yard grow infinitely unruly.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lady Alimony,</I> I, i.
<P>11. <B>inexplicable</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, shows without words to explain them.
<SC>Steevens</SC>: Rather, shows which are too confusedly conducted to explain them-
selves. There is one of these in Heywood's <I>The Four Prentices,</I> 1615, as may be
seen from the following: &lquo;Enter Tancred, with Bella Franca richly attired, she
<I>somewhat affecting him,</I> though she <I>makes no show of it.</I>&rquo; [I, i, p. 442, ed. Dodsley,
1825.] Surely this may be called an <I>inexplicable dumb show.</I>

moralities, and represented as of a most violent character, so that a ranting actor might
always appear to advantage in it. Sh. uses it as an adjective in 1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> V, iv,
114. It is the <I>Trivigante</I> of the Italians, or <I>Tervagant</I> of the French Romancers.

<P>13. <B>Herod</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: The character of Herod in the ancient mysteries was
always a violent one. Thus, in <I>The Chester Plays</I> [p. 153, ed. Sh. Soc.], Herod

greateste above degree, That is, that was, that ever shalbe,&rquo; &amp;c. Chaucer, speaking
of the parish-clerk, Absolon, says: &lquo;He pleyeth Herodes vp on a scaffold hye.&rquo;&mdash;
<I>The Milleres Tale</I>&mdash;3384, Hengwrt MS. <SC>Douce</SC> gives a long extract from an
ancient Pageant, performed at Coventry by the Shearmen and Taylors, in 1534, but
the composition of which is of a much earlier date. To illustrate the present pas-
sage, and to give an idea of the boundless rant of the braggart tyrant, it is sufficient
to cite such lines as these: [I am] the myghttyst conquerowre that eyer walkid on
grownd;&rquo; &lquo;All the whole world from the north to the sowthe, I ma them dystroie
with won worde of my mouthe.&rquo; And of his enemies, &lquo;with a twynke of myn iec
not won be left alyve.&rquo; At one place the stage-direction gives unlimited freedom to
the actor to tear a passion to tatters, and to make all split: &lquo;Here Erode ragis in thys
pagond, and in the strete also.&rquo;&mdash;See <I>Magnus Herodes,</I> in The Towneley Mysteries,
p. 140, ed. Surtees Soc.; <I>The Slaughter of the Innocents,</I> in The Coventry Mys-
teries, p. 183, ed. Sh. Soc.; <I>King Herod,</I> Ibid. p. 291; <I>The Slaughter of the Inno
cents,</I> in The Chester Plays, p. 172, ed. Sh. Soc.

<P>not read, the <I>face</I> and <I>body,</I> or did Sh. write, the <I>page?</I> The <I>page</I> suits well with
&lquo;form&rquo; and &lquo;pressure,&rquo; but ill with &lquo;body.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: The text means: to represent
the manners of the time suitable to the period that is treated of, according as it may
be ancient or modern. <SC>M. Mason</SC>: Read, &lquo;<I>every</I> age and body of the time,&rquo; and
then the sense will be: &lquo;show virtue her own likeness, and every stage of life, every
profession or body of men, its form and resemblance.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Perhaps Sh. did
not mean to connect these words. It is the end of playing, says Hamlet, to show
the age in which we live, and the body of the time, its form and pressure; to de-
lineate exactly the manners of the age, and the particular humor of the day.
<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I> 292): We might feel inclined to read <I>world</I> for &lquo;time,&rquo; but no
change is required. <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 8): Read <I>visage,</I> which is so near &lquo;very age&rquo;
in the <I>ductus literarum.</I> Compare &lquo;visage of the times,&rquo; 2 <I>Hen. IV:</I> II, iii, 3.
<SC>Silberschlag</SC> (<I>Morgenblatt,</I> No. 47, 1860, p. 1114): This is essentially the same
definition of the drama which Cervantes in <I>Don Quixote</I> puts into the mouth of the
Priest: &lquo;Comedy,&rquo; he says, &lquo;according to the opinion of Cicero, should be a mirror of
human life, a model of manners, a representation of truth.&rquo; Both Sh. and Cervantes
clearly drew their definitions from Cicero; Cervantes says so expressly, while Sh.
intimates in the phrase, &lquo;both at the first and now,&rquo; that he gave an ancient definition
of the drama, but he does not mention Cicero's name, because it was not his style,
in the works of his riper years, to display his knowledge, or to support his opinions,
by the citation of authorities. His use of &lquo;hic et ubique,&rquo; in I, v, 156, affords a
proof [noted <I>ad loc.</I>] that the end of that scene was written many years earlier
than the rest of the drama.

<P>26. <B>theatre</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Compare Jonson's <I>Poetaster,</I> 1601, &lquo;&mdash;&mdash;if I prove the

<P>26. <B>there be</B>] For instances of the more common use of <I>be</I> with the plural than

<P>28. <B>profanely</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: This seems to relate, not to the praise which he has
mentioned, but to the censure he is about to utter. Any gross or indelicate language
was called <I>profane.</I> <SC>Mason</SC>: This refers to the praise given to the players; Ham. con-
sidering it as a kind of profanation to praise persons highly who were so undeserving
of it. The construction is &lquo;highly, not to say profanely.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Hamlet says
that he does not mean to speak profanely by saying that there could be any such thing
as a journeyman Creator. [The profanity consists in alluding to Christians. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>30. <B>nor man</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): Farmer's conj. receives some countenance from

absurd than that of the Ff,&mdash;as if Christians and pagans were not men! The dis-
tinction, Christian, Turk, and Pagan, was not uncommon. See Howell, in Richard-
son's <I>Dict. s. v.</I> &lquo;pagan.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: This means, <I>nor even man.</I>
<P>31. <B>journeymen</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The notion of Nature keeping a shop and employ-
ing journeymen to form mankind was common in Shakespeare's time. See Lyly's
<I>Woman in the Moon,</I> 1597: &lquo;They draw the curtains from before Nature's shop,
where stands an image clad and some unclad.&rquo;
<P>31. <B>had made them</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Restored,</I> p. 173): According to the Qq
and Ff, Hamlet is supposed to reason that because he had seen some very prepos-
terous players, he should think, therefore, that Nature's journeymen had made <I>all
mankind,</I> for so <I>men</I> in this place without <I>some</I> or <I>those</I> prefixed must imply. Might
not Sh. more probably have written <I>them?</I> [Theobald gives two instances: <I>Love's
Lab. Lost,</I> III, i, 25, and <I>Com. of Err.</I> II, ii, 81, where &lquo;them&rquo; and <I>the men</I> have
been confounded. But as he does not allude to this emendation in his subsequent
edition, it is to be presumed that he withdrew it. It is to me, however, so clearly
the correct reading that I do not hesitate to follow it, although all other editors except
two have adhered to the text of the QqFf, which is &lquo;<I>had made men.</I>&rquo; <SC>Rann</SC> adopts
Theobald's emendation, and <SC>Hudson</SC> adopts Farmer's conj., &lquo;had made <I>the men</I>&rquo;
<SC>Clarendon</SC> suggests <I>'em.</I> <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>36. <B>clowns</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Stowe informs us (p. 697, ed. 1615) that among the
twelve players who were sworn the queen's servants in 1583, &lquo;were two rare men,
viz. Thomas Wilson, for a quick delicate refined <I>extemporall witte;</I> and Richard
Tarleton, for a wondrous plentifull, pleasant <I>extemporall witt,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. Again, in Tarle-
ton's <I>Newes from Purgatory:</I> &lquo;&mdash;&mdash;I absented myself from all plaies, as wanting
that merrye Roscius of plaiers that famosed all comedies so with his pleasant and
<I>extemporall invention.</I>&rquo; This cause for complaint, however, against low comedians
is still more ancient; for in <I>The Contention Betwyxte Churchyard and Camell,</I> &amp;c.,
1560, I find the following passage: &lquo;But Vices in stage plaies, When theyr matter
is gon, They laugh out the reste To the lookers on,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Malone</SC>: The clown very
often addressed the audience in the middle of the play, and entered into a contest
of raillery and sarcasm with such of the audience as chose to engage with him.
<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 246): There is a remarkable addition at this place in Q<SUB>1</SUB>, which is not
without marks of the hand of Sh. The phrases there found continued to be the
stock-wit of the clowns who appeared on the stage of the mountebanks, and who
seem silently to have withdrawn themselves about the close of the last century.
<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): The passage in Q<SUB>1</SUB>, which is mere prose, although chopped up
into apparent verse, is curious, because it seems levelled at William Kemp, who
about this date quitted the company of players to which Sh. had always belonged.
Perhaps, after Kemp rejoined the King's Players (before 1605), the passage was
omitted or subdued. We are to bear in mind that <I>Hamlet</I> was probably not com-
posed until the winter of 1601, or the spring of 1602, and it was about this date, . . .
that Kemp went over from the Lord Chamberlain's to Lord Nottingham's Players,
and of course did his best to promote the success of a competing association. It
would, therefore, not be surprising if, besides laying down a general axiom as to the
abuse introduced by the performers of the parts of clowns, Sh. had designed a par-
ticular allusion to Kemp. <SC>White</SC>: The passage in Q<SUB>1</SUB> was probably an extempo-
raneous addition to the text by the actor, and had but a passing application.
<SC>Halliwell</SC> is inclined to think that this addition in Q<SUB>1</SUB> should be retained in
the text.

<P>63. <B>Hath</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: <I>Hast</I> of the Qq is a solecism. Though the subject-nomi-
native &lquo;thou&rquo; is second person, the predicate-nominative &lquo;man&rquo; is third person, and
being the antecedent of the relative &lquo;that,&rquo; determines the person of the verb to
which &lquo;that&rquo; is the nominative or subject.
<P>64. <B>blood and judgement</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: According to the doctrine of the fou<*>
humors, <I>desire</I> and <I>confidence</I> were seated in the blood, and <I>judgement</I> in the phlegm,
and the due mixture of the humors made a perfect character. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Passions
and reason. [See IV, iv, 58.]
<P>66. <B>please</B>] For other instances of &lquo;please&rquo; in the subjunctive, see <SC>Walker</SC>,
<I>Crit.</I> i, 207.
<P>68. <B>core</B>] <SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 245): From this speech Anthony Scoloker, in <I>Daiphantus,
or The Passions of Love,</I> 1604, has stolen the following line: &lquo;Oh, I would weare
her in my heart's-heart-gore;&rquo; whereupon <SC>Clarendon</SC> asks, should not &lquo;gore&rquo; be <I>core?</I>
<P>69. <B>Something,</B> &amp;c.] <SC>Clarke</SC>: The genuine manliness of this little sentence,
where Ham. checks himself when conscious that he has been carried away by fervor
of affectionate friendship into stronger protestation than mayhap becomes the truth
and simplicity of sentiment between man and man, is precisely one of Shakespeare's
exquisite touches of innate propriety in questions of feeling. Let any one, who
doubts for a moment whether Sh. intended that Ham. should merely <I>feign</I> madness,
read carefully over the present speech, marking its sobriety of expression even amid
all its ardor, its singleness and purity of sentiment amid its most forcible utterance,
and then decide whether it could be possible that he should mean Hamlet's wits to
be touched. That his heart is shaken to its core, that he is even afflicted with mel-
ancholia and hypochondria, we admit; but that his intellects are in the very slightest
degree disordered, we cannot for one instant believe.
<P>72. <B>thee,</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: This comma after &lquo;thee&rquo; serves to show that the phrase,
&lquo;of my father's death,&rquo; is connected with &lquo;circumstance,&rquo; and not with &lquo;told,&rquo; and
in neat pointing, should not be omitted.

<P>74. <B>very comment</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The most intense direction of every faculty.
<P>74. <B>thy soul</B>] <SC>Knight</SC>: Hamlet having told Hor. the &lquo;circumstances&rquo; of his
father's death, and imparted his suspicions of his uncle, entreats his friend to observe
his uncle &lquo;with the very comment of <I>my</I> soul,&rquo;&mdash;Hamlet's soul. To ask Hor. to
observe him with the comment of his own soul (Horatio's) is a mere feeble exple-
tive. <SC>Collier</SC> in his first edition also advocated the reading of the Ff, but fol-
lowed the Qq and the (MS) in his second. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> &amp;c., p. 214) criti-
cises the upholders of the text of the Ff in this passage, and says that Knight's text
of this tragedy is &lquo;beyond all doubt the worst that has appeared in modern times.&rquo;
Dyce thinks that the important word &lquo;very,&rquo; as Caldecott has interpreted it above,
demands &lquo;thy.&rquo; <SC>Corson</SC> maintains just the opposite; he prefers <I>my,</I> as more ex-
pressive. Hamlet's meaning is, I would have thee so enter into my feelings, so
identify thyself with me, that when thou seest that act a-foot, even with the very
comment of <I>my</I> soul, thou wilt observe my uncle. &lquo;My&rquo; also gives force to &lquo;Even
with the very,&rquo; which has less force in the other reading. <SC>Dyce</SC> furthermore points
out <I>why</I> Ham. wished Hor. to watch his uncle so closely, when he tells him that
&lquo;after we will both our judgements join In censure of his seeming.&rquo;
<P>75. <B>occulted</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The word seems to occur here only.
<P>76. <B>one speech</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 247): The speech which Hamlet himself had
prepared for the players.
<P>77. <B>damned</B>] <SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 245): The ghost of a person sentenced for his wicked-
ness to damnation, and which in this instance has deceived us. Thus Spenser, <I>Fairy
Queen,</I> b. i, canto 2, st. 32. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: This is the third time that this theo-
logical reflection occurs to the Prince. See I, iv, 40; II, ii, 575.
<P>79. <B>Vulcan's</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: The connection of thought between Vulcan's realm and
the Christian Hell whence the &lquo;damned ghost&rquo; issues, is very common among Shake-
speare's contemporaries.
<P>79. <B>stithy</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> substituted <I>Smithy,</I> on the ground that &lquo;stithy&rquo; meant an
anvil, and &lquo;an anvil is far from being the dirtiest thing in a smith's shop.&rquo; But
<SC>Caldecott</SC> says that <I>stithy, stithe,</I> and <I>stith</I> were the same, and used indifferently
to express either the iron to work upon, or the forge, or the workshop; though in
later times <I>stith</I> has been confined to the sense of <I>anvil,</I> and &lquo;stithy&rquo; to that of <I>shop.</I>

which he had before assumed. See <I>Lear,</I> I, iii, 16: &lquo;Idle old man.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC>:
Sh. employs &lquo;idle&rquo; in the sense of <I>mad</I> several times; among others see Q<SUB>1</SUB> [line
930; in Appendix], and also [lines 1535-1537]. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Idle&rquo; is still used
in Suffolk in the sense of foolish, lightheaded, crazy. Compare III, iv, 11. <SC>Mo-
berly</SC>: I must appear to have nothing to do with the matter.
<P>87. <B>fares</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 248): We have here the two senses of the word &lquo;fare,&rquo;
which, like <I>est,</I> means both <I>is</I> and <I>eats.</I> The King inquires in the first sense, Hamlet
answers in the second.

<P>89. <B>promise-crammed</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: The King had promised him that he should
be next to himself; but Hamlet ought to have been first in the realm.
<P>90. <B>nothing</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: This answer is not founded on any act of mine.
<P>91. <B>mine</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: They grow not out of mine; have no relation to anything
said by me.
<P>92. <B>mine now</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: A man's words, says the proverb, are his own no
longer than he keeps them unspoken. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: They are now anybody's.
<SC>Moberly</SC>: I am mad, and therefore not answerable for what I said a minute ago.
<P>93. <B>university</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC>: To have kept Hamlet's love for Ophelia before
the audience in any direct form, would have made a breach in the unity of interest;
&mdash;but yet to the thoughtful reader it is suggested by his spite to poor Polonius,
whom he can not let rest. <SC>Farmer</SC> infers that the common players were occasionally
admitted to perform in the universities on the strength of an application for that
purpose in Vice Chancellor Hatcher's <I>Letters to Lord Burghley,</I> 1580. But <SC>Calde-
cott</SC> thinks this extract merely shows that <I>applications</I> of this sort were <I>occasionally
made;</I> not that they were accepted; on the contrary, the governors were always dis-
posed to find reasons for rejecting them. Wherefore, in the absence of direct evi-
dence, Caldecott thinks that the probability of stage plays having been performed in
the universities by professed actors is strongly negatived. That he was mistaken
will be seen from the reference to Q<SUB>1</SUB> by Clarendon. <SC>Malone</SC>: The practice of
acting Latin plays in the universities of Oxford and Cambridge is very ancient, and
continued to near the middle of the last century. They were performed occasionally
for the entertainment of princes and other great personages; and regularly at Christ-
mas, at which time a <I>Lord of Misrule</I> was appointed at Oxford, to regulate the
exhibitions, and a similar officer with the title of <I>Imperator</I> at Cambridge. The most
celebrated actors at Cambridge were the students of St John's and King's colleges:
at Oxford those of Christ-Church. In the hall of that college a Latin comedy called
<I>Marcus Geminus,</I> and the Latin tragedy of <I>Progne,</I> were performed before Queen
Elizabeth in the year 1566; and in 1564, the Latin tragedy of <I>Dido</I> was played before
Her Majesty, when she visited the university of Cambridge. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: In 1564.

<P>122. <B>sables</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: These words are an ironical apology for his mother's
cheerful looks: two months was long enough in conscience to make any dead hus-
band forgotten. The true reading is:&mdash;&lquo;<I>'fore</I> I'll have a suit of sables, <I>i. e.</I> before.
As much as to say&mdash;Let the devil wear black for me, I'll have none. <SC>Johnson</SC>: I
cannot see why Hamlet, when he laid aside his dress of mourning, in a country where
it was <I>bitter cold,</I> and the air <I>nipping and eager,</I> should not have a <I>suit of sables.</I> I
suppose it is well enough known that the fur of sables is not black. <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I>
&amp;c., i, 136): It is scarce worth remarking, being a fact of such notoriety, that
&lquo;sables,&rquo; the furs so called, are the finery of most northern nations; so that Hamlet's
saying amounts to a declaration, that he would leave off his blacks, since his father
was so long dead. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 538): The sense seems to be: If this be the case,
let the devil wear plain black; I'll get me a suit of sables, which, from their colour,
will have the appearance indeed of mourning, but at the same time will indulge my
appetite for finery and ornament to the utmost. <SC>Farmer</SC>: There is an equivoque
here. In Massinger's <I>Old Law,</I> we have: &lquo;A cunning grief That's only faced with
sables for a show, But gaudy-hearted.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: By the Statute of Apparel, 24
Henry VIII, c. 13 (article <I>furres</I>), it is ordained that none under the degree of an
<I>earl</I> may use <I>sables.</I> Bishop says, in his <I>Blossoms,</I> 1577, speaking of the extrava-
gance of those times, that a thousand ducates were sometimes given for &lquo;a face of
sables.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC> thinks that by the &lquo;devil&rquo; Hamlet would have it understood
that he meant his uncle. <SC>Wightwick</SC> (<I>The Critic,</I> 1854, p. 317; cited in <I>N. &amp;
Qu.,</I> 18 July, 1857) maintains that the contrast here is of color, not of material.

pictures,&rquo; wherein the definitions are given of certain colors, among them &lquo;Sabell
colour, <I>i. e.</I> flame-colour,&rquo; he infers that Ham. here says, &lquo;I'll have a suit of <I>sabell,</I>&rquo;
<I>i. e.</I> of flame color. &lquo;A misspelling,&rquo; he adds, &lquo;has produced all the previous con-

<P>126. <B>hobby-horse</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Amongst the country May-games there was
a hobby-horse, which, when the puritanical humor of those times opposed and dis-
credited these games, was brought by the poets and ballad-makers as an instance of
the ridiculous zeal of the sectaries; from these ballads Ham. quotes a line or two.
<SC>Nares</SC>: A small horse; also a personage belonging to the ancient morris-dance,
when complete, and made, as Mr Bayes's troops are on the stage, by the figure of a
horse fastened round the waist of a man, his own legs going through the body of the
horse, and enabling him to walk, but concealed by a long foot-cloth; while false
legs appeared where those of the man should be, at the sides of the horse. Lat-
terly the <I>hobby-horse</I> was frequently omitted, which appears to have occasioned a
popular ballad, in which was the line now quoted by Ham. It is also quoted in
<I>Love's Lab.</I> III, i, 30. <SC>Dyce</SC> adds to this note of Nares's: Many readers will prob-
ably recollect the spirited description of the Hobby-horse in Scott's <I>Monastery;</I> but,
since Mr Bayes's troops have been long banished from the stage, it may be necessary
to mention here that they are part of the <I>dramatis person&oelig;</I> in the Duke of Bucking-
ham's once-celebrated satirical play called <I>The Rehearsal.</I> <SC>Collier</SC>: A ballad seems
to have been written on the omission of the Hobby-horse in May-games. &lquo;The

<P>127. <B>The dumb-show</B>] <SC>Pye</SC>: This appears to contain every circumstance of
the murder of Hamlet's father. Now there is no apparent reason why the Usurper
should not be as much affected by this mute representation of his crimes as he is
afterwards when the same action is accompanied by words. The subsequent con-
versation between Hamlet and Ophelia precludes the possibility of its having been
a kind of direction to the players only. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Since the usage of the time
warranted, and, as it would seem, even demanded this dumh-show, how could it
have been omitted? Hamlet, intent on &lquo;catching the conscience of the king,&rquo; would
naturally wish that his &lquo;mouse-trap&rquo; should be doubly set; and could never be sup-
posed willing to relinquish any one of those engines, the use of which custom had
authorized. The King, in fact, takes alarm at the thought that the subject is to be
afterward brought forward in plain terms in the play, and expresses his apprehension
of &lquo;offence in that argument,&rquo; of which he was already in possession; and at this,
indeed, he &lquo;blenches.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC>: Mute exhibitions, during the time of Sh., and be-
fore and after, were often introduced to exhibit such circumstances as the limits of a
play would not admit to be represented. We presume, however, that Sh. had here
some stage authority for making the dumb-show represent the same action that is

<P>indicated in the dialogue. His dramatic object is [pointed out by Caldecott]. <SC>Hun-
ter</SC> (ii, 249): To represent the story of a play in dumb-show when the play itself
is going to be performed appears a most extraordinary mode of procedure, and noth-
ing like it has been traced in the usages of the English theatre, or, I believe, in the
theatres of the more polished nations of Europe. What approach nearest to it, and
may by some be mistaken for it, are the Dumb Shows in Sackville's <I>Gorboduc</I> and
Gascoign's <I>Jocasta.</I> But whoever considers these shows attentively will perceive
that they are something essentially different from the exhibition of the very action
which is immediately to follow with the accompanying dialogue. They are, in fact,
but so many moralizations, resembling the choruses of the Greek drama, the moral
lessons being read in action, rather than in words. I do not recollect any other
English play with a dumb-show even of this kind; and Ophelia's questions, &lquo;What
means this, my lord?&rquo; and &lquo;Will he tell us what this show means?&rquo; prove that shows
such as these made no part of the common dramatic entertainments of England.
[Gascoign's instructions respecting the dumb-shows in <I>Jocasta</I> are here given, to
show how utterly unlike they are to this in <I>Hamlet.</I>] No one has hitherto hit upon the
true origin of the show in <I>Hamlet.</I> It seems that such strange and unsuitable antici-
pations were <I>according to the common practice of the Danish theatre.</I> I first became
acquainted with this fact, which appears to explain what without it appears to carry
absurdity as far as it will go, when reading an unpublished diary of the seventeenth
century, the writer of which relates that about the close of the year 1688 there landed
at Hull about six thousand Danish soldiers, who were dispersed in the neighhoring
towns. Some of them were quartered at the little town of Hatfield, near Doncas-
ter, near to which the writer of the diary lived, who, having given some general
account of their habits, proceeds thus:&mdash;&lquo;Many of them while they stayed here acted
a play in their language, and they got a vast deal of money thereby. The design of
it was Herod's Tyranny, the Birth of Christ, and the Coming of the Wise Men.
They built a stage in our large court-house, and acted the same thereon. I ohserved
that <I>all the postures were shown first,</I> namely, the king on his throne, his servants
standing about him; and then, the scenes being drawn, <I>another posture came,</I> the
barbarous soldiers murdering the infants, and so on; and <I>when they had run through
all so,</I> they then began to act both together. All which time they had plenty of all
sorts of music of themselves, for [one] soldier played on one sort, and one another.
I heard some of them say that some of these players belonged to the King of Den-
mark's play-house, that was set a fire and burnt when most of the nobles were behold-
ing a play several years ago.&rquo; The writer of this diary was Abraham de la Pryme.

<P>129. <B>miching mallecho</B>] <SC>Hanmer</SC> defines the first word as &lquo;secret, covered,
lying hid;&rquo; and the second as &lquo;a wicked act, a piece of iniquity. Span. <I>malhecho.</I>&rquo;
<SC>Warburton</SC> maintains that the phrase means: &lquo;Lying in wait for the poisoner.&rquo;
And that it should therefore read: &lquo;miching <I>Malhechor,</I>&rquo; and so introduces it in his
text. <SC>Henley</SC> very properly points out that <I>malhechor</I> no more means a poisoner
than the perpetrator of any other crime. <SC>Grey</SC> (ii, 296): Why may not Sh. have
wrote <I>miching Malbecco,</I> from Spenser's description of him, <I>Fairy Queene,</I> iii, cantos
9, 10? <SC>Farmer</SC> (cited by Steevens): Were not these obscure words originally:
&lquo;This is <I>mimicking Malbecco,</I>&rquo; a private gloss hy a friend on the margin of the MS
<I>Hamlet,</I> and thence ignorantly received into the text? <SC>Heath</SC>: To <I>mich</I> is a word
still in common use in the western part of this island, and signifies, to lurk, to do
mischief, under a fair external appearance. <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> i, 136): This is said
of the person of the <I>Poisoner</I> in the Dumb Show, a representative of the King, who
was a man of mean figure (see III, iv, 64), and is therefore compared by the speaker
to the character called Iniquity, in the ancient moralities, whose figure (it is like)
was the same, an ill-looking, <I>munching</I> animal. <SC>Malone</SC>: In Norfolk <I>michers</I> sig-
nify <I>pilferers.</I> The signification of <I>miching</I> in the present passage may be ascer-
tained by a passage in Decker's <I>Wonderful Yeare,</I> 1603: &lquo;Those that could shift
for a time,&mdash;went most bitterly <I>miching</I> and muffled, up and downe, with rue and
wormwood stuft into their eyes and nostrills.&rquo; See also Florio, <I>Acciapinare:</I> &lquo;To
<I>miche,</I> to shrug or <I>sneake in some corner.</I>&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;<I>Mychyn</I> or stelyn pryuely.&rquo;
&mdash;<I>Prompt. Parv.</I> <SC>Knight</SC>: The <I>skulking crime</I> pointed out in the Dumb Show is,
in one sense of Hamlet's wild phrase, <I>miching malhecho;</I> his own secret purpose
from which mischief will ensue, is <I>miching mallecho,</I> in another sense;&mdash;in either
case &lquo;it means mischief.&rquo; <SC>Maginn</SC> (<I>Fraser's Maga.</I> Dec. 1839): In the Qq we find
the traces of the true reading: <I>mucho malhecho,</I> much mischief. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>):
&lquo;<I>Malhecho. . . . .</I> An evil action, an indecent and indecorous behaviour; malefac-
tion.&rquo;&mdash;Connelly's <I>Span. and Engl. Dict.,</I> Madrid. Compare: &lquo;<I>Tho.</I> Be humble,
Thou man of mallecho, or thou diest.&rquo;&mdash;Shirley's <I>Gentleman of Venice; Works,</I>
vol. v, p. 52. Maginn's alteration is doubtless wrong. <SC>Keightley</SC> did not think
so; he adopted it. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Minsheu (<I>The Guide into Tongues</I>) gives, &lquo;To
Miche, or secretly to hide himself out of the way, as Truants doe from schoole.&rquo;
<SC>Mackay</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 16 Oct. 1875) says that it is to the wooing of the Queen by
the Poisoner that Ham. refers as meaning mischief, not to the murder; in the latter
the mischief is past, in the former it is to come. This is the clue which reveals the

<P>154. <B>cheer</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cheerfulness. See <I>Rich. III:</I> V, iii, 74. The word
originally signified <I>face, countenance,</I> from Fr. <I>ch&egrave;re</I> (compare <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> III, ii,
314); hence, &lquo;to be of good cheer&rquo; was to exhibit joy in the face. It was then applied
to that which produces gratification, and denotes entertainment or fare, as in III, ii, 194.

<C>[178-203. <B>the dozen or sixteen lines.</B>]</C>
<P>discussion as to whether or not these were Hamlet's dozen or sixteen lines was
started by a note from <SC>Furnivall</SC> in <I>The Academy,</I> 3 Jan. 1874, to the effect that
both <SC>Seeley</SC> and himself, independently and without any knowledge of Clarke's
note on the subject, had hit upon these lines as those written by Ham. The dis-
cussion is carried on in the pages of <I>The New Sh. Soc. Trans.</I> 1 Series, pt. ii. p.
465, and as it there takes up some thirty or more pages, a mere digest of it can be
given here. <SC>Malleson</SC> contends that these are not the lines written by Ham. 1.
They do not apply to the King's character or position, but rather to Ham. himself.
2. There is nothing in them of the torrent, tempest, and whirlwind of passion that
Ham. was so anxious should not be torn to tatters. And, lastly, there was one
<I>scene</I> which Ham. tells Hor. is to be the test, during which he is to watch the King
with every faculty of his being, while Ham. will do the same during one <I>speech.</I>
Beyond doubt the <I>scene</I> is where poison is poured into the Player King's ear, and
here, likewise, at the crisis of the plot is to be found the <I>speech,</I> viz. &lquo;Thoughts black,
hands apt, drugs fit,&rquo; &amp;c., and this is Hamlet's addition to the play. Had the King not
blenched, we should have had probably the rest of the dozen lines, which might have
contained a hint of the Poisoner's next aim, the seduction to a sudden second marriage
of the seeming-virtuous Queen. It was the success of this alteration or addition that
Ham. declared would get him a fellowship in a cry of players, and this success was due
to the &lquo;talk of the poisoning,&rquo; and this &lquo;talk of the poisoning&rquo; is found only in this
speech of Lucianus. <SC>Seeley</SC>, on the other hand, believed that the dozen or sixteen
lines were some of those which make up the long speech beginning &lquo;I do believe
you think what now you speak.&rquo; To avoid conjecture as much as possible, we must
consider two characteristics which the inserted speech <I>must necessarily</I> have: 1. It
must consist of some dozen or sixteen lines. 2. Being an insertion, it must be such
a speech as can be removed without affecting the action of the play. Now, these
two characteristics belong to this speech of the Player-King, and to it alone. It is
exceptionally long, and the whole of it could not be spared, hut it is quite easy to
spare about a dozen or sixteen lines from the middle of it, and such a retrenchment
would bring the speech to about the average length of the other speeches. There
is no reason why Ham. should make his lines &lquo;charge the King with murder, or to
drive the moral of the play home to the King's conscience.&rquo;<SUP>*</SUP> The play might be
trusted to do that; no speech could make the application plainer. It is impossible
for the speech beginning &lquo;Thoughts black,&rquo; &amp;c., to be the inserted speech, because
it satisfies none of the conditions. It is not a dozen or sixteen lines, but only six;
it is not an inserted speech, but belongs essentially to the action. It is also impos-
sible to suppose exactly that it was broken off by the King's rising, for the six lines
in question form only one sentence, and must therefore belong entirely to the play
itself in its original form, unless the murder were to be done in dumb show, which
nobody supposes. His uncle's guilt is by no means the absorbing topic of Hamlet's
thoughts; it is an annoying subject that weighs upon his mind without interesting it,
and his only desire is to postpone and keep at arm's length everything connected
with it, and with his duty to punish it. His real feeling for his uncle is only con-
tempt, as for a vulgar knave, whom there is no satisfaction in thinking about,&mdash;and
it would be source of wonder if he should think about him enough to take the

<C>[178-203. <B>the dozen or sixteen lines.</B>]</C>
<P>trouble to write a dozen or sixteen lines to make clear what was already as clear as
the day. But the subject that really does fill Hamlet's mind, to the exclusion of
what ought to engage his attention more, is his mother, and she it is with whom these
inserted lines deal. From what we know of Hamlet's feelings she would be, <I>&agrave;
priori,</I> the subject of his inserted speech. Furthermore, if the speech were about
the murder, it would be of no help in the progress of the play, nothing would be re
vealed to us by it. Whereas, if the speech dealt with the mother, it would be a broad
hint to us not to trust Hamlet's professions, and that the experiment of the play, with
all its parade of ingenuity and of vengeance to follow, is a mere blind by which
Ham. hides both from himself and Hor. that he does not intend to act at all, but will
go on for ever brooding over the frailty of his mother and of all womankind. To
this <SC>Malleson</SC> rejoins: Ham. never says he <I>has written</I> a passage of so many lines,
but that he <I>intended to write</I> some uncertain number, a dozen or sixteen. When he
sat down with the play before him, he may have written twenty or twenty-six, and
indeed, if the Player-King's speech be accepted as partly Hamlet's, all of it might
be claimed for him except the first two and the last two lines, which, omitting the in-
tervening twenty-six, go fairly together. There is no reason why the inserted lines
must be such as can be removed without affecting the play; may not Ham. have
substituted his lines for those which he struck out? If lines 178-203 were made, as
Seeley contends, to catch the conscience of the Queen, there appears to be in them
when closely analyzed nothing with any special reference to her, and accordingly she is
perfectly unmoved by them; her response, when appealed to by Hamlet as to how she
likes the play, betokens perfect self-possession. Afterwards, to be sure, she is thrown
into &lquo;most great affliction of spirit,&rquo; but it is entirely on her husband's account,&mdash;as
far as she was concerned, this speech was pointless. Grant that the plot of the play,
by itself, sufficiently emphasized the King's guilt, there is nothing unnatural in
Hamlet's wishing to make assurance doubly sure. In <SC>Seeley's</SC> final remarks he
admitted that Hamlet's instructions to the Player suggest a speech that is in some
sense passionate, but that in reality Ham. takes the occasion of a particular speech
to give a general lecture on elocution, or on the general way in which a passion
should be expressed. And these lines, which may appear tame to us, may have
horne a much more intense feeling to Ham. The insertion is introduced to tell
us something about Ham. that we should not otherwise have known. Its object
was not to catch the conscience of the Queen, but to give us an additional in-
sight into the dreamy, unpractical character of Ham. He had been from the
first brooding over his mother's conduct, and the play offers him an opportunity
to relieve his feelings; the lines may not produce much effect upon her,&mdash;he knows
how unimpressionable she is,&mdash;but his object will be gained if he only writes them.
<SC>Furnivall</SC> sums up: Technically, Seeley's position is very strong, but &lquo;on the
merits&rquo; he breaks down,&mdash;he has a capital case at Law, but none in Equity. I
cannot resist Malleson's argument, that Hamlet's inserted speech is the <I>one</I> speech
in which he tells Hor. the King's guilt is to unkennel itself. But I hold very
strongly that Lucianus's speech is not the speech, and that, in fact, the speech is not
in the printed play. Either the King's conscience was more quickly stung than
Ham. anticipated, and so the written speech was never needed; or (as Mr Matthew
has suggested) Sh. contented himself with showing us, or letting us assume, that
Ham. alterd the play, and put his &lquo;dozen or sixteen lines&rquo; into action instead of

<C>[178-203. <B>the dozen or sixteen lines.</B>]</C>
<P>words; if he had not modified the play, what credit could he have claimd for him-
self as a play-writer or adapter. The inconsistency of Shakespeare's having made
Ham. first talk so much about inserting a speech, and then leaving it out after all,
is what one might fairly expect in the recast <I>Hamlet</I> after its other startling incon-
sistencies, <I>e. g.</I> Hamlet's age and Ophelia's suicide. What can it matter whether an
actual speech of a dozen or sixteen lines, though often announct, be really in the
play or not? <SC>Simpson</SC> calls attention to the fact that just as the historical drama
takes for granted those events which are made known by previous allusions, so the
sub-play generally omits all those details which have been previously described or
alluded to. Thus in <I>Mid. N. D.</I> we have both the play as presented before Theseus
and a rehearsal of it. The lines rehearsed are different from any in the actual play.
&lquo;Looking at the practice of the time and at the previous likelihoods of the case, I see
no reason whatever for expecting to find that Sh. would have put into the sub-play
the dozen lines that he makes Ham. promise.&rquo; <SC>Bathurst</SC> (p. 70) says that he sees
&lquo;no symptoms of the lines which Ham. was to insert.&rquo; <SC>Gervinus</SC> (2te Band, p.
102, 3te Auflage) believes that Sh. meant the passage from line 177 to 187 to apply
to Ham. &lquo;Indeed, Gonzago acted the part of Hamlet's father. Ham. as well as his
mother must have a taste of &ldquo;wormwood.&rdquo;&rquo; My friend Dr <SC>Ingleby</SC> has kindly sent
me extracts from a Paper on this subject, which is announced for reading to the
<I>New Shakspere Society,</I> 9 February, 1877. In these extracts Dr Ingleby dissents
from all that has been assumed heretofore on this subject in that Society's <I>Transactions,</I>
and maintains his own view, very briefly thus: The court-play is but a part of <I>Ham
let;</I> that Ham. writes no speech at all, whether of six, twelve, or sixteen lines, nor
recites such a speech; Sh. simply wrote the entire play, <I>not</I> writing any additions <I>in
person&acirc; Hamleti,</I> still less writing an addition to a play which he had previously
written in the character of the author of an Italian morality. To trace into its
issues every suggestion in the play, <I>so that the eveni should justify the hint,</I> is &lquo;to
consider too curiously.&rquo; A drama is a work of art, a contrivance for imposing upon
the spectator, causing him to take no account of actual time, place, and circum-
stance, making him almost forget that he is in a play-house. In real life a Hamlet
might compose and insert a few lines to add point and force to an ordeal, like that
of the court-play, to which the fictitious Hamlet subjects the supposed criminal;
and if we had the play before us, we might detect the insertion by means of our
various tests of metre, phraseology, &amp;c. If we failed to discover the added lines,
the fault is ours; the lines would be there. Now to suppose that Sh. in composing
<I>Hamlet</I> followed out the exact course that a real living prince would have followed,
is to impute to him a lack of the simplest art of the playwright, and a neglect of
the artifices which the drama places at his command. Whereas, Shakespeare's pro-
cedure was probably this: In the course of enlarging the first sketch of his <I>Hamlet</I>
he conceived the design of making it a vehicle for the highest possible instruction
in the art of elocution. The play-scene was already devised, and he had, therefore,
to introduce the Players as arriving at Elsinore. Here was the chance he wanted.
He would make Ham. instruct the Player, and through him all players, how to
act. But how was this to be brought ahout? Ham. could hardly be supposed to
know by heart the r&ocirc;les of a strolling player. Wherefore, Sh. makes Ham. speak
as if he had already recited to the Player a speech of his own composition, and
hereupon give his instructions. Thus, having found or made the occasion. Sh. had

<P>to prepare the audience for the supposed recitation, and this was done by represent-
ing Ham. at a former interview imparting to the old Player his intention of writing
&lquo;a speech of some dozen or sixteen lines&rquo; (<I>i. e.</I> a speech of <I>several</I> lines) for inser
tion in <I>The Murder of Gonzago.</I> But all the while Shakespeare's object (kept
wholly out of view) was to prepare the audience for his own lesson (<I>voce Hamleti</I>)
on elocution. It is a rule of dramatic art that, a dramatic expedient not essential
to the plot, introduced for a collateral object, is to be left out of consideration as
soon as that object is attained. As soon, therefore, as Ham. has given the old Player
his lesson, the <I>dramatic need</I> of the &lquo;dozen or sixteen lines&rquo; is satisfied, and we have
no further concern with them. The suggestion, however, served (1) to prepare the way
for Hamlet's advice; (2) to suggest the possibility, vague to the last degree, that Ham.
had the old play touched and tinkered to suit his purpose more completely. The
phrase, &lquo;some dozen or sixteen,&rquo; does not mean what it says; it is even more indefi-
nite than &lquo;ten or a dozen,&rquo; or &lquo;a dozen or fourteen,&rquo; which Mrs Quickly uses in <I>Hen.
V:</I> II, i; the prefix &lquo;some&rquo; adds vagueness to what was vague already. These
lines, by the very nature of the case, can never have been in <I>Hamlet.</I> [It is to task
the credulity of an audience too severely to represent the possibility of Hamlet's
finding an old play exactly fitted to Claudius's crime, not only in the plot, but in all
the accessories, even to a single speech which should tent the criminal to the very
quick. In order, therefore, to give an air of probability to what every one would
feel to be thus highly improbable, Sh. represents Ham. as adapting an old play to
his present needs by inserting in it some pointed lines. Not that such lines were
actually inserted, but, mindful of this proposal of Hamlet's, the spectator is pre-
pared to listen to a play which is to unkennel the King's occulted guilt in a certain
speech; the verisimilitude of all the circumstances is thus maintained. No matter
how direct or pointed the allusion to the King's guilt may be, we accept it all, secure
under Shakespeare's promise that the play shall be made to hit Claudius fatally.
And we hear the fulfilment of this promise in Hamlet's cry of exultation over the
success of his attempt at play-writing. The discussion, therefore, that has arisen
over these &lquo;dozen or sixteen lines&rquo; is a tribute to Shakespeare's consummate art.
Ingleby, I think, is right in maintaining that Sh. did not first write <I>The Murder of
Gonzago,</I> and then insert in it certain lines, as though written by Hamlet. And
Sievers, the Clarkes, Malleson, and others are also right, I think, in believing that
certain lines of the court-play are especially applicable to Claudius, and which we
may imagine are those that Ham. told the Player he would give him. It is the very
impression which, I think, Sh. wished to convey. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>224. <B>offence</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: Here again, as before in I, v, 137, this word is used in
a double sense. The King means a <I>moral</I> &lquo;offence,&rquo; and Hamlet means a <I>physical</I>
&lquo;offence,&rquo; or crime.
<P>227. <B>Mouse-trap</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: In reference to II, ii, 580.
<P>227. <B>Tropically</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Figuratively, by a <I>trope</I> or <I>turn</I> we give things.
<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 282): <I>Trapically</I> of Q<SUB>1</SUB> is an unmeaning word, except that we may see
a faint shade of meaning in the play being a <I>figurative</I> representation of an actual
deed, and this, combined with the opportunity of playing on the word <I>trap,</I> is the
true reason that we meet with this word thus oddly introduced.
<P>228. <B>image</B>] See <I>Macb.</I> II, iii, 74.
<P>228. <B>Vienna</B>] <SC>Collier</SC>: The <I>Guiana</I> of Q<SUB>1</SUB> perhaps arose from the shorthand-
writer having misheard the name.
<P>229. <B>duke's</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 252): Q<SUB>1</SUB> explains why everywhere else he is a <I>king.</I>
The character was a <I>duke</I> throughout, as the play was originally written, and when
<I>king</I> was to be substituted for <I>duke,</I> this passage remained by some accident uncor-
rected. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 281) shows by many instances that <I>king, duke,</I> and <I>count</I>
were confounded in sense, and that to the poet they were one and the same, all in-
volving alike the idea of sovereign power; and thus might easily be confounded
with each other in the memory.
<P>229. <B>Baptista</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: In Italian, I think, the name always of a man. <SC>Rit-
son</SC>: I believe it is never used singly, but compounded with <I>Gian</I> (for <I>Giovanni</I>),
and meaning, of course, <I>John the Baptist.</I> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 252): I have seen a few
instances in which the name was borne by women in England. Sh. was not solicit-
ous about it. It had a feminine termination; that was enough.
<P>231. <B>we</B>] See I, iv, 54.
<P>231. <B>free</B>] See II, ii, 537.
<P>232. <B>wince</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: A proverb. Thus, in <I>Damon and Pythias,</I> 1582: &lquo;I
know the gall'd horse will soonest wince.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: See Lyly's <I>Euphues,</I> p.
119 (ed. Arber): &lquo;For well I know none will winch except she be gawlded.&rquo; See
<I>Mother Bombie,</I> I, iii.

Whom I have slain in reaching for a crown;&rquo; and of the two lines that follow,
Hamlet's speech is a satirical condensation: &lquo;The screeking raven sits croking for
revenge Whole herds of beasts comes bellowing for revenge.&rquo;

<P>263. <B>feathers</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: It appears from Decker's <I>Gul's Hornbooke</I> that feathers
were much worn on the stage in Shakespeare's time.
<P>264. <B>turn Turk</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: See <I>Much Ado,</I> III, iv, 57; and, in Greene's <I>Tu
Quoque,</I> 1614: &lquo;This it is to turn Turk, from an absolute and most compleat gentle-
man, to a most absurd, ridiculous, and fond lover.&rquo; It means no more than to
change condition fantastically. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: To undergo a total and ruinous change.
<P>264. <B>Provincial</B>] <SC>Warton</SC>: Hamlet means the roses of <I>Provence,</I> a beautiful
species; therefore read <I>Provencial</I> [<SC>Capell, Malone</SC>, and <SC>Steevens</SC> adopted this
reading] or <I>Proven&ccedil;al.</I> <SC>Douce</SC>: Change is unnecessary. There is no evidence that
<I>Provence</I> was ever remarkable for its roses; whereas, <I>Provins,</I> about forty miles
from Paris, was formerly very celebrated for the growth of this flower, which, accord-
ing to tradition, was imported into that country from Syria by a Count de Brie.
<SC>Johnson</SC>: When shoe-strings were worn they were covered, where they met in the
middle, by a ribbon gathered in the form of a rose. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cotgrave gives
both localities: &lquo;Rose de Provence. The Prouince Rose, the double Damaske Rose;&rquo;
and &lquo;Rose de Provins. The ordinarie double red Rose.&rquo; In either case it was a
large rose. The Province or Damask Rose was probably the better known. Gerarde,
in his <I>Herbal,</I> says that the damask rose is called by some &lquo;Rosa provincialis.&rquo; Fair-
holt (<I>Costume in England,</I> p. 238) quotes from Friar Bacon's <I>Prophecy,</I> 1604:
&lquo;When roses in the gardens grew, And not in ribbons on a shoe: Now ribbon roses
take such place, That garden roses want their grace.&rquo; At p. 579 he gives several
instances of the extravagances to which this fashion led. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> wildly pro-
poses and adopts &lquo;provisional&rquo; for the following reason: &lquo;The passing strangeness
of the assumption that actors procured fresh (?) roses from the town of Provins
occurred neither to Douce nor to the critics who follow him. It is probable that
nothing more than parti-colored paper was used as a substitute.&rquo; Hence, &lquo;Since
&ldquo;Provincial&rdquo; yields no meaning, it is clear that Sh. here wrote <I>provisional</I> (like the
Italian <I>provisionale</I>), that is, a pair of makeshift-roses.&rquo;
<P>265. <B>razed</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: I once suspected that we ought to read &lquo;<I>raised</I> shoes.&rquo;
It was the known custom of the tragedians of old, that they might nearer resemble
the heroes they personated, to make themselves as tall in stature as they possi-
bly could. But perhaps it may have been &lquo;<I>rayed</I> shoes,&rquo; that is, <I>striped, spangled.</I>
<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Razed shoes&rquo; may mean <I>slashed</I> shoes, <I>i. e.</I> with cuts or openings in
them. Sh. might have written &lquo;<I>raised</I> shoes,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> shoes with high heels. Stubbes,
<I>Anatomie of Abuses,</I> 1595, has a chapter on corked shoes, &lquo;which,&rquo; he says, &lquo;beare
them up two inches or more from the ground, &amp;c., some of red, blacke, &amp;c., razed,
carued, cut, and stitched,&rquo; &amp;c. To <I>raze</I> and to <I>race</I> alike signify to <I>streak.</I> See
Markham's <I>Country Farm:</I> &lquo;&mdash;baking them all (<I>i. e.</I> wafer cakes) together be-

<P>267. <B>share</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The actors in Shakespeare's time had not annual salaries
as at present. The whole receipts of each theatre were divided into shares, of which
the proprietors of the theatre, or <I>house-keepers,</I> as they were called, had some: and
each actor had one or more shares, or part of a share, according to his merit. See <I>Var.</I>
1821, iii, [p. 171. Also <SC>Collier's</SC> <I>Annals of the Stage,</I> iii, p. 429.] <SC>Clarendon</SC>:
In Henslowe's Diary (p. 5) is a memorandum of &pound;15 being lent to Francis Hens-
lowe for a share with the Queen's players, and [p. 8, three years afterwards, in 1596]
&pound;9 for a half share with another company. [In <SC>Halliwell's</SC> very valuable <I>Illus-
trations of the Life of Shakespeare,</I> 1874, pp. 86-91, certain petitions and answers
are reprinted, that were filed in 1635, in the Lord Chamberlain's office, and although
in date they are after Shakespeare's day, they nevertheless throw great light on the
early financial management of the Globe and Blackfriars theatres, and of the value
of the shares in them. The substance of one of these petitions, which shows us
what the <I>house-keepers</I> were, and that they and the actors were not always in accord,
is as follows: &lquo;Robert Benefield, Eyllardt Swanston, and Thomas Pollard doe
further humbly represent unto your Lordship. That the houskeepers beeing but
six in number, vizt., Mr. Cutbert Burbadge, Mrs. Condall, Mr. Shankes, Mr. Taylor,
Mr. Lowen and Mr. Robinson (in the right of his wife), have amongst them the
full moyety of all the galleries and boxes in both houses, and of the tireing-house
dore at the Globe. That the actors have the other moyety, with the outer dores;
but in regard the actors are halfe as many more, vizt., nine in number, their shares
fall shorter and are a great deale lesse then the houskeepers; and yet, notwithstand-
ing out of those lesser shares the sayd actors defray all charges of the house what-
soever, vizt., wages to hired men and boyes, musicke, lightes, &amp;c., amounting to 900
or 1000 <I>li.</I> per annum or thereaboutes, beeing 3 <I>li.</I> a day one day with another;
besides the extraordinary charge which the sayd actors are wholly at for apparell
and poetes, &amp;c. Whereas the sayd houskeepers out of all their gaines have not
till Lady Day last payd above 65 <I>li.</I> per annum rent for both houses, towardes which
they rayse betweene 20 and 30 <I>li.</I> per annum from the tap houses and a tenement
and a garden belonging to the premisses, &amp;c., and are at noe other charges whatsoever,
excepting the ordinary reparations of the houses. Soe that upon a medium made of
the gaynes of the howskeepers and those of the actors one day with another through-
out the yeere, the petitioners will make it apparent that when some of the hous-

emendation will strike many as the more likely reading, <SC>White</SC> thinks it strange
that modern editions should retain &lquo;I&rquo; of QqFf. <SC>Stratmann</SC> agrees with Malone.
<P>269-271. <SC>Dyce</SC>: Another quotation, surely; &lquo;pajock,&rquo; of course, excepted.
<P>271. <SC>Jove</SC>] <SC>Hudson</SC>: The meaning is, that Denmark was robbed of a king who
had the majesty of Jove.
<P>272. <B>pajock</B>] <SC>Pope</SC>: This alludes to the fable of the birds choosing a king; in-
stead of the eagle, a peacock. <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Restored,</I> p. 94) proposed: First,
<I>meacock,</I> a &lquo;<I>cravenly</I>&rquo; bird, and metaphorically a dastardly effeminate fellow; Second,
<I>paddock,</I> a toad; Third, <I>puttock,</I> a ravenous kite, a devourer of the state and people.
Of these three Theobald repeated only the second in his edition, with the note: &lquo;I
think Ham. is setting his father's and uncle's characters in contrast to each other:
and means to say, that by his father's death the state was stripped of a godlike mon-
arch, and that now in his stead reigned the most despicable poisonous animal that
could be; a mere <I>paddock</I> or <I>toad.</I> This word I take to be of Hamlet's own sub-
stituting. The verses repeated, seem to be from some old ballad; in which, rhyme
being necessary, I doubt not but the last verse ran thus: <I>A very, very</I>&mdash;ass.
<SC>Farmer</SC>: A <I>peacock</I> seems proverbial for a fool. Thus, Gascoigne, in his <I>Weeds:</I>
&lquo;A theefe, a cowarde, and a <I>peacocke</I> foole.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Sh. means that the King
struts about with a false pomp, to which he has no right. See Florio, 1598: &lquo;<I>Pauon-
neggiare.</I> To iet vp and down fondly gazing vpon himselfe, as a peacocke doth.&rquo;
<SC>Martinus Scriblerus</SC> (<I>Explanations,</I> &amp;c., Edinburgh, 1814): The original word
soundeth to me like a foreign word introduced into our language. Following out
this hint, if thou wilt look, reader, into any Italian Dictionary, thou wilt see that the
word <I>baiocco</I> means a piece of money, of about three farthings value, and there was
a silver coin of that value in Queen Elizabeth's time, which seemed to figure in
Shakespeare's imagination as something abundantly ridiculous. See <I>King John,</I> I.

<P>i, 143. When Hamlet, therefore, calls the King a <I>paiock,</I> he merely means to use
one of the most contemptuous expressions which occurred to him in the moment;
so that I would not alter the text. <SC>Dyce</SC>: &lquo;Pajock&rquo; is certainly equivalent to <I>pea-
cock.</I> I have often heard the lower classes in the north of Scotland call the peacock
&mdash;the &lquo;pea<I>-jock;</I>&rquo; and their almost invariable name for the turkey-cock is &lquo;bubbly-<I>jock.</I>&rquo;
<SC>Halliwell</SC> quotes Dyce, and adds: there can be little doubt but that the word in
the text is a similarly corrupted form. <SC>Elze</SC>: If <I>paddock</I> be inadmissible, <I>bawcock</I>
may be suggested. See <I>Hen. V:</I> IV, i, 44; and <I>Twelfth Night,</I> III, iv, 125. <SC>Eden
Warwick</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 7 Dec. '61), finding from Bunsen's <I>Egypt's Place, &amp;c.</I> that
the word <I>Pataikoi,</I> the name of the ancient Ph&oelig;nician gods, still survives at the
present day in Rome, applied to a coin with a hideous, worn-out impression, which
is called a &lquo;Patacco,&rquo; suggested that &lquo;paiocke&rquo; is a misprint for <I>patokie.</I> <SC>Leo</SC> (<I>N.
&amp; Qu.,</I> Jan. 21, '65): &lquo;Hamlet means <I>ass,</I> and does not intend to weaken what he
means by supplying it by such an innocent word as &ldquo;peacock,&rdquo; &ldquo;paddock,&rdquo; &amp;c. He
says, &ldquo;A very, very . . . ,&rdquo; and then he says <I>nothing more,</I> but <I>hems</I> in a rather cha-
racteristic way; and so gives to the hearer the opportunity to supply by rhyming
what he has left unsaid. And so I suppose the word in question did not belong to
the verse, but was a stage-direction, which I should like to understand as&mdash;&ldquo;hiccup.&rdquo;
&ldquo;A very, very . . . [<I>hiccups.</I>&rdquo;&rquo; [Can this be surpassed? <SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Latham</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I>
12 Aug. '71) suggests <I>Polack.</I> In <I>Hamlet</I> Danicisms may be expected, and this
word, besides its primary, national meaning, had, owing to the ill feeling between
the Poles and the Danes, a secondary meaning equivalent to <I>blackguard</I> or Philistine.
<SC>T. McGrath</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 23 Sept. '71) suggests <I>paj-ock,</I> i. e. <I>paj,</I> equivalent to <I>patch,</I>
a contemptuous fellow, and <I>-ock,</I> diminutive. Hence &lquo;pajock&rquo; or <I>patchock,</I> a paltry
clown; and cites Spenser, <I>A View of the present State of Ireland,</I> p. 636, Globe ed.:&mdash;
&lquo;Some in Leinster . . . are degenerate, and growen to be as very patchockes as the wild
Irish.&rquo; <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> 293): I agree with Theobald, as the King is afterwards
called a &lquo;paddock,&rquo; and there is probably an allusion to the poisoning. <SC>Tschisch-

<I>hajduk.</I> I have not been able to discover at what period <I>Haiducks</I> were introduced
into European courts, but it is quite possible that it took place towards the close of
the sixteenth century. <SC>Anonymous</SC> (<I>New Shakespearian Interpretations,</I> Edin.

lest the pecocke might soone find them. And Aristotle sayth that the pecocke hath
an unsteadfast and evill shapen head, as it were the head of a serpent, and with a
crest. And he hath a simple pace, and a small necke, and areared, and a blew
breast, and a taile ful of bewty, and he hath the foulest feet and riveled . . . and he
hath an horrible voice. And as one sayeth, he hath a voice of a feend, the head of
a serpent, and the pace of a theefe. And Plinius sayth that the pecocke hath envie
to man's profit, and swalloweth his owne durt: for it is full medicinable, but it is
seldom found.&rquo; This last is a curiously dark touch of malevolence. Ham. could

<P>not have selected the name of bird or beast that expressed with greater emphasis
the hateful union of corrupted passion and evil life that now usurped the throne
and bed of Denmark. <SC>John Davies</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 11 March, '76): This is prob
ably the Low German (Friesic) <I>pojek,</I> or <I>pajek,</I> a boy. In Sweden the modern form
is <I>pojke,</I> but the provincial and older form is <I>pajke</I> = <I>payek.</I> In the north of Eng-
land it is shortened into <I>pack,</I> and in Denmark into <I>pog.</I> In all these countries
it is a term of reproach. A northern peasant woman in England will call her child
a dirty or a naughty <I>pack,</I> especially when some offence against cleanliness has been
committed. It is often pronounced broadly, <I>paack,</I> not unlike <I>paiocke.</I> In the
present passage it is equivalent to a mere dirty boy, probably with some reference to
his sensual habits. [I think Dyce's testimony is conclusive. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>gleam of Hamlet's old regard for his schoolfellows shines out here for a moment;
but it fades again instantly, and he ends with a jesting allusion to the catechism,&mdash;
intended to avow, rather than to conceal, his feeling that he is using his tongue in a
way forbidden, as much as picking and stealing are to his hands.
<P>320. <B>pickers and stealers</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Hands. <SC>Whalley</SC>: The phrase is
taken from our church catechism, where the catechumen, in his duty to his neighbor,
is taught to keep his hands from picking and stealing. <SC>Nares</SC>: Examples are com-
mon of swearing by the fingers, called in cant phrase, &lquo;the ten bones.&rquo; See 2 <I>Hen.
VI:</I> I, iii, 193. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;<I>Pykare</I> or lytylle theef.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Prompt. Parv.</I> <SC>Claren-
don</SC>: &lquo;By this hand!&rquo; is a frequent form of asseveration. See <I>Temp.</I> III, ii, 56, 78;
<I>Mer. of Ven.</I> V, i, 161.
<P>321. <B>your cause</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The cause of your disorder. So &lquo;your sover-
eignty of reason,&rquo; in I, iv, 73.
<P>325. <B>voice</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: See I, ii, 109.
<P>327. <B>proverb</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The remainder of this old proverb is preserved in
Whetstone's <I>Promos and Cassandra,</I> 1578: &lquo;Whylst grass doth growe, oft sterves
the seely steede.&rquo; Again, in <I>The Paradise of Daintie Devises,</I> 1578: &lquo;To whom of
old this proverbe well it serves, While grass doth growe, the silly horse he starves.&rquo;
Ham. means to intimate that whilst he is waiting for the succession to the throne
of Denmark, he may himself be taken off by death.

<P>329. <B>recorders</B>] <SC>Chappell</SC> (<I>Popular Music of the &lquo;Olden Time,</I>&rquo; p. 246, and
note): Old English musical instruments were commonly made of three or four
different sizes, so that a player might take any of the four parts that were required
to fill up the harmony. So Violins, Lutes, Recorders, Flutes, Shawms, &amp;c., have
been described by some writers in a manner which (to those unacquainted with
this peculiarity) has appeared irreconcilable with other accounts. Sh. (in <I>Hamlet</I>)
speaks of the Recorder as a little pipe, and says, in <I>Mid. N. D.,</I> &lquo;he hath played
on his prologue like a <I>child</I> on a recorder;&rquo; but in an engraving of the instru-
ment<SUP>*</SUP> it reaches from the lip to the knee of the performer; and among those
left by Henry VIII were Recorders of box, oak, and ivory, great and small, two
base Recorders of walnut, and one <I>great</I> base Recorder. Recorders and (English)
Flutes are to outward appearance the same, although Lord Bacon in his <I>Natura<*>
History,</I> cent. iii, sec. 221, says the Recorder hath a less bore, and a greater above
and below. The number of holes for the fingers is the same, and the scale, the
compass, and the manner of playing, the same. Salter describes the <I>recorder,</I> from
which the instrument derives its name, as situate in the upper part of it, <I>i. e.</I> between
the hole below the mouth and the highest hole for the finger. He says, &lquo;Of the
kinds of music, vocal has always had the preference in esteem, and in consequence
the Recorder, as <I>approaching nearest to the sweet delightfulness of the voice,</I> ought
to have first place in opinion, as we see by the universal use of it confirmed.&rquo;
Ward, the military instrument-maker, informs me that he has seen &lquo;old English
flutes&rquo; with a hole bored through the side, in the upper part of the instrument, cov-
ered with a thin piece of skin, like gold-beater's skin. I suppose this would give
somewhat the effect of the quill or reed in the Hautboy, and that these were Re-
corders. Recorders were used for teaching birds to pipe.
<P>329. <B>To withdraw with you</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> i, 138): That is, to have done
with you, draw towards an end with you; and he singles out Guil., as of a darker
and more treacherous temper than the other. [Capell marks the phrase as an
Aside.] <SC>M. Mason</SC>: These words were probably spoken to the Players, whom
Ham. wished to get rid of. Read, therefore, &lquo;So, withdraw you;&rquo; or &lquo;So with-
draw, will you?&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: Here Malone added the stage-direction: [<I>Taking
Guildenstern aside.</I>] But the foregoing obscure words may refer to some gesture
which Guil. had used, and which at first was interpreted by Ham. into a signal for
him to attend the speaker into another room. &lquo;To withdraw with you?&rquo; (says he).
&lquo;Is that your meaning?&rquo; But finding his friends continue to move mysteriously
about him, he adds, with some resentment, a question more easily intelligible.
<SC>Caldecott</SC>: The two royal emissaries at first only request that the Prince would
&lquo;vouchsafe them a word;&rquo; and they then acquaint him with the King's rage, and the
Queen's command to visit her. They then, <I>by a waving of the hand, or some such
signal,</I> as the exclamation of Ham. denotes, intimate that he should remove to a

<P>more retired quarter. Although aware that the above, their only proper business,

means no more than &lquo;to draw back with you,&rquo; to leave that scent or trail. It is a
hunting term, like that which follows. <SC>Staunton</SC>: It is simply a direction ad-

Ham. and his schoolfellows could hardly have taken place in presence of the
Players, and the disputed words may have been intended to mark the departure of
the latter. <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>: If the reading and punctuation given in our text
be right, the words seem to be addressed to Guil. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: For this use of the
infinitive, compare III, iv, 216; and <I>King John,</I> I, i, 256. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Just step
aside for a moment. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: Perhaps we should read, &lquo;<I>Go,</I> withdraw
with you.&rquo;
<P>330. <B>wind</B>] <SC>Singer</SC>: This phrase is borrowed from hunting, and means to get
the animal pursued to run with the wind, that it may not scent the toil or its pur-
suers. &lquo;Observe how the wind is, that you may set the net so as the hare and wind
may come together; if the wind be sideways it may do well enough, but never if
it blow over the net into the hare's face, for he will scent both it and you at a dis-
tance.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Gentleman's Recreation.</I> <SC>Moberly</SC>: As if you were stalking a deer.
<P>333. <B>unmannerly</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: If my duty to the <I>king</I> makes me press you
a little, my love to <I>you</I> makes me still more importunate. If that makes me <I>bold,</I>
this makes me even <I>unmannerly.</I> <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 540): If you think me too bold in
what I have said by the command of your mother, to offer anything on the single
motive of my love to your person would be unmannerly. <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: Read&mdash;my
love is <I>not</I> unmannerly. My conception of the passage is, that, in consequence of
Hamlet's moving to take the recorder, Guil. also shifts his ground, in order to place
himself <I>beneath</I> the prince in his new position. This, Ham. ludicrously calls &lquo;going
about to recover the wind,&rquo; &amp;c., and Guil. may answer properly enough, and like a
courtier: <I>if my duty</I> to the king makes me <I>too bold</I> in pressing you, upon a disagree-
able subject, <I>my love</I> to you will make me not <I>unmannerly,</I> in showing you all pos-
sible marks of respect and attention. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: If my sense of duty have led
me too far, it is affection and regard for you that makes the carriage of that duty
border on disrespect. See &lquo;Forgive me this my virtue,&rquo; III, iv, 152. <SC>Singer</SC>:
Ham. may say with propriety, &lquo;I do not well understand that.&rquo; <SC>Keightley</SC>: &lquo;I
read, &ldquo;If my duty be too bold, my love [is] too unmannerly. . . .&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>:
Probably Sh. intended Guildenstern's words to express an unmeaning compliment.
As Ham. did not well understand them, commentators may be excused from at-
tempting to explain them.

<P>336. <B>Guil.</B>] <SC>Dr B. Nicholson</SC>: Hitherto Ros. and Guild. have so uniformly
worked in common that the artistic management of the scene, as well as the fuller
force thereby gained, demands that Hamlet's request be addressed first to one and
then to the other. Nor, though Guil. may or may not be the leader of the two, is
Ros. silent; in fact, in the previous dialogue, Ros. is the one who is set before us as
trying to get the wind of Ham. In this reply, therefore, let &lquo;Guil.&rquo; be changed
to Ros. [Probably these same reasons influenced the following emendation of
Staunton, line 339. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>339. <B>you</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: Should not this be addressed, and the reply which follows
be assigned, to Rosencrantz? See the dialogue in Q<SUB>1</SUB>.
<P>341. <B>govern</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: One would almost suppose this word to be here tech-
nical, from the use made of it on this subject in <I>Mid. N. D.</I> V, i, 123.
<P>341. <B>ventages</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The holes of a flute.
<P>342. <B>thumb</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC> attempts to justify the misprint of Q<SUB>2</SUB>Q<SUB>3</SUB> by supposing
that the <I>umber</I> was &lquo;the ancient name for that piece of movable brass at the end
of a flute which is either raised or depressed by the finger.&rquo; In support, he adduces
instances of the use of the words <I>umber,</I> and <I>umbriere,</I> which, however, mean the
visor of a helmet. <SC>Tollet</SC> supports the reading on practical grounds: if a re-
corder had a brass key like the German flute, we are to follow Q<SUB>2</SUB>Q<SUB>3</SUB>; for then the
<I>thumb</I> could not govern the ventages; if, however, it had not a brass key, then the
reading of the Ff must stand. <SC>Nares</SC>, in refutation, says that the brass key is more
modern than the time of Sh.
<P>343. <B>eloquent</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: I feel a certain seriousness&mdash;that's hardly the word&mdash;
about &lquo;eloquent,&rquo; not in keeping; whereas, in the use of <I>excellent</I> there seems to
be implied the idea that the music that can be got out of the little instrument is
superior to what one would suspect. The word &lquo;excellent&rquo; should be pronounced
with a downward circumflex on &lquo;ex-,&rquo; imparting a patronizing tone.
<P>344. <B>stops</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: The sounds formed by stopping the holes. See line <B>17</B>
of Induction to 2 <I>Hen. IV.</I> <SC>Singer</SC>: Rather the mode of stopping those ventages
to produce notes.

<P>363. <B>backed . . . weasel</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> preferred <I>ouzle</I> to &lquo;weasel,&rquo; because, first,
a &lquo;weasel&rquo; is not <I>black</I> (to read &lquo;back'd&rquo; only avoids the absurdity of giving a
false color to the &lquo;weasel&rquo;); secondly, by reading &lquo;ouzle,&rquo; there is humor in com-
paring the same cloud to a <I>Beast,</I> a <I>Bird,</I> and a <I>Fish.</I> <SC>Heath</SC>: The resemblance
of a cloud to an animal is generally concluded from its shape, not its color. &lquo;Weasel,&rquo;
then, is the true reading, and Polonius, in his eagerness to humor a madman, un-
luckily pitches upon the very portion of a weasel in which it most differs from a
camel. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Tollet observes that we might read, &lquo;it is <I>beck'd</I> like a weasel,&rquo;
<I>i. e.</I> weasel-snouted. So, in Hollinshed's <I>Description of England,</I> p. 172: &lquo;if he
be <I>wesell-becked.</I>&rquo; Quarles uses this term of reproach in his <I>Virgin Widow:</I> &lquo;Go
you <I>weazel-snouted,</I> addle-pated,&rquo; &amp;c. Tollet adds, that Milton in his <I>Lycidas</I> calls
a promontory <I>beaked, i. e.</I> prominent like the <I>beak</I> of a bird or a ship.
<P>366. <B>Then</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Then will I assent to your request, as yours is assenta-
tion to everything I say.
<P>366. <B>by and by</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Immediately. Compare <I>Matthew,</I> xiii, 21, where
&lquo;by and by&rquo; is the translation of <G>eu<*>qu/s</G>.
<P>367. <B>bent</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Bent&rquo; is used by Sh. for the utmost degree of any passion
or mental quality. The expression is derived from archery; the bow has its <I>bent</I>
when it is drawn as far as it can be. [See <SC>Wellesley</SC>, II, ii, 328; also II, ii, 30.]
