<P>374. <B>bitter business</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This expression is almost burlesque. The
Quarto is much nearer Shakespeare's words, who wrote &lquo;<I>better</I> day,&rquo; which gives the
sentiment great force and dignity. &lquo;The horror of the season fits me for a deed
which the <I>pure</I> and <I>sacred</I> day would quake to look on.&rquo; This is said with great
classical propriety. According to ancient superstition, <I>night</I> was prophane and exe-
crable, and <I>day</I> pure and holy. <SC>Heath</SC>: Warburton objects that the phrase is
almost burlesque. It is so; but it is so only from the abuse of the word &lquo;bitter,&rquo;
which is crept into our language from amongst the vulgar, long since the days of
Sh., and which can have no weight in the present case. If alteration be necessary,
I should suppose Sh. wrote &lquo;the <I>bitter'st</I> day.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: Though at present this
is a vulgar phrase, yet it might not have been such in Shakespeare's time. <SC>Dyce</SC>, in
his <I>Few Notes,</I> &amp;c., p. 141, not knowing that he had been anticipated by Warburton,
proposed &lquo;<I>better</I> day.&rquo; And although in both of his eds. he preferred the reading
of the Ff, he would not allow that &lquo;better&rquo; was indefensible, but cites in his ed. ii
the following note by <SC>Mitford</SC>: &lquo;The word is <I>better.</I> The &ldquo;<I>better</I> day&rdquo; is opposed
to the &ldquo;witching time of night.&rdquo; It is the <G>zepo\n h(map</G> of Homer, <I>Il.</I> <G>q</G>. 66.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Gent.
Maga.</I> Feb. 1845, p. 125. &lquo;I may add, too,&rquo; continues Dyce, &lquo;that John Kemble,&mdash;
whose performance of the Prince of Denmark is among the most vivid recollections
of my youth,&mdash;invariably [said &ldquo;<I>better</I> day.&rdquo;] See <I>Hamlet,</I> revised by J. P. Kemble,
1814, p. 51.&rquo; <SC>Cartwright</SC> (<I>New Readings,</I> &amp;c., p. 37): Read, &lquo;And do such
business as the <I>light of day.</I>&rquo;
<P>375. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: The utmost at which Ham. arrives, is a disposition, a mood, to
do something;&mdash;but what to do is left undecided, while every word he utters tends
to betray his disguise. Yet observe how perfectly equal to any call of the moment
is Ham., let it only not be for the future.

<P>as it precludes approbation or silent admission of the moral taste discovered in this
play by its author. It is, besides, dramatically improper; for, in the first place, his
mother had done nothing to deserve it; it is not even insinuated against her that she
was acquainted with the manner of her former husband's death. Her offence was
marrying again too soon, and, in addition to this, that her second husband was
brother to the first. In the next place, such a deed would not only delay the execu-
tion of the high behest of the Ghost, which is the main purpose of the drama, but
would in all probability have entirely frustrated it; and Ham. cannot be supposed
not to have foreseen that such would be the result. Ham. a matricide would have
become instantly an object of universal odium. In fact, the truth cannot and ought
not to be concealed that, popular as this play is, not in England only, but all the
world over, there are parts in it which seem quite at variance with the ordinary
modes of thinking of its author.

&lquo;however my mother may be hurt, wounded, or punished.&rquo;

<P>7. <B>lunacies</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: This unnecessary Alexandrine we owe to the players.
Sh. wrote <I>lunes, i. e.</I> madness, frenzy. See <I>Wint. Tale,</I> II, ii, 30; <I>Merry Wives,</I>
IV, ii, 22. <SC>Johnson</SC>: I take <I>browes</I> of the Qq to be, properly read, <I>frows,</I> which,
I think, is a provincial word for <I>perverse humours,</I> which being not understood was
changed to &lquo;lunacies.&rquo; But of this I am not confident. <SC>Steevens</SC> suggested that
perhaps Sh. designed a metaphor from horned cattle, whose powers of being danger-
ous increase with the <I>growth of their brows!</I> <SC>Henley</SC> improved on this, and main-
tained that the image under which the King apprehends danger from Ham. is that
of a <I>bull!</I> &lquo;which, in his frenzy, might not only gore, but push him from his throne.&rquo;
<SC>Elze</SC>: It is not improbable that Sh. wrote either <I>frowns</I> or <I>brains.</I>
<P>9. <B>many many</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): The (MS) has &lquo;<I>very</I> many,&rquo; thus setting right
a manifest misprint of the Ff. [Adopted in the text by Collier (ed. ii) and Elze.]
<SC>Staunton</SC>: This expression, signifying numberless, should certainly be hyphened,
like <I>too-too, few-few, most-most,</I> &amp;c. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Compare &lquo;little little,&rquo; <I>Hen. V:</I>
IV, ii, 33.
<P>13. <B>noyance</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Harm. Here used in a stronger sense than our

meaning, applied to the &lquo;feeble stinges&rquo; of &lquo;gnattes.&rquo;

<P>15. <B>cease</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The demise. Throughout Sh. a strong sense is attached
to this verb &lquo;cease.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;Cease&rquo; and &lquo;Dies&rquo; are tautological in word, not in
sense. The <I>death</I> of Majesty <I>comes</I> not alone. <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 10): &lquo;Cease&rquo; as a noun

that death dies not alone, and that it is a massy wheel as well as like a gulf; whereas

<P>72. <B>well</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC>: This speech well marks the difference between crime and

audible soliloquy, it is far less improbable than is supposed by such as have watched

remarkable; the degree of merit attributed by the self-flattering soul to its own
struggle, though baffled, and to the indefinite half-promise, half-command, to per-
severe in religious duties. The solution is in the divine <I>medium</I> of the Chris-
tian doctrine of expiation; not what you have done, but what you are, must de-
termine.

<P>73. <SC>Hanmer</SC> (<I>Some Remarks,</I> &amp;c., 1736, p. 41): This speech of Hamlet's has
always given me great offence. There is something so very bloody in it, so inhu-
man, so unworthy of a hero, that I wish our poet had omitted it. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Dr
Johnson's mistaking [see note, line 95] of the marks of reluctance and procrastination
for impetuous, horror-striking fiendishness!&mdash;of such importance is it to understand
the germ of a character. But the interval taken by Hamlet's speech is truly awful!
<SC>Hazlitt</SC> (p. 107): This refinement of malice here expressed by Ham. is in truth
only an excuse for his own want of resolution. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 255): In the whole
range of the drama there is, perhaps, nothing more offensive than this scene. Ham.
is made to doat on an idea which is positively shocking. Besides, as an excuse
for not then executing the command, under the spell of which he lived, it is poor
and trivlal. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Ham. had before said (I, ii, 182): &lquo;Would I had met my
dearest foe in heaven,&rquo; &amp;c. This notion of killing soul and body must therefore be
the natural impulse of his mind. It seems simpler to admit this view of Hamlet's
speech here than to consider it, as Coleridge does, to be at least half an excuse for
not doing <I>now</I> the act of vengeance from which his soul shrinks, though an unbend-
ing law has imposed it on him. <SC>Horn</SC> (ii, 56): Now comes the moment for revenge,
but <I>only</I> for revenge, not for righteous punishment, which must be preceded by a
full, perhaps also by a <I>public, conviction.</I>

<P>82. <B>audit</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: From these lines, and some others, it appears that Sh.
had drawn the first sketch of this play without his Ghost; and, when he added that
machinery, he forgot to strike out these lines. For the Ghost had told him
very circumstantially how his audit stood; and he was now satisfied with the real-
ity of the vision. <SC>Ritson</SC>: As it appears from the Ghost's own relation that
he was in purgatory, Hamlet's doubt could only be how long he was to continue
there.
<P>83. <B>our . . . thought</B>] Both <SC>Caldecott</SC> and <SC>Delius</SC> connect &lquo;our&rquo; with &lquo;cir-
cumstance,&rquo; the former paraphrasing: &lquo;the measure or estimate of what may have
reached us,&rquo; the latter, &lquo;according to human relations and thoughts.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>,
on the other hand, connects &lquo;our&rquo; with &lquo;thoughts,&rquo; and paraphrases: &lquo;the circum-
stance and course of our thought,&rquo; adding, &lquo;We have a similar use of the possessive
pronoun, I, iv, 73; III, ii, 321.&rquo; In <I>Two Gent.</I> I, i, 36, and <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> III, iii,
114, &lquo;circumstance&rquo; means the details of an argument. So here &lquo;circumstance of
thought&rquo; means the details over which thought ranges, and from which its conclu-
sions are formed.

<P>cannot be accused of plagiarism for having adopted <I>hint</I> in his text. <SC>Johnson</SC>: To
&lquo;hent&rquo; is used by Sh. for to <I>seize,</I> to <I>catch,</I> to <I>lay hold on.</I> &lquo;Hent&rquo; is therefore <I>hold,</I>
or <I>seizure.</I> &lquo;<I>Lay hold on</I> him, sword, at a more horrid time.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;Have
a more fierce, rash, or headlong grasp or purpose.&rquo; &lquo;<I>Hyntyn</I> or <I>hentyn,</I> rapio,
arripio.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Prompt. Parv.</I> <SC>White</SC>: &lquo;A more horrid having, taking, opportunity.
<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Feel or be conscious of a more terrible purpose.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): A
hold, an opportunity to be seized. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Equivalent to <I>grip.</I> Hamlet, as
he leaves hold of his sword, bids it wait for a more terrible occasion to be grasped
again. <SC>Moberly</SC>: A more fell grasp on the villain. <SC>John Davies</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I>
11 March, 1876): More probably here used in a sense common in some of the
western counties, meaning the <I>course</I> or <I>passage of the ploughshare up the furrow.</I>
This is the W. <I>hynt,</I> O. W. <I>hent</I> (<I>Zeuss,</I> 100, 101), a way, a course; compare Lat.
<I>sent-is,</I> Gothic <I>sinths.</I> Hamlet's words would convey to the mind of a West-coun-
tryman a very forcible image; the sword, in its shearing through the flesh, being
compared to the passage of a ploughshare through the earth.

<P>age in which he lived. The true question is not whether this practice were founded
in religion, but whether or not Sh. gave a faithful picture of human nature in a bar-
barous age. With our ruder Northern ancestors, revenge, in general, was handed
down in families as a duty, and the more refined and exquisite, the more honorable
it was; and this character or feature of it is to be found in every book that in those
times applies to the subject. And it was a subject brought upon the stage by subse-
quent tragedians as late as the middle of the seventeenth century. Sh. has here in
some sort laid a ground for the introduction of it by making the King himself pro-
claim (IV, vii, 129): &lquo;Revenge should have no bounds,&rquo; and he makes even the
philosophizing and moralizing Squire of Kent, in his beloved retirement from the
turmoils of the world, exclaim on killing Cade, 2 <I>Hen. VI:</I> And as I thrust thy
body in with my sword, So wish I, I might thrust thy soul to hell.&rquo; <SC>Wordsworth</SC>
(<I>Shakespeare's Knowledge of the Bible,</I> p. 208) finds for Ham. the same palliation
as does Caldecott.
<P>96. <B>physic</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: Hamlet calls his temporary forbearance a physic which
does not impart life to his foe, but prolongs his illness.
<P>96. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Hamlet here flies off to an <I>ideal</I> revenge, in order to quiet his filial
feelings without violating his conscience; effecting a compromise between them, by
<I>adjourning</I> a purpose which, as a man, he dare not execute, nor, as a son, abandon.
He afterwards asks Horatio:&mdash;&lquo;Is't not a <I>perfect conscience,</I> to quit him with this
arm?&rquo; which confirms the view here taken, as it shows that even then his mind was
not at rest on that score.
<P>97, 98. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Oh what a lesson concerning the essential difference between
wishing and willing, and the folly of all motive-mongering, while the individual
self remains!

<P>42. <B>rose</B>] It is only by keeping steadfastly in mind the many benefits which we
have received at the hands of the early commentators that we can listen with any
patience to their dispute about the meaning of this phrase. <SC>Warburton</SC> thinks it
refers to an actual flower worn on the side of the face. <SC>Steevens</SC> accepts the flower
but denies the &lquo;side of the face,&rquo; because the text reads &lquo;forehead;&rquo; it cannot mean
a <I>blush,</I> &lquo;because the forehead is no proper place for a <I>blush</I> to be displayed in.&rquo;
It must be a rose on the forehead, and in proof a figure, in a painted glass window
representing a <I>Morrice-Dance,</I> is cited that bears a <I>flower on the forehead!</I> (I
hope here be truths!) It makes very little matter that this flower turns out to
be a Deptford Pink; the flower is there, and the <I>rose</I> in <I>Hamlet</I> follows as of course.
<SC>Malone</SC> is rather overpowered by this display of learning, but ventures to suggest
that <I>rose</I> might &lquo;only mean the <I>roseate hue.</I>&rquo; And then, as if frightened at his own
boldness, hastens to add that &lquo;the forehead certainly appears to us an odd place for
the hue of innocence to dwell on;&rquo; and yet Sh. <I>has</I> represented a <I>smile</I> there, as in
<I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> II, ii, 205, and moreover, &lquo;that part of the forehead which is situated
between the eyebrows seems to have been considered by our poet as the seat of
innocence and modesty,&rquo; as in IV, v, 119. <SC>Boswell</SC> closes the discussion forever
by saying that &lquo; &ldquo;rose&rdquo; is put generally for the <I>ornament,</I> the <I>grace,</I> of an innocent
love.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC> refers to the proverb frequent in Sh., and found in <I>The London
Prodigal,</I> 1605: &lquo;As true as the skin between any man's brows.&rquo; And, lastly, <SC>Singer</SC>
refers to Ophelia's description of Ham. as &lquo;the rose of the fair state.&rquo;
<P>44. <B>blister</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Brands as a harlot. Compare <I>Com. of Err.</I> II, ii, 138.
<P>46. <B>contraction</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: For &lquo;marriage contract.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Anni-
hilates the very principle of contracts. <SC>White</SC>: There seems to be no better ex-
planation than Warburton's. But I suspect that there is corruption. <SC>Tschisch-
witz</SC>: Probably a misprint for <I>contractation,</I> formed by analogy with the Ital. <I>con-
trattazione.</I> [This conjectural emendation (which <SC>Stratmann</SC> terms judicious,
and compares with <I>affectation</I> of the Ff for &lquo;affection&rquo; of the Qq in II, ii, 422)
Tschischwitz inserts in the text, and instructs us to read &lquo;body of&rquo; as a trochee. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;Contraction&rquo; here means the <I>marriage contract;</I> of which Hamlet holds
religion to be the life and soul, insomuch that without this it is but as a lifeless body.

fine sense&rquo; in comparison with the &lquo;sad stuff&rquo; of the original. [See I, i, 158.]
<P>50. <B>doom</B>] That is, doomsday. See <I>Macb.</I> II, iii, 74. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Heaven bl<*>shes
at you, and the solid mass of earth is sick to think of it, as if it were waiting for the
day of judgement. <SC>Malone</SC> asks: Had not Sh. St Luke's (xxi, 25, 26) description
of the last day in his thoughts? <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Knowledge of the
Bible,</I> p. 305) replies: &lquo;No doubt he had; but why not also the parallel descriptions
of Matthew and of Mark? Yes, and still more, of Peter, 2 <I>Ep.</I> iii, 7-11; and John,
<I>Rev.</I> xx, 11. The truth is, I fear, that whatever else our poet's critics have been
strong in, they have, for the most part, not been strong in knowledge of the Scrip-
tures; and that the book which they should have looked to first and most for help
in the illustration of his works is the book which has been generally looked to last
and least.&rquo;
<P>51. <B>Is thought-sick</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> omits the hyphen, and affirms &lquo;Is&rquo; to be
the &lquo;historical Present,&rquo; that is, &lquo;Is thought [to be] sick.&rquo;
<P>52. <B>and . . . index</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> [following the distribution of speeches in Qq]:
To the Queen's question, &lquo;what act?&rquo; Ham. replies: &lquo;That roars so lond <I>it</I> thunders
<I>to</I> the <I>Indies.</I>&rquo; He had before said, Heav'n was shocked at it; he now tells her it
resounded all the world over. This gives us a very good sense where all sense was
wanting. <SC>Edwards</SC> (<I>Canons,</I> &amp;c., p. 156, 7th ed.): Sh. uses &lquo;index&rquo; for title, or
prologue. The Index used formerly to be placed at the beginning of a book, not
at the end, as now. Thus, also, in <I>Rich. III:</I> II, ii, 149; and <I>Oth.</I> II, i, 263.

<P><SC>Malone</SC>: Bullokar's <I>Expositor</I> defines an &lquo;Index&rquo; by &lquo;A Table in a booke.&rquo; The
<I>table</I> was almost always <I>prefixed</I> to books. <I>Indexes,</I> in the modern sense, were very
uncommon. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): <I>Index,</I> a prelude, anything preparatory to another.
<SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: The explanations of &lquo;<I>in</I> the index&rquo; are very lame. Instead of
&lquo;in,&rquo; we should manifestly read <I>is,</I> and the sense is, &lquo;What act, that roars so loud
and thunders, is my accuser?&rquo; &lquo;index&rquo; being understood in its ancient judicial
sense.
<P>53. <B>picture</B>] <SC>Davies</SC> (<I>Dram. Misc.,</I> Dublin, 1784, vol. iii, p. 63): It has been the
constant practice of the stage, since the Restoration, for Ham. to produce from his
pocket two pictures in little of his father and uncle, not much bigger than large coins
or medallions. Instead of movable scenery, which was first introduced from France
by Betterton in 1662, Shakespeare's stage made use of tapestry. Two full-length
portraits in the tapestry of the Queen's closet might be of service in this scene.
<SC>Steevens</SC>: It is evident from the words, &lquo;A station,&rquo; &amp;c., that these pictures, which
are introduced as miniatures on the stage, were meant for whole lengths, being part
of the furniture of the Queen's closet. Ham., who in a former scene had censured
those who gave &lquo;forty, fifty ducats apiece&rquo; for his uncle's &lquo;picture in little,&rquo; would
hardly have condescended to carry such a thing in his pocket. <SC>Malone</SC>: The in-
troduction of miniatures in this place appears to be a modern innovation. A print
prefixed to Rowe's edition of <I>Hamlet,</I> 1709, proves this. There the two royal por-
traits are exhibited as half-lengths, hanging in the Queen's closet; and either thus,
or as whole-lengths, they were probably exhibited from the time of the original
performance to the death of Betterton. To half-lengths, however, the same objec-
tion lies as to miniatures. <SC>Steevens</SC>: We may also learn that from this print the
trick of kicking the chair down on the appearance of the Ghost was adopted by
modern Hamlets from the practice of their predecessors. <SC>Caldecott</SC> objects to
miniatures, because the audience could not then be permitted to judge of what they
hear, nor make any estimate of the comparative excellence of the features, nor could
the &lquo;station&rquo; and the &lquo;combination and the form&rquo; be adequately represented in so
confined a space. Completely to do away with the objection that it is not probable
that Ham. should have about him his uncle's picture, a Bath actor once suggested
the snatching of it from his mother's neck. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 256): Perhaps Holman's
way was the best. The picture of the then King hung up in the lady's closet, but
the miniature of the king who was dead was produced by Ham. from his bosom.
[<SC>Fitzgerald</SC> (<I>Life of Garrick,</I> ii, 65) suggests that the pictures be seen with the
mind's eye only; a suggestion adopted by <SC>Irving</SC> and <SC>Salvini. Fechter</SC> follows
the suggestion of the Bath actor mentioned by Caldecott, and tears the miniature
from his mother's neck and casts it away. <SC>Rossi</SC> not only tears it from his mother's
neck, but dashes it to the ground and stamps on the fragments. <SC>Edwin Booth</SC>
makes use of two miniatures, taking one from his own neck, and the other from his
mother's.&mdash;<SC>A. I. Fish</SC>.]

Marlowe and Milton, and intransitively in Jonson's <I>Fox,</I> I, i: &lquo;With these thoughts
so battens.&rquo;
<P>69. <B>hey-day</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Thus, in Ford's <I>'Tis Pity She's a Whore,</I> 1633:
&lquo;&mdash;&mdash;must The hey-day of your luxury be fed Up to a surfeit.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: <I>High
day</I> is Johnson's explanation. It must mean the meridian glow. See &lquo;such high-
day wit.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Mer. of Ven.</I> II, ix, 98. <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: German <I>Heyda! Heysa!</I> excla-
mations of high spirits, active enjoyment. Hence, <I>hey-day,</I> the vigor and high
spirits of youth, where the spelling is probably modified under an erroneous im-
pression that there is something in the meaning of the word which indicates a
certain period of life. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The meaning is obvious, but the derivation
uncertain.
<P>71. <B>step</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): <I>Stoop</I> is from the (MS) with evident fitness, in refer-
ence to the disadvantageous comparison Ham. is drawing. <SC>Elze</SC> pronounces this a
brilliant emendation.
<P>71. <B>Sense</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: From what philosophy our editors learnt this, I cannot
tell. Since <I>motion</I> depends so little upon <I>sense,</I> that the greatest part of <I>motion</I> in
the universe is amongst bodies devoid of <I>sense.</I> We should read: &lquo;Else, could you
not have <I>notion,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> intellect, reason, &amp;c. This alludes to the famous peripatetic
principle of <I>Nil fit in</I> intellectu, <I>quod non fuerit in</I> sensu. <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 140): &lquo;Sense&rquo;
is <I>reason;</I> since she <I>moved</I> and performed other actions that belonged to humanity,
the presumption was she had the <I>reason</I> belonging to it. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Whichsoever
of the readings be the true one, the poet was not indebted to this boasted philoso-
phy [referred to by Warburton] for his choice. <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Sense&rquo; has been already
used for <I>sensation</I> in line 38, above. <SC>Staunton</SC>: The meaning is: &lquo;Sense (<I>i. e.</I>
the sensibility to appreciate the distinction between external objects) you must have,
or you would no longer feel the <I>impulse of desire.</I>&rquo; This signification of &lquo;motion&rquo;
might be illustrated by numerous examples from our early writers, but the accom-
panying out of Sh. will suffice: <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> I, iv, 59; <I>Oth.</I> I, iii, 95; <I>Ibid.</I> I,
iii, 334. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Motion&rquo; is emotion, as in <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> cited above.
<SC>Moberly</SC> inclines to Staunton's explanation.

<P>90. <B>grained</B>] <SC>Marsh</SC> (<I>Lectures on the English Language,</I> New York, 1859, p.
67, et seq.): <I>Granum,</I> in Latin, signifies a seed or kernel, and it was early applied
to all small objects resembling seeds, and finally to all minute particles. Hence it
was applied to the round, seed like form of the dried body, or rather ovarium, of an
insect of the genus <I>coccus,</I> which furnished a variety of red dyes. <I>Granum</I> becomes
<I>grana</I> in Spanish, <I>graine</I> in French, and <I>grain</I> in English, meaning a dye produced
by the coccus insect, often called in commerce <I>kermes.</I> The color obtained from
kermes or grain was peculiarly durable. When, then, a merchant recommended his
purple stuffs as being dyed in <I>grain,</I> he originally meant that they were dyed with
<I>kermes,</I> and would wear well; and this phrase was afterwards applied to other
colors, as a mode of expressing the quality of durability. See <I>Com. of Err.</I> III, ii,
108; and <I>Twelfth Night,</I> I, v, 256. In both these examples [as also in the present
instance from <I>Hamlet</I>] it is the sense of permanence (a well-known quality of the
purple produced by the <I>grain</I> or <I>kermes</I>) that is expressed. It is familiarly known
that if wool be dyed before spinning, the color is usually more permanent than when
the spun yarn or manufactured cloth is first dipped in the tincture. When the origi-
nal sense of <I>grain</I> grew less familiar, and it was used chiefly as expressive of <I>fast-
ness</I> of color, the name of the effect was transferred to an ordinary known cause, and
<I>dyed in grain,</I> originally meaning dyed with kermes, then dyed with fast color, came
at last to signify dyed in <I>the wool</I> or other raw material. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cotgrave has
&lquo;Graine: . . . graine wherewith cloth is dyed in graine; Scarlet dye, Scarlet in graine.&rquo;
<P>91. <B>leave</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;To part with, give up.&rquo; See <I>Two Gent.</I> IV, iv, 79;
<I>Mer. of Ven.</I> V, i, 172.

closes the discussion by showing that the character in the old moral-plays, known as
the &lquo;Vice,&rquo; was doubtless so named from the <I>vicious</I> qualities attributed to him, and
from the mischievous nature of his general conduct. <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Hist. of Eng. Dram.
Poetry,</I> ii, 264, <I>et seq.</I>) gives the best account of this curious personage in a passage
quoted by <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): As the Devil now and then appeared without the Vice,
so the Vice sometimes appeared without the Devil. Malone tells us that &lquo;the prin-
cipal employment of the Vice was to belabor the Devil;&rquo; but, although he was
frequently so engaged, he had higher duties. He figured now and then in the
religious plays of a later date, and, in <I>The Life and Repentance of Mary Mag-
dalen,</I> 1567, he performed the part of her lover, before her conversion, under the
name of Infidelity; in <I>King Darius,</I> 1565, he also acted a prominent part, by
his own impulses to mischief, under the name of Iniquity, without any prompting
from the representative of the principle of evil. Such was the general style of the
Vice, and as Iniquity he is spoken of by Sh. (<I>Rich. III:</I> III, i, 82) and Ben Jonson
(<I>Staple of News,</I> second Intermean). The Vice and Iniquity seem, however, some-

where he came.&rquo; In <I>The Longer thou livest the more Fool thou art,</I> and in <I>Like
will to Like,</I> the Vice is disposed of nearly in this summary manner: in the first,
Confusion carries him to the Devil, and in the last, Lucifer bears him off to the in-
fernal regions on his shoulders. In <I>King Darius</I> the Vice runs to hell of his own
accord, to escape from Constancy, Equity, and Charity. According to Bishop Hars-
net (in a passage cited by Malone,&mdash;<I>Shakespeare,</I> by Boswell, iii, 27), the Vice was
in the habit of riding and beating the Devil, at other times than when he was carried
against his will to punishment.

<P>121. <B>hair . . . Starts</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC> [reading &lquo;hair . . . Start&rquo;]: &lquo;Hair,&rquo; in fact,
may be considered as a noun of multitude, and the intervention of the plural sub-
stantive, &lquo;excrements,&rquo; would also suggest the plural verb.
<P>121. <B>excrements</B>] <SC>Pope</SC>: The hairs are excrementitious, that is, without life or
sensation. <SC>Malone</SC>: See <I>Macb.</I> V, v, 11-13. <SC>Whalley</SC>: Not only the hair of
animals having neither life nor sensation was called an excrement, but the feathers
of birds had the same appellation. Thus, in Izaak Walton's <I>Compleat Angler,</I> P.
I, c. i, p. 9, ed. 1766: &lquo;I will not undertake to mention the several kinds of fowl
by which this is done, and his curious palate pleased by day; and which, with their
very excrements, afford him a soft lodging at night.&rquo; <SC>Nares</SC>: Everything that
appears to vegetate or grow upon the human body; as the hair, the beard, the nails.
<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): &lquo;And albeit hayre were of it selfe the most abiect excrement that
were, yet should Popp&aelig;as hayre be reputed honourable. I am not ignorant that
hayre is noted by many as an excrement, a fleeting commodity. . . . . An excrement
it is, I deny not,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;Chapman's <I>Justification of a strange action of Nero,</I> &amp;c.
1629, sig. <SC>b 2. Clarendon</SC>: Bacon, <I>Natural History,</I> cent. 1, sect. 58, says, &lquo;Living
creatures put forth (after their period of growth) nothing that is young but hair and
nails, which are excrements and no parts.&rquo;
<P>122. <B>an end</B>] See I, v, 19.

<P>161, 162. <B>eat . . . devil</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: &lquo;Habits devil&rquo; arose from the supposed

Thirlby. That is, custom, which, by inuring us to ill habits, makes us lose the ap-
prehension of their being really ill, as easily will reconcile us to the practice of good
actions. Theobald, in his correspondence with Warburton (Nichols's <I>Illust. of Lit.</I>
ii, 574), says: &lquo;I would read and point &ldquo;doth eat Of <I>habit's evil,</I>&rdquo; &amp;c., <I>i. e.</I> of

<SC>Johnson</SC>: I think Thirlby's conjecture wrong; <I>angel</I> and <I>devil</I> are evidently opposed.
<SC>Malone</SC>: I incline to think with Dr Thirlby. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I would read: <I>Or</I> habit's
devil. The poet first styles <I>custom</I> a <I>monster,</I> and may aggravate and amplify his
description by adding, that it is the &lquo;d&aelig;mon who presides over habit.&rquo;&mdash;That mon-
ster custom, or habit's devil, is yet an angel in this particular. <SC>Boswell</SC>: &lquo;Habit's
devil&rquo; means a devil in his usual habits. <SC>Becket</SC> (i, 60) and <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent.
Maga.</I> 1845) both conjectured &lquo;If habit's devil;&rquo; the latter paraphrases: &lquo;If that
monster, custom, which in general is the devil of habit, leading to evil, yet in this
thing acts the good part of angel,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;That monster, custom, who
devours all sense, all just and correct feeling, (being also) the evil genius of (our)

or devil, who makes mankind insensible to the quality of actions which are habit-
ual.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC>: The edd. who have made &lquo;habits&rquo; the genitive case cannot explain
their own reading. As we print the passage it means: custom, who destroys all
nicety of feeling,&mdash;sense,&mdash;sensibility,&mdash;who is the devil that governs our habits,&mdash;
is yet an angel in this, &amp;c. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 1): Our punctuation means, &lquo;that

word is here <I>devill,</I> while just below and elsewhere it is uniformly <I>divell</I> when
the evil spirit is meant. <SC>Delius</SC> (ed. i): The opposition between &lquo;angel&rquo; and
&lquo;devil&rquo; shows that the latter as well as the former refers to &lquo;monster, custom:&rquo;

the subordinate clause. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): We now adopt Thirlby's emendation,

intended. Still, the passage is decidedly corrupt. <SC>White</SC>: The text of the Qq

<P>164. <B>livery</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: Just as a new dress or uniform becomes familiar to us by

good and fair actions which we inwardly desire to do.
<P>169. <B>master</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: For the insertion of the word <I>curb</I> I am answerable.

<I>either,</I> and substituted <I>master</I> in its place. The modern editors have accepted the
substituted word, and yet retain <I>either;</I> by which the metre is destroyed. The word
omitted in the first copy was undoubtedly a monosyllable. <SC>Steevens</SC>: This very
rational conjecture may be countenanced by the same expression in <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> IV,

<I>throne,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. Its alliteration explains its omission, and why &lquo;cast out,&rquo; the wording
of every version, was changed into &lquo;throw out.&rquo; It restores to the line its musical
tone. It gives the exact sense required. Persistence in well-doing, whether by
doing good or by leaving evil undone, exorcises the Tempter with wondrous potency;
but persistence in evil so destroys rebelling conscience, that the prince of this world
unresistingly ascends our vacant throne, and makes of us willing and unrespective
servants for his work. Lastly, it gives not only the exact sense, but the full sense,
required by the context, whether above or below it. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: It seems more
probable that something is omitted which is contrasted with &lquo;throw out,&rquo; and this
may have been &lquo;lay&rquo; or &lquo;lodge.&rquo; The latter was the technical word used in Hars-

for all, or baffle his attacks whenever they arise. <SC>Ingleby</SC> (<I>Sh. Hermeneutics,</I> p.
125) records two emendations suggested to him by friends: <SC>Sylvester</SC> proposes,
&lquo;either <I>mask</I> the devil,&rquo; of which Q<SUB>4</SUB> is the corruption. Compare III, i, 47-49.
And <SC>C. J. Munro</SC> &lquo;half-seriously&rquo; suggests: &lquo;And <I>entertain</I> the devil.&rquo; &lquo;It is not

suggests <I>fire, rouse, stir, serve, feed,</I> &amp;c. Besides which, there are many dissylla
bles that befit the sense and measure, as <I>abate, abase,</I> &amp;c. And why not read
&lquo;<I>over-maister,</I>&rquo; which occurs in a former scene? Thus we see what a wealth of
suggestion has been ignored! We venture to call attention to the evident require-
ments of the passage: &lquo;The stamp of nature&rquo; is not new to us in this connec-
tion, nor in this play; we have had it twice in the second ghost-scene, viz. &lquo;the
vicious mole of nature,&rquo; and &lquo;the stamp of one defect.&rquo; Now Hamlet would say,
&lquo;Use almost can change, or convert, this stamp of nature;&rquo; so that an antithesis is
not only <I>not</I> required, but is impertinent. Use, he would say, can either <I>subdue</I>
&lquo;habit's devil&rquo; by following out his own prescription of <I>gradual weaning from evil,</I>
or (if the worst come to the worst, and revolution be necessary) <I>cast him out;</I> and
either of these can such use, or change of habit, effect &lquo;with wondrous potency.&rquo; The
keynote of the whole passage is &lquo;Reformation, by gradually subduing evil habits;&rquo;
and so far from Hamlet's advice, &lquo;assume a virtue if you have it not,&rquo; being a recom-
mendation of hypocrisy, it is given solely with the view of facilitating inward amend-
ment, and is therefore honest and sincere. The missing word, then, must at least
import <I>the subduing of the devil of habit.</I> In the First Quarto we have the expres-
sion, &lquo;And win [<I>i. e.</I> wean] yourself hy little as you may&rquo; from the sin to which you

<P>[the Queen] have habituated yourself. Now, that <I>weaning by little and little,</I> or
gradually weaning the will and affections from the customary sin, &lquo;recurring and
suggesting still,&rquo; is just what the missing word, were it recovered, would assuredly
be found to express or imply. <I>Lay</I> and <I>shame</I> are equally acceptable in sense, and
both afford a perfect rhythm. Perhaps shame is the finer reading of the two. At
the same time it must be owned that Hamlet's prescription is calculated to do little
for the sinner; at best, we fear, to &lquo;skin and film the rancorous place.&rquo; We can
hardly say that conjecture has yet determined the best reading here, though it cannot
be said that sufficient indications are wanting for its guidance. Unfortunately, it is
in the very nature of the case that some doubt should continue to vex this passage,
after conjecture has done its work.

<P>212. <SC>Staunton</SC>: A consideration of the exigencies of the theatre in Shakespeare's
time, which not only obliged an actor to play two or more parts in the same drama,
but to perform such servile offices as are now done by attendants of the stage, shows
that this line is a mere interpolation to afford the player an excuse for removing the
body. We append a few examples where the same expedient is adopted for the
same purpose. Among them the notable instance of Sir John Falstaff carrying off
the body of Harry Percy on his back,&mdash;an exploit as clumsy and unseemly as Ham-
let's &lquo;tugging out&rquo; Pol., and, like that, perpetuated on the modern stage only from
sheer ignorance of the circumstances which originated such a practice: <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I>
III, i, 201; <I>Rich. II:</I> V, v, 118, 119; 1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> V, iv, 160; 1 <I>Hen. VI:</I> I, iv,
110; <I>Ibid.</I> II, v, 120, 121; <I>Ibid.</I> IV, vii, 91, 92; 2 <I>Hen. VI:</I> IV, i, 145; <I>Ibid.</I> IV,
x, 86, 87; <I>Ibid.</I> V, ii, 61-65; 3 <I>Hen. VI:</I> II, v, 113; <I>Ibid.</I> II, v, 121, 122; <I>Ibid.</I>
V, vi, 92, 93; <I>Rich. III:</I> I, iv, 287, 288; <I>Lear,</I> IV, vi, 280-282; <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> V,
viii, 21, 22; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> III, ii, 261; <I>Ibid.</I> V, v, 78, 79; <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> IV, ix, 31, 32;
<I>Ibid.</I> IV, xiv, 138. These instances from Sh. alone, and they could easily be multi-
plied, will suffice to bring into view one of the mconveniences to which the elder
dramatists were subject through the paucity o<*> actors; and at the same time, by ex-
hibiting the mode in which they endeavored to obviate the difficulty, may afford a
key to many passages and incidents that before appeared anomalous.

<P>217. <B>Good night, mother</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 257): This scene has always been ad-
mired as one of the masterpieces of this great dramatic writer; and there are in it
undoubtedly fine opportunities for the display of an actor's powers,&mdash;striking situa-
tions, and also fine poetry. But the question arises, To what purpose all this excite-
ment and bustle? The scene appears to have been written for its own sake, not
helping forward the story. Except that Pol. is accidentally killed in the course of
it, the parties are left precisely where they were, Ham. having only in this forcible
manner signified to his mother the displeasure which he felt at her conduct. But as
the play was originally written this scene had a purpose. Ham. reveals to his mother
his knowledge of his uncle's guilt, and his purpose of revenge; and she engages to
conceal and to assist. From this time the Queen keeps up appearances with her
husband, but is secretly a friend to Ham.; and there is an entire scene, afterwards
withdrawn, between her and Hor., in which Hor. communicates to her confidentially
the return of Ham. from England, when the dialogue ends with her saying: [see
Appendix, p. 77, lines 1779-1781.] This removes all ambiguity respecting the part
which the poet intended the Queen should take; according to the present regulation,
her precise situation is not clearly exhibited.

<P>6. <B>Compounded</B>] <SC>Jennens</SC> retains the reading of Q<SUB>2</SUB>Q<SUB>3</SUB> and interprets it as an
imperative, otherwise Ham. tells an untruth, for he had not buried the body.
<P>12. <B>to</B>] For the indefinite use of the infinitive, see III, iii. 85, and <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 356.
<P>12. <B>of</B>] See I, iv, 18; <I>Macb.</I> III, vi, 27; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 170.
<P>12. <B>sponge,</B>] <SC>Corson</SC> defends the comma, maintaining, and rightly, that the sen-
tence is not exclamatory. &lquo;In modern English we should say &ldquo;in being demanded
by a sponge, what,&rdquo;&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Hamlet's madness is made to consist in the
free utterance of all the thoughts that had passed through his mind before;&mdash;in fact,
in telling home-truths.
<P>12. <B>replication</B>] <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. a Lawyer,</I> p. 34): This is an exception of the
second degree made by the plaintiff upon the answer of the defendant.
<P>15. <B>soaks</B>] <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 343), in this speech of Hamlet's, would transpose the
sentences, so that lines 19, 20, containing the simile of a sponge, should follow im-
mediately &lquo;authorities&rquo; in line 16; and for &lquo;soaks up&rquo; he would read <I>sucks up,</I> and
for &lquo;gleaned&rquo; he suggests <I>glutted.</I>
<P>15. <B>countenance . . . authorities</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The first means <I>favour,</I> as in
I, iii, 113; V, i, 26. The latter, <I>offices of authority.</I>
<P>17. <B>nuts</B>] <SC>Farmer</SC> conjectured, &lquo;like an ape, <I>an apple.</I>&rquo; To this <SC>Malone</SC> ob-
jected, on the ground that Sh. then would have written &lquo;<I>as</I> an ape,&rquo; &amp;c., not &lquo;<I>like</I>
an ape.&rquo; But <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 116) suspected Farmer to be right, having found
in Hugh Holland a construction precisely similar: &lquo;Where, like in Jove's [braines],
Minerva keeps a coile.&rquo;
<P>19. <B>needs</B>] <SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 193) finds an equivoque here between <I>to need</I> and <I>to
knead.</I>

<P>22. <B>sponge . . . dry again</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;When princes . . . have used courtiers
as <I>sponges to drinke</I> what juice they can from the poore people, they take pleasure
afterwards to <I>wring them out</I> into their owne cisternes.&rquo;&mdash;R. C.'s Henr. Steph. <I>Apology
for Herodotus,</I> 1608. Vespasian, when reproached for bestowing high office upon per
sons most rapacious, answered, &lquo;that he served his turne with such officers as with
<I>spunges,</I> which, when they had drunke their fill, were the fittest to be <I>pressed.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Bar-
nabe Rich's <I>Faultes, faults and nothing but faults,</I> 1606; also Suetonius, <I>Vespas.</I> c. 16.
<P>22. <B>ear</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: A proverb since Shakespeare's time.
<P>26-27. <B>The . . . body</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: This answer I do not comprehend. Perhaps
it should be,&mdash;The body is <I>not</I> with the King, for the King is not with the body.
<SC>Jennens</SC>: The body, being in the palace, might be said to be with the King; though
the King, not being in the same room with the body, was not with the body. <SC>Stee-
vens</SC>: Perhaps this,&mdash;The body is in the King's house (<I>i. e.</I> the present King's), yet
the King (<I>i. e.</I> he who should have been king) is not with the body. Intimating that
the usurper is here, the true King in a better place. Or it may mean&mdash;<I>the guilt of
the murder lies with the King,</I> but the King is <I>not where the body lies.</I> <SC>Douce</SC>: The
body, <I>i. e.</I> the external appearance or person of the monarch, is with his uncle; but
that the real and lawful king is not in that body. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The King is not yet
cut off from life and sovereignty: his carcase remains to the King; but the King is
not with the body or carcase that you seek; the King is not with Polonius. But
Hamlet's answers are necessarily enigmatical. A more natural meaning is suggested.
The image raised, the impression made upon the King's fears by the fate of Polo-
nius, makes his body or carcase present to the fancy of the King, who knew and has
said that &lquo;it had been so with him had he been there;&rquo; but the King is not with the
body, <I>i. e.</I> is not lying with Polonius. Others interpret, plainly enough, if admissi-
bly: The body is with the King, <I>i. e.</I> intombed, or in the other world with the late,
the real king; but the King, <I>i. e.</I> he who now wears the crown, the usurper, is not
with the body. <SC>Singer</SC>: It may mean: The King is a body without a kingly soul,
a thing&mdash;of nothing. <SC>Elze</SC> agrees with Eschenburg's explanation: The corpse is
here with the King, but the King is not with it, <I>i. e.</I> he is as yet no corpse. <SC>Hud-
son</SC>: The meaning of this intended riddle, to the best of my guessing, is: The
King's body is with the King, but not the King's soul: he's a King without kingli-
ness. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Apparently a sententious maxim from some political book. &lquo;The
body politic is joined to the King, yet the King is not to be considered part of the
body politic, but a thing apart.&rquo; [The present editor agrees with <SC>Clarendon</SC>, that
Ham. is talking nonsense designedly.]
</CC>

<P>29. <B>Of nothing</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Should it not be read: <I>Or</I> nothing? When the
courtiers remark that Ham. has contemptuously called the King a <I>thing,</I> Ham. de-
fends himself by observing that the King must be a <I>thing</I> or <I>nothing.</I> <SC>Farmer</SC>
and <SC>Steevens</SC> cite instances of the use of this not uncommon phrase, and <SC>Whalley</SC>
cites <I>Psalm</I> cxliv, 4: &lquo;Man is like a thing of nought.&rquo; [&mdash;Prayer Book Version.
&lquo;&mdash;&mdash;of vanity.&rquo;&mdash;Authorized Version.] <SC>Nares</SC> quotes Beau. &amp; Fl. <I>Humorous Lieu-
tenant,</I> IV, vi: &lquo;And though a thing of nothing, thy thing ever.&rquo; [&mdash;p. 517, ed.
Dyce.]
<P>29. <B>Hide . . . after</B>] <SC>Hanmer</SC>: There is a play among children thus called,
<SC>Singer</SC>: Most probably what is now called &lquo;whoop&rquo; or &lquo;hide and seek.&rquo; <SC>White</SC>:
The exclamation is merely one of Hamlet's signs of feigned madness. <SC>Moberly</SC>:
Ham. sheathes his sword (&lquo;a Toledo or an English fox&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;point of fox,&rquo; &amp;c., prob-
ably from the name of a celebrated maker like Andrea di Ferrara), and, as if he
were playing hide and seek, cries &lquo;now the fox is hid: let all go after him.&rquo;
<P>9, 10. <B>diseases...relieved</B>] <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Euphuism,</I> p. 11): &lquo;But I
feare me wher so straunge a sicknesse is to be recured of so vnskilfull a Phisition, that
either thou wilt be to bold to practise, or my body too weake to purge. But seeing
<I>a desperate disease is to be committed to a desperate Doctor,</I> I wil follow thy counsel.
and become thy cure.&rquo;&mdash;[<I>Euphues,</I> p. 67, ed. Arber.]

<P>61. <B>set</B>] <SC>M. Mason</SC>: One of the common acceptations of the verb &lquo;set&rquo; is to value
or estimate; as we say, to set at nought. <SC>Malone</SC> thinks that it is an elliptical ex-
pression for <I>set by.</I> <SC>Singer</SC> denies the ellipsis, and quotes, without giving the au-
thority, &lquo;To <I>sette</I> or tell the pryce; <I>&aelig;stimare.</I>&rquo; [Barett's <I>Alvearie</I> has: &lquo;To set, of
tell the price. Indicare,&rquo; which makes nothing against Malone; because &lquo;To set&rquo;
is not used absolutely, but the full phrase is &lquo;to set the price.&rquo; <SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>
says that &lquo;set&rquo; would not have been thus used had it not been familiar in the phrases,
<I>set at nought, set at a pin's fee,</I> &amp;c.
<P>63. <B>conjuring</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Rest.</I> 109): If the &lquo;letters,&rquo; importing the te-
nour of the process, were to <I>that</I> effect, they were certainly congruing; but of no
great use, when the sovereign process imported the <I>same</I> thing. Now a process
might import a command, and letters <I>conjuring</I> a compliance with it be sent, and be
of great efficacy, where the execution of the command was to be doubted of. More-
over, Ham. when he changed the substance of the commission would be likely to
retain the form, and we find him using &lquo;earnest conjurations.&rquo; As to the accent, Sh.
generally accented the first syllable. <SC>Clarendon</SC> thinks &lquo;conjuring&rquo; probably a
misprint, although it yields a fair sense.
<P>65. <B>hectic</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Used as a substantive in Cotgrave: &lquo;Hectique: Sicke
of an Hectick, or continuall Feauer.&rquo; Only here, either as substantive or adjective,
in Sh.

<P>25, 26. <B>Two . . . straw</B>] <SC>As You Like It</SC> (Gent. Mag. lx, 403): These lines
are certainly given to Ham. very wrongfully, as they undoubtedly belong to the Capt.
Ham. appears entirely ignorant of the object of the Norwegian army. The Capt.
speaks with contempt of the little patch of ground, which for five ducats he would
not farm, to recover which so many souls were to be sacrificed and so much money
expended. After this, Ham. begins very properly, &lquo;This is an imposthume,&rquo; &amp;c.
<SC>Tschischwitz</SC> goes still farther, and gives the whole speech down to &lquo;dies.&rquo; to the
Capt., on the ground that this speech does not accord with what Ham. says after-
wards, where honor is the cause that impels him to the struggle, not an &lquo;imposthume
of much wealth and peace.&rquo;

<P>54. <B>Is not to stir</B>] [Does the &lquo;not&rquo; belong to the copula or to the predicate? I
think it belongs to the copula, and that there should be a comma after it: &lquo;Is not,

attribute of greatness; it is rather the attribute of smallness, of a mere love of
fighting; but it <I>is</I> the attribute of greatness to stir instantly and at a trifle when
honor is touched. The mere fact that For. is astir, and Ham. is still, does not prove
the former to be the greater man, or make him an example to the latter. But be-
cause, for the merest fantasy that his honor was touched, he was going to his grave

<P>as to a bed, <I>herein</I> lies the contrast and example to Ham. Moreover, when &lquo;not&rquo;
is joined to the copula, and a comma placed after it, the force of &lquo;But&rquo; is felt, thus:
True greatness is not (predicate), <I>but</I> it is this. Include the &lquo;not&rquo; in the predicate,
and &lquo;But&rquo; becomes inconsequent: True greatness is (predicate), <I>but</I> it is this. <SC>Ca-
pell</SC> perceived this, and added a second <I>not</I> as a compromise, embracing both read-
ings: &lquo;Is not, <I>not</I> to stir,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Delius</SC> does not actually add the second <I>not,</I> but
he says it is understood, or rather that the &lquo;not&rquo; belongs to both copula and predicate.
This discussion may seem trifling enough, but we must remember that: Rightly to
punctuate is not, to put a stop without great argument, but greatly to find quarrel in
a comma when Shakespeare's at the stake. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>his army,&mdash;with this flash of a better fortune for Denmark athwart the deepening
drama, the Act should end. Ending here, the interval consumed by the voyage to
England, the return of Laer. from Paris, and the expedition of For. to Poland and
back, is thrown <I>between</I> the Acts,&mdash;its natural place. This proposed exteusion of
the Third Act would make this greatest of tragedies the most symmetrical too; while
the Fourth Act, relieved of a confusion which is now mistaken for an anticlimax,
would be devoted with a single purpose to its two superb contrasts: the revenge of
Laer. with the revenge of Ham., and the utter madness of Oph. with the semi-
counterfeit lunacy of her lover. A gain almost as great for the closet as for the
stage. <SC>Marshall</SC> (p. 77): The interval which elapses between this scene and the
preceding is at least a month, and probably more. [Page 193.]&mdash;This may be seen
by an examination of the remaining scenes. No break can occur at the end of this
scene; the conversation between the King and Laer. in sc. vii is evidently part
of that which ends this scene; the time occupied by sc. vi is merely sufficient
for the King to explain to Laer. the circumstances of Polonius's death. We find
from sc. vi that Ham. has returned, having been taken by the pirates on his second
day out; how long he was detained by them does not appear; it must have been for
some time, since between Acts IV and V there cannot elapse much more than two
days, and at the end of Act V we find ambassadors announcing the death of Ros.
and Guil., and For. returned from Poland, so that it is evident that the break im-
plied by a new Act ought to occur at the end of IV, iv. Moreover, if Ophelia's
madness were introduced at the beginning of a new Act, it would be more effective,
and the interval which is supposed to have occurred would give color to the causes
which produced it. [See notes on Act IV, p. 311.]

<P>25. <B>cockle-hat</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The description of a pilgrim. While this kind
of devotion was in favor, love intrigues were carried on under this mask. Hence
the old ballads and novels made pilgrimages the subjects of their plots. The cockle-
shell hat was one of the essential badges of this vocation; for the chief places of
devotion being beyond sea or on the coasts, the pilgrims were accustomed to put
cockle-shells upon their hats, to denote the intention or performance of their de-
votion.

<P>40. <B>God 'ild</B>] &lquo;God reward you.&rquo; See <I>Macb.</I> I, vi, 13.
<P>41. <B>daughter</B>] <SC>Douce</SC>: This is a common story among the vulgar in Gloucester-
shire, and is thus related: &lquo;Our Saviour went into a baker's shop where they were
baking, and asked for some bread to eat. The mistress of the shop immediately put a
piece of dough into the oven to bake for him, but was reprimanded by her daughter,
who, insisting that the piece of dough was too large, reduced it to a very small size.
The dough, however, immediately afterwards began to swell, and presently became
of a most enormous size. Whereupon the baker's daughter cried out, &ldquo;Heugh,
heugh, heugh,&rdquo; which owl-like noise probably induced our Saviour for her wicked-
ness to transform her into that bird.&rquo; This story is often related to children, in order
to deter them from such illiberal behavior to poor people. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: The plumage
of the melancholy bird, and the color of the baker, in correspondence with her
father's &lquo;white shroud,&rquo; and probably her own habit, may have suggested, to a bewil-
dered mind, this singular allusion. <SC>Elze</SC>: As little did the baker's daughter expect
to be turned into an owl as it occurred to my father and myself to anticipate the
kind of death we should die. <SC>Doering</SC> (p. 79): Oph. feels that she has acted
towards Ham. in an equally heartless manner.
<P>43. <B>conceit</B>] Imagination. See III, iv, 114. <SC>Moberly</SC>: The King seems to

<P>46. <B>Saint Valentine's day</B>] <SC>Halliwell</SC>: This song alludes to the custom of the
first girl seen by a man on the morning of this day being considered his Valentine or
true-love. The custom continued until the last century, and is graphically alluded to
by Gay. The custom of the different sexes choosing themselves mates on St Valen-
tine's day, 14th February, the names being selected either by lots or methods of
divination, is of great antiquity in England. The name so drawn was the Valentine
of the drawer. <SC>Douce</SC> traces the custom to the <I>Lupercalia</I> of Rome, during which

<P>77. <B>muddied...unwholesome</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: These refer primarily to the blood,

<P>79. <B>greenly</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Unskilfully, with greenness, without <I>maturity</I> of judge-
ment.
<P>80. <B>hugger-mugger</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Sh. probably took the expression from North's
<I>Plutarch,</I> p. 999, ed. 1631 [p. 121, ed. Skeat]: &lquo;Antonius thinking good . . . . that
his bodie should be honorably buried, and not in hugger-mugger.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Its
meaning is seen in Florio's <I>Dict.:</I> Dinascoso, <I>secretly, hiddenly, in hugger-mugger.</I>
[See <SC>Wheatley's</SC> <I>Dict. of Reduplicated Words.</I>]
<P>81. <B>Divided</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC>: Compare V, ii, 221.
<P>85. <B>wonder</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The mysterious death of Pol. filled his son with doubt
and amazement.
<P>85. <B>in clouds</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (Nichols's <I>Lit. Hist.</I> ii, 575): Thirlby has conjectured
<I>inclos'd, i. e.</I> private, close in his apartment, and cites IV, vii, 130, in confirmation.
But change is needless; the text means: &lquo;to be reserved and mysterious in his con-
duct.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: At lofty distance and seclusion, <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> suggests
&lquo;keeps in his wonder, wraps himself in clouds.&rquo;
<P>88. <B>Wherein</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Wherein (that is, in which pestilent speeches) neces-

<P>91. <B>murdering-piece</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;A case shot is any kinde of small bullets,
nailes, old iron, or the like, to put into the case, to shoot out of the ordinances or
murderers; these will doe much mischiefe.&rquo;&mdash;Smith's <I>Sea Grammar,</I> 1627. Thus, in
Beau. &amp; Fl. <I>The Double Marriage,</I> IV, ii, 6: &lquo;A father's curses . . . like a murder-
ing-piece, aim not at one, But all that stand within the dangerous level.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC>:
A murdering-piece, or murderer, was a small piece of artillery; in Fr. <I>meurtri&egrave;re,</I>
which took its name from the loopholes and embrasures in towers and fortifications,
that were so called. &lquo;<I>Meurtri&egrave;re,</I> c'est un petit canonniere comme celles des
tours et murailles, ainsi appell&eacute;, parceque tirant par icelle a desceu, ceux ausquels
on tire sont facilement meurtri.&rquo;&mdash;Nicot. &lquo;<I>Visiere meurtri&egrave;re,</I> a port-hole for a mur-
thering Peece in the forecastle of a ship.&rquo;&mdash;Cotgrave. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): &lquo;Murdering-
pieces,&rquo; if we may trust Coles, were not always &lquo;small,&rquo; for he gives &lquo;A murdering-
piece, <I>Tormentum murale,</I>&rquo; and afterwards &lquo;Tormentum murale, <I>a great gun.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lat.
and Eng. Dict.</I>
<P>93. <B>Switzers</B>] <SC>Reed</SC>: In many of our old plays the guards attendant on kings
are called &lquo;Switzers,&rquo; and that without any regard to the country where the scene
lies. <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Law, logicke and the Switzers, may be hired to fight for any body.&rquo;
&mdash;Nash, <I>Christ's Teares over Jerusalem,</I> 1594.

<P>115. <B>unsmirched</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Clean, not defiled. This seems to be an allusion

seems the only place where Sh. uses this word, meaning <I>unsullied.</I> We have else-
where &lquo;smirched&rquo; and &lquo;besmirched&rquo; for <I>dirtied.</I>

<P>119-121. <B>There's...will</B>] <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Proof, as indeed all else is, that Sh

<P>119. <B>divinity</B>] <SC>Boswell</SC>: In Chettle's <I>Englandes Mourning Garment</I> is the fol
lowing anecdote of Queen Elizabeth: While her Majesty was on the river near
Greenwich, a shot was fired by accident, which struck the royal barge, and hurt a
waterman near her. &lquo;The French ambassador being amazed, and all crying Treason,
Treason! yet she, with an undaunted spirit, came to the open place of the barge,
and bad them never feare, for if the shot were made at her, they durst not shoots
againe: such majestie had her presence, and such boldnesse her heart, that she de-
spised all feare, and was, as all princes are or should be, so full of divine fullnesse,
that guiltie mortalitie durst not beholde her but with dazeled eyes.&rquo;
<P>119. <B>hedge</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: See <I>Job,</I> i, 10; and iii, 23.

<P>126. <SC>Theobald</SC> gives this note of <SC>Warburton's</SC>, which, not being in Warburton's
own edition, was probably a MS communication: Laertes is a good character. But
being in rebellion, Sh. avoids any appearance of sanctioning such conduct by put-

horror at his actions. The jealousy of the two reigns in which Sh. wrote would
not dispense with less exactness. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Mercy on Warburton's notion of

the extreme turpitude of his consent to become an agent and accomplice of the
King's treachery; and to this end he re-introduces Oph. at the close of this scene to
afford a probable stimulus of passion in her brother.

<P>sent her most precious senses after the object of her inflamed affection. <SC>Warburton</SC>:
The cause of Ophelia's madness was grief, occasioned by the violence of her natural
affection for her murdered father; her brother, therefore, with great force of expression,
says: &lquo;Nature is <I>fal'n</I> in love, and where 'tis <I>fal'n.</I>&rquo; [Thus Warburton's text.]
To distinguish the passion of <I>natural affection</I> from the passion of love between
the two sexes, <I>i. e. Nature,</I> or <I>natural affection is fal'n in love.</I> <SC>Johnson</SC>: These
lines might have been omitted in the Folio without great loss, for they are obscure
and affected; but, I think, they require no emendation. <I>Love</I> (says Laertes) is the
passion by which <I>nature is most</I> exalted and <I>refined;</I> and as substances, <I>refined</I> and
subtilised, easily obey any impulse, or follow any attraction, some part of nature, so
purified and <I>refined,</I> flies off after the attracting object, after the thing it loves.
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Fine&rquo; seems to mean &lquo;delicately tender,&rquo; and &lquo;instance&rquo; &lquo;proof&rquo; or
&lquo;example.&rquo; &lquo;The thing it loves&rquo; is here Polonius; the &lquo;precious instance,&rquo; Ophelia's
natural soundness of mind. Her sanity has followed her father to the grave. <SC>Col-
lier</SC> (ed. 2): Lines 157-159 are struck through with a pen in the (MS), probably
because they were not understood.

<P>167. <B>wheel</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: We should read <I>weal.</I> She is now rambling on the
ballad of the steward and his lord's daughter; and in these words speaks of the
state he assumed. <SC>Heath</SC>: Possibly by &lquo;wheel&rquo; is here meant the burden of the
ballad. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) says that &lquo;most critics seem now to agree with Steevens [<I>sic</I>]
in&rquo; thus referring it to the burden or refrain; but <SC>Clarendon</SC> asserts that no satis-
factory example has been found of the word in this sense. <SC>Steevens</SC> cites a very
apposite illustration &lquo;from memory, from a book of which&rquo; he could not &lquo;recollect
the exact title or date;&rquo; unfortunately when Steevens does not adduce line, page,
and title, his illustrations are to be received with caution; his wit was too ready at a
pinch, and the simple reference to a &lquo;black-letter quarto in my possession&rquo; was con-
venient, much like Sir Walter Scott's &lquo;<I>Old Play.</I>&rquo; The illustration in question
(which has been repeated by several edd. since his day) is as follows: &lquo;The song
was accounted a good one, thogh it was not moche graced by the <I>wheele,</I> which in
no wise accorded with the subject-matter thereof.&rquo; A conclusive quotation, if&mdash;&mdash;.
Steevens adds that &lquo;Rota&rquo; is the ancient musical term in Latin for the burden of a
song. <SC>Johnson</SC> suggests: &lquo;perhaps the lady stolen by the steward was reduced to
<I>spin!</I>&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC> divests this suggestion of its tragic element by supposing that the
wheel is here used in its ordinary sense, and that these words refer to the occupation
of the girl who is supposed to sing the song alluded to by Oph. <SC>Staunton</SC> says it
was, perhaps, the practice on the old stage for Oph. to play the &lquo;wheel,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> the
refrain, upon her lute before these words. [If &lquo;wheel&rquo; ever meant <I>refrain,</I> the
meaning apparently had become obsolete when F<SUB>2</SUB> was printed. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>170. <B>rosemary</B>] See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> IV, v, 79, and notes. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 259):
The mind of Oph. is thrown off its poise by the shock which she had received;
she thinks of marriage: with that comes the idea of rosemary, the sweet-scented
rosemary, and she addresses him who should have been the bridegroom, Ham.
himself, as her &lquo;love.&rquo; She then feels her disappointment. Ham. is not there, and
she turns to another flower wrought up in her wild attire, pansies, as more fitting her
condition,&mdash;a flower connected with melancholy, then often called <I>thought,</I> and
taking its name from it. &lquo;There's a daisy; I would give you some violets, but,&rquo; &amp;c.
When the mind is unsettled, it is usual for some idea to recur which has been intro-
duced at a critical period of the person's life. Now, when Laer. was warning Oph.
against encouraging the attentions of Ham., he urged her to consider his trifling but
as &lquo;A <I>violet</I> in the youth of primy nature.&rquo; These words had remained imprinted
on her mind, associated with the idea of Ham. and the idea of her brother, and they
now recur to her memory when she again converses with her brother on the same
unhappy subject. The violets withered when her father died. When Ham. had
slain Pol. there was a final obstacle interposed to their union. <SC>Staunton</SC>: There
is method in poor Ophelia's distribution. She presents to each the herb popularly
appropriate to his age or disposition. To Laer., whom in her distraction she prob-
ably confounds with her lover, she gives &lquo;rosemary&rquo; as an emblem of his faithful
remembrance; and &lquo;pansies&rquo; to denote love's &lquo;thoughts&rquo; or <I>troubles.</I> <SC>Delius</SC>:
Probably these flowers existed only in Ophelia's fantasy, and there was no distribution
of real flowers to the persons present.
<P>171. <B>pansies</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;For thoughts, because of its name, <I>pens&eacute;es.</I>&rquo; In <I>N.
&amp; Qu.,</I> 22 Oct. 1864, <SC>Fabius Oxoniensis</SC> gives a number of the names by which
this flower is known among rustics and old writers; see also <SC>Beisly</SC> (<I>Sh. Garden,</I>
p. 156).
<P>173. <B>document</B>] <SC>Edinburgh Review</SC> (<I>Shakespearian Glossaries,</I> July, 1869):
This word is here used in its earlier and etymological sense of instruction, lesson,
teaching. This early signification is well illustrated in the <I>Fairy Queen</I> [i, 10, 19&mdash;
Clarendon], &lquo;her sacred booke . . . . She unto him disclosed every whit, And
heavenly documents thereout did preach.&rquo; The word was habitually used in this
sense in Shakespeare's day, but has now wholly lost its primitive signification, and
is restricted to its secondary sense of written precepts, instructions, and evidences.
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cotgrave gives &lquo;Document: m. A document, precept; instruction,
admonition; experiment, example.&rquo;

<P><I>dissemble.</I> <SC>Nares</SC>: This was generally considered an inflammatory herb, and was
certainly emblematic of flattery. [Several instances are given.] <SC>Staunton</SC>: For
the King she has &lquo;fennel,&rquo; signifying &lquo;flattery&rquo; and &lquo;lust;&rquo; and &lquo;columbines,&rquo;
which marked ingratitude. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): We may certainly suppose that she
offers the King &lquo;flattery,&rquo; though we do not agree with Staunton in supposing that
here <I>fennel</I> signifies &lquo;lust&rquo; also. <SC>Beisly</SC> (p. 157) cites Holland's <I>Pliny</I> [p. 77, ed.
1635]: &lquo;Fennel hath a singular property to mundifie our sight, and take away the
filme or web that ouercasteth and dimmeth our eyes.&rquo; This property is noticed by
most of our early writers on plants, and it is in reference to this quality that Oph.
presents it to the King to clear his sight, just as the rosemary was given to Laer. to
aid his memory.
<P>175. <B>columbines</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: In <I>All Fools,</I> by Chapman, 1605: &lquo;a columbine?
No; that thankless flower fits not my garden,&rquo;&mdash;II, i. Gerard and other herbalists
impute few, if any, virtues to them; and they may therefore be styled <I>thankless,</I>
because they appear to make no grateful return for their creation. S[<SC>tephen</SC>]
W[<SC>eston</SC>]: Columbine was an emblem of cuckoldom on account of the horns of its
nectaria, which are remarkable in this plant. <SC>Holt White</SC>: It was also emblem-
atic of forsaken lovers: &lquo;The columbine in tawny often taken Is then ascribed to
such as are forsaken.&rquo;&mdash;Browne's <I>Britannia's Pastorals,</I> b. i, song ii, 1613. <SC>Dyce</SC>
(<I>Gloss.</I>): But here Oph. is not assigning the columbine to herself, and, except her-
self, there is no &lquo;love-lorn&rquo; person present.
<P>176, 177. <B>rue . . . Sundays</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The reason why &lquo;rue&rquo; was called
&lquo;herb of grace&rquo; is because that herb was a principal ingredient in the potion which
the Romish priests used to force the possessed to swallow when they exorcised them.
These exorcisms being performed generally on a Sunday, in church before the whole
congregation, is the reason why she says we call it &lquo;herb of grace o' Sundays.&rquo;
[<SC>Dyce</SC> says Warburton was only repeating what he had read in the works of a great
divine,&mdash;Jeremy Taylor; see <SC>Todd</SC> <I>post.</I>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe there is a quibble
meant in this passage; &lquo;rue&rquo; anciently signifying the same as <I>ruth, i. e.</I> sorrow. Oph.
gives the Queen some, and keeps a proportion of it for herself. There is the same
kind of play with the same word in <I>Rich. II:</I> III, iv, 104. &lquo;Herb of grace&rquo; is one
of the titles which Tucca gives to William Rufus, in Decker's <I>Satiromastix.</I> I
suppose the first syllable of the surname <I>Ru</I>fus introduced the quibhle. <SC>Henley</SC>:
The following passage from Greene's <I>Quip for an Upstart Courtier</I> will furnish the
best reason for calling <I>rue</I> herb of grace o' Sundays: &lquo;&mdash;some of them smil'd and
said, <I>Rue</I> was called <I>Herbegrace,</I> which, though they scorned in their youth, they
might weare in their age, and that it was never too late to say <I>Miserere.</I>&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>:
&lquo;Herb of grace&rquo; was not the <I>Sunday name,</I> but the <I>every-day</I> name of &lquo;rue.&rquo; In
the common dictionaries of Shakespeare's time it is called &lquo;herb of grace.&rquo; See
Florio s. v. <I>ruta,</I> and Cotgrave s. v. <I>rue.</I> There is no ground, therefore, for sup-

<P>posing with Warburton that &lquo;rue&rquo; was called &lquo;herb of grace&rquo; from its being used in
exorcisms performed in churches on Sundays. Oph. only means, I think, that the
Queen may with peculiar propriety on <I>Sundays,</I> when she solicits pardon for that
crime which she has so much occasion to <I>rue</I> and repent of, call her &lquo;rue&rquo; &lquo;herb of
grace.&rquo; After having given the Queen &lquo;rue,&rquo; to remind her of the <I>sorrow</I> and <I>con-
trition</I> she ought to feel for her incestuous marriage, Oph. tells her she may wear it
with a <I>difference,</I> to distinguish it from that worn by Oph. herself; because her tears
flowed from the loss of a father, those of the Queen ought to flow for her guilt.
<SC>Todd</SC> (ap. Caldecott) cites Jeremy Taylor's <I>A Dissuasive from Popery,</I> Part I, ch.
ii, sect. ix: &lquo;They [the Romish exorcists] are to try the devil by holy water, incense,
sulphur, rue; which from thence, as we suppose, came to be called herb of grace.&rquo;
<SC>Caldecott</SC> cites a passage from Edward Alleyn's letters [<I>Var.</I> 1821, vol. xxi, p. 390,
and <I>Sh. Soc.</I> vol. ix, p. 26], which seems to imply that &lquo;herb of grace&rquo; and &lquo;rue&rquo;
were different plants: &lquo;Every evening&rquo; [Alleyn is telling his wife, whom he calls
&lquo;good sweete mouse,&rquo; to take precautions against the plague raging that year, 1593,
in London] &lquo;throwe water before your dore and in your bake sid, and have in your
windowes good store of reue and herbe of grace.&rquo; That this &lquo;herb of grace&rquo; was
wormwood Malone shows by referring to the reply from Alleyn's parents to this
letter: &lquo;for your good cownsell . . . . we all thanck you, which wasse for keping
of our howsse cleane . . . . and strainge our windowes with wormwode and rewe.&rquo;
<I>-Sh. Soc.</I> vol. ix, p. 30.
<P>178. <B>difference</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This seems to refer to the rules of heraldry, where
the younger brothers of a family bear the same arms <I>with a difference,</I> or mark of
distinction. So, in Holinshed's <I>Reign of King Richard II,</I> p. 443: &lquo;&mdash;because he
was the youngest of the Spensers, he bare a border gules for a difference.&rquo; There
may, however, be somewhat more implied here than is expressed. You, madam
(says Oph. to the Queen), may call your <I>rue</I> by its Sunday name, <I>herb of grace,</I> and
so wear it with a difference to distinguish it from mine, which can never be anything
but merely <I>rue, i. e.</I> sorrow. <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Between the ruth and wretchedness of
guilt, and the ruth and sorrows of misfortune, it would be no difficult matter to dis-
tinguish. <SC>Skeat</SC> [<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 25 Dec. 1869): There is no difficulty here if we do
not force the words into some heraldic phrase. It merely means this: I offer you
rue, which has two meanings; it is sometimes called <I>herb of grace,</I> and in that sense
I take some for myself; but with a slight difference of spelling it means <I>ruth,</I> and
in that respect it will do for you. This explanation is not mine,&mdash;it is Shakespeare's
own; see <I>Rich. II:</I> III, iv, 105, 106. [A discussion on the meaning of this phrase
is also to be found in <I>Edin. Rev.</I> July, 1869; <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 25 Sept. 1869; 23 Oct.
1869, and 8 Jan. 1870.]

<P><I>fessio Amantis,</I> 1554, speaking first of the funeral of Chaucer, and then of Gower,
says: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; he lieth buried in the monasterie of Seynt Peter's at Westminster, &amp;c.
<I>On whose soules and all christen, Jesu have mercie.</I>&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: So, with this most
touching prayer, Oph. goes to meet her death. It displays admirably her simple and
loving spirit, and seems to be a protest beforehand against the hard-hearted law
which hinders her having the full Christian burial-rites.
<P>194 <B>of</B>] For instances of &lquo;of&rquo; used for <I>on,</I> see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 175 and &sect; 181.
<P>195. <SC>Jennens</SC>: &lquo;Do you see this?&rquo; is spoken to the King; and &lquo;O God!&rquo; is only
an exclamation expressing the anguish of Laertes's mind on the sight of his sister's
frenzy. [So in Jennens's text. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>196. <B>commune</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: To <I>common</I> of F<SUB>1</SUB> is to &lquo;commune,&rquo; which, pro-
nounced as anciently spelt, is still in frequent provincial use. So, in <I>The Last Voy-
age of Captaine Frobisher,</I> by Dionyse Settle, bl. l., 1577: &lquo;Our Generall, repayred
with the ship boat to common or sign with them.&rquo; Again, in Holinshed's account
of Jack Cade's insurrection: &lquo;&mdash; to whome were sent from the king the archbishop,
&amp;c., to common with him of his griefs and requests.&rquo; <SC>Boswell</SC>: Surely the word
<I>common</I> in F<SUB>1</SUB> means, I must be allowed to participate in your grief, to feel <I>in com-
mon</I> with you. [<SC>Grant White</SC>, in his excellent <I>Sh. Scholar,</I> p. 421, was beguiled
by the &lquo;homely strength&rquo; of the F<SUB>1</SUB> text into approval of Boswell's interpretation of
it, much to <SC>Dyce's</SC> &lquo;surprise,&rquo; who pronounced it &lquo;most erroneous;&rquo; the two words,
<I>common</I> and &lquo;commune,&rquo; are mere variations in spelling of the same word; they were
both accented alike, on the first syllable,&mdash;as Grant White afterwards remarked in
his edition. And <SC>Hudson</SC> says Milton so accents &lquo;commune,&rquo; and so also eve<*>
Wordsworth. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>198. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: That is, &lquo;of your wisest friends, whom you will.&rquo;

<P>the close of the interview with his mother: &lquo;O 'tis most sweet When in one line
two crafts directly meet.&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;If the word <I>crafts</I> had its present maritime significance
in Shakespeare's time, the pun alone is conclusive of a pre-arranged capture. <I>How</I>
arranged is neither here nor there; but opportunities of chartering a free cruiser
could not have been wanting to a prince of Denmark, and, what is more significant,
<I>the fleet of Fortinbras was then in port at Elsinor.</I> There is an understanding, just
ever so vaguely glanced at, between the two young princes. But the following lines
admit of but one interpretation: &ldquo;<I>Let it work; For 'tis the sport to have the en-
giner Hoist with his own petar; and 't shall go hard</I> <SC>But I will delve one
yard below their mines And blow them at the moon</SC>!&rdquo; One would think
it required a miraculous allowance of critical obtuseness to ignore a counterplot so
strikingly pre-announced. . . . To make assurance doubly sure, comes the letter to
Hor., &ldquo;In the grapple <I>I boarded them;</I> on <I>the instant</I> they got clear of <I>our ship;</I>
so I <I>alone</I> became their prisoner. They dealt with me like <I>thieves of mercy;</I> <SC>but
they knew what they did</SC>.&rdquo; Can circumstantial proof go farther? Could any
twelve men of sense, on such a record, acquit Ham. of being an accessory before, as
well as after the fact?&rquo; [See <SC>Snider</SC>, Appendix, Vol. II, p. 183.]
<P>21. <B>as</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: We must either take &lquo;as&rquo; = <I>as though,</I> or supply <I>withal</I>
after &lquo;death.&rquo;
<P>23. <B>will make</B>] For instances of the omission of the relative, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 244,
and <I>Macb.</I> V, vii, 7.
<P>24. <B>bore</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The calibre of a gun, or the capacity of the barrel. &lquo;The
matter would carry heavier words.&rquo; <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> cannot persuade himself that
&lquo;bore&rquo; is not a verbal substantive from &lquo;to bear,&rquo; and means &lquo;capacity for bearing.&rquo;
<P>28. <SC>Clarke</SC>: This simple yet strong conclusion to his sedate but most earnest
letter to his bosom-friend might, we think, fully serve to denote Hamlet's per-
fect sanity. Madmen do not write in a style thus condensed and pertinent; if
they are warm they are violent, if they are fervent they are excited; but here is
warmth of friendship with staid expression, fervour of feeling with sobriety of
assurince.

<P>18. <B>general gender</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The <I>common race</I> of the people. <SC>Delius</SC>:

<P>20. <B>spring</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: This simile is neither very seasonable in the deep interest
of this conversation, nor very accurately applied. If the spring had changed base
metals to gold, the thought had been more proper. <SC>Reed</SC>: The allusion is to the
qualities of the dropping-well at Knaresborough, in Yorkshire. Camden (1590, p.
564) thus mentions it: &lquo;Sub quo fons est in quem ex impendentibus rupibus aqu&aelig;
guttatim distillant, unde <I>Dropping Well</I> vocant, in quem quicquid ligni immittitur,
lapideo cortice brevi obduci et lapidescere observatum est.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Lily
has: &lquo;Would I had sipped of that ryuer in Caria, which turneth those that drinke
of it to stones.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Euphues,</I> p. 63, ed. Arber.
