<P>&lquo;gyves,&rquo; but in &lquo;graces.&rquo; How can corporeal &lquo;gyves&rquo; be converted into incorporeal,
abstract &lquo;graces&rquo;? That is more than even the well at Knaresborough could do.
An abstract noun in this connection ruins the whole metaphor, and is illogical.
If we substitute some abstract noun for &lquo;gyves,&rquo; while restoring logical propriety,
we deprive the simile of all significant clearness, force, and depth, and to introduce
the wonder-working spring in order to compare together two abstract qualities
would be pointless, and assuredly not in accordance with Shakespeare's genius
and style. Read, therefore: <I>graves. Graves,</I> now spelled <I>greaves,</I> is found also in
2 <I>Hen. IV:</I> IV, iv, 50, where, as here, something mean becomes ennobled. For
the spelling, compare &lquo;thraves,&rquo; instead of <I>threaves</I> (Chapman's <I>Iliad,</I> xi, 477);
and &lquo;stale,&rquo; instead of <I>steale</I> or <I>stele</I> (<I>Ib.</I> iv, 173). <SC>Stratmann</SC> praises this emen-
dation of Elze's as judicious.
<P>22. <SC>Jennens</SC> finds the reading of the Ff so unnatural and impossible that he
adopts that of Q<SUB>2</SUB>Q<SUB>3</SUB>, reading <I>so loved, arm'd,</I> and paraphrases, &lquo;Too slightly timbered
for one so loved and armed with the affections and veneration of the people.&rquo; The
<I>armes</I> of Q<SUB>4</SUB> are put for the person <I>armed,</I> and the love applied to them which is
meant for him. In both these readings we have the idea of a suit of armor reverbe-
rating an arrow back to its bow, which is not only possible, but just. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
The reading of the Ff, however, is supported by Ascham's <I>Toxophilus;</I> &lquo;Weake
bowes, and lyghte shaftes can not stande in a rough wynde.&rquo; [p. 151, ed. Arber.]
<P>25, 26. <B>have . . . driven</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 425: Here note that though the first line
could be re-transposed, and Laer. could naturally say, &lquo;I have lost a father,&rquo; on the
other hand he could not say, &lquo;I have driven a sister,&rquo; without completely changing
the sense. &lquo;Have&rquo; is here used in its original sense, and is equivalent to &lquo;I find.&rquo;
When &lquo;have&rquo; is thus used without any notion of action, it is separated from the par-
ticiple passive. See I, ii, 215; III, iii, 38.
<P>27. <B>praises</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: If I may praise what has been, but is now to be found
no more.

<P>112. <B>begun by time</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The meaning may be, <I>love</I> is not innate in us,
and co-essential to our nature, but begins at a certain time from some external cause,
and being always subject to the operations of time, suffers change and diminution.
<SC>M. Mason</SC>: The King reasons thus:&mdash;&lquo;I do not suspect that you did not love your
father; but I know that time abates the force of affection.&rquo; I therefore suspect that
we ought to read: &lquo;love is begone by time.&rquo; I suppose that Sh. places the syllable
<I>be</I> before <I>gone,</I> as we say <I>be-</I>paint, <I>be-</I>spatter, <I>be-</I>think, &amp;c., or possibly we should
read &lquo;by-gone.&rquo; <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 14): The dominant idea of the speech is that love
is abated by time. Read &lquo;love is <I>begnawn</I> by time,&rquo; an expression which exactly
conveys the sense required, while the change requisite for perverting it into the
received text is slight. Compare <I>Rich. III:</I> I, iii, 222; <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> IV, v.
293.
<P>112. <B>by time</B>] <SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 197): Read <I>betime.</I> The King means, &lquo;love begins
at an early period of life, but as our affections ripen this affection suffers abatement.&rquo;
<SC>Keightley</SC>: I cannot make any good sense out of this. I suspect that &lquo;time&rquo;
may be owing to the same word lower down. The love spoken of seems to be that
of children for parents, and possibly the word was <I>childhood, birth.</I>
<P>113. <B>proof</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: In transactions of daily experience. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Cir-

<P>117. <B>still</B>] Always, constantly. See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> V, iii, 106, and notes.
<P>118. <B>plurisy</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: I would believe, for the honor of Sh., that he wrote
<I>plethory.</I> But I observe the dramatic writers of that time frequently call a fulness
of blood a <I>pleurisy,</I> as if it came not from <G>rleupa\</G>, but from <I>plus, pluris.</I> [This
emendation Warburton communicated by letter to Theobald, who replied that it had
also occurred to him, but that he was doubtful of it, partly from &lquo;the <I>accental</I> sylla-
ble falling so wrong in the verse, the <I>o</I> being long&rquo; [here Theobald's Greek misled
him], and partly because Sh. might have mistaken the nature of pleurisie, as Beau
&amp; Fl. seem to have done: &lquo;those too many excellencies, that feed Your pride, turn to
a pleurisy.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Custom of the Country</I> [II, i, p. 417, ed. Dyce]. In his edition Theobald
added: &lquo;thou grand decider . . . that heal'st The earth when it is sick, and cur'st
the world O' the pleurisy of people.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Two Noble Kinsmen</I> [V, i, p. 417, ed. Dyce].
<SC>Tollet</SC>, in the <I>Var.</I> 1821, cites: Mascal's <I>Treatise on Cattle,</I> 1662, p. 187, &lquo;Against
the blood, or <I>plurisie</I> of blood. The disease of blood is, some young horses will
feed, and being fat will <I>increase</I> blood, and so <I>grow to a plurisie,</I> and <I>die.</I>&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>
cites: &lquo;Must your hot itch and plurisy of lust . . . be fed Up to a surfeit.&rquo;&mdash;<I>'Tis
Pity She's a Whore,</I> IV, iii [Ford's <I>Works,</I> p. 177, ed. Dyce]. Other instances are
given by <SC>M. Mason</SC> and <SC>Nares</SC>, in all of which the word is spelled &lquo;plurisy,&rquo; and
means <I>a surfeit, a plethory.</I> Whence <SC>Nares</SC> affirms that it means &lquo;a plethora or
redundancy of blood. Not the same as <I>pleurisy,</I> but derived from <I>plus, pluris,</I>
more.&rquo; And Nares is followed in the derivation from <I>plus, pluris,</I> by <SC>Dyce, Col-
lier, Staunton, White</SC>, and <SC>Hudson. Gifford</SC> also explains: &lquo;Thy plurisy of
goodness is thy ill&rquo; (Massinger's <I>Unnatural Combat,</I> IV, i, p. 196, ed. Gifford) by
&lquo;thy superabundance of goodness: the thought is from Sh.,&rquo; and cites the present
passage from <I>Hamlet.</I> <SC>Coleridge</SC>, in his <I>Notes,</I> says, &lquo;I rather think that Sh. meant
<I>pleurisy,</I> but involved in it the thought of <I>plethora,</I> as supposing pleurisy to arise
from too much blood; otherwise I can not explain &ldquo;this &lquo;should&rquo; is like a spend-
thrift sigh That hurts by easing.&rdquo; In a stitch in the side every one must have
heaved a sigh that &ldquo;hurt by easing.&rdquo; Since writing the above I feel confirmed
that &ldquo;pleurisy&rdquo; is the right word; for I find that in the old medical dictionaries the
pleurisy is often called the &ldquo;plethory.&rdquo; &rquo; In fine, Sh. and the early dramatists were
misled by the sound into supposing that pleurisy was the same as plethory, and it
was accordingly spelled &lquo;plurisy,&rquo; as indicating the symptoms implied in its supposed
derivation from <I>plus, pluris.</I> It is better to retain that spelling, although there is no
disease, I believe, so named, or rather so spelled, at present. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>119. <B>too-much</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: Like &lquo;a great amiss,&rquo; &lquo;the why and wherefore,&rquo; and
the like. English had at this time something like the flexibility of the Greek, and
had no difficulty in throwing out phrases like <G>to\ a(/gan</G> and <G>to\ rpi/n</G>.

<P>128. <B>spendthrift sigh</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This nonsense should be read &lquo;a spend-
thrift's <I>sign,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> though a spendthrift's entering into bonds or mortgages gives him
a present relief from his straits, yet it ends in much greater distresses. <SC>Heath</SC>:
This refers to a very idle opinion, still prevalent among the common people, that
every sigh draws drops of blood from the heart and tends to shorten life. <SC>Calde-
cott</SC> cites <SC>Dr Sherwen</SC>: To have conceived, previous to the discovery of the cir-
culation of the blood, that sighing sucked the blood, was an idea natural enough
for after, or rather during, a deep sigh the blood flows more freely through the pul-
monary artery and its ramifications in the different lobes of the lungs; and it might
have appeared to the old physiologists to be thus drawn away from the heart and the
general mass into the lungs. How it got back again into the heart, they did not
know. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The meaning is that the mere recognition of a duty without
the will to perform it, while it satisfies for a moment, enfeebles the moral nature.
We have the same notion of sighs wasting the vital powers in 2 <I>Hen. VI:</I> III, ii,
63; <I>Mid. N. D.,</I> III, ii, 97. [See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> III, v, 58.] <SC>Moberly</SC>: He who
vainly acknowledges that he &lquo;should&rquo; have done a thing is like a spendthrift sighing
for his squandered estate.

<P>160. <B>that</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;That&rquo; follows &lquo;when,&rquo; after a parenthesis or other in

<P>160. <B>prepared</B>] <SC>White</SC>: The Qq are decidedly wrong. &lquo;A goblet might be
well spoken of as prepared for the nonce, but not as preferred [offered] for the

<P>161. <B>nonce</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: For the special occasion. The phrase was originally
&lquo;for the once,&rquo; the &lquo;n&rquo; being added for euphony. [See <SC>M&auml;tzner</SC>, vol. i, p. 181.]
<SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 260): There is little in our poel's writings more painful than such a
scene as this; the cool deliheration with which Laer. comes into such a plot is so
inconsistent with his character as exhibited in the other parts of the play; the clum-
siness of the whole contrivance, and the barefaced manner in which the King is
made to expose his villainous purpose to one who is already half his enemy, that
one is tempted to ask where the mighty spirit is fled which dictated some portions of
this most unequal performance. What an abandonment also of the <I>great design</I> of
the tragedy (as announced in the First Act), that there should be a train laid which
is to bring about the catastrophe while the principal actor is not cognizant of it, and
has, of course, no part in it. The death of the King is in consequence brought
about without that intention of the mind of Ham. which was necessary to connect
it with the early scenes of the play, and to give dignity to the great catastrophe.

<P>know what passed in the mind of Oph. when she placed herself in so perilous a situ-
ation. After the facts had been weighed and considered, the priest in the next Act
pronounces that <I>her death was doubtful.</I> <SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 197): As the Queen seems
to give this description from ocular knowledge, it may be asked why, apprised as
she was of Ophelia's distraction, she did not take steps to prevent the fatal catastro-
phe, especially as there was so fair an opportunity of saving her while she was, by
her clothes, borne &lquo;mermaidlike-up,&rquo; and the Queen was at leisure to hear her
&lquo;chanting old tunes.&rquo; T. C. [<SC>Thomas Campbell</SC>?] (<I>Blackwood's Maga.,</I> Feb.
1818, p. 511): Perhaps this description by the Queen is poetical rather than dramatic;
but its exquisite beauty prevails, and Oph., dying and dead, is still the same Oph.
that first won our love. Perhaps the very forgetfulness of her throughout the re-
mainder of the play, leaves the soul at full liberty to dream of the departed. She
has passed away from the earth like a beautiful air,&mdash;a delightful dream. There
would have been no place for her in the agitation and tempest of the final catas-
trophe. We are satisfied that she is in her grave. And in place of beholding her
involved in the shocking troubles of the closing scene, we remember that her heart
lies at rest, and the remembrance is like the returning voice of melancholy music.
<SC>Hudson</SC>: This passage is deservedly celebrated, and aptly illustrates the Poet's power
of making the description of a thing better than the thing itself, by giving us
his eyes to see it with. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: This speech of the Queen is certainly un-
worthy of its author and of the occasion. The enumeration of plants is quite as
unsuitable to so tragical a scene as the description of the Dover cliff, in <I>Lear,</I> IV,
vi, 11-24. Besides, there was no one by to witness the death of Oph., else she
would have been rescued.
<P>185. <B>drown'd?</B>] <SC>Corson</SC>: It would appear from the Queen's reply that Laertes's
speech must have been meant to be interrogative. If exclamatory, the iteration
thereupon of the Queen, &lquo;Drown'd, drown'd,&rquo; is almost ludicrous, and makes one
feel that the poor girl has had indeed, as Laer. says in the next speech, &lquo;too much
of water.&rquo;
<P>186. <B>drown'd</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Beau. &amp; Fl. ridicule this passage: &lquo;I will run mad

full Lady,</I> III, ii, p. 68, ed. Dyce. <SC>Elze</SC> finds another allusion to this passage in
the same play of <I>The Scornfull Lady,</I> II, iii, p. 41: &lquo;Drown'd, drown'd at sea.&rquo;

the hero, and such a phrase could hardly be avoided. There are, however, undoubt-

<P>189. <B>trick</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Our habit, a property that makes a part of us. <SC>Clar-

<P>193. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: That Laer. might be excused in some degree for not cooling,

<P><B>Scene I.</B>] <SC>Schlegel</SC> (ii, 194): The only circumstance from which this piece
might be found less theatrical than other tragedies of Sh. is, that in the last scenes
the main action either stands still or appears to retrograde. This, however, was in-
evitable, and lies in the nature of the thing. The whole is intended to show that a
consideration, which would exhaust all the relations and possible consequences of a
deed to the very limits of human foresight, cripples the power of acting.

<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>: Until within a very recent period it was customary for one of the
Grave-diggers to preface his labors by divesting himself of about a dozen waistcoats,
an operation which always created great merriment, and which, perhaps, had come
down hy tradition from the players of Shakespeare's own time. The Doctor, in <I>The
Duchess of Malfi,</I> according to a stage-direction in ed. 1708, &lquo;puts off his four cloaks,
one after another,&rquo;&mdash;a similar stratagem to create the laughter of the audience.
<P>4. <B>straight</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Make her grave from east to west, in a direct line, parallel
to the church; not from north to south, athwart the regular line. <SC>Jennens</SC> first
pointed out that &lquo;straight&rquo; here means simply <I>forthwith;</I> and <SC>Steevens</SC> corroborated
it by citations from III, iv, 1; <I>Oth.</I> III, iii, 87; <I>Merry Wives,</I> IV, ii, 81. <SC>Malone</SC>
added from Herhert's <I>Jacula Prudentum:</I> &lquo;There is no churchyard so handsome
that a man would desire straight to be buried there.&rquo; <SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 261) believes that
the Clown refers to the <I>place</I> where the grave should be; suicides were buried on
the north side of the church, in unconsecrated ground.
<P>4. <B>crowner</B>] <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. Illustrated by Old Authors,</I> p. 72): This word is
generally supposed to be a corruption of the Clown's, but it is merely the English of
the Law Latin <I>coronator,</I> from <I>corona,</I> a crown, which Holinshed also uses.
<P>9. <B>se offendendo</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Used for <I>se defendendo,</I> a finding of the jury in
justifiable homicide.

<P>21. <B>Crowner's Quest law</B>] <SC>Sir John Hawkins</SC>: I strongly suspect that this
is in ridicule of a case of forfeiture of a lease to the Crown, reported by Plowden
in his 3 Eliza. It seems that Sir James Hales drowned himself in a river in a fit of
insanity (produced, it is supposed, by his having been one of the judges who con-
demned Lady Jane Grey), and the question was whether this did not work a forfeit-
ure to the Crown of his lease. The coroner sat on him, and a verdict of <I>felo de se</I>
was rendered. The legal and logical subtilties arising in the course of the case
gave a very fair opportunity of sneering at &lquo;Crowner's Quest law&rquo;:&mdash;Walsh said that
the act consists of three parts. The first is the imagination, which is a reflection or
meditation of the mind, whether or no it is convenient for him to destroy himself,
and what way it can be done. The second is the resolution, which is a determina-
tion of the mind to destroy himself, and to do it in this or that particular way. The
third is the perfection, which is the execution of what the mind has resolved to do.
And this perfection consists of two parts, viz. the beginning and the end. The be-
ginning is the doing of the act which causes death, and the end is the death, which is
only a sequel to the act.&rquo; Much subtilty was expended in finding out whether Sir
James was the <I>agent</I> or the <I>patient;</I> or, in other words, whether <I>he went to the water</I>
or <I>the water came to him:</I>&mdash;&lquo;Sir James Hales was dead, and how came he to his
death? It may be answered, by drowning; and who drowned him? Sir James
Hales; and when did he drown him? In his life time. So that Sir James Hales
being alive caused Sir James Hales to die, and the act of the living man was the
death of the dead man. And then for this offence it is reasonable to punish the
living man who committed the offence, and not the dead man. But how can he be
said to be punished alive when the punishment comes after death?&rquo; &amp;c., &amp;c. <SC>Ma-
lone</SC> thinks that Sh. must have heard of this case in conversation, for it was deter-

that playhouse (see Collier's <I>Annals of the Stage,</I> i, 388). Is it then unlikely that

<P>59-62, &amp;c. <SC>Theobald</SC> was the first to discover that the Clown here sings some
stanzas from a poem, which, because it was printed in a collection of <I>Songes and
Sonnettes, written by the ryght honorable Lorde Henry Haward, late Earle of Surrey,
and other,</I> and published by Tottel in 1557, Theobald inferred was written by the
noble lord whose name by precedence of rank stood on the title-page. But Gas-
coigne, who was ten years old when Surrey was beheaded, attrihutes the poem in
question to Lord Vaux, in an <I>Epistle to a Young Gentleman,</I> prefixed to his Posies:
&lquo;The L. Vaux his dittie, beginning thus <I>I loath,</I> was thought by some to be made
upon his death-bed,&rquo; &amp;c. And <SC>Warton</SC>, in his <I>Hist. of Eng. Poetry,</I> iii, 45, con-
siders that &lquo;undoubted evidence&rquo; is found that Thomas Lord Vaux was the anthor,
in a manuscript in the British Museum (<I>Harleian</I> MS, 1703) in which we have a
copy of this poem, beginning <I>I lothe that I did love,</I> with this title: &lquo;A dyttye or
sonet made by the lord Vans [&lquo;vaux,&rquo; ap. Arber, p. xiii], in the time of the noble
quene Marye, representing the image of Death.&rquo; It is thus given in Arber's Re-
print of Tottel's <I>Miscellany,</I> p. 173:

<P>74. <B>jowls</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: If proof were wanted of the exquisite propriety and force
of effect with which Sh. uses words, and words of even homely fashion, there could
hardly be a more pointed instance than the verb &lquo;jowls&rquo; here. What strength it
gives to the impression of the head and cheek-bone smiting against the earth! and
how it makes the imagination feel the bruise in sympathy!

always used in a bad sense by Sh.

<P>85. <B>mazzard</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: A head; usually derived, but with very little probability,

been a burlesque word, and was as likely to be made from <I>mazer,</I> a bowl, as from
anything else; comparing the head to a large goblet. <SC>Wedgwood</SC> confirms Nares's
derivation. &lquo;In a similar way, Italian <I>zucca,</I> properly a gourd, and thence a drink-

<P>88. <B>loggats</B>] The nature of this game has been much discussed, but what appears
to be the most exact description is thus given by <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;&ldquo;Loggats,&rdquo; diminu-
tive of <I>log.</I> The game so called resembles bowls, but with notable differences. First,
it is played not on a green, but on a floor strewed with ashes. The Jack is a wheel
of lignum-vit&aelig; or other hard wood, nine inches in diameter and three or four inches
thick. The loggat, made of apple-wood, is a truncated cone 26 or 27 inches in length,
tapering from a girth of 8 1/2 or 9 inches at the one end to 3 1/2 or 4 inches at the
other. Each player has three loggats which he throws, holding lightly the thin end.
The object is to lie as near the Jack as possible. The only place we have heard of

<P>such scenes and such characters with deliberate intention, and with a view to artistic
relief and contrast, there can hardly be a doubt. We must take it for granted that
a man whose works show everywhere the results of judgement sometimes acted with
forethought. I find the springs of the profoundest sorrow and pity in this hardened
indifference of the Grave-diggers, in their careless discussion as to whether Ophelia's
death was by suicide or no, in their singing and jesting at their dreary work. <I>We</I>
know who is to be the guest of this earthen hospitality,&mdash;how much beauty, love,
and heart-break are to be covered in that pit of clay. All we remember of Oph.
reacts upon us with tenfold force, and we recoil from our amusement at the ghastly
drollery of the two delvers with a shock of horror. That the unconscious Ham.
should stumble on <I>this</I> grave of all others, that it should be <I>here</I> that he should pause
to muse humorously on death and decay,&mdash;all this prepares us for the revulsion of
passion in the next scene, and for the frantic confession: &lquo;I loved Ophelia; forty
thousand brothers Could not with all <I>their</I> quantity of love Make up my sum!&rquo; And
it is only here that such an asseveration would be true even to the feeling of the
moment; for it is plain from all we know of Ham. that he could not so have loved
Oph., that he was incapable of the self-abandonment of a true passion, that he would
have analyzed this emotion as he does all others, would have peeped and botanized
upon it till it became to him a mere matter of scientific interest. All this force of
contrast, and this horror of surprise, were necessary so to intensify his remorseful
regret that he should believe himself for once in earnest. The speech of the King,
&lquo;Oh, he is mad, Laertes,&rquo; recalls him to himself, and he at once begins to rave.

<P>94. <B>quiddits</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: A contraction of <I>quiddity,</I> which is from [Mid. Lat.]
<I><*>iditas,</I> not from <I>quidlibet.</I> It was used, as quiddity also was, for a subtilty, or nice
efinement. Generally applied to the subtilties of lawyers. <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: Mid. Lat.
<I>quiditas,</I> the whatness or distinctive nature of a thing, brought into a by-word by the
nice distinction of the schools.

objects to this, that the scholastic phrase was uniformly <I>quodlibet,</I> never <I>quidlibet.</I>

<P>95. <B>tenures</B>] <SC>Elze</SC> (<I>The Athen&aelig;um,</I> 20 Feb. 1869) thinks that this word has

therefore be inserted between &lquo;recognizances&rquo; and &lquo;fines&rquo; in line 99.
<P>96. <B>sconce</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: A colloquial and jocose term, like costard, pate, maz-
zard, &amp;c.
<P>99, 100. <B>statutes, recognizances, fines, double vouchers, recoveries</B>] <SC>Rit
son</SC>: A recovery with <I>double voucher</I> is the one usually suffered, and is so denomi-
nated from <I>two</I> persons (the latter of whom is always the common crier, or some
such inferior person) being successively <I>vouched,</I> or called upon, to warrant the
tenant's title. Both &lquo;fines&rquo; and &lquo;recoveries&rquo; are fictions of law, used to convert
an estate tail into a fee simple. &lquo;Statutes&rquo; are (not acts of parliament, but) <I>statutes-
merchant</I> and <I>staple,</I> particular modes of <I>recognizance</I> or acknowledgement for se-
curing <I>debts,</I> which thereby become a charge upon the party's land. &lquo;Statutes&rquo; and
&lquo;recognizances&rquo; are constantly mentioned together in the covenants of a purchase
deed.
<P>100. <B>fine of his fines</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: This is the end of, or utmost attained by,
the operation of all this legal machinery. <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. a Lawyer,</I> p. 10): The
first &lquo;fine&rquo; means not a penalty, but an end. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Compare <I>All's Well,</I>
IV, iv, 35.
<P>101. <B>fine dirt</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 316): Foule? <SC>Dyce</SC> (e<*>d. 2): I believe the
old text is right here. <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. a Lawyer,</I> p. 10) acutely interprets this &lquo;fine,&rquo;
like the preceding &lquo;fine,&rquo; in the sense of <I>last.</I> &lquo;His fine pate is filled, not with fine
dirt, but with the <I>last</I> dirt which will ever occupy it, leaving a satirical inference to
be drawn, that even in his lifetime his head was filled with dirt.&rquo;

<P>103. <B>indentures</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Indentures were agreements made out in dupli-
cate, of which each party kept one. Both were written on the same sheet, which
was cut in two in a crooked or <I>indented</I> line, in order that the fitting of the two
parts might prove the genuineness of both in case of dispute.
<P>105. <B>box</B>] <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. a Lawyer,</I> p. 10): Ham. compares a grave to a box,
because conveyancers and attorneys keep their deeds in wooden or tin boxes.
<P>105. <SC>Staunton</SC> cites some passages parallel to the foregoing dozen lines from
Randolph's comedy of <I>The Jealous Lovers,</I> published at Oxford, 1668.
<P>109. <B>assurance</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;Assurance of lands is where lands or tenements
are conveyed by deed.&rquo;&mdash;Jacob, <I>Law Dict.</I> Here, of course, there is a reference
also to the ordinary meaning.
<P>110. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: O, the rich contrast between the Clowns and Ham. as two

like truth, for its antiquity, and treasured up, like a tune, for use.
<P>111. <B>sirrah</B>] See <I>Macb.</I> IV, ii, 30.

<P>130. <B>card</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC> explained this as the card on which the different points of
the compass are described, as in <I>Macb.</I> I, iii, 17. <SC>Malone</SC> understood it as only
another name for <I>chart,</I> and paraphrased its use in the present instance by: &lquo;we
must speak with the same precision and accuracy as is observed in marking the true
distances of coasts, the heights, courses, &amp;c., in a sea<I>-chart.</I>&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> selected this as
the definition of the present passage in his <I>Glossary.</I> <SC>Staunton</SC> says it is &lquo;rather
an allusion to the <I>card</I> and <I>calendar</I> of etiquette, or <I>book of manners,</I> of which more
than one were published during Shakespeare's age.&rquo; <SC>Ritson</SC> notes its use by Osric,
V, ii, 109. Whatsoever its immediate derivation, &lquo;to speak by the card&rquo; undoubt-
edly means <I>to speak with precision.</I>

lone</SC>: That is, so spruce, so quaint, so affected. There is no allusion to <I>picked</I> or
pointed shoes. [<SC>Douce</SC> agrees with Malone here, because this fashion had expired

<P>153. [The words of the Grave-digger are so explicit that the age of Ham. has been
generally accepted as that of thirty years, and none the less generally has it been
felt that this age does not accord, as Blackstone says, with the impression of his
youth which Ham. in the earlier scenes gives us. <SC>Halliwell</SC> [see Text. Notes] at-
tempts to avoid the difficulty by the aid of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, but this aid will hardly bear analysis. In
line 1922 of Q<SUB>1</SUB> the Clown says &lquo;heres a scull hath bin here this dozen yeare;&rquo; the con
versation for sixteen lines then turns upon Ham., and his being sent to England. At
the end of it Ham. says, &lquo;whose scull was this?&rquo; It is by no means certain that the
former skull is here referred to; the Clown may have just turned up another. It
does not follow, therefore, of necessity that it was Yorick's skull that had lain in the
ground a dozen years, and Q<SUB>1</SUB> fails us here at the most important point. <SC>Grant
White</SC>, at the beginning of his story of <I>Hamlet the Younger,</I> says that the Prince
was twenty years old when the tragedy opens, and at the close his essay, probably
overlooking this statement, says that Ham. was thirty years of age in the Fifth Act.
No one would impute to so shrewd a scholar as <SC>Grant White</SC> the supposition that
the action of the tragedy lasted ten years. <SC>Eduard</SC> and <SC>Otto Devrient</SC>, in their
ed. of Sh., contend, and with much force, for Hamlet's extreme youth [see Ap-
pendix, Vol. II], and modify their text accordingly. <SC>Furnivall</SC> (<I>New Sh. Soc.
Trans,</I> Part ii, 1874, p. 494), speaking of the &lquo;startling inconsistencies&rquo; in regard
to Hamlet's age, says: &lquo;We know how early, in olden time, young men of rank were
put to arms; how early, if they went to a University, they left it for training in Camp
and Court. Ham., at a University, could hardly have passt 20; and with this age
the plain mention of youth [in I, iii, 7; I, iii, 11-12; and I, iii, 123-4] agrees.
With this, too, agrees the King's reproach to Ham. for his intent in going back to
Wittenberg; and Hamlet's own revolt-of-nature at his mother's quick marriage to
his uncle. Had he been much past 21, and had he had more experience of then
women, he'd have taken his mother's changeableness more coolly. I look on it as
certain, that when Sh. began the play he conceivd Ham. as quite a young man.
But as the play grew, as greater weight of reflection, of insight into character, of
knowledge of life, &amp;c., were wanted, Sh. necessarily and haturally made Ham. a
formd man; and, by the time that he got to the Grave-diggers' scene, told us the Prince
was 30,&mdash;the right age for him then; but not his age when Laer. and Pol. warnd
Oph. against his blood that burnd, his youthful fancy for her,&mdash;&ldquo;a toy in blood&rdquo;&mdash;
&amp;c. The two parts of the play <I>are</I> inconsistent on this main point in Hamlets state.

<P>What matter? Who wants 'em made consistent by the modification of either part?
The &ldquo;thirty&rdquo; is not in Q<SUB>1</SUB>; yet who wants to go back to that?&rquo; <SC>Minto</SC> (<I>The Exam-
iner,</I> 6 Mar. 1875) contends that apart from the Grave-digger's speech and the thirty
years of the wedded life of the Player King and the Player Queen (and he is at a
loss to understand how these passages came into the play), &lquo;the natural construction
is that Ham. and his associates were youths of seventeen, fresh from the University.
That was the usual age in Shakespeare's time at which young nobles set out on their
travels, and there is no reason to suppose that he thought of altering the University
age in his play, and no hint that Ham. was so very much older than his companions.&rquo;
. . . . &lquo;A proper conception of Hamlet's age is essential to the understanding of the
play. He is a youth called home from the University by his father's death; a youth
of the age of Romeo, or of young Prince Hal at the time of his father's accession.&rquo;
. . . . &lquo;Hamlet's action is not the weak and petulant action of an emasculated man of
thirty, but the daring, wilful, defiant action of a high-spirited sensitive youth, rudely
summoned from the gay pursuits of youth, and confronted suddenly with monstrous
treachery, with crime that blurs the modesty and grace of nature, that makes the
very sunlight fire, and loads the sweet air of heaven with pestilence.&rquo; <SC>Marshall</SC>
(p. 181) thinks that Sh. intended Ham. to be nearer twenty than thirty; the general
features of his character are those of youth, and the frequent allusions throughout
the play to his being very young forbid the belief that he was really thirty years old.
The Grave-digger may mean that &lquo;he began to serve his apprenticeship thirty years
before; but he may not have come to the trade of grave-maker till some years later;
so that it does not necessarily follow that the day when King Hamlet overcame For.
tinbras was thirty years previously.&rquo; . . . . &lquo;The most material objection against Ham-
let's being more than between twenty and twenty-three years of age is that if he
were older his mother could scarcely have been the object of such a passion as that
of Claudius.&rquo;
<P><SC>Minto</SC> afterwards (in <I>The Academy,</I> 18 December, 1875) expressed his views at
greater length. Against the weighty authority of the Grave-digger is to be placed
Laer., whose advice to Oph. in simple prose means that she was not to trust Ham.,
because he was at an age of changeful fancies and fleeting attachments. Who would
speak of the love of a man of thirty as &lquo;a violet in the youth of primy nature&rquo;?
The very idea is a profanation of words, which carry such fragrance with them when
applied to the first love of budding youth. Again, the University age of young
noblemen at that time was from seventeen to nineteen, and Laer. had just left the
University; Ham. wanted to go back to it, and Hor. is under suspicion of playing
&lquo;truant.&rquo; The play is full of allusions to the youth of the personages coeval with
Ham. Fort. is &lquo;Young Fortinbras,&rquo; Laer. is &lquo;Young Laertes,&rquo;&mdash;the epithet in both
cases being repeated. The King speaks of skill with the rapier as a &lquo;very riband
in the cap of youth.&rquo; Hamlet's envy of Laertes's fame with the rapier has an
almost boyish air. Making Ham. thirty also adds some improbability to the suc-
cession of Claudius to his murdered brother; if at that age Ham. had tamely sub-
mitted to such a usurpation, and desired to go back to school in Wittenberg, he
would have been too contemptible a character to be fitted for any dramatist's hero.
Prof. <SC>Dowden</SC> having pronounced, in a notice of Werder's <I>Hamlet</I> (<I>The Academy,</I>
4 Dec. 1875), that theory incredible which &lquo;makes Ham., the utterer of the saddest

<P>and most thoughtful soliloquies to be found in Sh., a boy of seventeen,&rquo; <SC>Minto</SC>
replies that we are apt to underrate the precocity of boys of seventeen. &lquo;I venture to
say that sad and thoughtful questionings of the mysteries of life are more common
among boys under twenty than among men of thirty.&rquo; &lquo;Not only is it possible for sad
thoughts to come to a youth of seventeen, but it is at such an age, when the character
is not deeply founded, that the shattering of first ideals is most overwhelming. The
terrible circumstances that overthrew Hamlet's noble mind gave a stimulus to the
development of his thoughtfulness apart from an increase of years. The fresher
and brighter our conception of the gay boy-world out of which he was summoned,
the deeper becomes the monstrous tint of the horrible ambition, murder, and in-
cest, which appalled his vision and paralyzed the clear working of his mind when
he was first called upon to play a man's part in the battle of life. Too much has
been said of the philosophic temperament of Ham.; impulse and passion were more
in his nature than philosophy; his philosophy was not a serene growth, a natural de-
velopment of a mind predisposed to thought; it was wrung out of him by circumstances
terrible enough to make the most obtuse mind pause and reflect.&rquo; Prof. <SC>Dowden</SC>
(<I>The Academy,</I> 25 Dec. 1875) urged the following considerations in condemnation
of the theory that Ham. was a youth of seventeen: &lquo;The poet's youngest <I>heroines</I>
(children of the South) are aged fourteen (Juliet, Marina) and fifteen (Miranda).
The age of Perdita is sixteen. Sh. loved these earliest years of budding woman-
hood. What is the corresponding period of early manhood that charms the poet's
imagination? At what age does Sh. conceive that boyhood is blooming into adult
strength and beauty? I answer, from twenty-one to twenty-five. The stolen sons
of Cymbeline, boys just ready to be men, are aged twenty-three and twenty-two;
Florizel looks about twenty-one (<I>Wint. Tale,</I> V, i, 126); Troilus, a beardless youth
(two or three hairs upon his chin), is older: &lquo;he ne'er saw three-and-twenty.&rquo; I am
not aware that we can determine Romeo's age. Prince Hal at the time of his
father's accession was some twelve years old, but Sh. represents him as considerably
older. When the battle of Shrewsbury took place (Henry being in fact sixteen
years old), Sh., I believe, intends his age to be &lquo;twenty-two or thereabouts&rquo; (1 <I>Hen.
IV:</I> III, iii, 212). When Henry V ascended the throne, his age was twenty-six,
and there is no reason to suppose that Sh., who had up to that point made him older
than the Prince Henry of history, now represented him as younger. The Bishop of
Ely says: &lquo;My thrice puissant liege Is in <I>the very May-morn of his youth.</I>&rquo; Test
the tbeory of Hamlet's extreme youth by the other plays. Are we to imagine the
utterer of the soliloquy, &lquo;To be or not to be,&rquo; as five or six years the junior of the
boys of old Belarius, and that at a period of life when each added year counts for
much? Is Florizel,&mdash;one of Shakespeare's ideals of youthful grace,&mdash;four years
older than Ham.? Did Ham. begin his observations on society (V, i, 150) at four-
teen? Were his schoolfellows,&mdash;dispatched on a critical mission to England,&mdash;also
youths of seventeen? Can it be proved that any chief male personage in Shake-
speare's plays is aged seventeen, or eighteen, or even nineteen? The dating of the
Player-King's marriage is important in this discussion. His thirty years' wife (rep-
resenting Gertrude) is not too old to win a second husband's love; therefore Ger-
trude, although the &lquo;hey-day of her blood&rquo; is &lquo;tame,&rquo; is not necessarily too old; we
may imagine her forty-seven. But I am not greatly concerned to maintain the

<P>Player-King's and the Grave-digger's dates, except for the sake of resisting rash
tampering with Shakespeare's text. I can imagine Ham. as a man in the &lquo;May-
morn of his youth&rquo; at twenty-six or twenty-five. I am much concerned, however,
to oppose such a misreading of the play as would not only render the conception of
Ham. incoherent, but would pervert our view of an entire group of lovely charac-
ters,&mdash;the Florizels and Polydores and Ferdinands of Sh. And I would note that
Sh. found it possible to think of thirty as a youthful age. The Grave-digger him-
self speaks of &lquo;young Hamlet.&rquo; In <I>Much Ado</I> we read (of fashions in clothes):
&lquo;How giddily a' turns about all the hot bloods between fourteen and five-and-thirty.&rquo;
In the <I>Sonnets</I> Sh. names forty (not thirty) as the age when time has marred the
face. In the <I>Elegy</I> on Burbadge, that great actor is praised for his equal success
in the part of &lquo;young Hamlet&rquo; and of &lquo;old Hieronymo.&rquo; If Burbadge represented
Ham. as thirty years of age, still, in spite of the thirty years, Burbadge's Ham.
passed for young. I will, however, yield something, and if any critic will effi-
ciently knock upon the mazzard that &lquo;absolute&rquo; knave, the Clown, I accept as
satisfactory the age assigned by Marshall,&mdash;twenty-five.&rquo;

<P>163. <B>three and twenty</B>] <SC>Halliwell</SC>: I have ventured to alter the text here to
<I>a dozen</I> by the aid of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, in order to avoid a chronological difficulty, and for a similar
reason to alter &lquo;thirty&rquo; to <I>twenty</I> in line 153. It must be remembered that Ham. is
alluded to in the First Act as a very young man.
<P>169, 170. <B>This . . . sir</B>] <SC>White</SC>: If the repetition of these words were accidental
in the Ff, the chance must be reckoned among <I>gli inganni felici.</I> <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2): I
wish White had told us what force is added to the dialogue by the repetition. <SC>Cor
son</SC> partially answers Dyce's question by saying that the repetition serves to exhibit
the Clown's &lquo;sense of his official importance as he turns the skull over in his hands;&rquo;
[there also lurks in it a tone of hesitation, as though deliberating carefully the posi-
tion of the skull in the earth whence it was exhumed before deciding on the owner-
ship. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>170. <B>Yorick</B>] <SC>J. San</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 5 Oct. 1861): This is the German and Danish
<I>Georg, J&ouml;rg,</I> our <I>George;</I> the English <I>y</I> represents the foreign <I>j,</I> which has the same
sound. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Mr Magn&uacute;sson suggests to us that this name may be a cor-
ruption of Rorick, Saxo's Roricus, Hamlet's grandfather on the mother's side.
<SC>Latham</SC> (<I>Two Dissertations,</I> &amp;c., 1872, pp. 93 and 145): Name for name, the
&lquo;Yorick&rquo; of Sh. seems to be the <I>Eric</I> of <I>Der bestrafte Br&uuml;dermord.</I> If so, the
King is his own Jester. Be it so. A <I>Chronicon Erici Regis</I> actually exists. A
<I>Gesta Erici Regis</I> may have existed. Hence, by a confusion of which we only get
a general notion, out of <I>Gesta Erici Regis</I> may have come <I>Yorick, the King's Jester.</I>
[&lquo;Jerick&rquo; is the name of a &lquo;Dutch Bowr&rquo; in Chapman's <I>Alphonsus.</I> <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>176. <B>abhorred in</B>] <SC>White</SC>: What is abhorred? At what does Hamlet's gorge
rise? At the skull? He is not speaking of that. What he abhors, what his gorge
rises at, is <I>his imagination that here hung the lips that he has kissed.</I> This construc-
tion is sustained by the reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB>: &lquo;those lippes . . . they abhorre me.&rquo; <SC>Clarke</SC>:
&lquo;It&rquo; in this sentence, and in &lquo;my gorge rises at <I>it,</I>&rquo; is used in reference to the idea
of having been borne on the back of him whose skeleton remains are thus suddenly
presented to the speaker's gaze, the idea of having caressed and been fondled by one
whose mouldering fleshless skull is now held in the speaker's hand.
<P>177. <B>gorge</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): Throat, swallow, equivalent to stomach (Fr. <I>gorge</I>).
<P>180. <B>on a roar</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: We still say &lquo;to set on fire,&rquo; and in <I>Exodus,</I> xix,
18, we find &lquo;on a smoke&rquo; for &lquo;smoking.&rquo;
<P>181. <B>grinning</B>] <SC>Collier</SC>: The skull did not <I>jeer,</I> though it &lquo;grinned.&rquo;
<P>182. <B>chamber</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: The <I>table</I> of the Qq means her dressing-table. <SC>Douce</SC>
(ii, 264): There is good reason for supposing that Sh. borrowed this thought from
some print or picture he had seen. There are several which represent a lady at her
toilet, and an old man presenting a skull before the mirror.
<P>183. <B>favour</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Countenance or complexion. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: So in
Bacon, <I>Essay</I> xliii: &lquo;In beauty, that of favour is more than that of colour, and that
of decent and gracious motion more than that of favour.&rquo;

<P>201-204. <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 1): Are these four lines a quotation? <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> &amp;c.,
p. 445): They are marked in the (MS) as a quotation; and they seemed to have oc-
curred to the speaker as extremely apposite to what he had himself just said. We
have no notion whence the passage was taken. <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2) repeats his query,
and answers: &lquo;I believe not.&rquo; <SC>Clarke</SC>: Ham. is merely putting into rhyming
form the fancy that for the moment passes through his mind. Sh. has made this a
marked characteristic with Ham.&mdash;a tendency to doggerelize when he is speaking
lightly or excitedly; thus III, ii, 281, 282. Again at the close of the present scene,
where it is not so much a couplet that conventionally closes a scene as it is a fleer
extemporaneously put into rhyme, by way of light turning off from serious thought
and remonstrance to a manner that shall favor the belief in his madness.

radels, and then cast it all ouer with claie to keepe out the wind, which otherwise
would annoie them. Certes this rude kind of building made the Spaniards in
queene Maries daies to woonder, but cheeflie when they saw what large diet was
vsed in manie of these so homelie cottages; in so much that one of no small repu-
tation amongst them said after this maner: &ldquo;These English (quoth he) haue their
houses made of sticks and durt, but they fare commonlie so well as the king&rdquo;&rquo; (p.
233, ed. <I>New Sh. Soc.</I>).

<P>215. <B>warrantise</B>] <SC>Whalley</SC>: Is there any allusion here to the coroner's war-
rant, directed to the minister and churchwardens of a parish, and permitting the
body of a person who comes to an untimely end to receive Christian burial? <SC>Clar-
endon</SC>: This suggestion of Whalley's receiyes support from the conversation of the
Clowns at the beginning of the scene, but is scarcely consistent with what follows in
the next line, where &lquo;great command&rquo; evidently refers to the influence of the king,
which had been exercised so as to interfere with the usual proceedings. The rubric
before the Burial Office forbids it to be used for persons who have laid violent hands
upon themselves. For the word &lquo;warrantise,&rquo; see Cotgrave: &lquo;Garentage: m. War-
rantie, warrantize, warrantage.&rquo;
<P>215. <B>doubtful</B>] <SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 199): But the Queen, who was witness of the fact,
has told us that the death was accidental, from the breaking of an &lquo;envious sliver&rquo;
of a tree. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Only so far as that she was a lunatic, and had died by her
own act; the presumption in such a case being held to be that the act was wilful;
and there being always a <I>doubt</I> whether Christian burial could then be demanded;
although, as Burn's <I>Ecclesiastical Law</I> states, there is no record of its having been
actually refused in any instance.
<P>216. <B>order</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: That is, the course which ecclesiastical rules prescribe.
<P>218. <B>for</B>] For instances of &lquo;for,&rquo; meaning <I>instead of,</I> see I, iii. 131, and <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 148.

<P>219. <B>Shards</B>] Fragments of broken tiles or pots. See <I>Macb.</I> III, ii, 42.
<P>220. <B>crants</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> pronounced this an &lquo;evident corruption of <I>chants,</I> the
true word,&rquo; on the ground that a <I>specific</I> rather than a <I>generic</I> term was required to
answer to &lquo;maiden strewments.&rquo; <SC>Edwards</SC> whose book, <I>Canons of Criticism,</I> was
written in ridicule of Warburton's edition, suggests derisively (7th ed., p. 147) that
Warburton had better have &lquo;pitched upon <I>grants, wants, pants,</I> or any other, pro-
vided it rhymes to <I>chants;</I> because it would seem by the very next speech of the
Priest that these same <I>chants</I> were the only things denied her [&lquo;To sing a requiem&rquo;].
If Warburton's reading be approved, we should, to restore <I>integrity,</I> make a slight
alteration in line 221, and read &ldquo;Her maiden <I>'struments</I>&rdquo; for <I>instruments.</I> Music,
not only vocal, but instrumental also.&rquo; <SC>Heath</SC> supposes &lquo;crants&rquo; to be a misprint
for <I><*>rants,</I> that is, &lquo;the ceremonies granted by custom to those who died unmarried,&rquo;
and that Sh. afterwards substituted <I>rites.</I> <SC>Johnson</SC>, on the authority of an anonymous
correspondent, was the first to explain &lquo;crants&rquo; as the German word for <I>garlands;</I>
adding, that &lquo;to carry garlands before the bier of a maiden, and to hang them over
her grave, is still the practice in rural parishes.&rquo; &lquo;Crants,&rquo; therefore, was the original
word, which Sh., discovering to be provincial, and perhaps not understood, changed
to a term more intelligible, but less proper. &lquo;Maiden <I>rites</I>&rquo; give no certain or
definite image. <SC>Malone</SC> doubted whether this and many other changes in the
Folio were made by Sh., as an attentive comparison of the Qq and Ff would show.
<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i) emphasises the fact on which both Warburton and Dr Johnson lay
stress, viz.: that a specific, definitive image is here essential, and that <I>rites</I> does not
fulfil this requirement, while &lquo;crants&rquo; does. Of the advocates for <I>rites,</I> <SC>Knight</SC> and
<SC>White</SC> are the chief; the former urges that &lquo;the &ldquo;maiden strewments&rdquo; are the
flowers, the garlands, which piety scatters over the bier of the young and innocent.
The <I>rites</I> included these.&rquo; White agrees with him, that &lquo;crants&rquo; would hereby be a
mere repetition. <SC>Elze</SC> cannot avoid the conviction that &lquo;crants&rquo; is a sophistication,
since a most unusual and foreign word would never be applied to a most usual and
domestic ceremony. In <SC>Dyce's</SC> second ed. he gives this note of <SC>Lettsom's</SC>: &lquo;Most
of the edd. explain &lquo;crants&rquo; by <I>garlands;</I> but the German <I>Kranz</I> is singular, and
the singular seems indispensable here. From a note to Prior's <I>Danish Ballads,</I> it
would seem that young unmarried Danish ladies wear, or wore, chaplets of pearl;
at least, &lquo;fair Elsey&rquo; is described as wearing one; and the translator (vol. iii, p. 111)
says that this is the same as the &lquo;virgin <I>&cacute;rant</I> (<I>sic</I>) of Oph.&rquo; Guided by this, <SC>Dyce</SC>,
in his <I>Gloss.,</I> defines &lquo;crants,&rquo; a crown, a chaplet, a garland, and cites Jamieson,
<I>Etym. Dict. of the Scottish Lang.:</I> &lquo;<I>Crance . . . .</I> Teut. <I>krants,</I> corona, corolla,
sertum, strophium, Kilian. Germ. <I>Kranz,</I>&rquo; &amp;c. It is perhaps worth noting that
Jamieson, in this same passage cited by Dyce, gives an instance of the plural: &lquo;Thair
heids wer garnisht gallandlie With costly crancis maid of gold.&rquo;&mdash;Watson's <I>Collec-
tion of Choice Songs,</I> &amp;c., ii, 10. <SC>Halliwell</SC> gives a wood-cut of a funeral garland
seen by <SC>Fairholt</SC> in 1844, suspended in St Albans Abbey. &lquo;It was then.&rquo; says

<P>259. <B>do for her</B>] F. G. T. (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> vol. iv, p. 156, 1851) denies that Ham. really
rants: &lquo;Ham., a prince, is openly cursed, and even seized by Laer., and yet he only
remonstrates. He uses phrases so homely that there is something very like scorn in
them: &ldquo;What wilt thou <I>do</I> for her?&rdquo; is the quietude of contempt for Laertes's insult-
ing rant; and so, if my memory deceive me not, the elder Kean gave it. &ldquo;<I>Do</I> for
her&rdquo; being contrasted with Laertes's braggadocio &ldquo;<I>say.</I>&rdquo; Then come the possibilities:
weep, fight, fast, tear thyself (all, be it noted, common lovers' tricks), drink up eisel,
eat a crocodile. Here the crocodile probably refers to those put up in spirits in
apothecaries' shops. Here we have possibilities put against the rant of Laer.; the
<I>doing</I> against the <I>saying;</I> things that <I>could be done,</I> for Ham. ends with &ldquo;I'll do it.&rdquo;
But his quick imagination has caught an impetus from its own motion, and he goes
on: &ldquo;Nay, I'll even out-prate you,&rdquo; and then follows his superior rant, not uttered
with vehemence, but with quiet philosophic scorn.&rquo;

<P>263. <B>Woo't</B>] <SC>Singer</SC>: <I>Woo't,</I> or <I>woot'o,</I> in the northern counties, is the common
contraction of <I>wouldst thou.</I> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 271): Can any good reason be
given why we should write <I>woo't</I> or <I>woul't</I> here and not elsewhere? <SC>Lettsom</SC>
(<I>Footnote</I> to Walker): Halliwell, in his <I>Dict.,</I> has &lquo;<I>Woot.</I> Will thee. West.&rquo; In
the passage before us the context requires <I>wilt,</I> and this, indeed, is the text of Q<SUB>1</SUB>.
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: A colloquialism by which Ham. marks his contempt for Laer. In
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> IV, ii, 7; IV, xv, 59, it indicates affectionate familiarity.
<P>264. <B>eisel</B>] With the exception of &lquo;the dram of eale,&rquo; no word or phrase in this
tragedy has occasioned more discussion than this <I>Esill</I> or <I>Esile,</I> which, as it stands,
represents nothing in the heavens above, or the earth beneath, or the waters under
the earth, if from the last we exclude the <I>vessels</I> of Q<SUB>1</SUB>. <SC>Rowe</SC> and <SC>Pope</SC> blindly fol-
lowed the blind compositors of the QqFf. <SC>Theobald</SC> saw the difficulty so clearly
that subsequent criticism has chiefly ranged itself on one or other of the two interpre-
tations suggested by him, viz. that the word either represents the name of a river,
or is an old word, meaning vinegar. Theobald's objection to its being the name of a
river is that it must be some river in Denmark, and that he knew of none there so
called, nor any other, <I>idem sonans,</I> nearer than &lquo;the Yssel, from which the Province
of <I>Over-yssel</I> derives its title in German Flauders.&rquo; This objection comes strangely
from Theobald, for none knew better than he that Sh., who did not hesitate to make
Ham. swear by St Patrick, would have been just as likely to mention a river in
farthest Ind as in Denmark, if the name flashed into his mind, and would have been
intelligible to his audience. &lquo;Besides,&rquo; continues Theobald, &lquo;Ham. is not proposing
impossibilities to Laer., as the drinking up a river would be, but he rather seems to
mean, Wilt thou resolve to do things the most shocking and distasteful? and, behold,
I am as resolute.&rquo; <SC>Hanmer</SC>, forgetful of his own good rule of not giving &lquo;a loose to
fancy,&rquo; changed &lquo;Esill&rquo; into <I>Nile,</I> without a note or comment, in his first edition, to
indicate that it was not Shakespeare's word; and then, to fill up the measure of the
verse, introduced another <I>woo't</I> before &lquo;eat.&rquo; <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> &amp;c., i, 146) says it is
&lquo;palpable&rquo; that a river is intended, but there is no absolute necessity, because a croco-
dile is mentioned, that the river must be the Nile, and Hanmer's better reading would
have been <I>Nilus,</I> which would have suited the metre without the addition of <I>woo't.</I>
(See <I>post</I> Elze.) Capell then goes on to say that &lquo;Sh. sought a river in Denmark,
and, finding none that would do for him, coin'd the word&mdash;<I>Elsil;</I> in a supposition

That undirtakith to drynk up Seyne.&rquo; <SC>Nares</SC> considers the challenge to drink <I>vinegar,</I>
in such rant, so inconsistent and even ridiculous that we must decide for the river,
whether its name can be exactly found or not. <SC>Caldecott</SC> agrees with Steevens,
that it refers to the Yssel, the most northern branch of the Rhine, one which flows
nearest to Denmark, and by Zutphen into the Zuyder Zee. Caldecott adds strength
to Steevens's supposition, that it might refer to the Vistula or <I>Weissel,</I> by showing,

self any concern about them; Sh. took his geography from more accessible sources,
and from points nearer home. <SC>Knight</SC> adopts Caldecott's interpretation. In <I>N. &amp;

by asserting that &lquo;eisel&rquo; means <I>Wormwood Wine,</I> a nauseously bitter medicament

would have been valuable, but unfortunately the premises from which he drew his
conclusion were weak. &lquo;In Thomas's <I>Ital. Dict.</I> 1562,&rquo; says Singer, &lquo;we have &ldquo;As-
sentio, Eysell,&rdquo; and Florio renders <I>Assentio</I> by <I>Wormwood.</I> What is meant, how-
ever, is Absinthites or <I>Wormwood wine.</I>&rquo; The inference here is that Florio refers to
a liquid Wormwood, whereas he defines &lquo;Assentio, <I>. . . . the herbe Wormwood,</I>&rquo;
which, I am afraid, weakens Singer's conclusion. In the same journal (vol. iv, p.
64, 1851) J. S. W. sums up the controversy, and decides in favor of a river, hecause
to drink a potion of vinegar &lquo;is utterly tame and spiritless in a place where anything
but tameness is wanted, and where it is quite out of keeping with the rest of the

<C>[264. &lquo;<B>drink up eisel.</B>&rquo;]</C>
<P>speech.&rquo; <SC>Elze</SC> contends vigorously for <I>Nilus,</I> not only because &lquo;crocodiles&rquo; are
immediately mentioned, but because in Elizabethan times the Nile was the home,
and the synonym, for everything wondrous and monstrous, and was moreover held
to be one of the mightiest of rivers, if not the mightiest. To drink up the bound-
less Nile is an hyperbole than which nothing could hetter befit the occasion; Ham.
wished to express a pure impossibility. To Delius's well-put objection that it is
difficult to see how so familiar a word as Nile could be sophisticated into <I>vessels,
Esile,</I> and <I>Esill,</I> Elze opposes the supposition that the Dutch <I>Yssel</I> or the Danish
<I>Oesil</I> was a marginal gloss of some wiseacre who thought it more appropriate to the
unities of the drama, and which by accident crept into the text. In <I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 12
Feb. 1859, <SC>Cuthbert Bede</SC> offers a citation which would bring the river much
closer to the doors of the Giobe theatre than any yet proposed: &lquo;The Saxon etymon
of <I>Iseldon,</I> according to Mr Sharon Turner, is <I>Ysseldune, i. e.</I> the Down of the Yssel,
which I take to have been the original name of some river, most likely of the river
of Wells, which flowed into the Fleet River; but I consider also that <I>Ysel</I> or <I>Eysel</I> is
the same as <I>Ousel,</I> the diminutive of <I>Ouse</I> or <I>Eyse,</I> in the British language, signify-
ing either a river or water.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Yseldon; a Perambulation of Islington,</I> by T. E.
Tomkins, Esq. <SC>Halliwell</SC> thinks that the Oesil or Isell is referred to, and adds,
&lquo;obscure streams certainly, but the reading is hardly to be rejected on that account,
for the name would be at least as familiar to an Elizabethan audience as that of the
mountain of Ossa, mentioned in the same speech. Sh. in all probability adopted
both names from the older play on <I>Hamlet.</I>&rquo; <SC>Dr Scadding</SC> (<I>Canadian Journal,</I>
No. LXI, 1866, p. 70) also advocates <I>Nilus,</I> and attributes to &lquo;indistinctness of
writing, perhaps, the wrong orthography of a <I>y</I> for an <I>i,</I> and an accidental transposi-
tion of syllables in the printing-office&rquo; the conversion of &lquo;<I>Nilus</I> into <I>Eysell, Eisil</I> or
<I>Esil</I> (in these several ways the modern text is given), conjectured by the commenta-
tors to be variously <I>esil</I> (that is, perhaps, <I>vinegar</I> in the sense of <I>poison</I>] or <I>vessels</I>
(that is, huge caldrons) or&rquo; some proper name. <SC>Keightley</SC> adopts <I>Yssel,</I> because
its name may have been familiar to the English mind from the fact that it was at
Zutphen, on its banks, that Sir Philip Sidney received his death-wound.
<P>Thus far I have cited only those who are in favor of the name of a river, and have
given all their arguments except one, which I have not repeated in every instance, be-
cause all more or less emphasize it; and this argument, which many find convincing,
lies in the words &lquo;drink <I>up;</I>&rquo; this, it is claimed, means <I>to drain, to exhaust,</I> and must
apply to a river or to something concrete,&mdash;it cannot apply to vinegar or to anything
in the abstract; Ham. never could have challenged Laer, to drink up all the vinegar
in the world,&mdash;there was a limit even to professed rant. <SC>Malone</SC> was the first to note
that this phrase, &lquo;drink up,&rquo; does not of necessity mean to exhaust totally, citing in
proof Shakespeare's 114th <I>Sonnet,</I> where it is synonymous with merely <I>to drink:</I>
&lquo;Drink up the monarch's plague, this flattery,&rquo; and again in the same <I>Sonnet:</I> &lquo;And
my great mind most kingly drinks it up;&rquo; and in <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> II, iii, 211, &lquo;his silence
drinks up his applause&rquo; (through an oversight Malone cites this from <I>Timon</I>). &lquo;In
Shakespeare's time,&rquo; adds Malone, &lquo;to <I>drink up</I> often meant no more than simply to
<I>drink.</I> So in Fiorio, <I>Ital. Dict.</I> 1598: &ldquo;<I>Sorbire,</I> to sip or sup up any drink.&rdquo; In like
manner we sometimes say, &ldquo;when you have swallowed down this potion,&rdquo; meaning
when you have swallowed it.&rquo; He might have cited from <I>Hamlet,</I> I, iv, 10: &lquo;drains

<C>[264. &lquo;<B>drink up eisel.</B>&rquo;]</C>
<P>on Jonson's <I>Every Man in his Humour,</I> IV, v (<I>Works,</I> p. 122, ed. 1816, cited by
Dyce): &lquo;It may just be observed that <I>off, out,</I> and <I>up,</I> are continually used by the
purest and most excellent of our old writers, after verbs of destroying, consuming,
eating, drinking, &amp;c.; to us, who are less conversant with the power of language,
they appear, indeed, somewhat like expletives; hut they undoubtedly contributed
something to the force, and something to the roundness, of the sentence.&rquo; In con-
firmation of this use of <I>up,</I> <SC>Dyce</SC> cites the following passages: <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I>
IV, iii, 305; <I>All's Well,</I> IV, iii, 250; <I>King John,</I> IV, iii, 133; <I>As You Like It,</I> II,
i, 62; <I>Tro &amp; Cres.</I> III, ii, 189. If more instances be needed, at least half a dozen
can be found by reference to <SC>Schmidt's</SC> invaluable <I>Lexicon,</I> s. v. 7; or to <SC>Mrs
Furness's</SC> <I>Concordance to Shakespeare's Poems,</I> s. v. &lquo;up.&rquo; The passages, however,
cited by Malone and Dyce do not satisfy <SC>Grant White</SC> of the soundness of Gif-
ford's explanation; he thinks that in all of them &lquo;up&rquo; conveys the sense either of
totality or completeness, as in the lines from <I>Love's Lab. Lost, All's Well,</I> and <I>Tro.
&amp; Cres.</I> III, ii, 189 (and herein Schmidt agrees with him); or of eagerness or in-
satiability, as in the lines from 114th <I>Sonnet</I> and <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> II, iii, 211. The
use of &lquo;up&rquo; in the present passage seemed, therefore, to Grant White fatal to the in-
terpretation of &lquo;eisel,&rquo; or vinegar. But granting that the sense of &lquo;totality or com-
pleteness&rquo; is inapplicable here, is not &lquo;eagerness or insatiability&rquo; the very sense
required? I cannot but believe, therefore, that in the present passage, &lquo;drink up
esill,&rquo; means no more than &lquo;to quaff esill,&rquo; whatever that may be.
<P>I now turn to the second interpretation by <SC>Theobald</SC>, who says: &lquo;I am persuaded
the poet wrote &ldquo;eisel,&rdquo; that is, Wilt thou swallow down large draughts of <I>vinegar?</I>
The proposition, indeed, is not very grand; but the doing it might be as distasteful
and unsavory as eating the flesh of a crocodile. And now there is neither an im-
possibility nor an anticlimax; and the lowness of the idea is in some measure re-
moved by the uncommon term.&rquo; Thereupon he cites Chaucer, <I>The Romaunt of the
Rose,</I> line 217: &lquo;&mdash;breed Kneden with eisel strong and egre;&rquo; Shakespeare's 111th
<I>Sonnet:</I> &lquo;Potions of eisel &lquo;gainst my strong infection;&rquo; and Sir Thomas More's
<I>Poems</I> (p. 21, ed. 1557): &lquo;remember therewithal How Christ for thee tasted eisel
and gall.&rquo; <SC>Capell</SC>, in his dissent from this interpretation, indulges in a gird of
most unusual humour for him: &lquo;if Eisel, an old word that signifies vinegar, be the
right reading, it must be because 'tis wanted for sauce to the crocodile.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>,
too, has his merry fling at it: &lquo;neither is that challenge very magnificent which only
provokes an adversary to hazard a fit of the heart-burn or the colic.&rquo; <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii,
263) thinks that the &lquo;Potions of eysell&rquo; in the 111th <I>Sonnet</I> prove that it was not
any river so called, but a desperate drink. &lquo;The word,&rquo; he adds, &lquo;occurs often in a
sense of which <I>acetum</I> is the best representative, associated with verjuice and vine-
gar. It is a term used for one ingredient of the bitter potion given to our Saviour
on the cross, about the composition of which the commentators are divided. Thus,
the eighth prayer . . . . in the <I>Salisbury Primer,</I> 1555, begins thus:&mdash;&ldquo;O blessed
Jesu! . . . . I beseech thee for the bitterness of the aysell and gall that thou tasted,&rdquo;
&amp;c.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. 2): It was a fashion of the gallants of Shakespeare's time to do some
extravagant feat as a proof of their love in honor of their mistresses, and among other
the swallowing of some nauseous potion was the most frequent. . . . . In Thomas's
<I>Ital. Dict.,</I> 1562, we have &lquo;Assentio. <I>Eysell,</I>&rquo; and Florio renders the same word by
<I>Wormwood.</I> <SC>Dyce</SC>: &lquo;For my own part I certainly believe that <I>eisel</I> is meant here

<P>the word (and it was common enough formerly) is&rquo; spelled <I>Eysell</I> in the 111th <I>Son-
net,</I> ed. 1609. &lquo;In the &ldquo;hyperbolical&rdquo; passages cited by Malone, <I>what</I> rivers do
those poets mention? The <I>Rhine,</I> the <I>Thames,</I> the <I>Meander,</I> the <I>Euphrates,</I>&mdash;and
not such obscure streams as the <I>Yssell,</I> the existence of which the commentators
had some difficulty in detecting.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> says that the (MS) makes no change in
<I>Esile.</I> <SC>Grant White</SC> confesses himself unable to conjecture what the word means;
if a river be intended, &lquo;we must regard the word as a remnant of a play, or tale, un-
known to us, which preceded Shakespeare's tragedy.&rquo; In <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> (Aug. 10, 1872),
<SC>John de Soyres</SC> says that he remembers in a book of Scandinavian legends an
account of Thor's trials of strength with the Giants, and that one of these trials was
to drink a lake Esyl dry, and suggests that this is Hamlet's allusion. The <SC>Claren-
don Editors</SC> &lquo;consulted Mr Magn&uacute;sson on this point, and he writes as follows:
&ldquo;No such lake as Esyl is known to Norse mythology or folklore. Thor's only trial
at drinking an impossible draught was at Utgar<G>d</G>aloki's, where he had to empty a horn
the other end of which mouthed into the sea: in consequence, he only achieved
drinking the ocean down to the ebb mark.&rdquo;&rquo; The citation from the 111th <I>Sonnet</I>
convinces <SC>Moberly</SC> that the same word there, is used here; Moberly adds: &lquo;a large
draught of vinegar would be very dangerous to life.&rquo; There yet remain, however,
four interpretations to be mentioned. First: In <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> (Oct. 5, 1872) <SC>John
Kershaw</SC> calls attention to a passage in Fletcher's <I>Wife for a Month,</I> IV, iv [p. 566,
ed. Dyce], where Alphonso [who is burning up with poison and indulges in the most
extravagant figures of speech] says: &lquo;I'll lie upon my back, and swallow <I>vessels.</I>&rquo;
&lquo;What more probable, therefore, than that Fletcher's &ldquo;swallow vessels&rdquo; had its
origin in Shakespeare's &ldquo;drinke up vessels&rdquo; of Q<SUB>1</SUB>?&rquo; Second: <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> prints
<I>Esule</I> in his text, and explains it as <I>Euphorbia Esula,</I> spurge, a poisonous plant,
whose juice was employed anciently as an emetic. Third: <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Sh. Lexicon,</I> s. v.
<I>Eysell</I>): &lquo;Hamlet's questions are apparently ludicrous, and drinking vinegar, in order
to exhibit deep grief by a wry face, seems much more to the purpose than drinking
up rivers. As for the crocodile, it must perhaps be remembered that it is a <I>mournfu</I>
animal.&rquo; Fourth: The late Rev. <SC>J. B. Dykes</SC>, Mus. Doc. (in a MS note sent to me

was fearful lest Laertes's rage and rebellion should break out anew; and that his
interference would be more likely to have weight with Laer. than that of the Queen,

for Ham. would be perfectly understood. <SC>Knight</SC>: The assignment in the Ff of so

a coarse sensualist proceeds from a typographical error.
<P>274-276. <B>Anon . . . . drooping</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> &amp;c., ed. 2, p. 445): A new
prefix by the (MS) assigns these lines to the Queen, while the two preceding are
given to the King. It seems likely that the King should interpose to tell the
spectators of the funeral, &lquo;This is mere madness, And thus a while the fit will work on
him.&rquo; In some consistency with this view, the King just afterwards desires Hor. to
follow Ham., who has rushed out. [<SC>Collier</SC>, in his ed. 2, adopted this distribution
of the speeches.]
<P>275. <B>When that</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> reads <I>E'er that,</I> because &lquo;it is the patience of
birds, during incubation, that is here spoken of. The pigeon generally sits upon
two eggs, and her young when first disclosed are covered with a yellow down.&rquo;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 547): The young nestlings of the pigeon when first disclosed stand in
need of the kindly warmth of the hen for a considerable time. <SC>Steevens</SC>: During
three days after she has hatched her couplets, the pigeon never quits her nest, except
for a few minutes in quest of a little food for herself; as all her young require in
that early state is to be kept warm, an office which she never entrusts to the male,
<SC>Johnson</SC>: Perhaps it should be <I>E'er yet. Yet</I> and <I>yt</I> are easily confounded.

<P>279, 280. <B>Let . . . day</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;Things have their appointed course,
nor have we power to divert it,&rquo; may be the sense here conveyed, though the pro-
verb is usually applied to those who for a time fill stations to which their merits
give them no claim. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> detects here a reference to Laer., the King,
and to Ham. himself. &lquo;Let the herculean power of Laer. do what it may, and
the cat, which creeps stealthily in the dark, mew, the faithful dog will have his
turn at last.&rquo;
<P>280. <B>day</B>] <SC>B. Street</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 5 Sept. 1868): These lines are so familiar that
we pay little attention to their wording, and what seems the correct reading, &lquo;dog
will have its <I>bay,</I>&rquo; has not been suspected. That it is <I>bay,</I> and not &lquo;day,&rquo; appears
so probable as to be almost certain if we consider that a dog might have its day of
popularity without any detraction from a very Hercules,&mdash;at least without any ex-
pressed disparagement of him; the idea is the expression of detraction on the part
of an inferior against his better. Each animal severally employing its natural utter-
ances in carping at worthiness; the cat mewing its cavils, the dog barking its dislike.
In <I>The Athen&aelig;um,</I> 3 Oct. 1868, &lquo;A. O. S.&rquo; showed that the phrase is older than Sh.
by giving an extract from a letter from the Princess Elizabeth to her sister, Queen
Mary: &lquo;&mdash;as a doge hathe a day, so may I,&rquo; &amp;c. In <I>The Athen&aelig;um,</I> 19 Nov.
1870, <SC>P. A. Daniel</SC> adduced two other instances of the use of the phrase. In <I>The
Interlude</I> (printed in 1573), entitled <I>New Custom,</I> II, iii: &lquo;Well if it chaunce that
a dogge hath a day,&rquo; &amp;c. Also, in Jonson's <I>Tale of a Tub,</I> II, i: &lquo;A man hath his
hour, and a dog his day.&rquo; This was written in 1663, &lquo;later,&rquo; adds Daniel, &lquo;than
<I>Hamlet,</I> no doubt, but Jonson would scarcely have adopted a <I>meaningless</I> bit of
slang.&rquo; <SC>Elze</SC> (<I>Shakespeare-Jahrbuch,</I> Bd. xi) adds a fourth example from <I>Sum-
mer's Last Will and Testament,</I> ed. Dodsley, vol. ix, p. 37.
<P>282. <B>in</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 162: &lquo;In&rquo; is here used metaphorically, where we should say,
&lquo;in the thought of.&rquo;
<P>283. <B>push</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: The instant test. For &lquo;present,&rquo; see <I>Wint. Tale,</I> I, ii,
281. For &lquo;push&rquo; in the sense of &lquo;crisis,&rquo; &lquo;critical moment,&rquo; see the same play, V.
iii, 129, and <I>Macb.</I> V, iii, 20.

<P>mutinous or disorderly sailors anciently were linked together. The word is derived
from <I>Bilboa,</I> a place in Spain, where instruments of steel were fabricated in the
utmost perfection. To understand Shakespeare's allusion completely, it should be
known that, as these fetters connect the legs of the offenders very close together,
their attempts to rest must be as fruitless as those of Ham., in whose mind <I>there was
a kind of fighting that would not let him sleep.</I> Every motion of one must disturb
his partner in confinement. The <I>bilboes</I> are still shown in the Tower of London
among the other spoils of the Spanish Armada.
<P>6. <B>Rashly</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Ham., delivering an account of his escape, begins with
saying, That he <I>rashly</I>&mdash;, and then is carried into a reflection upon the weakness of
human wisdom. I rashly&mdash;praised be rashness for it&mdash;<I>Let us</I> not think these events
casual, but <I>let us know,</I> that is, <I>take notice and remember,</I> that we sometimes succeed
by <I>indiscretion</I> when we <I>fail</I> by <I>deep plots,</I> and infer the perpetual superintendence
and <I>agency</I> of the <I>Divinity.</I> The observation is just, and will be allowed by every
human being who shall reflect on the course of his own life. <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> suggested
that the rest of Hamlet's speech after &lquo;Rashly,&rquo; and Horatio's reply, &lquo;That is
most certain,&rquo; should be put in a parenthesis, so that &lquo;Rashly&rquo; may be joined in
construction with &lquo;in the dark Groped I,&rquo; &amp;c. He also reads: &lquo;And praised be
rashness, for it lets us know,&rquo; and does not put a period after &lquo;will&rquo; at the end of
the speech, but prints &lquo;will;&mdash;&rquo;. Although <SC>Staunton</SC> in a note said that he agreed
with Tyrwhitt's suggestion, he nevertheless did not conform his text thereto. Un-
doubtedly there is force in Tyrwhitt's arrangement. <SC>Collier</SC>: The reasoning in
this passage is consecutive in Hamlet's mind, but, perhaps, hardly so in his expres-
sions. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> follows Tyrwhitt, except that he prints &lquo;for it let us know,&rquo;
because &lquo;let&rquo; is clearly the perfect tense, since Ham. is speaking of an act that is
past.
<P>6-11. <SC>Strachey</SC> (p. 93): That is to say, that when we have exhausted all our
powers of thought and reasoning upon the consideration of the course we should
pursue, and when it yet remains dark to us,&mdash;&lquo;sicklied o'er with the pale cast of
thought,&rquo;&mdash;then a higher wisdom and providence than our own will assuredly come
to our aid, and employ some apparently unimportant accident,&mdash;something which to
us seems merely a rashness or indiscretion,&mdash;to strike the hour and give command
for action. This is Hamlet's final, crowning, discovery; a discovery which every
man of Hamlet's tendency of mind must make for himself before it is possible for
him to turn his intellectual powers to practical account and to make his philosophi-
cal speculations available to the every-day service of God and man. Till such a
man has learnt the value of <I>accidents</I> in breaking the thread of his meditations
when it is spun long enough, and has formed the habit of seizing and using these
accidents, he must remain an unpractical visionary.
<P>8. <B>Our</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC> prints: &lquo;Rashness . . . . lets us know; <I>Or</I> indiscretion,
&amp;c., and vaguely interprets, &lquo;Rashness acquaints us with what we cannot penetrate
to by plots.&rquo; <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 547) exposed the futility of this change.

<P>9. <B>fail</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> thinks that <I>pall</I> and &lquo;tail&rquo; were by no means likely to have been
confounded; he therefore adheres to the Ff, and cites <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> II, vii, 88.
<SC>Caldecott</SC> says that <I>pall</I> means &lquo;lose their spirit, poignancy, and virtue; become
abortive.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (in his first ed. retaining <I>pall</I> in his text) cites the parallel phrase:
&lquo;And if I <I>fail</I> not in my deep <I>intent,</I>&rquo; <I>Rich. III:</I> I, i, 149. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): Very
possibly &lquo;fail&rquo; of the (MS) is the true word. <SC>Clarendon</SC> interprets <I>pall:</I> &lquo;to grow
vapid, and tasteless, like wine; hence to become vain and worthless,&rquo; and cites the
passage from <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> cited by Malone. <SC>Ingleby</SC> (<I>The Sh. Fabrications,</I> p.
115) suggests that <I>fall</I> and &lquo;fail&rquo; were used as synonymous by Sh., and cites in
proof <I>Com. of Err.</I> I, ii, 37; and <I>Merry Wives,</I> I, i, 262; and <I>Sir John Oldcastle:</I>
&lquo;London, you say, is safely look'd unto, Alas, poor rebels, there your aid must fall.&rquo;
In a note on &lquo;if ye fall in't&rquo; in <I>The Two Noble Kinsmen,</I> III, vi, 236, <SC>Littledale</SC>
says that Ingleby has confirmed him in thinking that &lquo;fall,&rquo; and not <I>fail,</I> is the right
reading in that passage, and he gives a fuller note from Ingleby than is contained in
<I>The Sh. Fabrications</I> cited above, as follows: Compare line 272 [of this same scene
in <I>The Two Noble Kinsmen</I>]: &lquo;Let it not fall agen, Sir.&rquo; There are remarkable
instances of the use of this intransitive verb as a synonym of <I>fail.</I> Sh. affords us
only two certain examples of this: &lquo;her better judgement May <I>fall</I> to match you
with her country forms And happily repent.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Oth.</I> III, iii, 237. Here &lquo;fall&rquo; is not
<I>happen</I> (Schmidt, wrongly, <I>begin, get into</I>), but <I>fail.</I> [The second instance is the
present passage in <I>Hamlet,</I> where] <I>pall</I> is nonsense; and <I>fall</I> makes sense. <I>Fall,</I>
of course, is the opposite of <I>succeed.</I> Now our word for this is &lquo;fail.&rquo; There is
also one example in <I>The London Prodigal,</I> and two in <I>Isaiah,</I> xxxi, 3, and lvii, 14,
15. [<SC>Dyce</SC> disapproved of this suggestion of Ingleby's. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>10. <B>ends</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Dr Farmer informs me that these words are merely tech-
nical. A wool-man, butcher, and dealer in <I>skewers,</I> lately ohserved to him that his
nephew (an idle lad) could only <I>assist</I> him making them: &lquo;&mdash;he could <I>rough-hew</I>
them, but I was obliged to <I>shape their ends.</I>&rquo; Whoever recollects the profession of
Shakespeare's father will admit that his son might be no stranger to such terms.
I have frequently seen packages of wool pinned up with <I>skewers.</I> <SC>Caldecott</SC> says
that the phrase is douhtless technical, in so far as it is drawn from a handicraft, and
that, as the use of tools is general, the phrases belonging to them pass into general
use. <SC>Knight</SC> fleers at Farmer's suggestion; and <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 264) says &lquo;the sooner
it is expunged the hetter. <I>Rough-hew</I> is not and never was <I>technical.</I> It is a com-
mon English word applicable to all kinds of work where there is room for ordinary
manual labor before the master comes and applies a skilful hand. Thus, in Pals-
grave's <I>Table of Verbs,</I> 1530: &ldquo;I rough-hewe a pece of tymber to make an ymage
of;&rdquo; Florio, 1598: &ldquo;<I>Abbozzare,</I> to rough hew any first draught, to bungle ill-
favouredly.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC> has a note to the same effect, and cites Baret's <I>Alvearie.</I>
