captivating him. Then the encounter with the pirate puts an end to the chance of
undoing it; and thus he is driven, somewhat uneasily, to justify his action to Hor.
As the latter receives his narrative with something like surprise, and even with a
touch of compassion, we may conclude with safety that Hamlet's kindly nature
would have cancelled the letters but for the accident which hindered his doing
so.&rquo;

<P>38. <B>conjuration</B>] See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> V, iii, 68, where this passage seems to have

<P>42. <B>comma</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (Nichols's <I>Lit. Hist.</I> ii, 579), writing to his &lquo;most affec-
tionate friend,&rquo; Warburton, says that it should be either &lquo;<I>no</I> comma,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> as no bar
should stand between their friendships:&mdash;Or, &lquo;And stand a comma 'tween their
<I>enmities,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> as peace should intervene and prevent enmities.&rquo; He did not repeat
these suggestions in his ed., but adopted Warburton's emendation, and justifies it in a
note which he attributes to Warburton: &lquo;The poet without doubt wrote, &ldquo;And stand
a <I>Commere,</I>&rdquo; <I>i. e.</I> a guarantee, a common mother. Nothing can be more picturesque
than this image of Peace's standing, drest in her wheaten garland, between the two
Princes, and extending a hand to each. We thus frequently see her on Roman coins.&rquo;
But <SC>Warburton</SC>, in his ed., goes further, and says that <I>Commere</I> here means &lquo;a traf-
ficker in love, one who brings people together, a procuress.&rquo; [Cotgrave sustains
him in this meaning.] <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> &amp;c., i, 147) was taken by this allusion to
Peace as represented on coins, and so adopted <I>Commere.</I> <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 549) well
interprets: &lquo;As a comma stands between two several members of a sentence, without
separating them otherwise than by distinguishing the one from the other, in like

perhaps in his mind to write,&mdash;That unless England complied with the mandate,

next changed into &lquo;stand a comma.&rquo; In Q<SUB>2</SUB> &lquo;there is no elision mark [if Bailey

<P>44. <B>knowing</B>] Contracted, or slurred in pronunciation, into a monosyllable. See
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> p. 119), and <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 470. <SC>Stratmann</SC>: As <I>know</I> cannot be,

<P>47. <B>shriving-time</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 265): This was a term in common use for any
short period. All Ham. meant was that they should be put to instant death.
<P>47. <B>allow'd</B>] <SC>Hanmer</SC> (<I>Some Remarks,</I> &amp;c., p. 46): The punishment of Ros. and
Guil. was just, because they had devoted themselves to the service of the Usurper in
whatever he should command. <SC>Malone</SC>: From <I>The Hystorie of Hamblet,</I> it appears
that the faithful ministers of Fengon were not unacquainted with the import of the
letters they bore [see Vol. II, p. 103]. Sh. probably meant to describe their representa-
tives, Ros. and Guil., as equally guilty. So that Hamlet's procuring their execution,
though certainly not absolutely necessary to his own safety, does not appear to have
been a wanton and unprovoked cruelty. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I apprehend that a critic and
a juryman are bound to form their opinions on what they see and hear in the cause
before them, and not to be influenced by extraneous particulars unsupported by legal
evidence in open court. I persist in observing, that from Shakespeare's drama no
proofs of the guilt of Ros. and Guil. can be collected. They may be convicted by
the old <I>Hystorie;</I> but if the tragedy forbears to criminate, it has no right to sentence
them. This is sufficient for the commentator's purpose. It is not his office to inter-
pret the plays of Sh. according to the novels on which they are founded,&mdash;novels
which the poet sometimes followed, but as often materially deserted. Perhaps he
never confined himself strictly to the plan of any one of his originals. His negli-
gence of poetic justice is notorious; nor can we expect that he who was content to
sacrifice the pious Oph. should have been more scrupulous about the worthless lives
of Ros. and Guil. Therefore I assert that in the tragedy before us their deaths ap-
pear wanton and unprovoked; and the critic, like Bayes, must have recourse to
somewhat <I>long before the beginning of the play</I> to justify the conduct of its hero.
<SC>Pye</SC> (p. 326): There is not one word uttered by Ros. and Guil. throughout the
play that does not proclaim them to the most superficial observer as creatures
of the King, purposely employed to betray Ham., their friend and fellow-student.
<SC>Strachey</SC> (p. 96): Something more than Hamlet's own preservation is at stake; he
is the representative and avenger of the rights of the crown and laws of Denmark,
outraged by a murderer and a usurper, (for he was only elected because he con-
trived to murder the rightful possessor at a moment when his natural heir was ab-
sent); and he has to act under those circumstances, which at rare and long intervals
in the history of every country, call on some man to maintain the spirit of the laws
by disregarding for a moment their letter. It is Hamlet's duty to avenge the crown

<P>63. <B>thinks't thee</B>] The editors who follow Q<SUB>5</SUB> interpret this as equivalent to
&lquo;bethink thee.&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC> in dealing with this passage exhibited, as his admirable
editor, Lettsom, well says, profound critical sagacity, and, almost entirely unaided
by any old copies, put aside ancient and modern corruptions, and made his way at
once to the genuine reading: &lquo;It may be observed&rquo; (<I>Vers.</I> 281) &lquo;that <I>thinks it thee</I>
also occurs in the Elizabethan poets in the sense of <G>mw:n dokei_ soi.</G>&rquo; He then cites the
present passage, and gives the reading of the present text; and also corrects the same
phrase in Cartwright, <I>The Ordinary,</I> III, ii (Dodsley, x, 216): &lquo;&ldquo;Little think'st
thee how diligent thou art To little purpose.&rdquo; <I>Thinks't thee,</I> of course. (I under-
stand, by the way, that the <I>thinks</I> in <I>methinks</I> is, originally and etymologically, not
the same with our present verb <I>to think;</I> but that it is a corruption of another verb
signifying <I>to seem;</I> so that <I>methinks</I> is <I>as it appears to me.</I>)&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC> offers
another solution: Perhaps the true reading is &lquo;thinks thee,&rquo; the final <I>s</I> of the Quarto
being mistaken for <I>e.</I> The word &lquo;think&rquo; in this passage is not the same in origin
as &lquo;think&rquo; used personally, but comes from Anglosaxon <I>thincan,</I> to seem, appear,
which is used impersonally with all personal pronouns. The other word is <I>then-
can,</I> to think, and the distinction is maintained in the German <I>d&uuml;nken</I> and
<I>denken.</I> In <I>Rich. III:</I> III, i, 63: &lquo;Where it seems best unto your royal self,&rquo; for
&lquo;seems,&rquo; which is the reading of the earliest Qq, the later editions have &lquo;thinkst&rquo;
or &lquo;think'st.&rquo;
<P>63. <B>stand me</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 204: This phrase cannot be explained, though it is
influenced, by the custom of transposition. Almost inextricable confusion seems to
have been made by the Elizabethan authors between two distinct idioms: (1) &lquo;it
stands on&rquo; (adv.), or &lquo;at hand,&rquo; or &lquo;upon&rquo; (comp. &lquo;instat,&rquo; <G>rposh/kei</G>), <I>i. e.</I> &lquo;it is of
importance,&rquo; &lquo;it concerns,&rquo; &lquo;it is a matter of duty;&rquo; and (2) &lquo;I stand upon&rquo; (adj.),
<I>i. e.</I> &lquo;I <I>in-sist</I> upon.&rquo; In (1) the full phrase would be: &lquo;it stands on, upon, to me,&rquo;
but, <I>owing to the fact that &lquo;to me&rquo; or &lquo;me&rquo;</I> (<I>the dative inflection</I>) <I>is unemphatic, and
&lquo;upon&rquo; is emphatic and often used at the end of the sentence,</I> the words were trans-
posed into, &lquo;it stands me <I>upon.</I>&rquo; &lquo;Me&rquo; was thus naturally taken for the object of
<I>upon.</I> [In the present passage] it means &lquo;it is imperative on me.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>:
The construction is here interrupted by the parenthesis.

<P>71, 72. <B>It . . . there</B>] <SC>Strachey</SC> (p. 94): Note the usual cautiousness of Hor.,
who contrives to suggest to Ham. the very strongest of all motives for instantly put-
ting the King to death, under an indirect and very innocently-sounding remark.
<P>73. <B>mine</B>] <SC>Miles</SC> (p. 80): You never suspect the errand Ham. is on until you
happen to hear that little word, &lquo;<I>The interim is mine!</I>&rquo; It means more mischief
than all the monologues! No threats, no imprecations, no more mention of smiling
damned villain; no more self-accusal; but solely and briefly, &lquo;<I>It will be short;</I> the
interim is mine!&rquo; Then, for the first time, we recognize the extent of the change
that has been wrought in Ham.; then, for the first time, we perfectly comprehend
his quiet jesting with the Clown, his tranquil musings with Hor. The man is trans-
formed by a great resolve: <I>his mind is made up!</I> The return of the vessel from
England will be the signal for his own execution, and therefore the moral problem
is solved: the only chance of saving his life from a lawless murderer is to slay him;
it has become an act of self-defence; he can do it with perfect conscience. He has
calculated the return voyage; he has allowed the longest duration to his own exist-
ence and the King's. At the very moment he encounters the Clown in the church-
yard he is on his death-march to the palace at Elsinore.

<P>83. <B>water-fly</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: A water-fly skips up and down upon the surface of

being considered a bird peculiar to the south-west coast of England, though now
known to be much more widely distributed. As to its pronunciation, <SC>Skinner</SC>
derives the name <I>&agrave; sono naturali quem avis edit,</I> and <SC>Cotgrave</SC> translates <I>Caue</I>
(clearly a case of onomatop&oelig;ia), and <I>Cauvette,</I> by A Chough or Jacke Daw. Fi-
nally, <SC>Ritson</SC> (p. 92) says that the name of the Cornish bird is pronounced by
the natives <I>chow,</I> which is conclusive. <SC>Caldecott</SC> doubts much if, in the present
instance, from its association with wealth, it have any relation to that bird, but in-
clines to think it should be <I>chuff.</I> [Is not Caldecott right here? The <I>chow</I> is,
perhaps, applicable to Osr. on the score of chattering, but how about the spacious
possession of dirt, the special application made by Ham.? If <I>chuff</I> be here meant

<P>104. <B>remember</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>, in his ed., 1790, conjectured that Ham. was about
to say &lquo;remember <I>not</I> your courtesy,&rquo; because he could not possibly have said &lquo;re-
member your courtesy&rquo; when he wanted Osr. to put his hat on. Malone be-
lieved that <I>courtesy</I> meant to uncover the head, and accordingly in <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I>
V, i, 103, he added <I>not</I> in Armado's speech, &lquo;I do beseech thee remember <I>not</I> thy
courtesy; I beseech thee apparel thy head,&rquo; and <SC>Dyce</SC> shared this opinion, for he
considered the &lquo;not&rquo; as indispensable. <SC>Staunton</SC> discarded the &lquo;not&rquo; in <I>Love's
Lab. Lost,</I> and in a note on the passage says: &lquo;Whatever may have been the mean-
ing of the words, or whether they were a mere complimentary periphrasis, without
any precise signification, the following quotations prove beyond a question that the
old text is right, and that the expression refers to the Pedant's standing bareheaded:
&mdash;&ldquo;I pray you <I>be remembred,</I> and cover your head.&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Lusty Juventus,</I> ed. Haw-
kins, p. 142. &ldquo;Pray you <I>remember your courts'y. . . . .</I> Nay, pray you be cover'd.&rdquo;
&mdash;<I>Every Man in His Humour,</I> I, i, ed. Gifford.&rquo; <SC>Grant White</SC>. (<I>The Galaxy,</I>
Oct. 1869) upholds Staunton, adding: It seems clear that Osric's completed speech
would have been, &lquo;remember <I>your courtesy.</I>&rquo; The phrase was a conventional one
for &lquo;be covered.&rquo; But why? The removal of the hat, in Shakespeare's time, even
more than now, was regarded as a mark of courtesy. I am unable to offer any
explanation of the phrase which is acceptable even to myself. I can only suggest
that the difficulty lies not in <I>courtesy,</I> but in some peculiar and, perhaps, elliptical
use of <I>remember.</I> <SC>Elze</SC> suggests &lquo;remember <I>thy bonnet.</I>&rquo;

<P>113. <B>yet but yaw</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I believe <I>raw</I> to be the right word; it is a word
of great latitude; it signifies <I>unripe, immature,</I> thence <I>unformed, imperfect, unskil-
ful.</I> The best account of him would be <I>imperfect</I> in respect of his quick sail. The
phrase &lquo;quick sail&rquo; was, I suppose, a proverbial term for <I>activity of mind.</I> <SC>Heath</SC>:
The meaning undoubtedly is that Laer. was but young (<I>raw</I>) in proportion to the
quick progress he had made in all gentlemanly accomplishments. <SC>Caldecott</SC>:
<I>Raw</I> is unready, untrained, and awkward. Compare <I>Per.</I> IV, ii, 60; <I>As You Like
It,</I> III, ii, 76. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> &amp;c., p. 220): &lquo;Nothing, I think, can be more cer-
tain than that the passage should stand thus: &ldquo;and <I>it</I> [which was often mistaken by
our early printers for &lquo;yet,&rquo; perhaps because it was written <I>yt</I>] but <I>yaw</I> neither in
respect of his quick sail.&rdquo; &ldquo;To <I>yaw</I> (as a ship), huc illuc vacillare, capite nutare.&rdquo;
&mdash;Coles's <I>Dict.</I> The substantive &ldquo;yaw&rdquo; occurs in Massinger: &ldquo;O, the <I>yaws</I> that
she will make! Look to your stern, dear mistress, and steer right, Here's that will
work as high as the Bay of Portugal.&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Very Woman,</I> III, v; <I>Works,</I> iv, 293, ed.
1805, where Gifford remarks: &ldquo;A <I>yaw</I> is that unsteady motion which a ship makes
in a great swell, when, in steering, she inclines to the right or left of her course.&rdquo;&rquo;
<SC>Elze</SC> thinks the possible solution of this difficulty is to consider &lquo;yaw&rquo; as a transitive
verb, and he thus interprets: &lquo;An inventory of Laertes s excellences would dizzy the
arithmetic of memory; yet it would not let it stagger hither and thither (like a badly-
steered ship), in view of his quick sail.&rquo; A quick-sailing ship holds a steadier course
than one that sails slowly. <SC>Staunton</SC> says he must admit his inability to understand
Dyce's reading, and adds: &lquo;Yet&rquo; is certainly suspicious, but the word displaced we
have always thought was <I>wit,</I> not <I>it,</I> and the drift of Hamlet's jargon to be this: his
qualifications are so numerous, and so far surpass all ordinary reckoning, that memory
would grow giddy in cataloguing, and <I>wit</I> be distanced in attempting to keep pace
with them. <SC>White</SC>: There seems to be no doubt that &lquo;<I>yt</I>&rquo; was mistaken for &lquo;yet.&rquo;
<SC>Clarke</SC> believes <I>raw</I> to be used in the same sense as in <I>As You Like It,</I> and inter-
prets: &lquo;your description is but inefficient and inadequate after all.&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 128:
The ellipsis of the negative explains &lquo;neither.&rquo; That is, &lquo;do <I>nothing but</I> lag clum-
sily behind neither.&rquo; &lquo;Neither,&rquo; for our <I>either,</I> is in Shakespeare's manner, after a
negative expressed or implied. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> says <I>raw</I> is merely a misprint for <I>row,</I>
and so gives it in his text, and thus interprets: &lquo;Memory, even with the help of arith-
metic, cannot overtake this swift sailer, but can only row while he sails. At the
present day we should say: and yet but sail neither in respect of his full steam.&rquo;
<SC>Clarendon</SC>: If this passage stands as Sh. wrote it, any meaning it may have has
defied the penetration of commentators to detect. If &lquo;vet&rquo; is a mistake for <I>yt</I> or <I>it,</I>

<P>to us. It is spoken ironically. <SC>Jennens</SC>: This speech is addressed to Osr. Hor.

will do't, sir, really,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> Are you defeated at your own weapons? Can't you un-

&lquo;Another tongue&rquo; does not mean, as I conceive, <I>plainer language</I> (as Dr Johnson

<P><I>in</I> a game of <I>a dozen passes,</I> or bouts, Laer. does not exceed you three hits; the
King hath laid on the principle of him who makes a bet, with the chance of gaining
<I>twelve for nine</I> that he may lose; or the King (by the advantage allowed to Ham.)
hath <I>odds,</I> tantamount to <I>four to three.</I> If the words, &lquo;he hath laid on,&rquo; refer to
Laer., it means that he has laid on the principle of one who undertakes to make
<I>twelve passes for nine</I> that his adversary shall make; on the <I>ratio</I> of twelve to
nine. <SC>Ritson</SC> (p. 212) maintains that there were to be but twelve passes in all,
and &lquo;Laer., to win, must have got eight hits, whereas Ham. would have won if he
had got only five; so that he had clearly the advantage of Laer., in point of number,
three whole passes or hits, and the odds were eight to five, which is in the same arith-
metical proportion of twelve to nine, in Hamlet's favor before they began to play.&rquo;
[This is, I think, virtually the same explanation as that given by <SC>Elze</SC>.] <SC>Seymour</SC>
(ii, 203): &lquo;If in the dozen passes Ham. shall be hit seven times, and Laer, only three,
the King will lose his wager.&rquo; <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.</I> 1845): The reading of the
Ff of <I>one</I> for &lquo;laid on&rquo; may be an error for <I>won,</I> or <I>on;</I> indeed the whole phrase,
&lquo;he hath laid on twelve for nine,&rquo; seems very like an interpolation from the margin.
One might say that, by a loose manner of speaking, not exceeding three hits may
mean <I>not exceeding more than two.</I> It may also be observed that these numbers
were probably represented by Arabic figures, and not by letters, and were more
liable to be altered and made corrupt. <SC>Quarterly Review</SC> (March, 1847, vol. lxxix,
p. 332): Osric never stoops to use the language of ordinary mortals. &lquo;He hath laid
on twelve for nine&rquo; is not he has laid twelve <I>to</I> nine, but he has wagered for nine
out of twelve. The King backs Ham. Laer., who is the celebrated fencer of the
age, is to give the Prince great odds:&mdash;the King stipulates out of the twelve passes
for nine hits from Laer, without his being declared winner. So also in the for-
mer part of the sentence, &lquo;he shall not exceed you three hits,&rquo; does not mean that
the sum of Laertes's hits over Hamlet's shall not be more than three. In a dozen
passes six hits each would place them on a par, and Osric calls Laertes's excess the
number of hits that he makes above his own half. This, the King bets, will not
surpass three, rendering the total amount to nine, which tallies with the other form
under which the bet is expressed. <SC>Moberly</SC>: &lquo;Each is to attack twelve times,
going on till a hit is made: and Laer. bets that he will hit Ham. twelve times before
Ham. can hit him nine times. That is: Ham. has three points given him, and with
these odds he trusts that he shall win.&rquo; <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> assumes that &lquo;a dozen&rquo; is
merely an indefinite number, and gives an elaborate calculation on the basis of
twenty-one rounds. [It may be said of all these calculations what <SC>Clarendon</SC> says
of one of them, they are doubtless correct, but do not explain the form in which the
wager is put.] <SC>Steevens</SC> refers this very &lquo;unimportant passage&rquo; to the members of
the Jockey Club, at Newmarket, &lquo;who on such subjects may prove the most enlight-
ened commentators, and most successfully bestir themselves in the cold unpoetic
dabble of calculation.&rquo;

I will . . . . hall: It is the breathing . . . . me&mdash;if it please his majesty, let,&rquo; &amp;c.,
or else, &lquo;Sir, I will . . . . hall, if it please his majesty. It is the breathing time,&rquo;
&amp;c. It was Hamlet's customary breathing time, whether his majesty pleased
or not.
<P>169. <B>will gain</B>] For instances of &lquo;will&rquo; used for <I>shall,</I> see <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 238;
and <I>Crit.</I> ii, 348). <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 319, says that &lquo;will&rquo; is probably used here by attrac-
tion with a jesting reference to the previous &lquo;will.&rquo; &lquo;My purpose is to win if I can,
or, if not, to gain shame and the odd hits.&rquo;

<P>181. <B>the time</B>] The present age. See <I>Macb.</I> I, v, 61; I, vii, 81; V, viii, 24.
<P>181. <B>outward habit</B>] <SC>Henley</SC>: Exterior politeness of address.
<P>181. <B>yesty</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: <I>Histy</I> of Q<SUB>2</SUB>Q<SUB>3</SUB> may have been a mistake for <I>hasty.</I>
<P>183. <B>fond and winnowed</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: &lquo;Fond&rquo; should undoubtedly be <I>fann'd,</I>
alluding to corn separated by the fan from chaff. The opinions here spoken of may
mean the opinions of great men and courtiers, men separated by their quality from
the vulgar, as corn is separated from the chaff. This &lquo;yesty collection&rquo; insinuates
itself into people of the highest Quality, as yeast into the finest flour. <SC>Johnson</SC>:
&lquo;If Q<SUB>5</SUB> preserved any traces of the original, Sh. wrote &ldquo;<I>sane</I> and <I>renowned,</I>&rdquo; which is
better than &ldquo;<I>fann'd</I> and <I>winnowed.</I>&rdquo; The meaning is: these men have got the cant
of the day, a superficial readiness of slight and cursory conversation, a kind of frothy
collection of fashionable prattle which yet carries them through the most select and
approving judgements. This airy facility of talk sometimes imposes upon wise men.
Who has not seen this observation verified?&rquo; <SC>Jennens</SC> follows Q<SUB>2</SUB>, but modifies it in
his text to &lquo;profane and tres-renowned,&rquo; &lquo;which is the French method of forming
superlatives, <I>i. e.</I> the most renowned;&rquo; and paraphrases: such a superficial collec-
tion of knowledge as carries them through the most common (<I>profane</I>) and even
the most renowned opinions, <I>i. e.</I> opinions, or branches of learning, which bring re-
nown to the learned in them. <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Fond,&rquo; <I>i. e. foolish,</I> is evidently opposed
to &lquo;winnowed,&rquo; <I>i. e. sifted, examined.</I> Their conversation was yet successful enough
to make them passable not only with the weak, but with those of sounder judgement.
The same opposition in terms is in the readings of the Qq: <I>profane</I> and <I>vulgar</I> are
opposed to <I>trenowned</I> or <I>thrice renowned.</I> <SC>Tollet</SC>: <I>Fanned</I> and &lquo;winnowed&rquo; occur
together in Markham's <I>Husbandry,</I> pp. 18, 76, 77. So also &lquo;fan and wind&rquo; in <I>Tro. &amp;
Cres.</I> V, iii, 41. <SC>Caldecott</SC> interpreted the phrase: &lquo;All judgements, not the simplest
only, but the most sifted and wisest.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC>. (<I>Remarks,</I> &amp;c., p. 221) pronounces
Warburton's emendation &lquo;admirable,&rquo; and one which &lquo;evidently restores the genuine
reading.&rquo; <SC>White</SC> (<I>Sh. Scholar,</I> p. 422) advocates &lquo;fond and winnowed,&rquo; and inter-
prets: &lquo;They go through and through (<I>i. e.</I> they stop at no absurdity in) the most
fond (<I>i. e.</I> affected or foolish) and winnowed (<I>i. e.</I> elaborately sought out) opinions.&rquo;
But <SC>White</SC>, having found that &lquo;fan&rquo; and &lquo;winnow&rquo; are &lquo;often coupled in the

&ldquo;fondly cherished,&rdquo; &ldquo;dearly esteemed,&rdquo; while &ldquo;winnowed&rdquo; means &ldquo;choice,&rdquo; &ldquo;se-
lect.&rdquo; &ldquo;Fond&rdquo; is thus used in I, v, 99.&rquo; <SC>B. Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 16 Jan. 1864):
Ham. of course means that Osr. and his compeers have not that inward wit neces-
sary to parley true euphuism, but only the outward trick of the language, which
while it passed with folks of like mind, would not stand the trial of better judge-
ment. . . . . If for &lquo;winnowed&rquo; or <I>trennowed,</I> we read <I>vinewed</I> or <I>vinnewed</I>&mdash;and
<I>blue vinney</I> is Dorsetshire, and <I>vinewedst</I> is spelt in the Ff of <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> &lquo;whinidst,&rquo;
&mdash;we have a change that restores the sense,&mdash;a word not incongruous with, but sug-
gested by, the metaphorical yesty collection, and a repetition of that Shakespearian
expression, a &lquo;mouldy wit.&rquo; . . . . The &lquo;yesty collection&rquo; is the frothiness of sour
and stale beer, which passes with those of corrupted and vitiated taste; but when
tried and blown upon by the more sober judgement flies off, and does not remain
like the true head of sound liquor or wit. Subsequently (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 31 Dec. 1864),
Nicholson added that he had forgotten the variant of <I>vinewed,</I> which is <I>fenowed</I> or
<I>fennowed.</I> &lquo;The last was doubtless the form chosen by Sh. in this passage.&rquo;
<SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 17) changes this whole passage thus: &lquo;only got the tune of the time,
and <I>out of the</I> habit of encounter [got] a kind of yesty <I>diction</I> which . . . . the most
<I>profound</I> and <I>renowned</I> opinions.&rquo; In support, he adds: 1. That the verb &lquo;got&rquo;
governs both the &lquo;tune of the time&rquo; and &lquo;a kind of yesty <I>diction,</I>&rquo; the latter of which
the persons concerned got, &lquo;out of the habit of encounter.&rquo; 2. That <I>diction</I> has been
used by Ham. just before in the phrase, &lquo;to make true <I>diction</I> of him.&rquo; 3. That
&lquo;most profound and renowned&rquo; comes much nearer the old reading than &lquo;most fond
and winnowed.&rquo; Besides, <I>most</I> winnowed is not English. We should not say of
one sack of wheat amongst several that it was the <I>most</I> winnowed, but that it was
the <I>best</I> winnowed. <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> proposed and adopted in his text: &lquo;<I>profound</I>
and winnowed,&rquo; on the ground that two opposite ideas, like &lquo;fond&rquo; and &lquo;winnowed,&rquo;
cannot be connected by &lquo;and&rquo; so long as &lquo;most,&rquo; by qualifying both, combined
them in one idea. &lquo;People of Osric's class are like chaff that is to be found in
a <I>deep and well-sifted</I> heap of wheat.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;Opinions conceitedly fine and
winnowed clean of the dust of common sense; such opinions as are affected by
lingual exquisites of all times. <SC>Clarendon</SC> inclines to Tschischwitz's reading:
&lquo;<I>profound</I> and winnowed&rquo; as affording a proper contrast with &lquo;yesty collection.&rquo;
<SC>Moberly</SC>: &lquo;A set of frothy expressions suited perpetually to express the absurdest
and most over-refined notions.&rquo;

<P>203. <B>gain-giving</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Restored,</I> p. 127): The same as <I>mis-giving.</I>
We thus use <I>gainsay.</I>
<P>206. <B>repair</B>] See I, i, 57.
<P>207. <B>augury</B>] <SC>Cornhill Magazine</SC> (&lquo;Presentiments,&rquo; October, 1866, p. 459):
This passage is one of the simplest, as it is one of the strongest, proofs of Shakespeare's
belief in presentiments. In all the instances he gives us, the moral to be drawn is
that the warning is neglected and the fate comes. At first we might think that
Hamlet's feeling was natural. He had detected the King's villainy, and he knew
his own counterplot would not long be secret. But it is plain that he suspected
nothing in the challenge to fence with Laer. He never once examined the foils, or
measured them, but picked up the first that came to hand, and took the length on
trust. Just before, when Hor. warned him, he had said, &lquo;The interim is mine,&rquo; and
he clearly looked forward to having things his own way till the next news from
England. [See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> V, i, 1.]
<P>208-211. <B>If . . . betimes?</B>] <SC>Tschischwitz</SC> (<I>Sh. Forschungen,</I> i, 62) calls attention

<P>them? Therefore, come what will, I am prepared.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;The reading of the
Quarto was right, but in some other copy the harshness of the transposition was
softened, and the passage stood thus: <I>Since no man knows aught of what he leaves.</I>
For <I>knows</I> was printed in the later copies <I>has</I> by a slight blunder in such typographers.
I do not think Warburton's interpretation of the passage the best that it will admit.
The meaning may be this: Since <I>no man knows aught of</I> the state of life which <I>he
leaves,</I> since he cannot judge what other years may produce, why should he be
afraid of <I>leaving</I> life betimes? Why should he dread an early death, of which he
cannot tell whether it is an exclusion of happiness or an interception of calamity?
I despise the superstition of augury and omens, which has no ground in reason or
piety; my comfort is, that I cannot fall but by the direction of Providence. Han-
mer's conjecture is not very reprehensible: Since <I>no man can call any possession
certain,</I> what is it to leave?&rquo; The Ff have received their best interpretation from
<SC>Caldecott</SC>, viz.: &lquo;Since no man has (<I>i. e.</I> has any secure hold, or can properly be
denominated the possessor, of) any portion of that which he leaves, or must leave,
behind him, of what moment is it that this leave-taking, or parting with a possession
so frail, should be made thus early?&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> truly remarks that no old copy is at
all well printed in this scene; and <SC>Dyce</SC> pronounces the present passage suspi-
cious. <SC>White</SC> thinks the Qq are manifestly wrong. <SC>Clarke</SC> prefers the Qq on
what, I think, is the true ground, so finely paraphrased by Johnson: That it is more
characteristic of Ham. to think little of leaving life, because he cannot solve its
many mysteries, than because he cannot carry with him life's goods. <SC>Clarendon</SC>
thinks that Johnson's is perhaps the true reading.
<P>213. <B>pardon</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I wish Ham. had made some other defence; it is un-

<SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 204) believes that the passage from &lquo;This presence,&rquo; &amp;c., line 215,
down to &lquo;enemy,&rquo; line 226, is an interpolation. The falsehood contained in it
is too ignoble. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 274): Arrange: &lquo;&mdash;I 'have done you wrong;
but pardon 't, As <I>you're</I> a gentleman. This presence knows.&rquo; [That is, in two lines,
the first ending &lquo;pardon't. <SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>247, 248. <B>Very . . . side</B>] <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 550) pronounces this passage, as at present
punctuated, stark nonsense, which is to be remedied by a comma after &lquo;lord,&rquo; and
a semicolon after &lquo;laid;&rquo; That is: &lquo;Your wager, my lord, is prudently laid; you
have given odds to the weaker side.&rquo; And the King's reply is in proof: &lquo;But since
that time he is greatly improved, therefore we are allowed odds.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>: The
odds were on the side of Laer., who was to hit Ham. twelve times to nine. It
was perhaps the author's slip. <SC>Jennens</SC> solved the difficulty, in nothing that the odds
here alluded to are those that were laid in the wager, viz. the greater value of the
King's stake as compared with Laertes's, and not to the number of hits, which is
what the King refers to in his reply. <SC>Ritson</SC> computes the value of the King's six
Barbary horses in comparison with the rapiers, &amp;c., as about <I>twenty</I> to one, and adds,
&lquo;these are the odds here meant.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: &lquo;I understand that your grace has
taken care that points shall be given me; but for all that, I fear that I shall be the
weaker. No, replies the King, I have seen you both, and the points given will
counterbalance his Paris improvement.&rquo;
<P>250. <B>better'd . . . odds</B>] <SC>Jennens</SC>: &lquo;Since the wager he gains if he should win
is better than what we shall gain if he loses, therefore we have odds, that is, we are
not to make as many hits as Laer.&rquo; <SC>Caldecott</SC>: &lquo;Better'd,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> stands higher in
estimation. <SC>Delius</SC> (and <SC>Moberly</SC> in the preceding note) refer &lquo;better'd&rquo; to La-
ertes's proficiency acquired in Paris. <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Expositor,</I> p. 298): If he (<I>i. e.</I>
Laer.) was bettered, in the ordinary sense of the word, how could the odds lie against
him? <I>You're</I> would give better sense than &lquo;he's;&rquo; but it does not satisfy me. A
line has evidently been lost, and the latter part may be addressed to the Queen.
The lost line may have been something like this: &lquo;'Tis true he did neglect his

<P>274. <B>fat</B>] Roberts, the player, in his <I>Answer to Pope,</I> 1729, stated that John
Lowin acted Henry VIII and Hamlet; it is also known on the authority of Wright,
in his <I>Historia Histrionica,</I> 1699, that Lowin acted Falstaff. Hence <SC>Steevens</SC> con-
jectured that, if the man who was corpulent enough to act Falstaff and Henry VIII
should also appear as Hamlet, this observation was put by Sh. into &lquo;the mouth of her
majesty to apologize for the want of such elegance of person as an audience might
expect to meet with in the representative of the youthful Prince of Denmark, whom
Oph. speaks of as the &ldquo;glass of fashion and the mould of form.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Wright
and Downes, the prompter, concur in saying that Taylor was the performer of Hamlet.
Roberts alone has asserted (and apparently without authority) that Lowin acted this
part. But, in truth, I am convinced it was neither Taylor nor Lowin, but prob-
ably Burbadge. Taylor apparently was not of the company till late, perhaps after
1615, and Lowin not till after 1603. <SC>Collier</SC>, in his <I>Memoirs of the Principal
Actors in the Plays of Sh.,</I> Sh. Soc. Publications, 1846, p. 51, shows conclusively
that Burbadge was the original Hamlet, and cites in proof the <I>Elegy</I> upon him,
copied from a MS in the possession of Heber, containing an enumeration of the
various parts in which Burbadge was distinguished. Shakespeare's words are there
used in reference to the fatness of the actor: &lquo;No more young Hamlet, though but
scant of breath, shall cry &ldquo;Revenge!&rdquo; for his dear father's death.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC>:
Does the Queen refer to Ham. or Laer.? <SC>Clarke</SC>: We believe that this refers not
to Burbadge, but to Ham. himself, who, as a sedentary student, a man of contem-
plative habits, one given rather to reflection than to action, might naturally be sup-
posed to be of somewhat plethoric constitution. This accords well with his not
daring to &lquo;drink&rquo; while he is heated with the fencing bout; with his being of a
&lquo;complexion&rquo; that makes him feel the weather &lquo;sultry and hot;&rquo; with his custom of
walking &lquo;four hours together in the lobby;&rquo; with his having a special &lquo;breathing
time of the day;&rquo; and with his telling Hor. that he has &lquo;been in continual practice&rquo;
of fencing,&mdash;as though he took set exercise for the purpose of counteracting his
constitutional tendency to that full habit of body which is apt to be the result of
sedentary occupation and a too sedulous addiction to scholarly pursuits. <SC>W. Aldis
Wright</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 9 March, 1867, p. 202) states that, in 1864, he received a letter
from Dr Ingleby, communicating a &lquo;fine reading&rquo; proposed by &lquo;Mr <SC>H. Wyeth</SC>, of
Winchester,&rquo; of <I>faint</I> for &lquo;fat.&rquo; <SC>Plehwe</SC> (<I>Hamlet, Prinz von D&auml;nemark,</I> Ham-
burg, 1862, p. 214) refers to IV, vii, 158, and conjectures that the same word is
here used: <I>hot.</I>
<P>277. <B>Good madam</B>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: Many thanks, madam.

<P>281. <B>Come . . . face</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: These very words (the present repetition of
which might have been spared) are addressed by Doll Tearsheet to Falstaff, when
he was heated by his pursuit of Pistol.
<P>283. <B>conscience</B>] <SC>Clarke</SC>: This symptom of relenting is not only a redeeming
touch in the character of Laer. (and Sh., in his large tolerance and true knowledge
of human nature, is fond of giving these redeeming touches even to his worst cha-
racters), but it forms a judiciously interposed link between the young man's previous
determination to take the Prince's life treacherously, and his subsequent revealment
of the treachery. From the deliberate malice of becoming the agent in such a plot,
to the remorseful candor which confesses it, would have been too violent and too
abrupt a moral change, had not the dramatist, with his usual skill, introduced this
connecting point of half compunction.
<P>286. <B>wanton</B>] <SC>Ritson</SC>: You trifle with me as if you were playing with a child.
<SC>Hudson</SC>: This is a quiet but very significant stroke of delineation. Laer. is not
playing his best, and it is the conscience of what is at the point of his foil that
keeps him from doing so; and the effects are perceptible to Ham., though he dreams
not of the reason.

<P>289. <B>Stage-direction</B>] <SC>Seymour</SC> (ii, 204): It is common in the exercise of the
sword for one combatant to disarm the other by throwing, with a quick and strong
parry, the foil out of his hand; and Ham., having done this, might, agreeably to
the urbanity of his nature, have presented his own foil to Laer., while he stooped
to take up that of his adversary; and Laer., who was only half a villain, could not
have hesitated to accept the perilous accommodation, and, indeed, had not time
allowed him to avoid it. M. C. (<I>New Monthly Maga.</I> vol. xiii, p. 301, March,
1820): After Ham. is hurt in the next round Laer. should master his foil. Ham.
thus on the point of being disarmed, should by a vigorous effort seize the sword of
Laer. Thus both parties would hold both weapons, and in separating each would
retain that of which he had a better hold. By these means an exchange might
easily take place. It is quite unnecessary that the parties should be ignorant of the
circumstance. Ham. is not aware of its importance; but Laer. sees his imminent
peril. Horror, remorse, and shame would make him parry imperfectly in the next
round, wherein he receives his mortal wound. <SC>Tieck</SC> (<I>Ludwig Tieck von Rud.
K&ouml;pke,</I> Leipzig, 1855, ii, 220, cited by Elze) thus explains the exchange of rapiers:
At the back of the stage there is a table, on which lie the rapiers. The combat-
ants take them up, fight a round, and replace them on the table, and conversation
occupies the pause between the rounds. The King then lets Osric, or some other
courtier, change the rapiers unobserved, so that the poisoned one falls to Ham. and
is taken up by him. For the King, whose character is always consistent, cannot
permit Laer. to survive, who had just headed a rebellion, and was moreover privy
to the whole plot against Ham. [See <SC>Tieck</SC>, Appendix, Vol. II.] <SC>Elze</SC> thinks
that in scuffling the rapiers are dropped, and are accidentally changed in picking
them up, and that Laer is too excited and Ham. too unsuspicious to notice the
change. <SC>Heussi</SC> attaches but little importance to the whole matter,&mdash;actors have
more adroitness in managing such things than scholars at their desks, anyhow; the
spectators need not see so very exactly that there has been an actual exchange. It
is enough that the combatants become violently incensed, and that a spectator at a
distance could not rightly say what was done in the scuffle. The issue makes it
clear enough. [No aid, that I can find, is to be obtained from <I>Vincentio Saviolo his
Practise,</I> 1595. In sig. H 3, directions are given for &lquo;fastning your left hand on the
hiltes of your enemies swoord.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] The following stage-directions are given in
<SC>Tom Taylor's</SC> Acting Edition of <I>Hamlet,</I> 1873: &lquo;[Laertes <I>wounds</I> Hamlet; <I>who
in return disarms him, and catches his foil.</I>]&rquo; After &lquo;<I>Ham.</I> Nay, come again,&rquo; line
290:&mdash;&lquo;[<I>He throws</I> Laertes <I>a foil, but, by mistake, retains the one he had disarmed
him of, and wounds him with it.</I>]&rquo; In <I>A Study of Hamlet,</I> by E. B. H. (London,
1875), the passage is thus given:&mdash;&lquo;[Laertes <I>wounds</I> Hamlet, <I>who in return disarms
him</I>&mdash;Laertes <I>then, to prevent himself being struck by</I> Hamlet, <I>rushes on him and
clutches his foil&mdash;they struggle.</I>] <I>King.</I> Part them! they are incens'd. [Hamlet
<I>leaves his foil in</I> Laertes's <I>grasp and picks up the poisoned one.</I>] <I>Ham.</I> Nay, come

&mdash;envenom'd too!&mdash;&rquo;]
<P>311. <B>but hurt</B>] <SC>Rohrbach</SC> (p. 37): Claudius's last words are characteristic; he
says that he is merely wounded, although he knows that the sword which has stabbed
him is poisoned. Thus tenacious is he of that which he has, this present life, until
Ham. forces down his throat the poisoned drink. To his latest breath he is the type
of strength and quick decision. Even his death, his last step, is quick and decided,
as had always been his style of action.

<P>313. <B>Drink</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 149): The literal sense of these words leads us to
imagine that Ham. pours some of the poisoned cup into the mouth of the King as
he lies gasping, or else dashes what is left on't upon him. But how, then, could
Hor. in either case say what he does in line 329? Ham. would hardly pour it so
gently as to leave much behind. It is probable that the expression is figurative, and
spoken upon making the King, who had declared he was only &lquo;hurt,&rquo; taste again of
his &lquo;sword.&rquo;
<P>313. <B>union</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: There may be a play here upon the word &lquo;union.&rquo;

<P>315. <B>temper'd</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Mixed, compounded. Compare <I>Exodus,</I> xxix, 2:
&lquo;cakes unleavened tempered with oil.&rquo;
<P>318. <B>Dies</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: We here find Laer., who was not wounded till after
Ham., first dying of a poison described as singularly quick in its operation. The
purposes of the drama might require that Ham. should survive, and the same quan-
tity of poison may affect different constitutions differently, but the poison of the
&lquo;anointed&rquo; sword, which had first entered the body, and was steeped with the blood,
of Ham., must, one would think, in the second instance have lost something of
its active quality, and would consequently have been more slowly operative upon
Laer. [Possibly Ham. gave Laer. a mortal thrust in return for the &lquo;scratch,&rquo; which
was all that Laer. was aiming at. So that Laer. dies of the wound, Ham. of the
poison. <SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>322. <B>mutes</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That are either auditors of this catastrophe, or at most
only mute performers, that fill the stage without any part in the action.

<P>345. <B>solicited</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, brought on the event. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 551):
That is, incited me to the act of vengeance I have just performed. <SC>Mason</SC>: The
sentence is left imperfect. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 274): &lquo;Solicit,&rquo; like many other
words derived from the Latin,&mdash;as <I>religion</I> for <I>worship</I> or <I>service,</I> &amp;c.,&mdash;had not yet
lost its strict Latin meaning. <SC>Lettsom</SC> (<I>foot-note to foregoing</I>): The original signi-
fication of the Latin word seems to have been <I>to move,</I> and the various meanings
attached to it by lexicographers are but modifications of this primary one. Ham.
seems to have been thinking of the events that had &lquo;solicited&rquo; or <I>moved</I> him to re-
commend Fort. as successor to the throne. <SC>Clarendon</SC>: Compare <I>Rich. II:</I> I, ii,
2. [See <I>Macb.</I> I, iii, 130.]
<P>345. <B>The rest is silence</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: If Hamlet's speech is interrupted by
his death, it would be more natural that these words should be spoken by Hor.
<SC>Moberly</SC>: To Ham. silence would come as the most welcome and most gracious
of friends, as relief to the action-wearied soul, freedom from conflicting motives,
leisure for searching out all problems, release from the toil of finding words for
thought; as the one sole language of immortality, the only true utterance of the
infinite.
<P>345. <SC>White</SC>: The <I>O, o, o, o,</I> of the Folio is the addition, doubtless, of some
actor.

an end. The concluding lines also are thus converted into a couplet: &lquo;Now cracks
a noble heart: good night, be blest, And flights of angels sing tbee to thy rest.&rquo;
Another &lquo;tag&rquo; is added afterwards, of a very poor and inanimate character, most
unlike the language of Sh. which, it seems, the performer of the part of Hor. was
also to deliver when the piece was abbreviated; it is as follows:&mdash;While I remain
behind to tell a tale, That shall hereafter turn the hearers pale.&rquo; Although the con-
clusion is hastened in this way, the old annotator has continued his corrections to
the end of the tragedy, as it has come down to us; but from what source he derived

<P>351. <B>cries on</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: To exclaim against. I suppose when unfair sportsmen
destroyed more quarry or game than was reasonable the censure was to cry <I>Havock.</I>
<SC>Caldecott</SC>: See <I>Oth.</I> V, i, 48. <SC>White</SC>: &lquo;This heap of dead proclaims an indis-
criminate slaughter.&rquo; <SC>Clarendon</SC>: &lquo;This pile of corpses urges to merciless slaugh-
ter, where no quarter is given.&rquo; In the <I>Statutes of Warre,</I> &amp;c., by King Henry VIII
(1513), quoted in Todd's ed. of Johnson's <I>Dict.,</I> it is enacted, &lquo;That noo man be so
hardy to crye havoke, upon payne of hym that is so founde begynner, to dye there-
fore; and the remenaunt to be emprysoned, and theyr bodyes punyshed at the
kynges will.&rquo; See also the <I>Ordinances of War</I> of Richard II and Henry V, pub-
lished in the <I>Black Book of the Admiralty</I> (ed. Twiss), i, 455, 462. The etymology
of the word is purely conjectural. Some derive it from the Welsh <I>hafog,</I> destruc-
tion; others from the A. S. <I>hafoc,</I> a hawk; others from the French <I>hai, voux!</I> a cry
to hounds.

<CC>
<P>359. <B>his mouth</B>] Of course this refers to the King, as <SC>Warburton</SC> long ago
pointed out. But, strange to say, <SC>Theobald</SC> referred it to Ham., a noteworthy slip
in one of the best editors Sh. ever had, and it is quite as remarkable that the slip
escaped the notice of the subsequent Variorum editors, who omitted no chance of
making merry over &lquo;poor Tib and his Toxophilus.&rquo;
<P>362. <B>jump</B>] See I, i, 65.
<P>368. <B>carnal</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Of sanguinary and unnatural acts, to which the perpe-
trator was instigated by concupiscence, or, to use Shakespeare's own words, by
&lquo;carnal stings.&rquo; Hor. alludes to the murder of old Hamlet by his hrother, previous
to his incestuous union with Gertrude. A <I>Remarker</I> asks, &lquo;Was the relationship
between the usurper and the deceased king a secret confined to Hor.?&rquo; No, but
the murder of Hamlet by Claudius was a secret which the young Prince had im-
parted to Hor., and to him alone; and to this it is he principally, though covertly,
alludes.
<P>369, 370. <B>Of accidental . . . cause</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: The first line refers to Pol., the
second to Ros. and Guil., whose deaths were &lquo;forced&rquo; on Ham.
</CC>

<CC>
<P>370. <B>put on</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Instigated. See <I>Cor.</I> II, i, 272. [See I, iii, 94.]
<P>371. <B>upshot</B>] <SC>Clarendon</SC>: This conclusion of the tragedy. In archery the
&lquo;upshot&rquo; was the final shot, which decided the match. It is used in the same meta-
phorical sense in <I>Twelfth Night,</I> IV, ii, 76.
<P>376. <B>rights of memory</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Some rights which are remembered.
<P>379. <B>voice will draw on</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Hor. is to deliver the message given
him by Ham., lines 343, 344, and justly infers that Hamlet's &lquo;voice&rquo; will be seconded
by others.
380. <B>same</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): The alteration by the (MS) is so much superior
to the QqFf in reference to the words &lquo;perform'd&rquo; and &lquo;stage,&rquo; which occur just
afterwards, that we make the change, not only without reluctance, but with thank-
fulness for the improvement upon the usual tame and unfigurative line. &lquo;Same&rquo; for
<I>scene</I> was the easiest possible misprint from carelessly written manuscript.
<P>382. <B>On</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: In consequence of. [See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 180.]
<P>382. <B>four captains</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 266): As may be seen in the monument in
Westminster Abbey of Sir Francis Vere, a soldier, who died 1608. This was no
doubt at that time the accustomed mode of burial of a soldier of rank.
</CC>

<CC>
<P>384. <B>put on</B>] <SC>Caldecott</SC>: Put to the proof, tried.
<P>390. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Ham. has gained the haven for which he longed so often; yet
without bringing guilt on himself by his death; no fear that his sleep should have
bad dreams in it <I>now.</I> Those whom he loved, his mother, Laer., Oph., have all
died guiltless or forgiven. Late, and under the strong compulsion of approaching
death, he has done, and well done, the inevitable task from which his gentle nature
shrank. Why, then, any farther thought, in the awful presence of death, of crimes,
conspiracies, vengeance? Think that he has been slain in battle, like his Sea. King
forefathers; and let the booming cannon be his mourners.
</CC>
